title: Lawsuit seeks to block proposed campground on Sanford’s Sand Pond
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new campground has been approved by Sanford’s planning board, but a lawsuit brought forward by a group of neighbors could bring development to a halt.
Michael Patterson, the developer behind the proposed Sand Pond Shores Camping Resort, said he purchased 115 acres on Sand Pond in 2021 with the intention of creating roughly 40 campsites on a portion of the property.
After years of hurdles, including a citywide moratorium on development to let the city reexamine its ordinances, the planning board approved Patterson’s development at its meeting Wednesday night.
Patterson has plans for about a dozen cabins and 30 RV sites on the east side of Sand Pond. If completed, it would be the second campground on the pond, joining Huttopia Southern Maine.
But four sets of neighbors argue in a lawsuit, filed in June in York County Superior Court, that the campground would violate the area’s common scheme of development and interfere with an easement.
The swath of land was previously owned by Miriam Siddall, who between the 1940s and 1990s sold lots along what is now known as Siddall Road. The four sets of plaintiffs say that those lots carried certain restrictions, including bans on commercial use, advertising and general unsightliness.
Those requirements apply to Patterson’s property, the plaintiffs say, and a campground would violate them. But Patterson says his deed specifically did not include those requirements, because of what he described as an effort by the Siddall family to promote development and get the highest possible return for selling the land. (Siddall died in 2001.)
Two of the sets of plaintiffs — Michael Estes and Richard Razumny — also argue that increased public use of Siddall Road from campground visitors would interfere with their easement and harm their daily lives.
The plaintiffs are asking the court to block Patterson from developing the land. Patterson, in a July response to the lawsuit, denied many of their claims.
Estes said in a phone interview last week that the question of which restrictions apply to whose land is his chief concern.
“How come his deeds don’t have the same restrictions as mine?” he said.
During the public comment period of Wednesday’s planning board meeting, some of the plaintiffs shared their concerns regarding the impact on Sand Pond, as well as the concerns of general disturbance brought about by campers.
“We’re not demons, the people who are opposing this campground,” said plaintiff Guy Chabot, who lives on Sand Pond Road.
“I’m certain if you were in my situation, you probably wouldn’t like having a campground in your backyard either,” Chabot added.
Chabot said Patterson has not approached him or his neighbors to discuss their concerns. Patterson said that was untrue, and that two Zoom meetings involving a third-party consultant took place with several neighbors “long before” the suit was filed.
“I love change,” Holly Bennett, another plaintiff, told the planning board. “What is happening in our neighborhood is not appropriate change.”
The planning board voted 6-1 to approve Patterson’s plan to use the site as a campground. Board member Lawrence Jackson-Rosen abstained because he was unable to attend the site walk, according to Patterson.
The campground received conditional approval, requiring slight design changes like the moving of a septic pump area. Patterson has until February to meet those conditions and hopes he can take care of them as soon as possible to begin the first phase of construction next year.
Despite its approval, the planning board warned Patterson that if the neighbors prevail in their lawsuit, any financial losses will be his to bear.
“I’m not going to wait,” Patterson said about beginning work on the development. “I’m gonna take my chances.”
The suit is pending. Patterson believes the next step will be a mediation session, but a date for that meeting has not been set.

title: Judge sets summer 2028 trial for the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk
text:
PROVO, Utah (AP) — The man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk will stand trial in the summer of 2028, a Utah judge ruled Monday.
Attorneys for defendant Tyler Robinson, 23, proposed a trial starting in 2029. But District Judge Tony Graf faced pressure from Kirk’s family and supporters, including President Donald Trump, to speed up court proceedings that already have lasted more than a year.
Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in the killing of Kirk, 31, as the activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. Robinson could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted.
Graf allocated 105 days for the trial, beginning with jury selection on June 21, 2028. He said the dates balance Robinson’s right to prepare his defense with the rights of Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, to a speedy resolution.
Erika Kirk’s attorney disagreed with the schedule but said there is no choice but to accept it.
“A trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie’s assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family,” attorney Jeffrey Neiman told the judge. He had argued the trial should start next October.
In a statement after Monday’s hearing, the Kirk family characterized Graf’s decision as a “delay” and said, “every additional day without justice prolongs our family’s pain.”
Robinson’s defense team declined to comment after the hearing.
The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting. His lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death.
Prosecutors had said they could be ready for trial by October 2027. Rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed a January 2028 start date.
Kirk helped galvanize young voters around Trump during the 2024 election. Trump weighed in on the trial in a social media post last month, saying Robinson should be tried “within a month.” The Republican president criticized Graf, a former prosecutor appointed judge last year, for “taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to.”
Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with the words “Hey Facist! CATCH!” and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.”
Robinson’s attorneys said in court documents that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson’s life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and to devote “substantial time” to issues such as jury selection.
___
Associated Press journalist Matthew Brown contributed from Billings, Montana.

title: Judge’s ruling could clear way for Lindsay Clancy to be tried again in deaths of her 3 kids
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A judge on Monday denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, potentially clearing the way for her to be retried next year in the deaths of her three young children.
Clancy’s defense team had asked the court to end the case based on an unusual argument that the judge shouldn’t have declared a mistrial in September when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. They argued that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue.
But Judge William Sullivan disagreed, saying he saw no other option than to declare a mistrial.
“Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy,” Sullivan wrote.
A spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz declined to comment.
Clancy has never denied that she killed her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued that Clancy had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior.
Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems, but they said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy, but they haven’t settled on whether they will pursue the same charges or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable for the jury.
The next hearing is Nov. 16.
In the motion to dismiss, one of Clancy’s lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued that the judge should have thoroughly interrogated jurors after the foreperson sent two notes saying the one juror who favored conviction wasn’t following the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.
Sullivan said that type of questioning is barred by law.
“Because the secrecy of jury deliberations is a bedrock of our judicial system, any inquiry into the jury’s deliberative process would improperly intrude into the jury’s function,” Sullivan wrote.
The judge also said he didn’t believe the jury foreperson’s claim that the holdout juror — identified in court papers by the pseudonym Juror Doe — wasn’t following the law.
“In context, the notes appear to express the foreperson’s belief that Juror Doe must be refusing to follow the law because Juror Doe would not agree with the majority’s view of the case,” Sullivan wrote. “Given that the jury unquestionably had reached an impasse, the Court did not and does not view the foreperson’s notes as reliable evidence of Juror Doe’s inability or refusal to deliberate or follow the law.”
On Monday, Sullivan also denied prosecutors’ request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury. Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally didn’t speak to reporters. Clancy’s lawyers argued that it would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech.
Sullivan also denied a defense motion to preserve certain records related to the first trial that potentially could have been used to further investigate the conduct of the juror who wanted to convict Clancy.
“In the Court’s view, Clancy is not entitled to any of the materials sought in this motion,” Sullivan wrote.

title: Maine deserves greater accountability on hospital commitments
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Denise McDonough is president of Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield in Maine,
and Patrick Woodcock is president and CEO of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce.
When it comes to healthcare, Maine is at a critical point.
Across our state, families are struggling with rising costs. Hospitals and other providers face significant financial and workforce pressures. Rural communities are working to preserve access to essential services. Employers and policymakers alike are asking how we can make healthcare more affordable while ensuring Mainers can get the care they need, when and where they need it.
At a moment like this, everyone in Maine’s healthcare ecosystem has a responsibility to put patients and communities first. That includes health plans like ours. It includes providers, policymakers and employers. And it includes Prime Healthcare Foundation.
When California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation sought approval to acquire Central Maine Healthcare, the case presented to Maine was clear: Central Maine was in financial distress and needed a partner with the resources and expertise to help secure its future.
Prime made significant commitments as part of that case. It pledged to invest $150 million in Central Maine’s facilities, employees and technology. It committed to maintaining access to care. And importantly, it assured Maine that local leadership and governance would continue to have a meaningful role in decisions affecting Maine patients, employees and communities.
Those commitments mattered. They mattered to state officials charged with evaluating the transaction. They mattered to community leaders. And they mattered to us. Like many others, we believed that if Prime followed through on its promises, the acquisition could provide needed stability while preserving a strong healthcare institution headquartered in Maine.
Today, there are reasons to be concerned that reality is not matching those commitments. We are seeing indications that consequential decisions affecting Maine healthcare are increasingly being made from afar. Questions remain about the existence and meaningful influence of the local governance that Mainers were told would remain in place. Patients have experienced disruption, and we are witnessing employee dissatisfaction at a time when retaining talented healthcare professionals is already one of Maine’s greatest challenges.
Healthcare is fundamentally local, and accountability to the communities we serve is important. Mainers benefit when decisions about access, affordability, and workforce stability reflect the needs of their communities and are informed by those who understand the challenges they face. Maintaining that local perspective and accountability is essential to ensuring Maine families have access to the care they need.
Maine cannot afford instability in its healthcare system. Our population is among the oldest in the country, many communities face shortages of healthcare professionals, and too many families already struggle with the cost of care. Every organization operating in this environment should be asking the same question: How do we preserve and expand access to high-quality, affordable healthcare for the people of Maine?
Prime has an important role in answering that question.
The path forward should begin with transparency and fulfillment of the commitments that helped make this acquisition possible. Mainers deserve a clear accounting of the promised $150 million investment: what has been invested, where it has been invested and what remains to be done. They deserve meaningful local governance with a genuine voice in decisions affecting Central Maine’s patients, employees and communities. And they deserve confidence that decisions about services will protect access to care rather than create additional disruption.
As healthcare and business leaders, we recognize the extraordinary pressures facing hospitals today. There are no easy answers, and responsible organizations sometimes must make difficult decisions. However, difficult circumstances make accountability and transparency more important, not less. Ultimately, we all benefit when there is stability, and it is essential that the community and the state have clarity on the challenges being faced and the steps being taken to address them. We remain committed to collaboration and welcome new opportunities to work together to address these challenges and strengthen Maine’s healthcare system.
This should not be about California versus Maine, or one healthcare organization versus another. It should be about keeping promises to the people who ultimately matter most: the patients, families, employees and communities who depend on Central Maine Healthcare.
Maine needs a strong and sustainable healthcare system. We need organizations willing to invest here, employ people here and become genuine partners in our communities. And when those organizations make commitments to Maine, we should expect them to keep them.
Prime came to Maine asking for the opportunity to help stabilize Central Maine Healthcare and secure its future. Maine gave it that opportunity. Now Prime must deliver.

title: Arthur Horace Kee III
text:
Arthur Horace Kee III, of Waldoboro, passed away unexpectedly on Nov. 7, 2026. He was born on Aug. 22, 1960.
Arthur was predeceased by his father, Arthur Horace Kee Jr. He is survived by his mother, Patricia Kee, of Waldoboro; sons, Arthur Horace Kee IV and his wife, Jessica, of Huger, S.C., and Alex Wesley Kee, of Portland; daughter, Abbie Katheren Kee, of Mount Pleasant, S.C.; brother, Jeffrey Kee and his companion, Sandra, of Waldoboro; sisters, Kathy Kee Steeves and her husband, Troy Steeves, and Cheryl Kee; along with many nieces and nephews.
Arthur had a close relationship with his nephew, Zach, whether they were listening to music, building things or simply spending time together.
Arthur’s family will honor his life in a private graveside service at the German Cemetery in Waldoboro.
Arrangements are under the care and direction of Hall Funeral Home of Waldoboro. To extend a condolence or share a story with the Kee family, please visit Arthur’s book of memories at hallfuneralhomes.com.

title: Van Buren Braces for Upcoming 12-hour Power Outage
text:
VAN BUREN, Maine (WAGM) - If you live in Van Buren, you’ll lose power on Thursday. Van Buren residents will experience an extended power outage lasting up to 12 hours. On Thursday the Van Buren Light and Power District will be replacing a malfunctioning substation transformer. So, officials have a few tips on how people can get through the extended outage.
Darren Woods, Director of the Aroostook Emergency Management Agency says: “It is a rough time of year to do it, but it is necessary. So, what homeowners need to be thinking about is what they can do at home to prepare. Some of the big things that we see that people forget is they’ll open and close their fridge a little too much. Things like putting freezer packs in your freezer and letting things freeze up. So, when the power does go out those packs can maintain the temperature within that unit. Keeping that unit closed as much as you can. That’s your freezer and your refrigerator and also thinking about things like well water. So, if you’re on a well that requires a pump and power for that well you have to think about the water you’re gonna need for drinking as well as for hygiene ahead of time.”
Since the temperature outside is getting colder, Woods also has some tips to keep residents warm during the outage. “You want to make you’ve got your home up to temperature. It might be a good idea to turn a couple of degrees higher than maybe you normally would have it. Just to let that cool down a little bit as you go through the outage. It’ll sustain you just a little bit longer. I’m positive Van Buren Light and Power will get that back on just as quickly as they can. So, we’re hoping that it’s gonna be less than a 12 hour, but people should really be prepared just in case.”
For those with generators, there are also some things to keep in mind.
“Making sure you do not run them inside. Keep your generator away from doors and windows and make sure you have good, working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors inside your home,” said Woods.
To help residents keep warm during the outage, the town of Van Buren will be opening a warming shelter at the town’s Community Center at 130 Champlain Street. Officials encourage residents needing a place to go during the extended outage should stop in and warm up.

Cruise ship pianist who fell overboard rescued from ‘middle of the ocean’ after 9 hours
text:
NEWPORT BEACH, Calif. (KCAL/KCBS) - Two fisherman helped save a Royal Caribbean pianist who fell overboard on a cruise ship then spent nine hours floating in the ocean nearly 20 miles off the California coast.
Sean Norton and Grant Garrett were headed back to Newport Beach after a Friday morning fishing trip when suddenly, their boat captain noticed someone in the water nearly 20 miles off the coast.
“I mean, it’s surreal,” Norton said. “Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up, and he was in total shock.”
Garrett said when the 37-year-old man came to, he told them he’s a pianist on the 14-deck Royal Caribbean cruise ship called the “Ovation of the Seas,” which was en route to Ensenada, Mexico, out of Long Beach.
“The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,’” Norton said.
After pulling the man from the water, the crew put out an emergency maritime call, and a group of Newport Beach lifeguards responded to help.
“It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean,” Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda said.
Lifeguard officials believe the man went overboard around 2:30 a.m. Friday, roughly nine hours before he was found. He was hospitalized but is expected to survive, according to the U.S. Coast Guard, which is investigating the incident and how he went overboard.
“You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees. A different year, no way he makes it,” Norton said.
The fishermen are grateful they found the man and were able to help him.
“I’m glad we were there, and I’m glad he’s doing okay,” Garrett said.
A Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson released the following statement regarding the incident: “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

Nvidia shares fall after report of CEO investigation
text:
Nvidia stock falls following company investigation into CEO
Nvidia stocks fell Monday following news that CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
The New York Times first reported Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy last month. On Sunday, Nvidia's board announced an investigation, and Huang issued a statement to employees posted on their website, admitting to the affair.
The AI chip supplier is the second highest valued company in the world, behind Apple and ahead of Microsoft, Google and Amazon. Its total market capitalization is estimated to be more than $4 trillion.
Founded in 1993, Nvidia started selling stocks to the public in 1999 at a value of four cents a share. The company's focus was graphics processing units, or GPUs, for video gaming.
The value of the company didn't take off until the launch of ChatGPT in 2022. At that time, the value of a share was about $17. Now, the bulk of its revenue is made from data centers.
Nvidia stock already took a tumble last week, dropping 10% from closing Thursday to closing Friday. Thursday was the worst day for major stock indexes since April 2025, according to Yahoo Finance. The declines impacted Nvidia along with other AI chipmakers.

title: Arrests made after crash, barricade breach near White House, reports say
text:
WASHINGTON (WJLA) - Two people were arrested Monday morning in two separate barricade-breaching incidents near the White House, according to the U.S. Secret Service.
The first incident happened before 10 a.m., when a car crashed onto a sidewalk near Lafayette Park.
The Secret Service said the “driver was combative with law enforcement” and was quickly arrested.
As a precaution, the Metropolitan Police Department’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal team was called to sweep the car. Roads around the park were closed.
Around the same time, in the same area, someone jumped a barricade. According to the Secret Service, that person was also arrested.
The incidents prompted a brief lockdown near the White House. The lockdown has since been lifted.
Both incidents remain under investigation.

title: Nancy H. Merchant | Obituaries
text:
Most obituaries tell the story of a life through a list of accomplishments and achievements. But Nancy “Gram” Merchant's life was never measured in accolades. It was measured in the way she made people feel, the memories she created, the traditions she carried on, and the extraordinary amount of love she poured into the people lucky enough to call her theirs.
Nancy made her home in Hall Quarry with her husband of 62 years, Robert “Bo” Merchant. Together, they built a life centered around family, laughter, and making ordinary days feel extraordinary.

title: “Wildwood”: Less wild, more wood
text:
Studio Laika is a film studio I hold in high regard, and for good reason. There are very few film studios left that do stop-motion animation and even fewer that make big-time, big-budget movies in the medium. Of course, you have your Aardman Animations, Rankin/Bass Animated Entertainment and artists like Ray Harryhausen, who did films like “The 7th Voyage of Sinbad” or “Jason and the Argonauts.” Studio Laika, however, has been able to keep the style of animation alive and well throughout the 21st century.
So when I went to see “Wildwood,” I was ready. I parked my butt in that theater seat, got the snacks, watched this movie and it just pissed me off! It ruined my whole week!
But hold on, for those of you who might not have gotten a chance to see this movie, let me break it down for you. The film follows Portland, Oregon, teen Prue McKeel (voiced by Peyton Elizabeth Lee), who, after deciding to ignore her parents’ warnings not to let her baby brother Mac leave the house, does so anyway and subsequently has him abducted by a murder of crows.
Together with her classroom acquaintance, a geek named Curtis Mehlberg (voiced by Jacob Tremblay), the two venture off into the aptly named “Impassable Wilderness,” or the “Wildwood.” Here, they find themselves caught in the middle of a war between the inhabitants of Wildwood and the despicable dowager Governess Alexandra (voiced by Carey Mulligan) with her army of red-coated coyotes. The governess intends to sacrifice Prue’s baby brother in order to reincarnate her dead son, who was taken by the forest ivy.
Right away, I want to say that this is a fantastic-looking film, as are all Studio Laika films. They have truly perfected their craft at this point and have managed to masterfully blend digital effects and stop-motion animation. Dare I say so, it makes “Coraline” look like a 10-year-old’s LEGO stop-motion animation. All the more impressive, seeing as they only started shooting the film in 2021. But I’ve said before, anyone can make a good-looking film nowadays. Even the best studio in its quest for perfect visuals will always leave something lacking. In this case, it was the writing!
The beginning of the movie makes us feel like we’re dropped right into the middle of a story when the characters have just reached their lowest point before the climax. Prue and Curtis’ introduction goes from kind enough to extremely irritating within the first 10 minutes.
The scene in the forest where they were forced to split was beyond forced, as Curtis urges Prue to continue without him and he’s captured by Governess Alexandra. At this point, he just goes back to being a cowardly, sniveling geek for the entire film until the climax. The climax is a big battle sequence, but the road to get there was full of so much character clutter, exposition dumps and fake-out climaxes that you’re ready for the movie to be over by the hour-and-a-half mark.
Now, I did think that the voice actors for this film were very good. I especially enjoyed William Knight, who played the Wild Hog Cabbie. It was the only part of the film that made me laugh. I don’t blame them for their characters stinking; I blame the writers. Sure, Prue is a moody teen and Curtis is a wimpy geek, but that doesn’t mean they have to be entirely unlikable! Plenty of other films did it well.
I think the biggest problem is that this film wants to be so grand, sweeping and amazing all at once, but forgets that it needs to use that two-hour runtime to properly set the pieces up for a satisfying payoff. You know a movie that did? “The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.” It had the same runtime, great special effects for the time, was based on a book of the same name and was vastly more gratifying to watch for grown-ups and kids alike.
The part where Curtis gets taken by the governess and tricked into thinking she was good? Yeah, that’s ripped from the plot of “Narnia” with Edmund Pevensie and the White Witch. I will die on this hill: For all the bloviation online about this film, “Wildwood” is nothing more than a worse “Narnia.” And you can take that one to the bank.

title: Bangor installs traffic cameras designed to keep cars moving
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - If you’ve ever sat alone at a red light wondering whether the signal knows you’re there, Bangor officials say new traffic detection cameras are designed to help.
The city has installed Miovision cameras at intersections across Bangor to detect waiting vehicles and help signals serve those traffic movements. City Electrician Chris Hawkins said the new equipment replaces aging infrastructure that required constant repairs.
“It’s solved a lot of the issues that we’ve had with the older systems,” Hawkins said.
A clearer view of traffic
Hawkins said the new cameras are better positioned to avoid direct sunlight than outward-facing cameras. That can give them a clearer view of vehicles approaching or waiting at an intersection.
The system also includes an artificial intelligence engine called Mateo, which collects traffic data to help local engineers track traffic patterns.
Not Flock cameras, city says
After the city posted about the installation on Facebook, officials addressed questions about the cameras.
“It is absolutely not a Flock camera,” Hawkins said. “It’s purposefully using a 400P resolution so facial ID is not possible, license plate readers are not possible, it’s not intended for it in any way.”
Hawkins said 42 cameras are active across most of Bangor. The installation took more than three years, and about a dozen more cameras are expected to be installed within the next year.

title: Deportation flight of Iranians from US scuttled at last minute, attorney says
text:
Deportation flight of Iranians from US scuttled at last minute, attorney says
A U.S. deportation flight of Iranian nationals bound for Iran by way of Pakistan was abruptly canceled Sunday morning, according to an attorney who spoke to some of the detainees slated for repatriation.
At least eight Iranians were loaded onto a plane Sunday morning in Mesa, Arizona, for a deportation flight headed to the country of Georgia, then on to Pakistan, according to Ali Rahnama, an attorney with the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund who filed emergency motions on behalf of some of the Iranian detainees. The flight was canceled without explanation, he said.
Court documents unsealed days ago in a civil lawsuit filed by the fund showed the Trump administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians to Iran, even as the war there drags on, via an unnamed third country. The lawsuit was filed in July and alleges that the U.S. government illegally shared confidential information about Iranians seeking asylum in the U.S. with Iranian officials.
There were three deportation flights to Iran between September 2025 and January 2026, with over 100 Iranian nationals deported. But the administration's confirmation of the new plans amid the war that began in February highlights its resolve in carrying out its hardline immigration crackdown, which has involved ramping up removals, including to places that critics say could endanger the lives of the returnees.
Homeland Security refuses comment
In response to questions Sunday from The Associated Press, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Immigration and Customs Enforcement does not comment on “prospective removal operations, including flight schedules, passenger manifests, destinations, or individual case details,” nor would the agency confirm future removal operations.
“As promised, the Trump Administration is employing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history,” the statement said.
The administration did not specify in the October court records when the deportations would be carried out. But in the past week, roughly a dozen Iranian nationals in immigration detention said they were notified that they were scheduled for an upcoming deportation flight to Pakistan and then to Iran, according to numerous attorneys who have since confirmed those plans with DHS.
Advocacy group says detainees have been contacted by Iranian officials
According to Rahnama, the eight detainees who boarded the flight on Sunday were visited by a senior official with the Iranian Interests Section — an Iranian representative office in the Pakistani Embassy in Washington that handles consular affairs — and were told that the Iranian government would transport them from Pakistan to Iran.
In the litigation brought by the Iranian immigrant advocacy group, at least a dozen Iranian detainees have said they’ve been contacted by Iranian officials who had knowledge of sensitive information on their asylum claims.
U.S. District Judge Ana C. Reyes, a nominee of President Joe Biden, has not ruled on the claims but ordered the U.S. government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country, and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.
In a court filing Sunday, the defense fund laid out what it had learned about plans for a removal flight Sunday and argued that the administration may have violated the judge’s directive to give advance notice of deportation plans.
Later Sunday, the government filed court documents in the case, but they were sealed and inaccessible to the public.
Group says individuals could face persecution
The Iranian American Legal Defense Fund has called for a halt to the removal flights, saying in a news release that they would “reportedly mark the first deportation of Iranians to Iran since the U.S.-Iran war began.”
The group’s executive director, Yasmin Chubin, said in a statement Sunday that it was difficult to comprehend why the U.S. would forcibly deport Iranians, including asylum seekers, to Iran, amid ongoing military hostilities.
The consequences of removal, Chubin said, “could be irreversible and individuals may face persecution, torture, or death.”
At least one person who had been part of the scuttled flight volunteered to go back to Iran after nearly two years of detention, Rahnama said, out of desperation to leave what he described as inhumane imprisonment. It’s not clear how many other of the deportees may have volunteered to leave.
____
Associated Press reporter Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Virginia, contributed to this report.

title: These 7 Maine college field hockey and soccer teams earned DIII tournament berths
text:
A disappointing end last season fueled the University of Southern Maine field hockey team in 2026.
The Huskies lost to Keene State in a shootout in last year’s Little East Conference semifinals. They avenged that loss Saturday, beating the Owls 1-0 to win the conference title and earn an automatic berth in the NCAA Division III tournament.
“We set this goal early on,” said USM coach Bonny Brown-Denico, who is in her 28th year leading the program. “Our seniors and captains have been outstanding, helping drive us to this ultimate goal.”
The Huskies were one of the seven Maine programs to earn a spot in NCAA DIII tournaments, whose fields were announced Sunday and Monday. The St. Joseph’s College and Thomas College men’s soccer teams and Husson University women’s soccer teams also earned automatic bids, while the Bowdoin field hockey, Bowdoin men’s soccer and Colby women’s soccer teams earned at-large bids.
Southern Maine (15-7) travels to Clinton, New York, to play Hamilton (11-5) on Wednesday. Hamilton earned an at-large bid.
“I told (the team), ‘If we get to the NCAAs, don’t be grateful just for getting there,'” Brown-Denico said. “‘Believe in yourselves and realize that on any given day, anyone can beat anyone.'”
The Huskies relied on senior leadership and a strong sophomore class this season. Lawrence High graduate Maddie Niles leads the team with nine goals and six assists. Senior forward Bri Townsend, a Nokomis graduate, has eight goals and four assists.
“They’ve taken on the responsibility of really getting better every single day,” Brown-Denico said. “They’ve been so easy with taking feedback and making corrections and instantly changing things when they need. My assistant coach always says, ‘You tell them one thing, they do it immediately.’ They’re the best students.”
The Bowdoin field hockey team earned an at-large bid after going 13-4 and losing to Middlebury 2-0 in the NESCAC semifinals. The Polar Bears have a bye into the first round and, at 11 a.m. Saturday in Brunswick, will host the winner of a game between Amherst and Endicott.
Senior Emily Ferguson has 10 goals and Hanna Balmelli has nine for Bowdoin this season.
The Thomas College men’s soccer team is 12-3-1 and beat Husson in a shootout on Saturday to win the North Atlantic Conference title and an automatic bid. The Terriers fell just short of the NCAA DIII tournament last season, losing to SUNY-Delhi in the conference title game.
“Last year was one of the best teams I’ve had, arguably, but not doing the small things well kind of cost us in the end,” said fifth-year Thomas coach Kyle Fletcher. “Something that we talked about at the beginning of the season was focusing on small details. I think it was a huge step in the learning process, as a coaching staff but as a program as well.”
David Ivarsson has 19 goals and nine assists, while Cody Robinson has nine goals for Thomas this season.
Thomas won’t have to travel far but got a tough draw. The Terriers will face Bowdoin (8-3-5) in the first round at 11 a.m. Saturday in Brunswick. The Polar Bears are ranked 25th in the United Soccer Coaches DIII poll and have three players with 10 points (Jack Banks two goals and six assists; Patrick Brady has four goals and two assists; and Adam Prince has five goals).
“Obviously, Bowdoin’s going to be a real tough test,” Fletcher said.
“The biggest (key),” Fletcher added, “is we can’t give them chances. They’re one of the best teams in the country. We’ve got our hands full. From the opening kick to the final whistle, we have to be at our best.”
The St. Joseph’s men’s soccer team is 9-2-8 and earned an automatic berth by beating Norwich University in the Great Northeast Athletic Conference championship game Saturday. The Monks, led by Windham graduate Nick Marion (10 goals, 8 assists) face Middlebury (10-2-3) at 11 a.m. Saturday in Vermont.
The Colby women’s soccer team (9-4-3) earned an at-large bid for its third trip to the NCAA Division III tournament. The Mules, led by Abigail Jarvi (8 goals), face the University of Mary Washington (12-2-4) on Saturday in Ewing, New Jersey.
Husson (10-5-2), which beat Lesley University 2-0 in the NAC final, will travel to Poughkeepsie, New York, on Saturday to play Tufts.

title: Late-Day Rain/Snow Showers Tuesday
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The rest of the region will have partly to mostly cloudy skies overnight, with lows ranging from the upper 20s in the north to the mid- and upper 30s closer to the coast.
Tuesday: Late-Day Rain/Snow Showers
Tuesday starts with periods of sunshine before clouds build from northwest to southeast. A few scattered snow showers are possible in northern Maine by early afternoon, but most of the region will stay dry during the daylight hours.
Highs will range from the upper 30s in the north to the 40s for most of the region. A few spots along the MidCoast could reach the low 50s.
Scattered rain and snow showers will arrive in the northwest by late afternoon. Most places will see rain, while areas north of Greenville and Millinocket have the best chance of light snow. Any snow accumulation should be less than an inch and mainly on grassy surfaces.
Rain showers will spread toward the coast by early Tuesday evening, with totals of only a few hundredths of an inch to a quarter of an inch.
Wednesday and Thursday: Drier stretch
Wednesday and Thursday will trend drier, with partly to mostly cloudy skies. Highs both days will range from the upper 30s to the low 50s across the region.
Late week: Watching Potential Storm
We are keeping a close eye on a potential storm from Thursday night into Saturday. There is still great uncertainty about its track, and a shift in the storm’s path could make a big difference in what we see.
Track 1: Through the Gulf of Maine. A track farther south would keep the region colder. Far northern Maine would be drier, while areas closer to the coast would have a better chance of a rain-and-snow mix.
Track 2: Well out to sea. This would be the least impactful option for land. Maine would stay dry, with impacts mainly over the water.
Please make sure to check back in for the latest details.

title: This woman helps cemetery visitors talk openly about death
text:
WASHINGTON (Aging Untold) — A historic cemetery in the nation’s capital has hired a death doula to help visitors have healthy conversations about mortality in what might be a first for such institutions.
An end-of-life doula, or death doula, is a person who offers services for end-of-life care, from planning final moments to providing respite for exhausted caregivers.
Promoting “death positivity”
Laura Lyster-Mensh, the death doula at Historic Congressional Cemetery, a national landmark in the heart of Washington, D.C., said her role focuses on promoting what she calls “death positivity.”
“The greatest thing that I can do here at the cemetery is promote death positivity and I walk around with people in the cemetery, and we just talk openly about death — unafraid, curious, sometimes awkward,” Lyster-Mensh said.
She acknowledged the concept might seem insensitive to those who are grieving.
“I think at first, to hear death positivity could seem even disrespectful,” she said. “I actually think that death positivity is about living better. Because what are we afraid of? When we turn that and we look at it as boundaries on our life that make life precious, we can feel better.”
Death cafes and conversation cards
Lyster-Mensh conducts her work through various methods, including regular events, including “death cafes.” She sets out tea, cookies and a deck of cards called “the death deck,” which is designed to start conversations about mortality.
“At first people will say, ‘Death, oh, I don’t want to do that.’ But you pull out one of these cards and you start talking and you learn things about the people that you care about and you start real conversations,” she said.
She said these conversations are often uncomfortable for people to initiate until it’s time or too late.
When asked for advice about living, Lyster-Mensh said people should slow down.
“I think we try to speed through everything. We try to speed through grief. We try to speed through happy moments, we hoard it. But you can’t really be present if you’re hoarding it,” she said.

Maine's November Night Sky Is Putting on One Heck of a Show
text:
I've always been fascinated by space. Seriously, I LOVE this stuff. I'm also a huge fan of planetariums, especially the incredible one at Boston's Museum of Science. There's just something about staring up at the stars and realizing how unbelievably massive our universe is that blows my mind.
And this November, Maine's night sky is giving us plenty of reasons to look up!
First, the Northern Taurids meteor shower peaks overnight November 11th into the 12th. WGME says You might only catch a handful of shooting stars per hour, but this shower is known for producing some pretty spectacular fireballs!
Then, November 17th and 18th bring the Leonid meteor shower, where you could spot up to 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions. Fun fact: Those shooting stars are actually tiny pieces of debris left behind by a comet.
And there's more!
On November 15th and 16th, Mars and Jupiter will appear close together in the early morning sky. They're actually millions of miles apart, but from Earth, they'll look like neighbors.
Then comes November's Beaver Moon on November 24th, which is also a supermoon this year. That means it'll appear slightly bigger and brighter than your average full moon.
According to NASA, Mercury will also be easier to spot before sunrise around November 20th, and Uranus reaches opposition on the 25th, making it a great time to break out the telescope.
One of my favorite things about living in Maine is that you don't have to travel far to find some incredible dark skies.
So grab a warm jacket, get away from the city lights, and look up!
Just cross your fingers that the Maine clouds cooperate.
Because sometimes the best show around doesn't require a ticket. Just a clear night and a little curiosity.

title: FBI investigating ‘suspected homicide’ aboard cruise ship out of Texas
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — The FBI is investigating a “suspected homicide” aboard a cruise ship that returned to port after departing from Texas, and a suspect is in custody, the agency said Monday.
The FBI did not say whether any charges had been filed. The name of the suspect was being withheld pending notification of the victim’s family, the agency said on the social platform X.
The MSC Seascape, which took off from Galveston, is a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins, more than 1,600 crew and can host nearly 5,900 guests, according to the company’s website.
“On reporting a guest incident aboard our ship, we were instructed by the authorities to return to the Port of Galveston,” MSC Cruises said in a statement. It added that it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.
The company said the vessel has resumed its voyage and left Galveston as of Monday afternoon.
MSC Seascape currently runs from Galveston to the Caribbean for five- and seven-night stays, according to the company’s website. The ship switched from Miami to Galveston last November, according to a statement.
Homicide investigations on cruise ships are uncommon. Earlier this year, a teenager was charged with murder and aggravated sexual abuse in the death of his 18-year-old stepsister on a Carnival Cruise ship out of Florida.

title: Investigation underway after 2 skydivers die when parachutes become entangled midair in California
text:
Investigation underway after 2 licensed skydivers die in California parachute collision
Two experienced skydivers who were taking part in an organized skydiving event in Southern California were killed after colliding midair and plummeting to the ground.
The Riverside County Sheriff's Office on Saturday identified the two who died as Georgia Jean, 56, of Box Elder, South Dakota, and Levi Pimentel, 29, of Aurora, Illinois.
Jean founded the company Circle Evolution, which “is the collaboration between conscious channel Georgia Jean and the non-physical collective The Circle of Light,” according to the company's website. Jean said in a bio that she started skydiving in 2015 and had more than 1,700 jumps.
Pimentel was listed on LinkedIn as a lead instructor at iFLY Naperville, an indoor skydiving company.
The accident occurred at about noon Friday at Skydive Elsinore, the company said in a statement, and both were licensed skydivers.
The Riverside County Fire Department said the two suffered traumatic injuries and were taken to a local hospital in critical condition.
Skydive Elsinore said the free fall portion of the dive and the opening of the parachutes were normal, but as they were preparing to land, the two skydivers collided at approximately 150 feet (about 46 meters) above the ground.
“The collision caused their parachutes to become entangled, and both sustained critical injuries when they reached the ground,” Skydive Elsinore said in a statement. They were pronounced dead at the hospital.
The Federal Aviation Administration was notified, the sheriff's office said. It will collect the skydivers’ parachutes and conduct an investigation.
The U.S. Parachute Association reports that in 2025, members made 3.47 million skydives and there were 16 fatalities. The organization said 5.6% of members reported suffering an injury that required medical treatment, with the most common being ankle injuries during landings.

title: 16-year-old ‘thankful’ to be alive after car part thrown into Halloween bonfire causes explosion
text:
PHOENIX (AZFamily/Gray News) - An Arizona man is facing charges after police say he threw a car part into a Halloween bonfire, causing an explosion that left a 16-year-old girl seriously injured.
Jaidynn Penberthy, 16, was seriously injured when Phoenix police say a man threw a car shock absorber into a bonfire during a Halloween party in the desert, causing an explosion.
The incident happened around 10:30 p.m. last Friday. Detectives say multiple partygoers were struck by debris, but only Penberthy was seriously injured.
Police believe 24-year-old Samuel Wolf Schnee is the man who caused the explosion. Court records show he was booked on three counts of aggravated assault and seven counts of endangerment.
‘Like a scene out of a horror movie’
Ethan Glass, Penberthy’s older brother, said she was standing 10 feet away when the blast knocked her unconscious.
“There was a lot of blood,” Glass said. “It was like a scene out of a horror movie.”
He said strangers performed lifesaving measures and called family members while Penberthy’s friends drove her for help and called 911. He said one girl helped by giving the 16-year-old a sternum rub to try to get her pulse back.
“She said that she lost her pulse for like a minute,” Glass said.
Penberthy suffered a broken jaw, multiple facial fractures, missing teeth and burns, according to her brother.
“The way the shrapnel, the piece, whatever it was hit her in the face, it struck her almost square in the mouth, nose, side going down kind of side of the face, just all around,” Glass said.
The 16-year-old was flown to a burn center and underwent facial reconstruction surgery. She still needs several more operations.
“She’s been crying a lot just from being in so much pain, and it’s hard to breathe,” Glass said.
Still, he said his sister is “very thankful that she’s alive.”
A GoFundMe has been set up to help with Penberthy’s medical expenses.
Suspect appears in court
Schnee appeared in court early Saturday morning, where state prosecutor Dawn Sauer called his alleged actions “extremely reckless.” She said Schnee admitted to throwing an old shock or strut into the fire.
“He claimed that he had drilled holes to release the harmful chemicals, but thus, he knew there were harmful chemicals inside,” Sauer said.
Schnee’s attorney, Jerald Schreck, said it had not been confirmed which item caused the explosion and injuries. He also argued that the state could not reasonably identify Schnee as the person who threw the item.
However, a judge found probable cause in the case.
“There are at least two or three witnesses that do identify the defendant [Schnee] as placing a shock in the fire,” the judge said.
The judge said proximate cause, a legal question of whether Schnee’s actions directly led to the injuries, would be an issue for trial.
Schreck asked the judge to release Schnee on his own recognizance while Sauer requested a $75,000 bond.
“He’s not a danger to the community because he’s been an Eagle Scout, he’s been a lifeguard helping people, he’s been prosocial, he has no criminal history, he’s not a flight risk because his family’s here,” Schreck said.
The judge acknowledged that Schnee posed a danger to others at the time of the incident but said she did not believe he poses a danger now and set a bond at $25,000.
Court records show Schnee later posted bond and was released.

title: Couple finds at least 25 snakes in newly purchased home
text:
SALVISA, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - Jessica and Johnathan Perry bought their first house in August, but their dream home in Kentucky came with an unwelcome surprise.
Three weeks after the purchase, the couple found their first snake.
“I was actually taking out the trash. My son and I were home alone and I walked out the door, and there was a snake on the porch. I immediately called my husband and then my dad to try to get somebody to come out here to get it,” Jessica Perry said. “Then, a few days later, we found another, and a few days later, another. Then one night, about a week after finding the first one, Johnathan and his friend came down in the basement and found two adults and several juveniles in the basement.”
An infestation
The Perrys said they have found at least 25 snakes inside the home.
“At this point, in just a few months, that’s an infestation,” Jessica Perry said.
Multiple home inspections before closing did not reveal a snake den beneath the front porch.
“We hired a contractor to come out and actually dig out the concrete. When they busted through the middle, there were dozens and dozens of snake eggs, new and what looked like several years old,” Jessica Perry said.
‘The Snake House’
Neighbors told the couple the home had a reputation.
“One neighbor had said that, ‘I’m surprised that the previous owners didn’t tell you all that the snakes were free with purchase,’” Jessica Perry said.
Jessica Perry also contacted a previous owner, who told her it was nicknamed the “snake house” when he was a child.
“Now that we have found out that it’s a decades-old problem, what worries us now is that there are multiple dens within the foundation of the home, and in order to eradicate and mitigate that, you essentially have to bust down the entire home, but that’s our worst fear,” Jessica Perry said.
The snakes are not venomous, but the Perrys are worried about their 5-year-old son.
“Not necessarily that we’d be scared that they’d bite him. Snakes like warmth. So, if they were to get in the upper level and get in the bed or whatever, they could curl up around his neck, per se,” Johnathan Perry said.
Searching the basement for snakes has become a daily routine. The family has gotten more cats and cleared brush near a creek, with more work planned for the spring.
“We just bought the home in August and we’re already financially out thousands and thousands of dollars trying to fix an unanticipated problem that we didn’t have, or we didn’t anticipate having when we purchased it,” Jessica Perry said.
“It’s sad to say on a new home we just bought that it’s become a chore, I guess, that every evening we get home, we ask each other, ‘Have you gone to the basement yet to check for snakes?’” Johnathan Perry added.
The work includes removing the back porch to check for another den and addressing potential foundation problems. The process is expected to take months and cost thousands of dollars.
A friend of the family has set up a GoFundMe to help pay for the additional work.
What to do if a snake is found indoors
Kat Dale, lead keeper at the Kentucky Reptile Zoo, said a person who is sure a snake is nonvenomous can carefully remove it.
“If the snake is scared, it might do a couple things, like it might try to bite because it doesn’t understand. It might also musk, which will release a very smelly odor to protect itself, or shake its tail. So, if you understand their behavior and are OK with their reactions when they’re frightened, you could handle it and get them out by hand,” Dale said.
Dale said another option is to guide the snake into a large container or lift it with the end of a broom or a similar object. She emphasized that extermination is not the answer: Snakes benefit nature and help control pests.
If a snake cannot be confidently identified, do not handle it; contact a qualified wildlife professional for help.

Coin flip settles a tie in a northern Kentucky election
text:
Heads or tails? Coin flip decides a Kentucky magisterial district election after race ends in a tie
A northern Kentucky election took an unusual turn after two candidates finished with the exact same number of votes.
Related video above: Mississippi and Alaska Senate races still too close to call post-midterms
Republican Benny Ray Renner and Democrat Kristen Gifford Fryman each received 91 votes in the race for magistrate in the 2nd Magisterial District in Robertson County, a rural county near the Ohio-Kentucky state line and around 58 miles from Cincinnati, Ohio.
Out of the 182 ballots cast, there was not a single vote that separated the two candidates once all precincts had reported their numbers back.
Following a recommendation from the Kentucky State Board of Elections, officials decided to settle the race the old-fashioned way — a coin flip.
It's unclear who chose heads and who chose tails, but officials with the Robertson County Clerk's Office told sister station WLKY that Fryman came out on top and won the election.

title: This artist uses sunlight to burn designs into wood
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Billy Keith is a solar artist. He uses sunlight as his tool to create artwork burned directly into wood.
“You learn a lot by standing in the sun all day,” Keith said.
Keith said he introduces himself as “the sun man,” and his goal is to make more art in public.
His work starts with something he cannot hold in his hand: sunlight.
Keith uses a large magnifying lens — a Fresnel lens — to concentrate the sun into a tiny point of light, hot enough to burn designs into wood. Keith works without stencils, printers or shortcuts, creating each piece freehand line by line.
“It’s taken me 16 years to get to where I can do this so fast and smooth over and over again,” he said.
Keith said part of the process is keeping the concentrated point of light moving. When he makes an error, he keeps going.
“No mistakes. I just Bob Ross that. Just keep on going. Happy accident,” he said.
Keith said he got into the art after what he described as a near-death experience.
“Near-death experience after a night out of drinking Easter weekend,” he said.
Keith said he heard what he described as a whisper telling him, “You’re done drinking. Make art with the sun.”
“I did not die… this is what I was saved to do, and I better be doing it,” Keith said.
Keith said each piece has a story. He’s made many trees, landscapes, animals, and plants just to name a few.
“This is the day I saved the cat from a tree,” he said.
Keith sells his work online and travels for events and festivals around the region. He said he likes creating art publicly so he can talk with people about it.
Keith said he can also make solar art in winter as long as the sun is out. He also uses bingo dabbers to paint his work, a method he said he discovered after finding a bingo dabber on the street.
If you would like to check out Keith’s art, click here: https://www.solarcombustion.art/.

title: NASA awards $10B in contracts for Moon Base cargo, nuclear rover
text:
NASA awards $10B in contracts for Moon Base cargo, nuclear rover
NASA announced over the weekend a suite of awards and mission updates to expand its Moon Base program, including the selection of eight companies for a commercial cargo delivery contract potentially worth $10 billion and the development of a nuclear-powered rover built from spare Mars rover hardware.
Related previous coverage in the player above: NASA's plans for a moon base could take shape by the end of 2026
The announcements, made Saturday at the MAX POWER aerospace expo and air show at the Kennedy Space Center, advance commercial robotic deliveries, launch and orbital transfer services, surface infrastructure, and science capabilities as the agency works with industry to establish a sustained presence near the Moon’s South Pole.
“We are building the Moon Base mission by mission,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said. “Today’s announcements expand nearly every part of that campaign, using the playbook that carried NASA through its greatest eras: fly often, learn, apply those lessons, and get better and more capable with every mission. When our astronauts return to the Moon, they will arrive with the first elements of the Moon Base already waiting for them on the surface.”
Carlos García-Galán, manager of the Moon Base Program, said that in the eight months since the program’s “Ignition,” the agency has consolidated efforts into a streamlined campaign for technology development and implementation. “Most importantly, we’ve taken action, awarding new contracts and forging new partnerships to accelerate development.”
To strengthen cargo lander capacity, NASA selected eight companies eligible to compete for future lunar surface delivery missions under a new Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) 2 framework: Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Intuitive Machines, ispace-U.S., Lockheed Martin Space, Northrop Grumman Space Systems, SpaceX, and Voyager Technologies.
The companies will manage, build, and operate landers carrying NASA science, technology, and infrastructure payloads. The 10-year, multiple-award, indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity master contract has a combined maximum value of $10 billion. NASA also raised the value of the existing CLPS 1.0 contract from $2.6 billion to $4.2 billion to support initial Phase One Moon Base objectives. The original contract remains in place through November 2028, with an additional five years to complete deliveries through November 2033.
NASA is moving forward with PROMISE (Polar Rover for Observation, Mapping, and In-Situ Exploration), a six-wheeled, nuclear-powered rover that will land at the South Pole to characterize the surface and subsurface, assess resource potential including ice in permanently shadowed regions, and provide data for landing site selection and future infrastructure. The rover can operate through long lunar nights.
The Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, a division of Caltech, will manage the mission and build the rover from spare flight components and engineering test models from the Curiosity and Perseverance Mars rovers. Using proven hardware and software reduces cost and shortens the timeline. Instruments include a drill to extract regolith from about 3 feet (1 meter) below the surface, spectrometers, temperature and radiation sensors, and cameras. It will also demonstrate NASA’s High Performance Spaceflight Computing system and advanced autonomy capabilities. Launch is targeted for late 2028 for an 18-month mission.
Blue Origin received a $94 million base contract, with a performance-based option worth an additional $140 million, to deliver and deploy PROMISE using its Mark 1 lander. The award expands a May 2026 task order to deliver two lunar terrain vehicles.
For transportation, NASA awarded six task orders totaling about $1.3 billion under its Venture-Class Acquisition of Dedicated and Rideshare (VADR) contract to Arrow Science and Technology, Blue Origin, and Impulse Space. The awards support three mission types: risk-reduction flights including the CAPSTONE 02 spacecraft to test navigation and communications; delivery of MoonFall drones and other assets to survey the South Pole ahead of astronauts; and demonstrations of orbital transfer vehicles to increase cargo capacity. Some missions will use Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Relativity Space’s Terran R, and SpaceX’s Falcon 9, with in-space transportation from Blue Origin, Firefly Aerospace, Impulse Space, and Quantum Space.
Separately, SpaceX was selected under an existing lunar logistics contract for a Cislunar Communications Deployment Demonstration. The company will launch communications satellites aboard a Starship to cislunar space in 2028 to inform future lunar networks.
On the surface, NASA plans to acquire commercial components for a Mini-Communications and Solar Tower (miniCAST). Awards went to Honeybee Robotics (a Blue Origin company) for energy storage, Redwire for power generation, and Yank Technologies Inc. for wireless power transfer. Engineers at Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, will assemble and test the systems. Work is expected to begin within months on components, with a solicitation for fully integrated power systems anticipated in early 2027.
NASA also intends to release a directed call under its Next Space Technologies for Exploration Partnerships (NextSTEP-3 B) solicitation to address high-priority data gaps through small missions, payloads, or commercial data purchases.
The efforts support Artemis astronaut missions of increasing complexity to the South Pole, advancing science and technology while establishing an enduring human presence that can serve as a foundation for crewed missions to Mars.
More information is available at nasa.gov/moonbase.

title: Ole Miss investigates video showing women making racist gestures outside student apartment
text:
Ole Miss investigating 'offensive' video showing women making racist gestures outside student's apartment
The University of Mississippi is investigating a video that appears to show two women making monkey gestures and noises outside a student’s apartment
Ole Miss investigating 'offensive' video showing women making racist gestures outside student's apartment
The University of Mississippi is investigating a video that appears to show two women making monkey gestures and noises outside a student’s apartment
A video captured by a doorbell camera at the University of Mississippi has left a first-year student and her two roommates feeling targeted.
It shows three white women walking past their apartment door, with two of them making monkey noises and gestures.
"It was somewhat laughable at first until things started sinking in. You start thinking about where you at, the type of atmosphere Mississippi brings in itself, and then the realization start setting in," said Vincent Ford, the student's grandfather.
Ford said the women's actions felt racially insensitive, considering the dark history of Black people being caricatured as monkeys and apes.
"My wife and I had a talk with my granddaughter and told her, 'Look, these types of things happen. We're going to get down to the bottom of it to make sure that you're safe,'" Ford said.  
He called for the university to hold the women accountable.
"If they did something that someone else felt was racial, then they need to be thrown off campus," Ford said.
The video has spread on social media, prompting the University of Mississippi to launch an investigation.
"We are aware of a video depicting offensive, hurtful, and unacceptable behaviors that conflict with our university values, and we condemn them. The university has reached out to those targeted by the actions to share information, resources and support," the university said in a statement.
Ford believes the political climate is contributing to incidents like this.
"When we have things happen on a political level, with the president on down, things like this will happen. And when they open up the floodgates, they normalize these types of things. It's our responsibility to make sure we look at it, we address it and say, 'Hey, this is not right,'" Ford said.
He said he wants his granddaughter to treat others with compassion, even when they are different.

title: SCOTUS and the high stakes North Dakota case
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) -A Supreme Court case out of North Dakota could have major implications for landowners everywhere. If justices side with federal law over state law, landowners likely would lose any incentive to pursue fair payment when the government takes their land, and they would risk sinking any potential payout into court fees.
When the government takes land, it has to pay the owner. That is called eminent domain, and it is in the Constitution. One pipeline company, working on behalf of the government, low-balled landowners, and the dispute turned into a multi-year legal battle. The landowners won but were left with $380,000 in legal fees.
North Dakota has a state law that says the pipeline company has to pay those legal fees. The federal government says the company does not have to. Bob McNamara argued the case Monday.
“What we’re saying is that when states try to protect private property owners, private companies have to respect those laws. Even private companies wielding the power of eminent domain,” McNamara said.
Justices appeared skeptical of that argument. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said, “unless Congress says state law is applicable, when you have federal condemnation by any actor, you would have federal law be the applicable rule.”

title: ‘A Christmas miracle’: Stolen nativity scene found miles away
text:
PALMER, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Community tips led to the recovery of a valuable nativity scene that apparently was stolen earlier this week, miles from where it was last seen.
The nativity scene, which sits inside a handcrafted wooden crèche cabin valued at tens of thousands of dollars, went missing from the parking lot at St. Michael’s Parish in Palmer sometime on Tuesday or Wednesday while sitting on a flatbed trailer, according to Father Michael Shields with the church.
Shields said community tips on Facebook led to a reported sighting along the Glenn Highway near Chickaloon.
“So one o’clock [Thursday] night, I got in my car to find it,” Shields said. “So I drove up to Chickaloon to see if I could find it.”
The pastor said he made the late-night drive down the highway but didn’t see it.
Palmer police, however, did. Officers contacted Shields as he was looking for the scene and confirmed they had found it, still in good condition.
Shields said it’s still not known who stole it, but he believes whoever took it abandoned it after the trailer’s tires went flat. He said it was found partly hidden among trees.
“It’s a Christmas miracle because honestly, I didn’t think we were going to get it back, to be honest,” he said.
The pastor said the nativity scene was created over seven years, built and paid for by the parishioners of his church. The figures were molded after the Italian image of Jesus, he said, adding that the figurines are valued at around $25,000 to $30,000.
Shields said the scene will be placed near the Palmer train depot near the center of town.
Shields was heartened by the community response as news of the theft spread quickly on social media.
“It went all through the Valley, Glennallen to Valdez,” he said. “And so everybody showed such beautiful concern and hope.”

title: Pope visits struggling Argentine home for people with disabilities to press economic message
text:
Pope visits struggling Argentine home for people with disabilities to press economic message
Pope Leo XIV doubled down Monday on his call for Argentina to look out for the weakest and most vulnerable as he visited a home for people with disabilities in a symbolically powerful rebuke of President Javier Milei’s austerity measures.
On his first full day in Argentina, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in the suburb of Claypole, south of the capital. The institution, founded by an Italian priest in 1935, shelters over 400 vulnerable people with disabilities across its 50 hectares (123 acres).
The center, known as the “city of charity,” has been severely impacted by Milei’s austerity measures, which have hit the healthcare and social service sector hard. Milei has taken his signature chain saw to specialized therapy programs that for decades have represented a lifeline for many of the estimated 5 million Argentines with disabilities, freezing payments and dismantling a vital safety net.
Related video:
Combined with inflation, the center has reported extreme economic distress and Leo’s visit comes just days before the Senate takes up a disability funding bill that Milei opposes.
A message also to Argentine business and labor
The visit kicked off a busy day for Leo in which the American pope, fulfilling the unfinished legacy of Argentine Pope Francis, is emphasizing Catholic social teaching that calls for putting the weakest and most vulnerable at the center of economic policy.
Upon arrival Sunday and with Milei at his side, Leo cited Francis’ frequent refrain that money must serve and not rule: “The economy must serve the person, not the person the economy,” Leo said in his first speech in Argentina.
It’s a message Leo is expected to repeat later Monday when he meets with business leaders, union representatives and leaders of popular movements at the Catholic University of Argentina.
Among those invited are domestic manufacturers battered by cheap imports since Milei scrapped long-standing trade barriers, and members of Argentina’s largest labor confederation, who took their worries over job losses and shrinking wages to the Vatican in September.
Since Milei took office in late 2023, his austerity agenda has made him an icon of the global conservative backlash against the liberal establishment. Much like its allies in the Trump administration, his government has portrayed the cuts to disability programs as part of a reform process aimed at eliminating fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.
A papal Mass nearly 40 years later
For many Argentines, the highlight of the day was to be Leo’s late-morning Mass at the “Monumento a los Españoles” that was expected to draw as many as 2 million people. It's the very same venue where, nearly 40 years ago, St. John Paul II became the last pontiff to celebrate Mass in the South American country.
Thousands of people arrived at midnight to secure a better spot for the Mass, Leo’s first in Argentina.
“We were dating when John Paul II visited 40 years ago,” recalled Teresa Videla, 63, who was accompanied by her husband and youngest son. “And now it’s very special for us to come back and see the visiting pope. So much has happened in the world, in the country, and we now have six children and 15 grandchildren.”
Leo has been welcomed by huge and adoring crowds in Buenos Aires, the second stop of his three-nation tour of South America.
Late Sunday, groups of faithful chanting “Pope Leo, Pope Leo,” and “Long live the pope” gathered in front of the Vatican's embassy, or nunciature, where Leo is staying. A smiling Leo stepped outside to greet them and offered his blessing.
