title: Jake Viola requests recount in Portland’s District 4 City Council race
text:
Jake Viola has requested a recount in the Portland City Council District 4 race after finishing just 12 votes behind incumbent Anna Bullett in last week’s election.
Viola made the formal request Monday, three days after the City Clerk’s office finalized the results. The tally was 3,421 to 3,409 in favor of Bullett, with another 917 ballots left blank.
“We’re separated by 12 votes out of nearly 8,000 cast,” Viola said after submitting the request. “When it’s that close, we owe it to the voters of District 4 to make sure every vote is counted.”
The city of Portland follows state statute and rules set by the Maine Secretary of State’s office in regard to recounts. While the hand recount has not yet been scheduled, state law says it must be held “as soon as reasonably possible at a time and place that affords the designated recount candidates a reasonable opportunity to be present.”
That statute also lays out that each candidate will provide a minimum of six counters to participate in the tallying. Because Viola’s vote total was within 1.5% of Bullett’s, he does not have to pay a deposit for the recount.
In response to the recount request, Bullett said Monday that she’s “grateful for the incredible turnout and engagement Portland voters had this cycle.”
“I look forward to the election results being certified and thank everyone for their support,” she said. “I have every confidence in the city clerk and her team and the accuracy of our elections.”
The other two City Council races on the Nov. 3 ballot were decided last week in ranked-choice runoffs, with former Mayor Kate Snyder taking an at-large seat and restaurateur Ilma López winning District 5.
Their victories were seen by supporters as bringing a necessary moderate shift to the City Council in the next term, and Viola was hoping to play a role in that new direction.
Viola, 35, cast himself as a candidate who would provide better communication and representation for constituents in District 4, and he campaigned on having experience in correcting municipal policies that cause unintended consequences.
Bullett, elected in 2023 and seeking a second term, campaigned on maintaining her focus on issues like pedestrian safety while using relationships established with city staff to more quickly resolve issues.

title: An abandoned safe was found in Falmouth — and its mysterious stash could now help heat homes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A puzzling stack of cash sat in the evidence room of the Falmouth Police Department for four years.
In August 2022, a resident walking the short trail through the woods between Falmouth’s Central Fire Station and the neighboring baseball fields spotted a safe on the ground and pointed it out to Falmouth police.
Cutting the safe open, police found $55,737 in bills.
“Cash of this magnitude is very unusual,” said Falmouth Police Chief John Kilbride. “I’ve never experienced anything like that in my 30 years.”
Following the discovery of the safe, Falmouth police reached out to other law enforcement across Maine and New Hampshire, asking if they had heard about a theft of a large sum of money from either an individual or a bank. The department also published newspaper notices about finding an unspecified amount of money, fulfilling their legal due diligence, said Kilbride.
Given that the cash went unclaimed and was dry in the safe — indicating it hadn’t been sitting outside for long — Kilbride said his best guess was that it was placed in the woods for a drug-related exchange.
After not hearing any leads for six months, the safe and its contents were officially classified as abandoned property, joining the department’s collection of unclaimed bikes, kayaks, wallets and jewelry. According to state statute, after the police department makes sufficient effort to find the owner and at least six months have passed, the chief of police can decide what to do with unclaimed property, including donate it to a nonprofit organization, trashing it or selling it to the highest bidder.
The Falmouth Police Department held onto the mysterious cash longer because Kilbride thought if the money was stolen from the home of an older adult, it might take more time for them or their family to notice it was missing. But after four years, he said it was time for the money to leave the evidence room.
Kilbride said he usually sends off unclaimed property as a donation to the Falmouth Lions Club’s auction or to a secondhand store. For this unusually large sum, he directed the $55,737 be deposited into the town’s account to be used for charitable purposes.
“This is the people’s money,” said Kilbride.
With a pile of cash that metaphorically fell from the sky and the direction to help residents, it didn’t take long for Town Manager Nathan Poore to craft a proposal.
“What do we do with this now? I thought now is the time to probably help people out with heating assistance,” he said.
The town has facilitated short-term heating assistance programs a handful of times over the past two decades, such as during the Great Recession and the pandemic. Each time, about $50,000 went to the program, said Poore.
Roughly half of Maine households rely on heating oil, with Maine consuming more residential heating oil per capita than any other state in the country, according to data from the American Community Survey. According to an announcement from the Maine Department of Energy Resources at the end of October, heating oil prices in Maine are at a record high, with costs up 82% over this time last year. Given this increase, Mainers will spend about $750 more than last fall to fill a standard 275-gallon oil tank.
Maine homeowners and renters can apply to the statewide Home Energy Assistance Program, which helps qualified applicants pay for heating costs. However, even with additional funds, the state assistance won’t go as far this winter, as record-high heating oil costs will reduce the average HEAP award’s purchasing power.
Falmouth residents who have completed a HEAP application and are approved will be eligible for the town’s program as well, said Poore. Awarded funds may be used toward heating fuel, an electricity bill or rent if rent includes utilities.
Poore said in the past, the town has had about 50 applicants for heating assistance. While he’s still working out the details following the Town Council’s likely approval of this allocation, Poore said he’ll probably start the program by granting $500 per applicant. Leftover funds would be distributed in additional rounds of assistance.
The Falmouth Town Council is expected to vote to approve this use of funds at its meeting Monday evening.
“I’ve never had the experience where we stumbled upon some found money and had to spend on charitable purposes,” said Poore, who has worked for the town for 20 years. “I don’t ever recall anything like this.”

title: Rochelle Fleming, lead singer of '70s disco and soul group First Choice, dies
text:
Rochelle Fleming, lead singer of '70s disco and soul group First Choice, dies
Rochelle Fleming, lead singer of the R&B and disco girl group First Choice, has died.
Fleming's manager announced her death in Philadelphia on behalf of her family.
Fleming was a Philadelphia native, and it was there that First Choice formed in 1971. The group’s soul and disco hits included "Armed and Extremely Dangerous," "Smarty Pants," "The Player (Part 1)," "Guilty," "Love Thang" and "Doctor Love." Their breakthrough came in 1973 with "Armed and Extremely Dangerous."
"'Let No Man Put Asunder' became particularly influential, embraced by generations of DJs and producers through remixes, samples and reinterpretations," BMG, the parent group of the band's record label, wrote.
The powerful vocalist continued singing after First Choice broke up in 1980, with solo dance records “Love Itch,” “Danger!” and “Suffer (The Consequences).”
“One of the greatest in R&B, Disco, and House music has left us,” the DJ Lenny Fontana wrote on Facebook. “She is probably one of the most sampled in current dance music as you will hear her voice on so many recordings. A humble person and to us an ICON! Rest in Eternal Peace as we all loved you.”
Christian Hope Baptist Church in Philadelphia also posted a tribute to Fleming, saying that even when Fleming became a renowned artist, she “came home” to sing at the church.
"When Rochelle stepped forward for a solo, the whole sanctuary leaned in. Her voice stirred our spirits, moved us to tears, and lifted us into praise. We looked forward to those moments, and we will carry them with us always."

title: New program will help people in Maine get to school, work, appointments and more
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
New program will help people in Maine get to school, work, appointments and more
The United Way is launching a new pilot project in Maine to help people get to appointments, work, school and more.
The program is called Keep ME Moving and is funded thanks to support from the John T. Gorman Foundation. The program will help people pay for small car repairs, bus passes, and Lyft rides.
The United Way says requests through 211 Maine related to transportation have increased 90% since 2020 and a recent survey conducted by the United Way in Cumberland and York counties found that transportation was a common challenge.
United Way officials say they expect demand will be high for the limited amount of money available for the program each month. You can also donate to Keep ME Moving to help it stay funded.
“We know that nearly four in ten households in Southern Maine are struggling, and the people experiencing those challenges are the experts on what would make a difference in their lives,” said United Way of Southern Maine President and CEO Dan Coyne. “What we heard repeatedly was that a relatively small transportation problem could quickly spiral into a much larger crisis. A missed shift at work, a missed medical appointment, or an unexpected repair can make it harder for a family that’s already stretching every dollar.”
A 2025 John T. Gorman Foundation report on transportation in Maine found that addressing transportation challenges will require both immediate support for families and longer-term policy solutions. Keep ME Moving is designed to help meet the immediate need.
Who is eligible?
Applicants are currently being accepted by referral from United Way non-profit and employer partners. To be eligible, people must live in a county served by the three United Ways in Maine, be within the ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed) income threshold, and have a transportation need related to one or more of the following areas:
- Medical, dental, or mental health appointments;
- Work or educational opportunity;
- Child care or school;
- Basic needs, such as groceries or pharmacy.
The fund is administered by United Way of Southern Maine in partnership with United Way of Aroostook.

title: Nvidia shares drop after co. investigates whether CEO was 'target of a foreign intelligence effort'
text:
Nvidia shares drop after co. investigates whether CEO was 'target of a foreign intelligence effort'
Shares of Nvidia are sliding before the market open on Monday as the chip company announced an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.”
Nvidia's announcement of the investigation on Sunday followed Huang’s acknowledgment that he had been intimate with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China.
During a routine briefing Monday, China’s Foreign Ministry dismissed the spying allegations, calling them a smear campaign against Beijing.
Related video: Trump says US won't put brakes on AI following Xi visit
Nvidia is a central player in the race to develop artificial intelligence. Its chips power many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China’s access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology.
Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in an analyst note that there's a small chance Huang is removed or steps down from the CEO post.
“Jensen is the core DNA of Nvidia and its AI success and ambitions are heavily tied to him staying on as CEO,” Ives wrote. “Jensen is not replaceable..there is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly as CEO and that speaks to the key risk now with Nvidia that investors will factor this dynamic to the stock.”
Still, Ives said there is a risk, as Huang could be removed as CEO depending on the board's investigation and that it will remain an overhang on shares near term.
Nvidia's stock dropped 5% in premarket trading. Shares hit an all-time high of $243.37 last month.

title: Trump pushes for permanent daylight saving time: ‘It’s so dark outside, so early’
text:
WASHINGTON D.C. (Gray News/AP) — President Donald Trump renewed his call to end the twice-yearly clock change by making daylight saving time permanent.
“Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act. It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?),” the president said on his social media platform, Truth Social.
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time.
On July 14, the House approved a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent. The vote was 308-117. However, the bill did not pass the Senate before Americans switched their clocks on Nov. 1.
Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight when Americans are most active. But opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.
Congress passed a law in 1973 establishing year-round daylight saving time as an experiment, which began in 1974. Lawmakers ended the experiment early as support declined, partly because of concern for children walking to school in the dark.
Trump, with the GOP coming off a shaky midterm election, promised to keep working to get the bill to his desk.
“I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done,” the president said. “The House sent it over to the Senate with great bipartisan support, numerous times (308-117), but the Senate didn’t take it up. We have far bigger priorities, but I will keep fighting for this!”

title: Making History Does Not Mean Changing It
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Like many on campus and across the country, I entered November in a dismal mood. After two years of watching America’s economy, institutions and global prestige melt away like a premature snowfall, I was expecting Democrats to phone it in like they had two years ago when Donald Trump stormed back into power on the promise of deregulated dictatorship. Even as the second term proved cataclysmic domestically and abroad, the Democratic Party seemed to be as uninspired as ever.
While moderates moved to squash progressives like Zohran Mamdani and Abdul El-Sayed, the world’s richest man embarked on a savage spending spree for Trump’s hand-picked candidates and the Supreme Court gutted the Voting Rights Act to enable Republican gerrymandering. Most polling favored Democrats, but so they had last time. My friends and I knew that Republicans had proven too disastrous to keep the House, but disagreed with our Senate predictions. Even so, we were unanimous in thinking that Susan Collins wasn’t going anywhere.
So you can imagine my surprise as the votes poured in on November 3rd. The Republicans lost the national popular congressional vote by 13 points, the worst loss since Watergate. As of today, Democrats have flipped seven Senate seats, including states like Kansas, South Carolina and Texas, where the party hadn’t been competitive in decades and have come within a hair’s length of taking Mississippi. In the House, Democrats have flipped over 40 seats and are on track for their biggest congressional victory since 2008. Among the states, six states now have new Democratic trifectas across both legislatures and the governorship, again, in states where Democrats normally take a drubbing. We also saw a medley of historic firsts: A female Native American governor in New Mexico, a female Black governor in Georgia, a Muslim senator in Michigan and an openly-gay senator in New Hampshire, as well as an overall record number for women and minorities running for public office. Democrats have much to be proud of this year. Nobody can deny that they have made history with these results.
But making history does not always mean changing it. Democrats should not rest on their laurels, nor should Republicans lament (or celebrate) the death of the MAGA movement. Midterm results generally tell us more about the past than the future: In 1994 and 2010, Republicans won big but failed to capture the White House in the next election. Past performance is not indicative of future results and the American people could tire of a Democratic Congress over the next two years if they don’t see enough change, or the wrong kind of change. That said, Democrats have a shot in 2028 if they remain disciplined, aligned with voters and committed to checking an executive branch gone haywire.
One thing is certain: The GOP just faced a massive rebuke for the past two years of mismanagement, especially where the economy is concerned. Voters sent a clear message that they are sick of inflation and blame Republicans for going to war with Iran, kicking off a trade war with the entire world and shepherding into law the Big Beautiful Bill, which sacrificed working peoples’ health insurance and food stamps to give the wealthiest Americans extravagant tax breaks. Trump proved to be a liability for the GOP as he showed the country that he cared far more about his ballroom project than he did about the price of groceries. At least Marie Antoinette wanted her people to eat.
The president, sounding eerily calm about his party’s disastrous performance last week, said in a 60 Minutes interview that Republicans would have fared better if he was on the ballot. Yet, in many ways, he was: Trump was at the forefront of efforts to undermine the electoral process in Republicans’ favor and he hand-picked many of the candidates who just lost safely red seats. As much as he likes to pretend that he’s a national superstar, the fact is that his approval rating hovers in the mid-to-low thirties and, both this year and in the 2018 midterms, an endorsement from him often spells electoral defeat. In reality, people can’t stand this guy. Also, over the past two years, as prices continued to rise, we heard further revelations of Trump’s abhorrent history of sexual violence, saw his unhinged rants on TV and Truth Social, and watched our president put himself before his country at every turn. Trump wasn’t on the ballot, and he should be thankful.
It really is that simple: Trump promised lower prices, they never materialized, so Republican voters stayed home, and his party suffered for it. “Woke” is not “back” (whatever that even means), this isn’t a sign that Americans are more progressive than we thought they were, and Democrats should not fight publicly to revive DEI programs or take up the issue of women’s sports, as much as I personally care about these issues. Alongside big wins for Democrats, we saw across the country pass a slew of socially-conservative ballot initiatives, including one in Maine that all-but-killed our needle exchange program. The 2026 electorate is the same one that helped put Trump in power two years ago.
If the Democratic party wants to keep what it has and take even more in two years, Democrats must, for now, live by the same mantra that saw Bill Clinton take back the presidency after more than a decade of Republican rule: It’s the economy, stupid.
Some suggestions for Democrats in office:
Problem: The Iran War has raised gas prices, and Americans don’t want to pay more than $4 per gallon. Solution: Congress should not authorize a single cent of defense spending until we arrive at a diplomatic solution that sees the Strait of Hormuz reopened.
Problem: Americans cannot afford homes because of tariffs on building materials. Solution: Congress should reclaim its constitutional power over tariffs and override the ones that Trump has put in place.
Problem: At the president’s behest, ICE is murdering people in the streets. Solution: Be the party of law and order. Hold the killers to account, publicly investigate ICE and the killings, and do everything short of a veto-proof majority to reign in federal law enforcement.
These are broad suggestions, I leave the specifics to my representatives, who you and I hand-picked for the job. Note what does not appear in my short list: Impeaching Trump, pushing for universal healthcare and other long-shot causes, and taking a knee in Capitol Hill. Democrats must steer clear of ineffectual political theater that won’t bring tangible change. Opposition parties often fail to avoid these pitfalls. That leads to a classic trap: Becoming a useful scapegoat for the president and his party. Trump is a master of seizing upon the negative and amplifying it to the whole country, so Democrats will pay dearly for any failed initiatives.
That leads me to the other key to lasting success for Democrats: They need to establish disciplined and unified messaging so that when Congress delivers, the president cannot take credit. That messaging means speaking with one voice against the war in Iran and the tariffs and reminding people of the economic hardship that this administration has put them through for the past two years. I admit that out-bragging this president is no small feat, but projecting sobriety and strength through unity will send a powerful message in a time of unfettered chaos.
That also means putting aside hot-button issues like Israel and gender-affirming care, at least until Democrats have rebuilt some political capital and beef is no longer a luxury for most Americans. Of course, these issues are controversial because they impact so many and they demand our attention. But remember that Democrats don’t have a veto-proof majority and control only one branch of the government. Trump can block any bill he doesn’t like, meaning Democrats can enact limited change at best. Trying to push through divisive legislation is far more likely to splinter the remarkably broad coalition that Democrats have just formed, reducing the odds of electing a Democratic president farther down the line who can go further than Congress can.
The next two years are a chance for Democrats to put their heads down and govern. Voters are tired and frightened by what this country has become. It is incumbent upon the Democratic party, as the clear winner of this year’s election, to rebuild their trust not just in the party, but in American institutions. Lofty proclamations about social progress and democracy won’t get it done. Instead, they must shine a light during dark times and make sure everyone can see it.

title: Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky files resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing his fellow Republicans to remove one of the Trump administration’s most prominent figures following sweeping election losses blamed in part on fallout from the war in Iran.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican, read the impeachment resolution from the House floor just hours after it opened for the first day of sessions after the midterms. It largely focuses on the war in Iran but also includes references to Hegseth’s role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela.
The congressman, who was defeated by a Trump-backed challenger in a primary earlier this year, said Hegseth’s actions amounted to “high crimes and misdemeanors.”
Hegseth, he said, “knowingly executed and implemented unlawful orders” and “remains a threat to the Constitution.”
President Donald Trump lashed out at Massie personally just hours after the congressman read the resolution, calling him a “loser” who “has a lot of hatred in his heart.”
A vote in the House could come by mid-week, but next steps are highly uncertain. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries supports the measure. If most Democrats follow him, Massie would only need support from a few Republicans to impeach Hegseth.
If the House votes to impeach, it would fall to to the Senate to either dismiss the charges or hold a trial. Republicans remain in the majority in both chambers, until the new Congress convenes in January with Democrats in control.
Sen. Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader, endorsed the impeachment push. “Hegseth must stand trial before the Senate,” he said.
Republican leaders, who are eager to use their final weeks in power executing their own agenda, expressed frustration at the move. House Speaker Mike Johnson, who has tried to prevent the vote, said impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that.”
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he wasn’t sure why the vote was being held now.
“We’ll see what their ultimate decision is over there,” he said of the House. “We’ll have to deal with it accordingly here.”
Hegseth issues his own defense and prepares for a fight
Hegseth is stepping up his public statements ahead of the vote, telling reporters that he’s eager to defend the military actions that he and Trump have taken against Iran, Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels and Venezuela’s previous leaders.
After giving a speech at the Naval War College in Rhode Island, he brushed aside the impeachment push.
“There’s a lot of politically motivated people who may have substantial policy disagreements, but their disagreements are with success,” he told reporters. He added that “if we want to litigate” the military actions that the Trump administration has taken, “I’m happy to do it all day long.”
Asked about Vice President JD Vance blaming the Iran war for the massive GOP losses in the election, Hegseth noted that Trump said he would do it again, and “I agree.”
Hegseth also announced that he would hold a rare news conference on Tuesday — his first in over 180 days — on the impeachment threat.
Hegseth argued that the war was necessary because “someone had to confront the Iranian regime’s pursuit of a nuclear weapon” and said “the choice was don’t act and wish it away or take a bold move.”
Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%.
Trump defended Hegseth to reporters on Monday, commending him for having “won the war” in Venezuela and “winning the war” in Iran, which continues to drag on.
Pentagon chief insists ‘Iran is devastated’
Hegseth reiterated that “Iran is devastated,” even though the Islamic Republic has been able to keep striking military bases in the Middle East that are used by the United States, causing billions of dollars in damage, as well as commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Disruptions to shipping in the waterway, where one-fifth of the world’s oil passed before the war, have led to higher energy prices that hit voters’ pocketbooks.
Hegseth’s defense of the war comes after about 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended his fellow Cabinet secretary, saying that he believes Hegesth has been doing “a great job” and that its unfair that a Republican is pushing the impeachment effort.
“I work with him. And so I see perhaps a side of him that the media doesn’t see and members of Congress may not see,” Rubio told reporters at the Group of Seven industrialized democracies gathering in Paris. “But I think Pete works really hard. He’s incredibly smart.”
___
Associated Press writers Kevin Freking, Lisa Mascaro, Joey Cappelletti and Farnoush Amiri contributed to this report.

title: A nature outing at MDI High School
text:
In the inimitable words of entertainer Garrison Keillor, “Birders are a weird lot.” That we are. Speaking for myself, I am always birding. No matter the core activity, I always have an ear peeled for birds. Hiking Sargent Mountain? Chickadees, nuthatches, kinglets, juncos, and woodpeckers are my soundtrack. Kayaking the Porcupine Islands? The plaintive call of Black Guillemots soothes my soul. Laying abed, there are countless nights when Barred Owls serenade, “Who cooks for you, who cooks for you all.” When actually birding, I often visit hotspots, places known for supporting loads of birds. Here on Mount Desert Island, the high school is tops.
The landscape makes this locale special, at least, from the viewpoint of a naturalist. The campus sits on a “whaleback,” ridges of glacial till or bedrock reminiscent of its namesake and formed during the Wisconsin glaciation. The ridgeline slopes into wetlands of Tamarack, Red Spruce, and Black Spruce. To the north, Kittredge Brook and its immediate watershed is a Maine Coast Heritage Trust preserve with a hiking trail extending between Pine Heath Road and the high school.

title: Joe Biden to limit memoir promotion tour, says cancer 'slows me down'
text:
Joe Biden to limit promotional appearances for upcoming memoir, says cancer 'slows me down'
Former President Joe Biden announced he will need to limit promotional events for his upcoming memoir release as he continues treatment for prostate cancer.
In a statement posted on social media, Biden said his memoir, "Promise Me, America," is slated to be released on Nov. 17, saying it covers his years as president and the challenges he and Americans faced.
"It's about who we are as a nation. What we stand for. And America's role in the world," Biden said about the memoir. "More than anything, it's about my faith in the American people and the great American experiment in self-governance and democracy."
Video: Former President Joe Biden has been diagnosed with an “aggressive” form of prostate cancer
Ahead of promotions for the memoir's release, the former president spoke on his cancer diagnosis, saying his doctors “continue to be encouraged” by how he is responding to treatment, though he said “some days are better than others."
“While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families,” Biden, 83, wrote. "It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes, it slows me down."
Biden said despite ongoing treatment, he will "not be able to hold as many conversations" about his book as he intended.
"I'm hopeful the words on the page speak for themselves," he wrote.
He concluded the statement, saying, "Promise Me, America, we'll never forget it."
The 46th president announced he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer in May 2025. He has since been undergoing treatment and has urged men to see their doctors for early detection.
"When prostate cancer is caught early, the five-year survival is close to 100%," Biden said in a social media post in September. "So have the conversation with your doctor. Don’t put it off."

title: Documentary on Bangor Humane Society to premiere Thursday in Orono
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The first documentary about the Bangor Humane Society will premiere Thursday evening, November 12th, at Black Bear Cinemas in Orono.
It’s produced by Five Road Films. Director and producer Keith Travers donated his time and resources to make the 45-minute documentary. He and his wife, Danielle Travers spent about a year filming the animals, 22 staff members and more than 100 volunteers at the shelter.
Woof LLC, Danforth’s Downhome Grocery and Mason’s Brewing donated to the project. Travers says he used that funding to purchase memory cards to store footage on.
“I was overwhelmed by the amount of people that volunteer their time and the passion that they have for that work,” said Travers. “I’ve done other documentaries but this one just kind of called out to me.”
Why the film was made
About a year earlier, Travers had heard about an email sent to the Bangor Humane Society. The tone of the email stuck with him.
“I deemed it pretty negative,” he says. “And I thought there was some misunderstandings about how the Humane Society works.”
Travers approached BHS about a documentary to show what really goes on behind the scenes.
“And we jumped in with all of our feet,” says Kathryn Ravenscraft, Director of Development & Communications for the Bangor Humane Society. “Yes, even our furry bosses were up for it too.”
Travers says he lost count of how many hours were put into filming and editing the 45-minute production. But he says, he was truly humbled by the amount of volunteers that donate their time to the amimal shelter.
“A lot of animals come in here under traumatic circumstances. They might be wandering the streets or people just can’t take care of them anymore. The people here, really, they go through a lot emotionally,” says Travers. “I wouldn’t says it’s shocking but I was overwhelmed by the amount of people that volunteer their time and the passion that they have for that work.”
What viewers may take away
Travers hopes those who watch the documentary will take understand the emotional rollercoaster that comes with working at an animal shelter.
“Maybe a little more compassion for the animals, but also for the people that are here,” says Travers. “I know sometimes people come in and they are upset because they didn’t get the service they think they deserve. And there’s usually a reason for that. So just to take a step back and understand what’s going on behind the scenes.”
“95 to 97% of our animals, the end is just walking out into their new lives. And that’s what we’re doing here. So it’s nice to be able to tell that,” says Ravenscraft.
Paws and take a bow
Humane: Inside Bangor Humane Society premieres on Thursday, November 12th at Black Bear Cinemas in Orono. The film starts at 6:30 p.m. but they’ll be rolling out the red carpet beforehand for some VIPs (that’s very important pets).
Tickets are $15. They can be purchased here.

title: Tigers Kevin McGonigle beats out Red Sox pitcher Payton Tolle for AL Rookie of the Year
text:
Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle won the American League Rookie of the Year award Monday night after a stellar all-around season that sets him up to be a franchise cornerstone for the next decade.
Red Sox left-handed pitcher Payton Tolle finished third in the voting, behind Cleveland pitcher Parker Messick.
McGonigle — who played most of the season at just 21 years old — had a .278 batting average and .806 OPS with 18 homers, 72 RBI, 28 doubles and 12 stolen bases while splitting time between third base and shortstop. He’s the first Tigers player to win the award since pitcher Michael Fulmer in 2016 and the first Tigers infielder since Lou Whitaker in 1978.
The Tigers thought enough of McGonigle’s potential that they signed him to a $150 million, eight-year deal in April, just a few weeks into his rookie season. He backed up that confidence by making the All-Star team and helping the Tigers remain in the playoff race for much of the summer.
McGonigle received 28 of 30 first-place votes. The balloting was conducted before the postseason.
Messick had a 12-9 record with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts while Tolle was 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts.
The National League winner will be announced later Monday night.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy, who took over in April after Alex Cora was fired, and led Boston tot he playoffs, is a finalist for AL Manger of the Year along with Kevin Cash of the AL champion Rays and Will Venable of the White Sox. The winner will be announced on Tuesday.

title: Supreme Court allows Trump administration to resume building border wall in Texas’s Big Bend
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.
The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
Landowners and business owners in the Big Bend region, environmentalists and others who’ve opposed the construction project were bitterly disappointed with the court’s decision.
“This horrific decision clears the way for contractors to bulldoze pristine desert and dynamite canyon walls before the courts have even decided whether this destruction is legal,” said Laiken Jordahl, national public lands advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the groups that sued to stop the construction. “They’re signing off on the permanent destruction of the wildest place in Texas, and the theft of a great American river from all of us.”
Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of barriers a week across the entire border with a goal of eventually covering the entire 2,000-mile border with a mixture of 30-foot-tall steel walls, vehicle barriers and surveillance technology designed to stop illegal immigration and smuggling.
The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations. Those rules are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.
Big Bend residents of both parties oppose the project
In Texas’s Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.
They’ve argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.
A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border’s lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.
The Trump administration filed an emergency appeal, saying there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend. More traffic could also be funneled there if there’s a gap in the wall, federal attorneys argued.
Customs and Border Protection head Rodney Scott said in an interview with The Associated Press that if the Big Bend area were left without a wall or other border infrastructure while other areas along the border get those fortifications, he’s convinced it would be swiftly overrun by cartels.
The Supreme Court agreed that the law sharply limits judges’ powers to intervene when the federal government decides speedy border barrier construction is necessary. The majority paused the lower court decision as the case plays out. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
CBP did not immediately respond to questions about how swiftly construction could restart. The agency started building an initial section of border wall in one area of the roughly 500-mile stretch that makes up the Big Bend region, but that was stopped with the judge’s order.
Construction activity in national park sparked outrage
The agency has encountered intense opposition from landowners up and down the region when it comes to getting permissions to enter their land to survey and build.
The Center for Biological Diversity sued over the construction, along with Friends of the Ruidosa Church and a river guide in the Big Bend area. Jordahl said it was the first time the government had waived a broad set of environmental laws inside a national park.
David Keller lives in the Big Bend region, is a member of the board of Conserve Big Bend and is a plaintiff in a separate lawsuit of landowners opposing the border wall projects.
He called the court’s decision devastating: “Everything is on the line again.”
Keller called the border infrastructure projects the “industrialization of one of the last best open undeveloped wild places in the lower 48 states.”
“We can’t afford to lose any more. Not an ounce. Not an acre,” he said. “We need wild country to be who we are, to be fully human, to be American I would say.”
The projects have drawn criticism from both Democrats and Republicans, including outgoing Republican Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, who wrote an op-ed arguing against the project published Monday in the San Antonio Express-News hours before the court’s decision.
“A combination of modern technology, adequate staffing, and meaningful cooperation with local officials and landowners offers a more sensible and effective path forward than indiscriminate construction of unnecessary barriers,” Cornyn wrote.
The government in August paused construction activity in Big Bend National Park that sparked outrage when bulldozers were spotted breaking ground in the park.
The government has repeatedly said no steel walls are planned for the national park. Initial plans included a new road as well as some vehicle barriers in the park. CBP has said in court filings that it will come forward with a finalized plan for what it intends to build in the national park but so far hasn’t done so while the case was at the Supreme Court.

title: There’s no room for Flock cameras in Vacationland
text:
OPINION: Automated license plate readers (ALPRs), more commonly referred to as Flock cameras, have been making headlines for months now. While many claim they are a necessity and the next step toward protecting public safety, a fair share of people see them as a threat to privacy and a product of government surveillance.
As it stands right now, there are currently an estimated 102 operational Flock cameras in the state of Maine. While this would rank Maine 47th out of 52 U.S. states and territories in terms of Flock camera surveillance, the state has certainly experienced its share of issues with the product.
The Brewer Police Department recently released a report detailing an instance in which its ALPR systems were using stored data beyond the 21-day limit allowed by Maine state law. Brewer’s director of public safety, Chris Martin, claimed he was given no warning that this was taking place, and upon finding out, he decommissioned the use of these ALPR cameras.
“The issue that I had was we never got a phone call,” Martin stated in a Sept. 9 interview with WABI. “We were still operating under the assumption that this was working properly.”
Martin expressed his disapproval of the situation, shifting the blame toward the vendor, stating they were “unable to hold up their end of the bargain.”
While it is still unclear why data continued to be stored and what the data was being used for, it is just one of many examples in Maine and across the country where these cameras pose a threat to public security.
In states such as Florida, Flock cameras have been used by police to stalk individuals by following their travel patterns. Jamarus Brown, a police officer trusted with upholding public safety, was reportedly accused of using Flock cameras to track his former girlfriend’s activities. Brown would later be arrested and sentenced to five years’ probation on charges of accessing a computer or electronic device without authority and misdemeanor stalking.
In North Carolina, police officer Elizabeth Snowman reportedly used Flock camera systems to track her boyfriend’s ex-wife. She, too, would later be arrested and charged with accessing a computer or electronic device without authority.
This repeated systemic misuse across multiple states has shown the gross negligence of people whom we are supposed to trust with upholding the law and is one of the reasons why we cannot trust this technology in our neighborhoods.
Whether it is the people operating the technology or the technology itself, it is clear that there are far too many issues to consider when talking about Flock cameras.
Many state and federal officials agree with this statement as well, raising concerns about the technology. Newly elected Maine Sen. Troy Jackson said if allowed to vote for a Flock ban, he would do it. Jackson stated, “We don’t know what else they’re using the data for. I don’t like that, and I would vote against it. I think we have to rein in big tech on a bunch of this stuff.”
This technology has raised many red flags across the state and has pushed cities such as South Portland to cancel their contract with Flock and remove all existing cameras from the area. Furthermore, the town of Fryeburg’s select board unanimously voted against the funding of Flock cameras and is going so far as to seek a permanent ban on the technology. During public comment, one resident described the technology as “Surveillance on everyone for a minority that might be stepping out of line.”
It’s worth noting that Flock cameras have definitely proved useful in many cases. In Centerville, Ohio, police used Flock technologies to track down a suspected armed robber in a case they claim had “few leads.” Centerville police used these technologies to track a car connected to another robbery a few towns over, later backtracking and using the information to find a suspect.
While I think that is certainly noteworthy and important in showing that these technologies have provided a public service, unfortunately, it does not negate the numerous cases where these technologies have failed us.
At the end of the day, the repeated misuse of this technology has shown the dangers it can pose to society. If we cannot trust the people using the technology or the companies providing it, we cannot trust the technology itself. It is for these reasons that we must do everything in our power to keep ALPRs and Flock cameras out of our state and neighborhoods.

title: Nvidia investigates whether CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by Chinese spy with whom he had an affair
text:
(AP) - Nvidia is opening an investigation into reports that CEO Jensen Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort,” the company’s board of directors said Sunday.
The announcement came after Huang acknowledged to the board that he had been intimate with a business executive whom, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for Beijing.
In a letter to Nvidia employees obtained by The Associated Press, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologized to his family and colleagues. He said he took “full responsibility” for his actions.
“Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life,” Huang wrote. “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility.”
Nvidia’s board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information. Huang “fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it,” the board said.
Huang, 63, will remain CEO during the investigation.
“Today’s news will not slow Nvidia,” company spokesperson John Rizzo said in a statement. “Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption.”
Nvidia has become a central player in the global race to develop artificial intelligence, with its chips powering many of the data centers and computing systems used to train and run AI models. Its advanced processors have also been a focus of U.S. export restrictions aimed at limiting China’s access to cutting-edge semiconductor technology.
The Times reported last month that U.S. intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and chip buyer, and determined that she was feeding information directly to Beijing. The two are not related, according to the Times.
Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.
The Nvidia CEO’s letter to employees did not name Alice Huang or address her apparent ties to Beijing. He did, however, refer to the national security concerns raised in news reports and said he supported the board’s investigation and would cooperate fully.
“I love our country and our company,” Jensen Huang said. “I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security.”
President Donald Trump said Sunday he hasn’t spoken to Huang about the latest development and praised him. “I hope everything’s fine then. He’s done such an incredible job,” Trump said, speaking to reporters before returning to the White House.
Asked whether he wished he had acted on intelligence when he was briefed about spying, Trump again praised Huang: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. He’s done an amazing job for our country.”
As to whether he’d take the CEO with him on his trip to Asia next week, Trump said he was open to it.
“I don’t know, but I’d certainly take him,” he said of Huang, who serves on the president’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday as he was departing the U.S. for a G7 meeting in Paris that he could not address the situation with Huang.
“I just can’t comment because of the nature of it,” he told reporters. “And I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia.”
Nvidia, the world’s most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street’s earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI’s best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.
___
Associated Press writer Michelle L. Price contributed to this report from West Palm Beach, Florida.

title: Neither voters nor Trump to blame for Collins’ loss
text:
Sen. Susan Collins now laments that she lost the election despite breaking with Trump, notably by voting once for impeachment. “It is never enough,” she is quoted as saying, offering that voters wanted tirades instead of results.
I fear that Sen. Collins is naive, in addition to calculating, as it seems obvious to voters like me that she and other Republican members of Congress have appeased Trump at our expense.
Collins voted more funding for ICE, despite its masked agents shooting and killing truly innocent people on our streets and terrifying thousands or millions of others. She voted to facilitate the passage of a bill cutting needed medical care and food to the poor, and driving our nearby hospital services to close. Collins provided key votes confirming judges who restrict women’s rights and empower one-person rule. And she voted to confirm the distorted and ill-informed Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. as head of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
How many more reasons do we need? Dare I use her campaign slogan? Thank you, Susan.
Tom Bradley
Portland

title: Homebuying in America: How a VA loan helped one Black veteran build wealth on her own terms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Homebuying in America: How a VA loan helped one Black veteran build wealth on her own terms
Gabrielle Pickens wasn’t thinking about homeownership until her daughter, Lily, was born in 2021. That moment changed everything. The single Black mother started thinking less about “someday” and more about what kind of stability she could build right now.
That’s when she turned to a benefit she earned during her seven years in the Navy: the VA loan. With competitive interest rates, no down payment requirement, and no private mortgage insurance (PMI), homeownership suddenly felt possible in a way it never had before. For her, becoming a homeowner was especially meaningful, given her credit challenges and the ongoing struggles she knew Black families can face in accessing homeownership.
“It’s either you’re a victim or a victor in your story,” she says. “What are you going to be?”
Pickens chose to be a victor. Four years later, after using a VA loan and rebuilding her credit, she stepped into her sunlit, two-bedroom, two-bath home with high ceilings and a spacious yard in the Chicago suburbs.
“I can only control what I do,” Pickens says. “I can’t beat the system of oppression. This is a group project.”
Setting the scene on homebuying
Before Pickens could take advantage of her VA loan benefits, she first had to improve her credit score. At the time, it was in the low 500s.
On average, Black Americans have lower credit scores than white Americans, shaped in part by long-standing gaps in access to wealth-building opportunities. Pickens thought her score would hold her back from homeownership, but her mindset changed when she attended a workshop through the Neighborhood Assistance Corporation of America, a nonprofit housing counseling and community advocacy organization. Pickens was surprised to meet many other people with credit challenges.
“There are so many ways that we end up with bad credit,” she says. “Nobody wakes up and says, ‘You know what? I’m about to mess my credit up.’ Life happens.”
Behind her homebuying experience
Working with a housing counselor, Pickens reviewed her finances every few months, paid down debt, corrected errors on her credit report, and built healthier credit habits. The effort paid off. Over roughly 18 months, Pickens increased her credit score from the low 500s to around 720 and saved $12,000 toward her home purchase.
Without the VA loan’s no-down-payment feature, Pickens says she likely would have needed years longer to save enough money to buy a home. The 6.125% interest rate she landed fit comfortably within her budget, and she paid only $2,000 in closing costs. As a disabled veteran, she also qualifies for a property tax exemption that helps keep her monthly housing costs low.
“I love it,” Pickens says. “I’m grateful for my mortgage rate and not being cash-strapped and trying to live above my means. A $1,000 mortgage for a two-bed, two-bath home in the suburbs? I’ll take it.”
An expert's take
Government-backed VA and FHA loans are critical for Black homebuyers because their low thresholds help open the door to homeownership. But as Andre Perry, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a nonprofit public policy organization based in Washington, D.C., stresses, more products such as these are needed to support Black homeownership.
Perry highlights programs with small or no down payment requirements and credit models that consider a person’s rent payment history. He also points to Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs) designed to expand access for historically underserved communities with lower mortgage rates or down payment assistance. While the Federal Housing Finance Agency directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to end SPCPs in March 2025, the programs weren’t entirely eliminated. Some lenders, especially larger ones, still offer them.
“These are the kind of innovations Black people need,” he says. “There are many people with incomes. They clearly are renting month-to-month, so they can have a mortgage. But they simply do not have the kind of product that enables them to get in the door. No pun intended.”
What this means for you
The median wealth of Black families is about a quarter of a million dollars lower than that of a median white family, making homeownership an especially important tool for narrowing wealth gaps. As home values rise and equity grows, a house can become a financial legacy for the next generation.
“This experience has given me the confidence to make other large purchases and take control of my wealth journey,” says Pickens. “The sky is the limit. It took me 35 years to buy my first home. It won’t take me 35 years to buy my second.”
While VA, FHA, and low- and no-down-payment loans can open the door to homeownership, they also come with a reality that’s often overlooked: buyers start with little or no equity. Because of how mortgage payments are structured, it can take time to build meaningful equity. Rising home prices often do most of the early “work” of increasing a homeowner’s wealth. But that also means there’s risk. If someone buys a home and then the market turns, home values could drop, leaving homeowners with an underwater mortgage, which means owing more than the home is worth.
Pickens is well aware of that risk and is approaching homeownership with a long-term mindset. She plans to make extra principal payments to pay down her mortgage faster. She is also eyeing strategic home renovations that can increase her home’s value over time.
“I know equity is coming. It doesn’t have to be today. I’m in it for the long haul.”
Her homeownership dream
For Pickens, buying a home wasn’t just about replacing rent with a mortgage payment. It was an investment in her future and a way to leave a legacy for Lily. Growing up on the South Side of Chicago, her home now gives her something different: fresh air, peace, quiet, and room to breathe. If she could distill her homeownership journey into a single message, it would read like a love letter to Lily.
“Go for what you want, girlfriend,” Pickens says. “With this house, Mommy did her best to get us here. You take it further than me. Don’t stop here. This is just the beginning. My ceiling is your floor.”

title: Police: Gunman who killed at least 6 people in Polish city square dies in hospital
text:
Police: Gunman who killed at least 6 people in Polish city square dies in hospital
The 24-year-old with far-right views who killed six people and wounded 15 others in a shooting in a Polish city square died in the hospital Monday, police said.
The attacker, wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into the Main Square in Krakow’s Old Town and opened fire. The location is a major tourist destination in Poland’s second-largest city, and several foreigners were among the dead and wounded.
Police said the man — who has not yet been officially named — initially continued firing even after he was wounded by police officers. He had been in critical condition since the attack and had been operated on multiple times.
Related video: Italian tourist recalls fleeing gunfire in Kraków
He died at 4:30 a.m. in the hospital, authorities said.
“We are first of all investigating if he was inspired by anyone, if someone helped him,” Eryk Stasielak from the Krakow branch of the national prosecutor's office told the AP. “We have secured his electronic devices and we will try to open them and get to the contents.”
Stasielak said prosecutors were also trying to understand how the attacker was able to come into possession of so many weapons and so much ammunition. He said it was too early to comment on the ideology of the man and several avenues were being investigated. Autopsies of the victims were being conducted starting Monday, he said.
Four women and two men were killed in the shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, authorities said. A man from the U.K. and a woman from Austria were also among the dead.
Authorities said on Monday morning that all wounded were in stable condition. The police officer who ultimately stopped the attacker remains in a serious state.
Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.
Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.
On Sunday night, mourners laid candles and flowers alongside the bullet holes in Krakow after the city’s central square turned into a site of bloodshed and grief.
“I come here so as not to get caught up in a spiral of fear and anxiety,” resident Maciej Sikorski told The Associated Press from the square. “In a situation like this, it’s all too easy to stop living — to start being afraid instead, and just vegetate. That is something I really want to avoid.”
Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act “constituting a terrorist offense.”

title: What is the 'Protect College Sports Act' and why does it face an uphill battle in the House?
text:
What is the 'Protect College Sports Act' and why does it face an uphill battle in the House?
A bipartisan Senate bill addressing college athlete payments and Olympic sports protections faces opposition in the House during Congress's lame-duck session.
What is the 'Protect College Sports Act' and why does it face an uphill battle in the House?
A bipartisan Senate bill addressing college athlete payments and Olympic sports protections faces opposition in the House during Congress's lame-duck session.
Congress returned to Capitol Hill today as lawmakers prepare to debate a bill aimed at regulating college sports.
What is the Protect College Sports Act?
The Protect College Sports Act, which passed the Senate with overwhelming bipartisan support, 77-22, would establish federal regulations for payments to college athletes for their name, image, and likeness, as well as set limits on how often athletes can transfer schools.
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Washington, negotiated the bill. Supporters of the legislation say it aims to reduce constant litigation and uncertainty across college sports. They also argue that without this legislation, schools under pressure to pay athletes in revenue-generating sports like football and basketball could cause smaller sports, which feed the Olympic pipeline, to fade.
Critics, however, argue the bill does not do enough to protect athletes or address the large sums of money flowing to coaches, colleges, and conferences.
Could the bill pass in the House?
The bill faces an uphill battle in the House, with nearly two months left in this session of Congress. The question now is whether Democrats, who mostly oppose the bill, will find any reason to support it during this lame-duck session.
If the bill does not pass the House, lawmakers will have to start over in the next session of Congress.

title: Patriots’ stars struggle in brutal loss to Packers
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Patriots coach Mike Vrabel underlined a universal truth about the NFL following his team’s lethargic 45-27 loss to Green Bay: If your team’s best players don’t perform well, your chances of winning typically evaporate.
New England’s best players — quarterback Drake Maye and cornerback Christian Gonzalez — had performances that rank among the worst of their career.
“We expect a lot more,” Vrabel said.
Maye threw three interceptions for the second time this season, two leading to 14 points for the Packers. He threw just one pick in his previous four games. He’s now tied with the Chargers’ Justin Herbert with an NFL-worst 11 INTs.
Gonzalez had just as bad a night. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, the cornerback gave up seven catches for 105 yards to Matthew Golden and three catches for 82 yards to Christian Watson. It made Gonzalez the only defender since at least 2018 to allow more than 80 yards receiving to two players in the same game.
“Christian had a few plays I’m sure that he’d like to have back,” Vrabel said. “We have high expectations for him, and he certainly does, too. So, I think it’s about answering the challenge this week and then coming back.”
What’s clear is that the team needs both players to course correct quickly as injuries throughout the roster continue to pile and a three-week run of games against Buffalo, Minnesota and Kansas City is less than a month away.
It has put even more emphasis on a matchup with the Detroit Lions on Sunday in Germany, the Patriots’ final game before their bye week. Lose, and they’ll fall to 5-5 and leave little room for error down the stretch.
“We’ve got to bounce back and know that there’s still some games left and we’re battling,” Maye said. “We’ve got to battle. I think that’s it.”
What’s working
Not a lot. But the Patriots did go 2 for 2 in the red zone. Still, this season they’ve converted on just 14 of 24 (58.3%) of their chances inside the 20.
What needs help
The run game. New England’s 94 yards rushing were its second fewest of the season and the second time in three games the Patriots failed to run for at least 100 yards
Stock up
WR DeMario Douglas. The receiver did his part to try to keep the offense moving, catching five passes for a season-high 102 yards.
Stock down
The offensive line. Maye was sacked a season-high four times. While the O-line came in dealing with injuries and had a few more Sunday, it’s something that must be cleaned up if the offense is going to get back on track this week.
Injuries
The biggest concern is running back Rhamondre Stevenson, who was able to jog off the field late in the third quarter, but it was announced later he suffered a knee injury. … Cornerback Carlton Davis III also suffered a knee injury in the second quarter. … In addition, left guard Ben Brown (knee) limped off a few plays after Davis late in the second quarter. … Special teamer Brenden Schooler also aggravated a hamstring injury. … Left tackle Will Campbell walked off with a knee injury in the fourth quarter.
Key number
5 — Number of teams the Patriots will face over their last eight games that currently have winning records.
Next steps
The Patriots head to Munich, Germany, on Wednesday to begin preparations for a matchup with the Lions at FC Bayern Munich Arena, home to the Bundesliga soccer team.

title: Enough about Sen. Margaret Chase Smith
text:
In a recent New York Times article, Senator Susan Collins compared herself to former Senator Margaret Chase Smith, saying they had both “taken a lot of tough votes.” And that she (Collins) had “stood up for what I believe in.”
The article ends with a quote from Collins, “I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment.”
Wrong. Sen. Margaret Chase Smith is remembered for a brave and principled stand against Joseph McCarthy’s “Red Scare.” Collins will be remembered as a calculating politician who carefully chose her “battles” in order to maintain a false reputation as a moderate in order to remain in power.
Collins had an opportunity, in her final term, to earn a “Margaret Chase Smith moment.” Collins knew what Trump and the MAGA culture he fostered was all about. She knew about the greed and corruption. Trump’s pardoning of the Jan. 6 criminals alone should have made that obvious.
Collins blames voter backlash against Trump for her loss. But it’s her appeasement to Trump that was the cause. If she had truly embraced Sen. Smith’s courage and stood for what was right, she might have won; Maine people admire courage.
John Gold
Saco

title: Gold Scam Targeting Maine Seniors Ends With Nine-year Sentence For Indian National
text:
An Indian National has been sentenced in Maine for an elaborate scam that targeted residents of several states.
Indian National Sentenced in Maine for Multi-State Gold Scam
We've reported on this type of scam before, in which criminals prey on people's insecurities about their savings and investments.
The U.S. Attorney for Maine says Prakashkumar Prajapati, 47, was in a Maine courtroom last week after pleading guilty to conspiring to commit wire fraud.
READ MORE: Avoid These 16 Crimes That Can Happen to Anyone
Prajapati is sentenced to nine years in prison and ordered to pay $1,897,386 in restitution.
Court records state that Prajapati worked with others in a multi-state scheme to defraud at least eight victims in five states, including Maine.
Maine Victim Instructed to Buy Gold and Give It to a Fake Government Employee
The scam begins with victims receiving calls from people posing as government officials.
These imposters instruct the victims to withdraw cash from their accounts and buy gold with it, which the 'government' will hold for safekeeping.
The callers then tell victims that a government agent will meet with them so they can hand over the cash and the gold.
Prajapati's role in the scam was to direct his co-defendant, Bharat Awasarmol, to meet with victims to take their gold and money.
Awasarmol was intercepted when FBI agents caught him accepting a package from a victim in Maine.
That victim told authorities the caller had posed as a Federal Trade Commission employee.
Maine Courts Sentence an Indian National For a Multi-State Scam Targeting Elderly Mainers
In all, the conspiracy targeted victims in Maine, New Hampshire, New York, New Jersey, and Virginia.
Prajapati caused $1,897,386 in losses to his victims, money he has been ordered to repay.
Awasarmol pleaded guilty in December 2025 and faces up to 20 years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for wire fraud conspiracy, and up to five years in prison and a fine of up to $250,000 for making a false statement.

title: This walking club for seniors calls members ‘Golden G.O.A.T.s.’
text:
GEORGETOWN COUNTY, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A walking club for seniors in South Carolina calls itself the “Golden G.O.A.T.s.”
The goal of the club is to stay fit and have fun. Members walk up to three miles three days a week.
Member joined to walk and be around people
“I’ve always enjoyed walking. I wanted to be able to be among people because I like people,” Virginia Holladay, a member of the group, said.
She addressed the unique name for the members.
“You know — you don’t want to be called an old goat. I think it’s a healthy benefit for us,” she said.
Camaraderie along with cardio
Aging Untold host Amy O’Rourke said the “camaraderie” is as important as the cardio.
“Golden G.O.A.T.s walking together hit me on so many levels. It’s the camaraderie of the interaction between all of them. It’s being in nature and feeling the ground and getting that fabulous air, and then all the exercise that they’re getting. They’re moving their body, so on every single level they’re hitting all the points that you want to hit,” O’Rourke said.
‘Iron G.O.A.T.’ title earned at nearly 600 miles
John Kester walked nearly 600 miles with the group and earned the title “Iron G.O.A.T.”
He said he likes the social aspect of the group.
“Talks continuously while we’re walking. We’ve gotten to learn about each other — so it’s a good social get-together,” Kester said.
O’Rourke also spoke about goals.
“When I think about having a goal and having that purpose, I think of how excited I would be, and I think others would be, having that goal and then accomplishing it, and then setting up the next one and having an inner purpose is so meaningful,” O’Rourke said.
