title: A New Format for the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall
text:
Athlete of the Fall Is Here With a New Large and Small School Format
Nine weeks of Athlete of the Week are complete, but there is still one major piece of the fall sports season left.
Now it is time to look at the entire body of work.
Nominations are officially open for the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall, and this year the awards will have a new format designed to better reflect the different sizes of athletic programs across the area.
Instead of crowning one boys winner and one girls winner, there will be four Athlete of the Fall awards:
Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall
Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall
Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall
Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall
How the School Divisions Will Work
The Athlete of the Fall divisions will not follow individual MPA sport classifications.
Instead, schools are being separated based on the overall size and participation level of their athletic programs.
The Large School Division will include:
Presque Isle
Caribou
Houlton
Fort Kent
All other Aroostook County schools covered during the fall season will compete in the Small School Division.
The goal is to create more balanced comparisons while still recognizing the very best seasons from across the County.
Nominations Will Be Organized by School, Not by Sport
Athlete of the Fall is an overall fall sports award, so athletes from soccer, cross country, golf and other eligible fall sports will all be considered together within their division.
Nominations will be organized by school, making it easier to see the top candidates from across the area.
There is also no one-athlete-per-school limit.
If a school has multiple athletes who put together exceptional seasons, they can all be nominated and considered for the final ballot.
A standout soccer player and a championship-level cross country runner from the same school should both have an opportunity to be recognized.
This Award Is About the Entire Season
Athlete of the Fall is different from Athlete of the Week.
A single huge game can make someone a strong weekly candidate. For this award, we are looking at everything an athlete accomplished from the beginning of the fall through the postseason.
That includes:
Season-long production and consistency, postseason performances, championships and major meet results, individual milestones, importance to the team, leadership, sportsmanship and overall impact.
An athlete does not need to have won Athlete of the Week to be nominated or selected as an Athlete of the Fall finalist.
Likewise, an Athlete of the Week victory does not automatically guarantee a spot on the final ballot.
This is a fresh evaluation of the complete fall season.
What to Include With Your Nomination
Coaches, athletic directors, parents, teammates, fans and community members are encouraged to submit nominations.
Please include:
The athlete's name
School
Sport
Season statistics or accomplishments
Postseason or championship performances
Awards, milestones or other notable achievements
Why you believe they deserve Athlete of the Fall consideration
The more information provided, the stronger the nomination can be when the final ballots are built.
Nominations Close Thursday at 5 P.M.
Athlete of the Fall nominations will remain open through Thursday, November 12 at 5 p.m.
Once nominations close, the top candidates will be selected for each of the four divisions and voting will begin shortly afterward.
That means we will have separate ballots for:
Large School Boys
Large School Girls
Small School Boys
Small School Girls
Nine weeks of weekly voting gave us a chance to recognize incredible individual performances.
Now we get to answer a bigger question.
Who put together the best complete fall seasons in Aroostook County?
Send in your nominations before Thursday at 5 p.m.

title: The system worked in Democrats’ favor. Now what?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Michael Conathan is a former U.S. Senate staffer, a climate and ocean policy expert and served as lead consultant for Maine’s Blue Economy Task Force. He lives in South Portland.
Last Tuesday, years of declining faith in the foundations of American government came to a head. In the face of real fear about the rise of fascism and the death of democracy, the country demonstrated the strength of our founders’ vision.
The blue wave that so many Democrats rode to victories in the midterm elections reminded us that votes still matter. That the collective is more powerful than the billions of dollars spent to drown us out. And that the overwhelming majority of our fellow citizens have had it with the bloviation and excess of the MAGA movement.
Democrats across Maine and around the country earned this historic victory. We built our case, each in our own way, to reach our own audience. The resulting win is not for the punditry or the donor class or the party machine. It’s for everyone who felt forsaken or duped. Everyone who repudiated the political sleight of hand that told us transgender kids in sports is a bigger problem than tax breaks for billionaires. Everyone who despaired as our neighbors were kidnapped and killed by government-sanctioned goon squads in the streets of Minnesota, Maine and Texas.
As the election’s euphoria and afterglow fades to examination and action, Democrats must consider what to prioritize. A wave of this magnitude constitutes a mandate. But a mandate for what?
On Donald Trump’s watch, Republicans made the mistake of taking their newfound voters for granted, assuming those who seized on his pledges of “Make Eggs Cheap Again” and “No New Wars” would join the GOP camp forever. They redrew districts that backfired spectacularly after discarding those promises. Ultimately, their red hubris led them into the path of an overwhelming blue tide.
Democrats should learn from Republican mistakes. As much as this election constituted an endorsement of progressive policies, it was first and foremost a course correction. The mad captain steering our country’s ship seized the wheel and spun us wildly off the chart. Voters have now given us a chance to straighten out and avoid the rocky shoals ahead.
As Democrats now take the controls in Washington and with an even greater majority in Augusta, we should remember that when at the helm of a ship it’s easy to oversteer. To get back on course, you at first turn sharply, then must anticipate the swing of the bow and straighten out before the wind, currents and tide push you too far in the other direction.
This election has brought us from one extreme back to the middle, not to its polar opposite. Republican strongholds in the South and Midwest have not suddenly become bastions of socialism, and they will not tolerate what they perceive to be the imposition of extreme progressive values. The same goes for many Maine districts that flipped blue last week.
An opportunity now exists to translate these wins into lasting, progressive policy change. But doing so will require compromise. Coalition building. Really listening to what voters want, what they fear and how they want to live.
Democrats will leverage their majority to pursue a bold agenda including national priorities such as universal health and childcare, equitable tax reform, climate action, civil rights and rational immigration policy, empathetic foreign policy and diplomacy.
Here in Maine, they will back Governor-elect Hannah Pingree’s stated priorities of housing, healthcare and strong communities. The first order of business is outlining specific actions to achieve those goals.
Then we must take time with independents and Republicans who voted blue. Welcome them the way we aspire to welcome immigrant neighbors. Don’t force them to assimilate immediately. Build bridges. Share meals. Listen. Hear their rationale. And, where we can find alignment, make changes and concessions that reflect their concerns.
We won’t all agree, and they won’t all stay. But this is the way to create a coalition with the staying power capable of creating lasting impact. This is critical, because accomplishing these goals will take time.
Politics is loud and flashy and pointed. But at its core, it exists to do the business of governing by making policy. Creating thoughtful, durable policy is quiet and slow and methodical. And, yes, boring. Which is exactly how the system was designed.
Winning is euphoric, and the victors should celebrate. Policymaking is tedious, and we have to do it anyway. Last week, the system functioned as designed. The guardrails held. The people have spoken.
Now the real work begins.

title: Adoptive and Foster Families of Maine sets Nov. 13 deadline for Christmas gift sign-ups
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Families who are fostering, adopting or raising a relative’s child have until Friday, Nov. 13, to sign up for help with Christmas gifts from Adoptive and Foster Families of Maine.
The organization is asking community members to sponsor gifts for children. Reporter Megan Waceken said the need is growing this year.
Need grows statewide and in Aroostook County
For nearly 30 years, Adoptive and Foster Families of Maine has connected the families it works with to community sponsors who provide gifts for Christmas morning.
Last year, the program provided gifts for about 1,400 children statewide. Resource Family Specialist Sarah Hatt expects closer to 2,000 this year, or about 600 more children.
In Aroostook County, the program provided around 125 gifts last year for children in foster, adoptive or kinship care, Hatt said. This year, the program is already at 140 gifts, and she expects the number to rise.
“A lot of them are oftentimes surprised at the amount of gifts or the quality of the gifts that sponsors will give to their children, and the kids are really happy,” Hatt said.
How to sign up
Families fill out a form listing their children’s clothing sizes and Christmas wishes.
“It asks for things that they’re hoping for Christmas, and ask for their favorite color, just different things like that so that sponsors can kind of feel like they’re getting to know them a little bit,” Hatt said.
Families who miss the Nov. 13 deadline can still sign up to be put on a wait list.
“If we can fill the need, we’ll certainly do it,” Hatt said.
Gift drop-off
Gift drop-off is Saturday, Nov. 21, from 9 a.m. to noon in the University of Maine at Presque Isle Campus Center. The organization then delivers the gifts to families in time to be opened on Christmas.
“A lot of the parents will contact us after and just we hear many positive things,” Hatt said. “They say how thankful they are for our program and how thankful they are for the sponsors and the community members that step up to help.”
The program is looking for sponsors now. If you’d like to become a sponsor you can contact Hatt at sarah@affm.net. Information on how to get involved is available on the organization’s website at affm.net/

title: Senate's first major action since midterms: Weighing sweeping energy legislation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Senate's first major action since midterm elections: Weighing sweeping energy legislation
The Senate on Monday is set to take up bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for data centers and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote on the bill, which senators and the president have pushed as a way to meet growing demand for electricity and other forms of energy that face yearslong delays in getting to the grid.
The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to get big energy projects started — both for clean energy and fossil fuel projects — and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over artificial intelligence data centers and rising electricity costs helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the massive, energy-hungry structures.
Trump urged senators to vote for it, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a social media post on Sunday. The bill will “ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote.
Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and in the oil and gas sector also support the bill.
However, many environmental organizations have panned the deal because they say it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals.
Midterm results could complicate bill's passage in lame-duck session
While the bill has received bipartisan support, the Democrats' sweeping midterm win could complicate its passage.
Some Democrats say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that produces needed clean energy but limits expansion of oil, natural gas and mining. Some critics have said the permitting bill as proposed could lead to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a “reckless” build-out of data centers powered by natural gas.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat who is expected to become speaker in January, criticized the bill last week, with his office saying it “falls short” in a number of areas.
Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, have strongly opposed the measure in recent days, citing concerns about its limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and Endangered Species Act.
The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to share its perspective before a project is approved, but supporters of an overhaul say that causes yearslong delays in federal permitting.
The bill's four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — released a detailed set of amendments Saturday designed to bolster support for the legislation.
The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years.
"Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” said Heinrich.
Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, and he particularly dislikes offshore wind. His administration has been paying energy companies to walk away from offshore wind projects under development. It has spent nearly $4 billion on such settlements.
Whitehouse said a provision in the permitting bill would end the buyouts, so the administration will no longer be able to use public money to pay clean energy developers to relinquish wind energy leases and oblige them to invest in fossil fuels instead.
Democrats are optimistic the bill will pass both chambers
At a press conference with Heinrich on Monday, Whitehouse said the bill is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations. And we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” next year.
Whitehouse said Trump's support should help the bill move toward a vote in the House.
Heinrich said he worked hard to incorporate feedback from tribal leaders on the initial proposal, adding that the amended version requires federal agencies to consult with tribes on projects that affect important cultural sites.
Sponsors also extended the window for objections to agency reports and strengthened opportunities for states to weigh in, Heinrich said.
If passed, he said, the bill will save households billions on electricity costs, create jobs, cut emissions and force big corporations to pay their full share for data centers instead of pushing energy costs on consumers.
Industry leaders are advocating for the bill's passage, including leaders of the American Clean Power Association, which represents clean energy developers, and the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group.
But Bradley Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it would be a “terrible mistake” to proceed with the bill in the waning days of the current Congress.
While changes announced Saturday address a few concerns, the bill also comes with a gauntlet of new — and at times conflicting — rules, Campbell said. He said the bill maintains a veneer of federal safeguards while in fact stripping the power of federal agencies, states, tribes and communities to identify and prevent serious harm to health and the environment.
Sara Amundson, president of the Humane World Action Fund, said the bill weakens the scientific foundation of the Endangered Species Act and could create new opportunities to exclude needed wildlife protections.
“This proposed rewrite of the ‘best available science’ standard could give agencies new grounds to unfairly dismiss credible research, including science showing that stronger protections are needed for species at risk," she said, urging lawmakers to drop the provision or oppose the bill.

title: Who’s going to run Hannah Pingree’s government? We have an early idea.
text:
AUGUSTA — Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree has no time to lose.
With less than 60 days until her inauguration, she’s got to make dozens of hires — decisions that will shape the course of her administration. An array of officials from the Gov. Janet Mills era have already announced over the past few months their plans to step down and let new faces join the Pingree administration.
We already know some of the key figures involved in staffing Pingree’s team. Pingree said she will announce the rest of the transition staff Tuesday morning during a news conference in Augusta.
The staffers we already know about have resumes that include working for both Democratic and Republican officials. They have ties to the Wabanaki Alliance, Planned Parenthood and other groups. They signify both Pingree’s pragmatism and — particularly on the issue of tribal sovereignty — her efforts to pivot away from Mills on certain fronts.
Pingree, 50, said after Tuesday’s election victory that she is now accepting applications on a rolling basis to serve in her administration. She and Mills had lunch Friday at the Blaine House after meeting with reporters in the morning to say how they are working together on the transition.
Without referring to former Gov. Paul LePage by name, Mills said “this is quite different than eight years ago,” alluding to less cooperation when she took over from the Republican.
It is too soon to speculate on who may lead certain departments. Pingree said she has been meeting with current agency heads and will interview or accept resumes for every Cabinet position. Asked about any plans to restructure or create new offices, she said she is open to “better ways to do things” and that she met a few weeks ago with former Gov. Ken Curtis, a Democrat who in 1972 made a major reorganization by consolidating 150 independent agencies into 16 departments.
Pingree is set to be sworn in on Jan. 6. Ahead of the inauguration, here are a few names of transition team and campaign staffers who will play key roles.
LEADING THE TRANSITION
The co-chairs of Pingree’s transition team are two people familiar to those who have closely followed the State House over the years.
Maulian Bryant is a member of the Penobscot Nation and the executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance, which represents the four Native American tribes in Maine and advocates for tribal sovereignty legislation that Mills vetoed in 2023. Although Mills and leaders of the tribes made progress on certain policy changes toward the end of her tenure, Pingree has said she will sign the sweeping proposal within 100 days that Mills blocked to allow the tribes to benefit from federal laws that do not currently apply to them.
Bryant was previously the Penobscot Nation ambassador to the state and remains a member of the tribal council and the Maine Climate Council.
Her transition team co-chair is Roger Katz, a former Augusta mayor who served as a Republican state senator from 2010-18. Katz, a lawyer, chairs the University of Maine System board of trustees. He is a moderate who has criticized his party’s more hardline figures like President Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage.
Katz and Pingree launched a political talk show together in 2014 called “The Maine Event” that aired on public television.
“Roger Katz and Maulian Bryant bring the experience and judgment I want at the table as we build this administration,” Pingree said in a statement. “They will be leading a group of volunteers from across Maine who will help me find leaders who put results first and reflect the best of Maine: integrity, accountability, public service and shared optimism about improving the lives of Maine people.”
MORE FAMILIAR FACES
Scott Ogden and Karen Geraghty will direct Pingree’s professional staff transition, focusing on more of the behind-the-scenes work that goes into getting a new administration up and running.
Ogden previously served as a spokesperson and deputy chief of staff to Mills, as well as an aide to U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine; former U.S. Sen. Olympia Snowe, R-Maine; and to U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, the 1st District Democrat. Ogden will coordinate personnel decisions, “legislative and policy agenda development” and “day-to-day operations,” according to a Pingree news release.
Geraghty previously led philanthropic efforts at Planned Parenthood of Northern New England and served as a Portland mayor and city councilor. She will direct planning of the inauguration.
Pingree’s team has not yet confirmed the location of the Jan. 6 inauguration, as the aging Augusta Civic Center that has hosted past inaugurations will be closed for renovation work.
OTHER PINGREE STAFFERS
It is not unheard of for campaign staffers to move into official roles if a candidate wins office. Pingree’s campaign manager, Jonny Asen, is one name to watch given his extensive resume.
Asen, who works in government relations and political consulting for the law firm Bernstein Shur, worked under former President Barack Obama for five years, rising to the rank of chief of staff for the White House’s legislative affairs director.
Asen also served as senior adviser to former Maine House Speaker Mark Eves, D-North Berwick, who led the state House of Representatives from 2012-16, and as chief of staff to Freeport Democrat Sara Gideon, who led the Maine House from 2016-20. Asen was then senior adviser for the Maine operation of former Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign. Harris won Maine handily while losing the 2nd Congressional District to Trump.
It is unclear how many campaign staff will stay on to work for Pingree’s administration, such as deputy campaign manager Ellie Edgell, who previously worked on campaigns in Michigan for figures such as U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
It is also not yet known who will serve as Pingree’s chief spokesperson. Pingree’s campaign spokesperson, Mary-Erin Casale, will serve in the transition role through the inauguration.
Pingree led Mills’ Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 until launching her gubernatorial campaign last year, so she has plenty of connections in that office who may continue to serve in her gubernatorial administration.
As for Mills, the 78-year-old former attorney general who is in her final weeks in office and who made an unsuccessful bid for the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate, she kept it brief Friday when asked what is next for her.
“Well, I have a few irons in the fire,” Mills said, “and I’ll know in January.”

Ranked choice voting counting process underway in Augusta
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Work is underway in Augusta to verify votes cast across Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
Unofficial first-round results show Republican Paul LePage leading Democrat Matt Dunlap. LePage received 49.894% of the vote, just short of a majority, so the state is preparing for a ranked-choice tabulation.
Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said the law requires that the Secretary of State’s office “produce a result for certification that is 50% plus one of the vote at a minimum.”
Dunlap concedes, count still must be certified
LePage leads by about 5,400 votes, and Dunlap has conceded the race. The state still has to complete the count and certify the winner.
Bellows says a change in the outcome is unlikely, but not impossible.
“If the vote verification process uncovered something surprising, for example, if a municipality had misreported the results and it had a statistical impact on the race, flipping the race to Matt Dunlap, and that was confirmed here in the presence of all of the observers and the media, then we would certify the race for Matt Dunlap,” Bellows said.
How the verification works
Workers are checking vote totals against those reported by towns, scanning ballots, and uploading vote records. If neither candidate has a majority after verification, the state will tabulate the next available choices on eliminated candidates’ ballots.
There were more than 6,000 blank ballots and more than 100 votes for an official write-in candidate.
As of Monday evening, ballots have been counted in these counties: Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Kennebec, Oxford, Penobscot, Waldo and Washington.
Campaign representative observes
Lauren LePage, the former governor’s daughter and a campaign representative, is watching the process.
“Yes, everything seems to be going very smoothly. The Secretary of State’s office has been very communicative with everyone in the room. And so, so far everything has been as it’s expected to be,” said Lauren Lepage.
She said her father is already in Washington, taking part in new member orientation for Congress.
Representatives for Dunlap’s campaign did not attend the tabulation proceeding Monday morning. Dunlap’s campaign has been contacted for comment and has not yet responded.
Bellows says the process could take four to five days. The public can watch it live on the Maine Secretary of State’s YouTube page.

title: WATCH: Artemis III crew talks at NASA's Max Power' air show, says 'Our team is ready'
text:
'Our team is ready': Artemis III crew speaks at NASA air show at Kennedy Space Center ahead of summer launch
The rocket is fully stacked, and the Artemis III astronauts are preparing for a summer launch.
“Our mission is going to contribute to such a big goal for the nation,” Mission Specialist Frank Rubio said.
Orlando sister station WESH's Meghan Moriarty spoke with the Artemis III team at NASA's "Max Power" air show Saturday.
Moriarty: What are you most confident in?
Rubio: “You know, the power of the NASA team. Ultimately, we know, like any mission, it's not going to go perfectly, but I'm really confident that our team is ready to deal with any off-nominal situations. I think we can accomplish the goal, which is ultimately to get Artemis IV and V to the surface of the moon.”
Moriarty: How honored are you to be part of a mission that is probably one of the most complicated to date?
Rubio: “Yeah, it's a privilege, right? We work all our lives in the math and engineering fields, and to be able to contribute to a really critical step toward achieving a final goal, it's a huge honor.”
Artemis III Commander Randy Bresnik also spoke with WESH. He highlighted the importance of the mission, saying it's necessary to practice in low Earth orbit ahead of future lunar landings.
Bresnik: “I've been blessed with the best crew, and we get to do the next most important step. It's important to get the SLS and Orion and crews launching again next year so we can have that muscle memory by 2028 when we land people on the moon.”
Artemis III is set to launch in mid-2028.

title: The look and feel of November through midweek
text:
The look and feel of November through midweek
The look and feel of November through midweek
A large upper-level low over northern Quebec will keep our weather unsettled through midweek, with occasional rain and mountain snow showers. Any showers this evening will taper off tonight, but another round is expected late Tuesday into Wednesday. The higher elevations could see some snow, with shower coverage becoming more limited Wednesday afternoon.
Temperatures will gradually cool through the week, returning closer to normal for this time of year. Highs will range from the 40s north to 50s south Tuesday, with most areas in the 40s by Thursday. Friday will be noticeably colder, with highs mainly in the 30s and 40s.
Looking ahead to late week, forecast models continue to disagree on the track of a potential coastal storm. There is growing support for a coastal track, but exactly how close it gets will determine our impacts. The best chance for accumulating snow will be in the White Mountains and higher elevations, with some wet snow possibly reaching the foothills. Along the coast, precipitation would most likely fall as rain. Strongest winds would also likely be near the coast, although confidence in wind impacts remains low for now.
There is still plenty of uncertainty with this system, particularly regarding snowfall amounts and wind. Behind the storm, temperatures should gradually return to more seasonable levels, with drier weather developing heading into next week.

Does Maine count votes for undeclared write-in candidates in state and federal elections?
text:
No.
In state and federal elections, Maine doesn’t count write-in votes for anyone who didn’t file a declaration of candidacy.
Votes for undeclared write-ins are recorded as blanks, but other votes on the ballot remain valid.
Blank votes still count toward the total ballots cast. In Maine’s 2026 2nd Congressional District race, preliminary results showed 123 votes for declared write-ins and 6,017 blanks. Because those votes count toward the total, no candidate reached a majority, requiring a ranked-choice runoff.
Municipal elections have different rules. Towns and cities may require write-in candidates to declare, but even those that do must count undeclared write-ins if no candidate appears on the ballot or a nominee withdraws.
Municipalities without that requirement also must count undeclared write-ins if they outnumber a listed candidate’s votes. Clerks are not required to count votes for fictional or dead people.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

Man accused of driving 100 mph, hitting 3 police cars during high-speed chase
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A North Carolina man faces multiple felony charges after allegedly leading police officers on a high-speed chase, authorities said.
The driver, identified as Devin Valdivia, 25, was arrested Saturday, Nov. 7. He faces 10 charges, including felony fleeing to elude arrest, felony assault on a law enforcement officer and driving while impaired.
Court documents allege Valdivia drove into oncoming traffic on Langtree Road and Statesville Highway, reached speeds of up to 130 mph while fleeing police and hit three police cars
The chase began Saturday night in Iredell County as officers responded to reports of a possibly impaired driver. Police said an officer attempted to pull over Valdivia on Langtree Road, but he fled before driving into oncoming traffic.
Valdivia allegedly hit a Mooresville police car before traveling south on Interstate 77, according to police. He exited at Sam Furr Road, where another crash happened between a police car and his vehicle. Police said Valdivia continued fleeing and drove into oncoming traffic.
He later returned to I-77 and took Exit 28. A short time later, his vehicle was involved in another crash with a third police car. Court documents allege Valdivia drove 100 mph in a 65-mph zone on I-77 and failed to maintain lane control.
Court records stated an officer suffered a fractured bone in his hand when Valdivia hit a police car during the pursuit.
Police said Valdivia eventually jumped from the vehicle and fled on foot before he was arrested. Arrest records state that Valdivia has prior convictions in Lincoln County for assault on a government official and attempted fleeing to elude arrest with a motor vehicle.
He also has a prior conviction for driving while impaired in Gaston County, according to the records.

title: Portland city leaders get first look at $48M relocation plan for Amtrak station
text:
Portland city leaders get first look at $48 million relocation plan for Amtrak station
Should the Amtrak train station in Portland be moved? That's the $48 million question.
The Portland City Council held a workshop Monday evening regarding the proposed relocation of the train station.
The Amtrak Downeaster is a popular mode of transportation for passengers heading from Portland to Boston, or up to Brunswick.
The current transportation center is located at Thompson's Point, along with the Concord Bus Terminal.
"I like where it's located now. It's very convenient. It's right off the highway. I like where it is," said Tammie Packard, who travels by train to Boston every three weeks.
The Northern New England Passenger Rail Authority (NNEPRA) was awarded $48 million in federal funding to relocate the train station along St. John Street, near Northern Light Mercy Hospital.
NNEPRA said the current train station is inefficient, costly and creates delays. The Rail Authority added that if Portland's train station is relocated, trains would no longer have to backtrack to the main line, which will save 15 minutes on every trip.
Falmouth resident Joel Kallich, who commutes to Boston, said he would like to see a train station that harkens back to the former Union Station, which was demolished in 1961 to make way for a strip mall.
But NNEPRA said the project is site-specific and will be closer to the Veterans Memorial Bridge.
"I would prefer it just in that location, but yeah, a lot of the stuff that's there that they tore down is terrible," Kallich said. "Let's clean it up and really make a gateway to the city."
City officials will have to agree with NNEPRA's preferred location, as the Rail Authority said there will not be another project if the current proposal does not go forward. NNEPRA said the $48 million in federal funding it received will not be able to be used for an alternative project or location.

title: FDA adds warning about rare vision loss to popular GLP-1s
text:
FDA adds warning about rare vision loss to popular GLP-1s
The FDA will now require makers of GLP-1s like Ozempic and Zepbound to add a warning to their labels about a rare side effect that can cause vision loss potentially associated with the drugs.
The eye condition, called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, or NAION, leads to sudden and often permanent vision loss. The vision loss happens when not enough blood flows to part of the optic nerve, which carries visual information to the brain.
According to the Food and Drug Administration, NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 receptor agonist products, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other pill-based and injectable drugs. After reviewing available data, the FDA concluded that there is "a potential increased risk of rare NAION events in patients taking GLP-1 RAs."
NAION is rare and typically occurs in people 50 or older, and the causes aren't fully understood. 
Symptoms include "sudden, painless vision loss in one eye" that people may notice upon waking; blurred or missing portions of vision, like blind spots or tunnel vision; distortion of colors; and blurry or hazy spots, the FDA said. Patients should contact their health care professional right away if they have any of these symptoms.
Risk factors for NAION may include smoking, diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea, anemia, and kidney disease.
NAION is not common, including among GLP-1 users. In making its decision, the FDA carried out a meta-analysis of GLP-1 development programs and found a higher rate of NAION in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs. But there were still not many cases: of 134,253 patients reviewed, there were 15 probable NAION events. Ten happened in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs, and five were in patients receiving placebo. There were none in patients who received other, non-GLP-1 RA glucose-lowering medication.
The FDA began looking into the problem after a medical paper was published in 2024 that linked NAION to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Ozempic.
Both Novo Nordisk, the company behind Ozempic and Wegovy, and Eli Lilly, which makes Zepbound, have previously denied any significant relationship between GLP-1s and NAION. Faced with lawsuits, they've pointed out in court that people with diabetes, which GLP-1s target, are at higher risk of blindness and other conditions named in GLP-1 lawsuits to begin with.
The FDA acknowledged those overlapping risk factors make it challenging to interpret reports it receives about adverse events tied to the drugs.
In other countries, including in the EU, U.K., Australia and Japan, some GLP-1 medications carry warnings about the condition.
People concerned about NAION should discuss the risks and benefits of GLP-1s with their healthcare provider. If you think you may have experienced it, you should talk with your doctor about whether to continue taking your GLP-1 RA medication or to stop it, the FDA said.

title: SCOTUS and the high stakes North Dakota case
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) -A Supreme Court case out of North Dakota could have major implications for landowners everywhere. If justices side with federal law over state law, landowners likely would lose any incentive to pursue fair payment when the government takes their land, and they would risk sinking any potential payout into court fees.
When the government takes land, it has to pay the owner. That is called eminent domain, and it is in the Constitution. One pipeline company, working on behalf of the government, low-balled landowners, and the dispute turned into a multi-year legal battle. The landowners won but were left with $380,000 in legal fees.
North Dakota has a state law that says the pipeline company has to pay those legal fees. The federal government says the company does not have to. Bob McNamara argued the case Monday.
“What we’re saying is that when states try to protect private property owners, private companies have to respect those laws. Even private companies wielding the power of eminent domain,” McNamara said.
Justices appeared skeptical of that argument. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson said, “unless Congress says state law is applicable, when you have federal condemnation by any actor, you would have federal law be the applicable rule.”

College Football Playoff doubles up, expands to 24 teams beginning next season
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(AP) - College football will expand its playoff to 24 teams beginning next year in a move that resets decades of tradition surrounding a once all-important regular season and dumps conference championship showdowns that used to be among the sport’s marquee events.
The announcement from the College Football Playoff and ESPN on Monday made official a deal that’s been in the works for months. The network reported it would pay an additional $1.7 billion over five years on top of the original $7.8 billion contract that runs through the 2031 season.
The new format will grant the Power Four conference champions automatic spots and give one more to the best team from the Group of Six. But that slot and the other 19 will be decided by a selection committee that will serve as the latest set of decision makers in college football’s long history of polls and opinions having lasting impacts on teams’ fates.
Beginning next year, around 30% of college football’s 68 power-conference schools will have a chance to play for the title, drawing the CFP closer to the NFL, which allows 43% of its teams into the playoffs. It leaves behind the last vestiges of yesteryear, when between four and eight teams entered December with a legitimate shot to win it all.
It’s a seismic shift that even ESPN conceded comes with some question marks. The network pays billions to televise regular-season games that might — or might not — have more meaning under the new system.
“In all honesty, it’s impossible to know for sure,” ESPN senior vice president Nick Dawson said in a conference call.
The revenue generated from the playoff expansion will presumably make up for the estimated $345 million the Power Four conferences generated in TV money for their title games. ESPN would then not be on the hook for $140 million of the extra money due to cancellation of the title games, the network reported.
How an expanded CFP will work
The top eight seeds will receive first-round byes in the new format and the playoff will start on the second weekend in December, with the first two rounds of games on campus. The traditional Army-Navy game will be played on the first weekend in December, which used to be reserved for conference title games.
Both the Southeastern and Big Ten conferences, whose approval was needed to adopt this change, and their Power Four brethren — the Big 12 and Atlantic Coast Conference — are banking that most of the additional spots will go to their members so their second-tier teams will have new motivation to keep spending big in an era of NIL payments and $50 million football rosters.
“I think it will be healthy for teams like our current situation, building to try to get to that point,” said coach Barry Odom, who is trying to rebuild at Purdue.
The first final for the 24-team playoff remains set for Jan. 24, 2028, in New Orleans. Traditional bowl games will still host the quarterfinal and semifinal rounds.
As for the rest of the bowls, most of them operated or televised by ESPN: “No decisions have been made at this time,” Dawson said.
As part of the expansion, the CFP is requiring Power Four teams to play at least 10 regular-season games against conference foes, other Power Four opponents and Notre Dame. Group of Six teams will have to play 10 games against conference opponents.
In theory, these requirements will keep everyone in the same ballpark when it comes to strength of schedule, which figures to play a huge role in the selection committee’s considerations.
Special treatment vanishes for Notre Dame
Notre Dame didn’t receive any guarantees, the way it did this year when, if it’s ranked in the top 12 by the CFP for what will be the last year of the 12-team postseason, it will get a spot.
Coach Marcus Freeman said he looks at the change as a net positive, in part because a team like his can now presumably afford more than one loss, and in part because of the new scheduling requirements. Notre Dame is one of only two independents left in major college football.
“I don’t want this to be like March Madness and have 60-something teams making the playoff,” he said. “But the more opportunities we have to make the playoff, it helps us.”
The new schedule also guarantees two off weeks during a regular season that will begin the week before Labor Day.
A bigger playoff changes the nature of the college regular season
The move to 24 teams marks the second expansion of the playoff since it began in 2014 as a four-team affair. Right after it moved to 12 in 2024, most thought it would eventually max out at 16, which was the SEC’s preference.
But the Big Ten wanted to go bigger, while the SEC balked at that, concerned about the league title game — a property it invented in 1992 and made billions from over the decades — along with the marketability of CFP games featuring third- and fourth-place finishers in power conferences.
ESPN took care of the money problem. Now, the question is whether fans will embrace an NFL-style free-for-all that could include about one-third of the Power Four’s 68 teams, depending on what happens with Group of Six schools whose role in these big-money power grabs seems to diminish with every move.
It’s the latest change for a sport that, for decades, built its distinct character and generated controversy by leaning on media and coaching polls to hand out national titles.
Like then, critics see a risk in giving more power to a selection committee that hasn’t really mastered four- or 12-team brackets. The exclusion of Florida State in 2023 and Notre Dame last season stand out as the best examples, and the first rankings this season left people scratching their heads again.
Skeptics also view the expanded playoff as another dilution of what is largely seen as one of the most important regular seasons in sports, replacing potential matchups between, say, Alabama and Georgia in an SEC title game with a 13 seed vs. 20 seed game that would pit, say, Kentucky and South Carolina.
Fan reaction “certainly weighed into the decision,” Dawson said.
“Ultimately, we just need to make a spectacular playoff,” he said. “The CFP has a responsibility to our fans, they’re the lifeblood of college football. We owe them to make this great. That really is our intent.”
As Big Ten commissioner Tony Petitti argued from the beginning, a postseason that gives bubble teams hope and keeps others vying for home-field advantage or byes will bring more eyes — not fewer — to the end of a regular season that sometimes boils down to only three or four traditional rivalry games with meaning.
Of course, nobody can be certain how things will play out. The only sure thing is that college football will never look quite the same.
“If they think it’s a good thing for college football, then I’ve got to believe that this is the route we’re headed,” Wisconsin coach Luke Fickell said, “and we’re going to make it a great thing for college football.”

title: 5 fun things to do while you’re in Scarborough
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kristen Lorden DeQuattro is an entertainment and events producer, artist manager and booking agent and hospitality professional.
She has lived in Scarborough for 25 years and is a huge fan of the town. Here are her recommendations:
Where do you like to eat?
In-season, for a date night, I like to go to Shade at the Higgins Beach Inn. The atmosphere is relaxed, the food is yummy, and as a seafood lover, I’m always glad to see one of my favorites — halibut — on the menu. For dessert, their blueberry pie is fantastic.
In the off-season I like Pine Point Grill. The atmosphere is cozy, the seating is comfortable, the food is very good and they have a happy hour during the week, so go early and take advantage of appetizer and drink specials. For breakfasts, Café Luna has been a great addition to Scarborough, especially for a breakfast meeting or if you want to grab an avocado toast and get a little work done away from the home office. It’s comfortable and has a more elevated café menu with delicious smoothies and bowls.
But when I just want a hearty breakfast sandwich, St. Joe’s wins! It’s tiny, absolutely no-frills, just a few seats to sit at, but they serve Carrabassett Coffee Company coffee and the food is great.
Where do you like to drink?
On a beautiful afternoon or evening between early summer and mid-October, I love grabbing a drink at the Black Point Inn and settling into an Adirondack chair on the hill overlooking Ferry Beach. The sunsets are absolutely stunning ,and it’s one of my favorite place to meet friends. On a nice day, if you’re looking for a casual afternoon drink or happy hour destination with a view, The Bait Shed at Pine Point is fun. The deck sits right over the water and it’s a great spot to share a lobster roll and their signature Jones Creek Lemonade. In the off-season and in any weather, I like the bar at Dunstan Tap & Table. The bar is good-sized, the staff is friendly and it has a welcoming vibe. It’s also the kind of place where you almost always run into someone you know. They have a large outdoor fire pit if you enjoy your drinks with Mother Nature, and the food is really good too.
Where do you like to connect with nature?
We are home to some of Maine’s most beautiful beaches like Scarborough Beach, Ferry Beach, Higgins Beach and Pine Point Beach, plus the salt marsh and the Eastern Trail. If I’m looking to get some exercise — which is almost never — I’ll meet a friend at the Eastern Trail for a brisk walk or a bike ride. If I want to breathe the fresh air and clear my head, I’ll go to Scarborough Beach at low tide… also excellent for finding sand dollars. The best sunrise is at Higgins Beach and the best sunset is the Black Point Inn.
Where do you like to shop locally?
I like Suburban Home Outfitters for furniture and home decor and connected to that is Gurley Antiques Gallery which is a fun place to poke around… there are lots of random and quirky items, but sometimes you’ll find just the right thing. For seasonal goodies: plants, hay bales, pumpkins, Christmas trees and greenery from Highland Farm is great. They also sell a small selection of handmade soaps, candles and interesting kitchen gadgets, plus pies and quiche.
What’s a hidden gem or can’t miss thing to do?
Scarborough’s greatest asset is its natural beauty. We’re surrounded by an abundance of visual gems and are constantly reminded of how lucky we are to call it home. 
A can’t-miss event that runs on one Sunday a month from May through October is Clamstock at the Clambake Seafood Restaurant. Don Campbell Band puts on a show in the parking lot while folks enjoy takeout in and outside of their cars. It started during the pandemic and has become a tradition. With the beautiful salt marsh as the backdrop, it’s probably one of the most scenic parking lots you’ll ever dance in.
Five Things is a feature in which locals give our readers suggestions for exploring the state of Maine, town by town. Have a city or town you think we should explore in the future? Tell News & Culture Editor Katherine Lee at [email protected].

title: 81-year-old woman trapped under car for hours in pouring rain before husband finds her
text:
HINGHAM, Mass. (WHDH) - Firefighters rescued an 81-year-old Massachusetts woman who spent four hours trapped under her car in the pouring rain.
Norman Wilbur says he knew something was wrong seconds after a cab dropped him off Friday night at his Hingham home. It turned out his wife, 81-year-old Peggy Wilbur, had gotten trapped underneath her car.
“I walked around, and I heard, ‘Help. Help.’ I said… ‘Peggy, is that you?’ And I looked. I couldn’t even see her because the car was up against it," Norman Wilbur said.
He called 911 as soon as he realized what happened, and Hingham Firefighters arrived within minutes. They used airbags and a spreading safety tool to lift the car off Peggy Wilbur.
Firefighters say the car was accidentally left in neutral and rolled toward the victim, pinning her against a rock wall. Her husband says she had been trapped for four hours in the pouring rain before he found her.
“You couldn’t see her because the wall was here and the car was right up to it,” Norman Wilbur said. “If the door hadn’t swung around, that added a buffer zone, enough of her legs between the wheels and the wall. If that didn’t happen, she would be in hot water.”
Norman Wilbur went with his wife to the hospital. She suffered serious injuries to her chest and legs and now faces a long recovery.
“She’ll be 82 this week, so she’s no spring chicken, as they say, but she’s a tough old Irish girl,” he said.
Firefighters say their thoughts are with the victim and her family.

Husson expands scholarship program to Aroostook County
text:
Husson University in Bangor is expanding its Opportunity Scholarship program to Aroostook County, offering free tuition every year to five students from Maine’s northernmost county.
The Clavette-Grainger Opportunity Scholarship is funded by Bruce and Cynthia (Clavette) Grainger, members of Husson’s Class of 1990 who met at the start of junior year and later married.
The scholarship is available to students who have earned a 3.0 GPA in high school, have a family adjusted gross income of $80,000 or less, qualify for a federal Pell Grant and live in or attend school in Aroostook County.
Recipients will receive assistance through a combination of federal, state and institutional aid.
First-year undergraduate students who are awarded the scholarship must attend school full-time in a four-year degree program on the Bangor campus.
This marks Husson’s third Opportunity Scholarship, joining the Cyr Opportunity Scholarship for Penobscot County students and the Harry S. Greenfield Opportunity Scholarship for Piscataquis County students.
“We are thrilled to expand the Opportunity Scholarship program to a third Maine county thanks to the generosity of Husson University Board of Trustees Vice Chair Bruce Grainger and his wife Cynthia Grainger,” said Husson President Lynne Coy-Ogan. “Both are proud Husson graduates who know the value of a Husson education.”
Students applying for undergraduate admission for fall 2027 are eligible for the scholarship. Applications are currently being accepted for fall 2027 admission and are reviewed on a rolling basis.
With 2,279 undergraduates enrolled in fall 2025, Husson was ranked No. 6 among Maine’s largest colleges and universities in the 2026 Mainebiz Book of Lists. The 2027 edition will be published in late December.

title: Homebuying in America: How a VA loan helped one Black veteran build wealth on her own terms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Homebuying in America: How a VA loan helped one Black veteran build wealth on her own terms
Gabrielle Pickens wasn’t thinking about homeownership until her daughter, Lily, was born in 2021. That moment changed everything. The single Black mother started thinking less about “someday” and more about what kind of stability she could build right now.
That’s when she turned to a benefit she earned during her seven years in the Navy: the VA loan. With competitive interest rates, no down payment requirement, and no private mortgage insurance (PMI), homeownership suddenly felt possible in a way it never had before. For her, becoming a homeowner was especially meaningful, given her credit challenges and the ongoing struggles she knew Black families can face in accessing homeownership.
“It’s either you’re a victim or a victor in your story,” she says. “What are you going to be?”
Pickens chose to be a victor. Four years later, after using a VA loan and rebuilding her credit, she stepped into her sunlit, two-bedroom, two-bath home with high ceilings and a spacious yard in the Chicago suburbs.
“I can only control what I do,” Pickens says. “I can’t beat the system of oppression. This is a group project.”
Setting the scene on homebuying
Before Pickens could take advantage of her VA loan benefits, she first had to improve her credit score. At the time, it was in the low 500s.
On average, Black Americans have lower credit scores than white Americans, shaped in part by long-standing gaps in access to wealth-building opportunities. Pickens thought her score would hold her back from homeownership, but her mindset changed when she attended a workshop through the Neighborhood Assistance Corporation of America, a nonprofit housing counseling and community advocacy organization. Pickens was surprised to meet many other people with credit challenges.
“There are so many ways that we end up with bad credit,” she says. “Nobody wakes up and says, ‘You know what? I’m about to mess my credit up.’ Life happens.”
Behind her homebuying experience
Working with a housing counselor, Pickens reviewed her finances every few months, paid down debt, corrected errors on her credit report, and built healthier credit habits. The effort paid off. Over roughly 18 months, Pickens increased her credit score from the low 500s to around 720 and saved $12,000 toward her home purchase.
Without the VA loan’s no-down-payment feature, Pickens says she likely would have needed years longer to save enough money to buy a home. The 6.125% interest rate she landed fit comfortably within her budget, and she paid only $2,000 in closing costs. As a disabled veteran, she also qualifies for a property tax exemption that helps keep her monthly housing costs low.
“I love it,” Pickens says. “I’m grateful for my mortgage rate and not being cash-strapped and trying to live above my means. A $1,000 mortgage for a two-bed, two-bath home in the suburbs? I’ll take it.”
An expert's take
Government-backed VA and FHA loans are critical for Black homebuyers because their low thresholds help open the door to homeownership. But as Andre Perry, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a nonprofit public policy organization based in Washington, D.C., stresses, more products such as these are needed to support Black homeownership.
Perry highlights programs with small or no down payment requirements and credit models that consider a person’s rent payment history. He also points to Special Purpose Credit Programs (SPCPs) designed to expand access for historically underserved communities with lower mortgage rates or down payment assistance. While the Federal Housing Finance Agency directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac to end SPCPs in March 2025, the programs weren’t entirely eliminated. Some lenders, especially larger ones, still offer them.
“These are the kind of innovations Black people need,” he says. “There are many people with incomes. They clearly are renting month-to-month, so they can have a mortgage. But they simply do not have the kind of product that enables them to get in the door. No pun intended.”
What this means for you
The median wealth of Black families is about a quarter of a million dollars lower than that of a median white family, making homeownership an especially important tool for narrowing wealth gaps. As home values rise and equity grows, a house can become a financial legacy for the next generation.
“This experience has given me the confidence to make other large purchases and take control of my wealth journey,” says Pickens. “The sky is the limit. It took me 35 years to buy my first home. It won’t take me 35 years to buy my second.”
While VA, FHA, and low- and no-down-payment loans can open the door to homeownership, they also come with a reality that’s often overlooked: buyers start with little or no equity. Because of how mortgage payments are structured, it can take time to build meaningful equity. Rising home prices often do most of the early “work” of increasing a homeowner’s wealth. But that also means there’s risk. If someone buys a home and then the market turns, home values could drop, leaving homeowners with an underwater mortgage, which means owing more than the home is worth.
Pickens is well aware of that risk and is approaching homeownership with a long-term mindset. She plans to make extra principal payments to pay down her mortgage faster. She is also eyeing strategic home renovations that can increase her home’s value over time.
“I know equity is coming. It doesn’t have to be today. I’m in it for the long haul.”
Her homeownership dream
For Pickens, buying a home wasn’t just about replacing rent with a mortgage payment. It was an investment in her future and a way to leave a legacy for Lily. Growing up on the South Side of Chicago, her home now gives her something different: fresh air, peace, quiet, and room to breathe. If she could distill her homeownership journey into a single message, it would read like a love letter to Lily.
“Go for what you want, girlfriend,” Pickens says. “With this house, Mommy did her best to get us here. You take it further than me. Don’t stop here. This is just the beginning. My ceiling is your floor.”

title: Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 1/2 years in a British prison for rape and sexual assault
text:
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10½ years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others during a time when his bawdy behavior was indulged and celebrated during his rise to stardom.
Judge Joel Bennathan denounced Brand’s “casual and arrogant disregard” for any woman who said no to him, and castigated him for the series of lies he told in testimony denying assaults that dated to 2004.
“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” Bennathan said. “You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”
Brand showed little emotion during the stinging rebuke. He turned to mouth the words “we’ll be OK” to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers after the hearing.
The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and provocative behavior on television and radio broadcasts, as well as battles with drugs and alcohol, had maintained his innocence and testified that all his encounters were consensual.
But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Prosecutor: Brand used fame to carry out crimes
The convictions — years after the #MeToo movement turned a spotlight on sexual abuse by the powerful and famous — raised questions about how Brand’s behavior was tolerated by TV and radio stations he worked for, including the BBC, and those around him.
“Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame,” prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said. “He used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity.”
Brand was supported by his wife, father and fans outside court
Brand wore a gray suit and an open collar shirt with a loose white tie. His long, graying hair was pulled back and knotted in a man bun atop his head. He clenched a crucifix in his right hand.
Defense lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to consider Brand’s good character, saying his only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995 and that he had performed charitable work and helped others overcome drug and alcohol abuse. He also asked the judge to consider the impact of the sentence on Brand’s family, particularly his three young children.
Brand was supported in Southwark Crown Court by his wife, Laura, and his father, Ron Brand. Laura entered the courthouse without Brand, who had been in since custody Thursday’s verdict.
A couple of Brand’s supporters, reflecting his recent conversion to Christianity, held a banner bearing crosses with the words: “Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth.”
Victims tell court it was difficult to see Brand celebrated in public
The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accounts from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand.
One of the women he was convicted of abusing spoke in court about the trauma the crime caused. The others provided statements read by the prosecutor.
A woman whom Brand groped during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004 said that the assault left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like “damaged goods.”
“It was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke,” she said.
Brand stared straight ahead as she spoke from behind a curtain that shielded her from public view to preserve her identity.
Bennathan said Brand’s entourage may have written off the sexual assault as “laddish,” the boorish and obnoxious behavior for which Brand was known and with which he thought he could get away.
“It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offense, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it,” the judge said.
Rape victim felt ‘powerless’
A former fan he was convicted of anally raping at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009 said that she was left feeling anxious and humiliated and had difficulty eating and sleeping, and went through periods of heavy drinking.
She said she spent months fearing that she might have contracted HIV and that it took years for her to speak up. She only came forward after police opened an investigation following the documentary.
“I felt that if I reported him, I would not be believed,” she said in the statement read by Karmy-Jones. “His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless.”
Winter, the defense lawyer, argued that Brand should be “regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given” following consensual sex.
The judge noted how disrespectfully Brand had treated the woman, including putting her in his phone contacts under “T” for “tart.”
A woman he was convicted of kissing and groping at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 said it had a lasting impact on her life.
“Since the sexual assault ... Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget,” she said. “Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump.”
A woman says she was silenced by ‘culture at the time’
The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a woman who said the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.
“Immediately after the incident I spoke up, and sadly it was brushed under the carpet by senior management,” she said. “There was a culture at the time which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore, which meant I did not give myself time to lament on it, boxed it up and pushed it aside.”
Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men’s bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.
Brand, who was known for edgy stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, rose to prominence in the early 2000s hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

title: Maine field hockey falls 2-1 at home against UAlbany in America East semifinals
text:
ORONO, Maine — On Tuesday, Nov. 3, the University of Maine field hockey team lost 2-1 to the University at Albany in the America East semifinals. The game was decided in a shootout, with the UAlbany Great Danes scoring on two of their five attempts and the UMaine Black Bears scoring on only one of their five attempts.
Despite the dreary weather, the first quarter started strong for Maine. Under a minute in, the Black Bears got their first penalty corner but weren’t able to get more than a blocked shot.
Throughout the first quarter, there was a lot of back-and-forth play. Both teams played with strong defense as they moved up and down the pitch. It wasn’t until the end of the quarter that the Great Danes got their first penalty corner, which led to a shot on goal for them. First-year goalkeeper Anabel Halkes stood tall and made a great save, and the ball went over the crossbar and behind the goal.
To start the second quarter, the Great Danes maintained some strong play and registered a shot, though it was blocked.
About halfway through the quarter, Maine scored its only goal of the game from a strong rush into UAlbany’s zone. The goal was scored by third-year forward and midfielder Emily Chisholm, who was assisted by fourth-year forward Saylor Kuefler.
Despite it being the Black Bears who scored the goal, they didn’t gain any momentum. Instead, it was the Great Danes who had the stronger play following the goal.
Following halftime, the Black Bears came back strong and maintained possession to make sure the Great Danes were spending most of their time defending their own zone.
Early in the third quarter, the Black Bears got a shot on goal, which was saved by UAlbany third-year goalkeeper Merle Vaandrager. Following that save, Maine got its second penalty corner of the game, taken by fourth-year back Eloise Penty, but the shot went off the post.
Two minutes later, UAlbany also got its second penalty corner of the game, which led to a shot that went just wide of the goal.
To start the fourth quarter, the tension was high. Everyone in the crowd knew a one-goal lead could be snapped. The Great Danes came out strong, with their momentum being helped by a green card on second-year forward Martha Barratt.
UAlbany got two penalty corners just a minute apart during the penalty. The Great Danes then got two shots on goal, both of which were saved by Halkes, who was standing tall while Maine’s defense was not. Following two penalty corners that UAlbany earned just seven seconds apart, the Great Danes scored with just over five minutes left in regulation time. The goal was scored by first-year back Quinty Reumer, who was assisted by fourth-year back Mara Küskes and fourth-year forward Emma Staron.
Following the goal, neither team was able to gain the lead in regulation despite another UAlbany penalty corner, as both teams played strong defense, which led to overtime.
In overtime, UAlbany got its eighth penalty corner of the game, and shortly after, Maine got its third.
Following Maine’s penalty corner, it looked like UAlbany scored a goal. However, after review, it was deemed that Halkes made the save. Following the call, UAlbany got its ninth penalty corner of the game, and Halkes made the save on a shot by second-year midfielder Mathilda Prada.
With neither team scoring in overtime, the game went to a shootout. UAlbany scored on its first two attempts, by fourth-year back and midfielder Pilar Lorenzini and Küskes, respectively. Kuefler scored on Maine’s third attempt. Neither team scored on any of its following attempts, leading to a loss for the Black Bears.
With this loss, the University of Maine’s field hockey season is over, while UAlbany went on to lose at home to the University of Vermont in the America East final on Friday, Nov. 6.

title: African restaurant opens in Portland Public Market
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A new restaurant featuring African specialties and other international fare opened recently in the Portland Public Market House on Monument Square.
Julia’s Afro-Global Kitchen launched Sunday on the second floor of the Public Market, joining Bub’s Home Kitchen. Jamaican restaurant Yardie Ting is the Public Market’s vendor on the first floor.
Owner Harly Ngouama said Julia’s Afro-Global Kitchen is named for her late mother, who owned a restaurant in their native Republic of the Congo.
Ngouama’s menu includes Congolese cuisine and other African specialties like pondu, a cassava leaf stew; jollof rice; salted fish; madesu beans with beef; and makosso soup with pork trotters. Julia’s also serves braised pork rib, barbecue goat, beef and chicken brochettes, and international dishes like shawarma, fried rice and pasta with cheese., with a $35 buffet special every Sunday.
Julia’s Afro-Global Kitchen is open Tuesday-Thursday from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., and Friday-Sunday from noon to 8:30 p.m.

title: Penobscot Valley wins fourth Class D state girls soccer championship in a row
text:
OAKLAND, Maine (WABI) - The Penobscot Valley Howlers were crowned Class D state girls champions on Saturday in Oakland, and they were led by a remarkable performance from their goalkeeper.
Brooklynn Raymond stopped an early penalty kick on a day in which she recorded 13 saves and a clean sheet in the Howlers’ 1-0 win over Monmouth Academy.
“I mean, just knowing that we could get back here, trusting each other, even through the losses, all the ties we had, knowing that we had what it took, we knew what it was like to be in a championship game. We knew we could do this again, despite all the talk on the outside,” said Raymond, senior goalkeeper.
It’s Penobscot Valley’s fourth-straight state title.

title: ‘He was loved by everyone’: Family mourns pilot killed in crash weeks before daughter’s birth
text:
WAYCROSS, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) — A pilot killed in a small plane crash at the Waycross-Ware County Airport has been identified as a husband and father.
Amanda Scheuing identified the pilot as her husband, Tim Scheuing.
According to the Federal Aviation Administration, a Beechcraft BE35 crashed during takeoff at Waycross-Ware County Airport around 11:15 a.m. Friday, Nov. 6.
Amanda Scheuing remembered her husband as a devoted father, husband and Christian.
“Words are hard to process right now.... He was the absolute best person I have ever known. I couldn’t have asked for a better husband or a better father for our kids,” she said.
She said they met while working together when she was 16 and began dating shortly afterward. The couple celebrated their 20th wedding anniversary this year and have a 16-year-old daughter, with another daughter due in three weeks.
“He was funny, quick-witted, adventurous and a helping hand to anyone,” she said.
Amanda Scheuing said her husband was a pilot, flight instructor and owner of Runway One Nine Aviation. She thanked the community for its outpouring of love.
“He was loved by everyone and touched so many lives,” she said.
She also thanked the emergency crews, first responders and airport staff, as well as the couple’s family, friends and church family.
The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the cause of the crash, with the FAA also investigating.
