title: Man dies after deer struck by another car flies into his windshield
text:
BOONE COUNTY, Mo. (KY3/Gray News) - A Missouri man died Thursday night after a deer struck by another vehicle flew into his Jeep, authorities said.
According to the Missouri State Highway Patrol, the crash happened on U.S. Route 40 in Boone County just after 5:45 p.m.
Troopers said an SUV, driven by a 75-year-old man from Clark, was headed east on the highway, east of Rocheport Gravel Road, when it hit a deer in the road.
The deer was then propelled into the westbound lane, directly in the path of a Jeep, driven by a 40-year-old man from Glasgow. The deer hit the windshield and top of the Jeep, entered the passenger compartment, and hit the driver, according to the crash report.
The Jeep went off the road and hit trees before stopping. Troopers said the driver was pronounced dead at the scene.
The SUV came to a controlled stop. Its driver was not injured, according to the crash report.

title: Trump after meeting with Qatari PM says he believes war with Iran is militarily ‘effectively over’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) - President Donald Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,” suggesting that — at least for now — he’s not prepared to resume the bombardment that has devastated the Islamic Republic and caused reverberations across the global economy.
The president made a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting earlier in the day with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.”
He added that Iran has been “decapitated” but said he is still looking to make sure there’s a long-term solution to ensuring that Iran’s nuclear program is defanged.
It was some of Trump’s most definitive comments about moving away from his threat to resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections had passed.
The president’s Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress to Democrats in last week’s elections. The elections were shadowed by dissatisfaction among the American electorate over the 8-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices that’s impacted nearly ever sector of the global economy.
Trump, over the course of the conflict, has repeatedly said he is on the cusp of ordering U.S. forces to escalate attacks if Iran’s leaders don’t quickly agree to U.S. terms to end the war, only to back down. In earlier cycles, he has also edged away with a last-minute declaration, sometimes at the behest of Gulf allies, that he’s going to give diplomacy more time.
In a posting on social media shortly before speaking to reporters, Trump once again asserted that Middle East allies — Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others — “would prefer the status quo.” Minutes later, in his exchange with reporters, he sought to assure war-weary Americans that there was “positive momentum” and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.”
“They’re talking to us, and they’re talking very politely, And we’ll see what happens,” Trump said. He added, “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.”
Trump, however, gave no hint of a drawdown of the thousands of U.S. troops who have been shifted to the waters off of Iran and maintain a naval blockade to stem the flow of Iranian oil into the global market.
“We’re keeping it going. We have the greatest military blockade ever,” Trump said.
Qatari officials last week presented proposals on Iran’s nuclear program, according to two Middle East government officials familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The White House declined to comment, though Trump last week alluded to ongoing indirect talks with Tehran.
All the while, Tehran continues to insist on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.
Earlier Monday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has come under fire over the conflict, said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including the possibility of telling Iran: “Hey, we’re done, and we’re going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it.”
The defense secretary has been one of the administration’s most prominent defenders of the war. Critics say the administration launched the war without proper authorization, violated the War Powers Resolution and subverted congressional war-declaring powers.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Hegseth, largely over his execution of the war.
Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with the Iranians and they sign a “strong agreement,” it’s “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” to resume strikes.
Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.
The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
—
AP writers Konstantin Toropin, Samy Magdy and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

title: Man accused of driving 100 mph, hitting 3 police cars during high-speed chase
text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A North Carolina man faces multiple felony charges after allegedly leading police officers on a high-speed chase, authorities said.
The driver, identified as Devin Valdivia, 25, was arrested Saturday, Nov. 7. He faces 10 charges, including felony fleeing to elude arrest, felony assault on a law enforcement officer and driving while impaired.
Court documents allege Valdivia drove into oncoming traffic on Langtree Road and Statesville Highway, reached speeds of up to 130 mph while fleeing police and hit three police cars
The chase began Saturday night in Iredell County as officers responded to reports of a possibly impaired driver. Police said an officer attempted to pull over Valdivia on Langtree Road, but he fled before driving into oncoming traffic.
Valdivia allegedly hit a Mooresville police car before traveling south on Interstate 77, according to police. He exited at Sam Furr Road, where another crash happened between a police car and his vehicle. Police said Valdivia continued fleeing and drove into oncoming traffic.
He later returned to I-77 and took Exit 28. A short time later, his vehicle was involved in another crash with a third police car. Court documents allege Valdivia drove 100 mph in a 65-mph zone on I-77 and failed to maintain lane control.
Court records stated an officer suffered a fractured bone in his hand when Valdivia hit a police car during the pursuit.
Police said Valdivia eventually jumped from the vehicle and fled on foot before he was arrested. Arrest records state that Valdivia has prior convictions in Lincoln County for assault on a government official and attempted fleeing to elude arrest with a motor vehicle.
He also has a prior conviction for driving while impaired in Gaston County, according to the records.

title: Here’s what Joe Biden has to say in his book about Trump’s involvement in Jan. 6 riots
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Former U.S. President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”
And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump’s years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should “follow him to his grave.”
Biden’s sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of “Promise Me, America,” published Monday by The Atlantic. The 46th president’s full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment, his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health.
“Donald Trump led an insurrection,” Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as the U.S. Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. ”His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.
“The rioters weren’t ‘peaceful protesters,” he wrote. “They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election.” He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons to the offenders.
“To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement,” Biden wrote. “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.”
Biden also laments Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change.
“All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors,” Biden wrote. “In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”
Democrats won big, but Biden’s reputation still lags
The memoir’s release comes on the heels of Biden’s fellow Democrats trouncing Republicans in the midterm elections, securing stunningly broad House and Senate majorities and flipping control of several statehouses in a comprehensive rebuke of Trump’s second presidency. But Trump’s return to power two years earlier was itself a rejection of Biden’s one White House term, and many voters still harbor skeptical views of his presidency and his party.
In a lengthy social media post on Sunday, Biden pitched his memoir as the best way he can explain his presidency, “the challenges we faced, the decisions I made and why I made them.”
During his four years in office, Biden confronted the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic fallout, and he worked to restore global alliances that Trump frayed. But he faced widespread concerns about his age, and he abandoned his reelection bid after a disastrous June 2024 debate with Trump. Dogged by lingering inflation and other concerns, Biden’s vice president, Kamala Harris, lost to Trump that November.
Months after leaving office, Biden announced that he’d been diagnosed with prostate cancer. He opened up about his condition in his Sunday social media post, saying he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped” and urging people to let the book speak for him.
Biden said his doctors “continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment.” But, he acknowledged, “Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”
Biden tells of an unusually complimentary Trump
In the excerpt, Biden recounts an unusual Oval Office meeting with Trump days after the 2020 election — well before the Jan. 6 riots.
“‘You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends,’” Trump said, according to Biden.
Trump even commented, “that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me,” Biden added.
Public polling at the time Biden dropped his reelection bid showed him trailing Trump, and Democrats pushed for him to yield out of fear that he could not win.
Biden said he used the meeting to give Trump “a tour of the world,” including the Ukraine-Russia war, NATO alliances, Israel and Gaza and China-U.S. relations. Biden said Trump “focused on the personalities” of world leaders rather than the substance of international relations.
He said that the two-hour meeting left him worried Trump would indeed dismantle much of his presidency. He wrote that Trump’s opening weeks — his Day One executive orders and everything that followed — confirmed his worries about a “crueler government” that “tried to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds” and a president who “took a wrecking ball to our traditions.”
The title echoes Biden’s memoir about his late son
The memoir’s title echoes an earlier Biden book, “Promise Me, Dad,” that he wrote about his son Beau’s cancer and death — a parallel that implicitly acknowledges the former president’s age, condition and the reality that he may not have a long post-presidency to see the direction of the country and the evolution of his legacy.
In that first book, released between Biden’s vice presidency and his 2020 presidential bid, he explained that the title came directly from a father-son conversation around Thanksgiving in 2014.
“Promise me, Dad. Give me your word that no matter what happens, you’re going to be all right,” Biden recalled Beau saying. Beau Biden died six months later.
In his Sunday post, Biden repeated an argument he made often when campaigning and during his presidency, saying the U.S. is unique because it was “built on an idea” that “all of us are created equal.”
“Promise me, America,” he concluded, that, “we’ll never forget it.”

title: Maine Shows Its True Colors in Ranking of America's Most Charitable States

title: Winslow to recount District 1 ballots
text:
After losing to incumbent Michael Joseph by just 12 votes, retired career firefighter Scott Holst called for a recount in Winslow’s District 1 Town Council race, Town Clerk Audra Fleury said.
Three candidates ran for Winslow’s District 1 council seat and just 18 votes decided the election. In the initial count, Joseph got 251 votes, Holst got 239, and Erin McCullough, who came in third, got 233.
Fleury said the recount will start at 9 a.m. Wednesday at 114 Benton Ave. Veteran’s Day is one of the town’s floating holidays, and so it will not interfere with the recount, which will be open to the public.
Holst worked in Winslow and Waterville as a firefighter for almost 45 years. He said after regularly attending council and school budget meetings he has ideas for how Winslow could better balance its municipal and school interests in the budget.
McCullough has lived in Winslow for 10 years. She said after working as a school councilor for 17 years she’s used to hard conversations and knows how to collaborate with others and find solutions to problems.
Joseph did not respond to the Maine Trust for Local News voter guide survey or to requests for comment during the election cycle. He won his council seat in 2023, when he described himself as a conservative Christian businessman looking to cut unnecessary spending.
In Winslow’s District 3 race, Daniel Potelle beat council Chair Fran Hudson by over 150 votes. Charles Lambert ran unopposed for the District 5 seat. If the recount names Holst or McCullough as winner, Winslow’s council seats will all have been won by newcomers.

title: Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Texas' Big Bend to resume
text:
Supreme Court clears the way for border wall construction in Texas' Big Bend to resume
The Supreme Court cleared the way Monday for the Trump administration to resume border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas for now, a blow to bipartisan opponents who had argued the project is a waste of money that threatens the unique landscape.
The border wall is a signature project of President Donald Trump, who has long vowed to build a wall from the Pacific Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico.
Republicans in Congress last summer funded the project with $46 billion, and Customs and Border Protection has been rapidly erecting 12 miles of border barriers a week across the entire border.
The government has pushed forward by issuing sweeping waivers to bypass regulations that are aimed at protecting the environment, but have historically slowed down major construction projects.
In Texas's Big Bend region, bipartisan opposition has rallied to fight back against the project, which would include 30-foot-tall steel walls in some areas as well as vehicle barriers and new roads.
They've argued that the barriers are a waste of money that threaten the local economy and lifestyle in an area of historically low illegal immigration. They say the job could be better done using only surveillance technology like drones.
A judge in Texas sided with opponents, finding that Congress likely had not clearly authorized such broad waivers for an area with the southern border's lowest rate of migrant apprehensions. She ordered an immediate stop to all construction-related activity in the area, which includes Big Bend National Park as well as land up and down river in state and private hands.
The Trump administration says there are illegal border crossings and drug seizures in Big Bend, and more traffic could be funneled there if there's a gap in the wall. Federal attorneys said the judge overstepped her authority since the law sharply limits court challenges to border construction waivers.
The high court's decision allows construction to continue while the case plays out.

title: James Gunn and Peter Safran Are Out at DC Studios CEOs
text:
James Gunn and Peter Safran Are Out as DC Studios CEOs
After four years, James Gunn and Peter Safran are out as the heads of DC Studios.
The surprising announcement was made today by Warner Bros., who also announced that they will be replaced by former Marvel producer Jeremy Latcham, who will become DC’s president and chief creative officer.
While the news comes shortly after Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. studio, it also comes with Gunn and Safran still working on their next big DC movie, Man of Tomorrow, the sequel to Gunn’s own Superman movie of 2025. That film is scheduled to open in theaters next summer.
It also comes after they just turned Clayface from an obscure Batman villain into a solid box-office hit. The Clayface movie, just the third film from Gunn and Safran’s DC Studios, has grossed over $100 million worldwide
READ MORE: The Best Performances in DC Movies Ever
Gunn and Safran were first given the titles of co-CEOs of DC Studios in the fall of 2022. By that point, Gunn had already directed The Suicide Squad for DC after years of leading the Guardians of the Galaxy franchise at Marvel. (He actually released Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 in 2023, after he was already DC co-CEO.)
When Gunn and Safran were formally introduced as the heads of DC, they unveiled an ambitious lineup of interconnected movies and television series. They included plans for films based on The Authority and Swamp Thing, and TV shows about Booster Gold, Amanda Waller, and Wonder Woman’s homeland of Themyscira. None of those projects have been made — and now seem almost certainly doomed to spend eternity in limbo.
The first movie of their combined DC Universe of film and television shows was Gunn’s own Superman in 2025. The film was a critical and commercial hit, although not a massive blockbuster along the lines of Christopher Nolan’s The Dark Knight. Their next film was this summer’s spinoff Supergirl, which was a critical and commercial disappointment, and earned just $126 million worldwide.
Apart from Peacemaker, which predated the Gunn/Safran regime, the only TV series they made fully set in their DCU was the animated Creature Commandos and the well-received Lanterns, which recently wrapped up its first season on HBO Max.
Here was Gunn and Safran’s statement on the news:
Four years ago, we set out to unite DC under one creative vision. In that time, we helped restore ‘Superman’ to the heart of DC, while opening new doors and telling new stories in film and television with ‘Peacemaker,’ ‘Creature Commandos,’ ‘Lanterns’ and ‘Clayface. We’re immensely proud of the team that turned that ambition into something real, including the actors, crews and executives we had the opportunity to collaborate with. We’ve shared a creative history with Jeremy going back to Marvel, and we’re eager to see the perspective he brings to DC’s next chapter. We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in Man of Tomorrow.
Jeremy Latcham’s credits include serving as associate producer on Iron Man, co-producer on Iron Man 2, and executive producer of The Avengers and Gunn’s own Guardians of the Galaxy.
His last production for Marvel was 2017’s Spider-Man: Homecoming. Since then he’s produced the films Bad Times at the El Royale, Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, and the Nate Bargatze comedy The Breadwinner.

title: Why your metabolism changes as you age — and what you can do now
text:
(Aging Untold) — Metabolism is how your body makes and uses energy, burns fuel, keeps up strength and recovers from day to day.
As we get older, that process can change and affect how we feel and how our bodies function.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said metabolism is about much more than the number on the scale.
Metabolism is the body’s ‘power plant’
“Metabolism really is the language of your cells, and your cells operate on energy,” Rogers said. “What’s supplying that energy is these little battery packs called mitochondria.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck compared metabolism to the body’s “power plant.”
Mitochondria are the batteries that power it and every organ has its own power plant, Rogers said.
“The brain requires a lot of power, the heart requires a lot of power,” Rogers said. “If you deplete that power in an organ that needs a lot, you’re going to start to see symptoms sooner.”
That is why changes in the eyes and ears show up in older people, she said.
“They require a lot of power, so that’s why you see the healing start to go and the eyesight start to go quickly,” Rogers said.
When cells can’t produce the energy they need, Rogers said, people can notice changes in how they think and feel.
“When you cannot produce the energy for all your cells that is needed, you’ll experience things like brain fog or fatigue or just simply being out of it,” Rogers said.
She said that energy supports the whole body.
“Your heart has to beat. Your brain has to think. You have to breathe. Your immune cells have to fight infection. Everything depends on having energy,” Rogers said.
Metabolism is more than weight
Cradduck said many people think of metabolism only in terms of weight gain. It also affects how an older person processes medications.
“Think of aging as losing energy,” Rogers said. “It’s the cellular energy that’s progressively being lost as you age. That’s why we start to see the symptoms that we associate with aging.”
Why strength training matters
As people age, they lose muscle and gain fat, a condition called sarcopenia, Rogers said. And many of the hormones people lose with age are tied to maintaining muscle mass.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said people often turn to weight loss and overlook strength.
“What I see happen is people will go on a weight loss thing, and they think they need to lose weight, and they forget that they really need the strength,” O’Rourke said. “So it’s a positive thing to gain weight because it could mean that your muscles are getting stronger.”
O’Rourke recommended strength training two to three times a week as people get older.
“To the younger people out there, I’d say start strength training now, so that you don’t have such a cascading effect when you get older,” O’Rourke said.
How muscle connects to glucose
Rogers explained that muscle plays a role in how the body uses glucose. She said glucose provides energy and has to be taken up by muscles to be used for energy.
“Insulin resistance is when your muscles will not take that glucose up, And that’s where prediabetes and all that starts, at the level of the muscle. So the more muscle that you can build, the better you can help that process,” Rogers said.
Type 2 diabetes is showing up earlier, Rogers said, and cited metabolic inflexibility, which she described as the inability to go back and forth between using fat for energy and using carbs for energy. Your cells should be able to go back and forth.
“That makes you very efficient, and we’re losing that efficiency because of things like toxins, inflammation,” Rogers said.
Building health instead of waiting to manage disease
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the focus can be on creating health and energy rather than waiting to manage disease.
Rogers listed muscle stimulation, inflammation control, toxin removal, good nutrition and good sleep.
Key takeaways
- Metabolism is about energy, not just weight. Every cell runs on energy, including the heart, brain, lungs and immune cells.
- Muscle is a primary metabolic driver. Losing muscle mass as you age is one thing that can slow metabolism.
- Aging is the slow loss of cellular energy. When mitochondria slow down, your overall vitality drops.
- Life is about function, not weight. A healthy metabolism gives you the physical strength to stay capable.

title: Netflix drops trailer for 'The Trials of Karen Read' docuseries
text:
Netflix drops trailer for 'The Trials of Karen Read' documentary series
Karen Read's two dramatic murder trials are now the subject of a Netflix documentary series, a new trailer for which was released on Monday.
Massachusetts investigators and the Norfolk District Attorney's Office argued Read hit her boyfriend, John O'Keefe, with her Lexus SUV outside of a home in Canton during a snowstorm on Jan. 29, 2022, following a night of drinking. Read's attorneys said someone else was responsible for killing O'Keefe and that Read is the victim of a law enforcement cover-up.
The Netflix documentary series is set to be released on Nov. 23, exclusively through that streaming platform. It boasts "exclusive interviews with those who were inside the house" along with jurors and people who knew O'Keefe.
Watch the trailer in the YouTube video embedded below.
Read was tried twice in consecutive years on a charge of second-degree murder. Her first trial ended with a hung jury, which told the judge several times that it was unable to reach a unanimous verdict.
Her legal team attempted to fight a second trial, but the courts found that double jeopardy protection did not apply because no verdict was recorded in the case.
Following the second trial, she was found not guilty in June 2025 of second-degree murder but convicted on a lesser charge of drunken driving.
Karen Read's legal saga
Since the verdict ended her second trial, Read and her related cases have continued to drag on.
She and Aidan Kearney, the blogger known as "Turtleboy," are the plaintiffs in a defamation lawsuit filed by witnesses who testified during her criminal trials, Jennifer McCabe, Brian Albert, Colin Albert and Brian Higgins.
Kearney was a vocal advocate for Read's claims, and prosecutors alleged that the two communicated about the case, sometimes through third parties. Kearney still faces witness intimidation cases stemming from the events.
Read and the two Canton bars where she and O'Keefe went before his death are the plaintiffs in a wrongful death lawsuit filed by O'Keefe's family.
Read also filed her own lawsuit against Massachusetts State Police and the Canton Police Department. Citing numerous inappropriate messages attributed to investigators, Read's team claims the agencies "negligently permitted virulent misogynists and bigots to target her and will answer for what they built, what they concealed and what they did to her."
Last year, Read also brought a lawsuit alleging that others were responsible for the death of her boyfriend and that investigators failed to pursue those leads. That case names investigators and witnesses who testified in her criminal trials as defendants.

title: How to talk about the end of life without feeling pressure to be strong
text:
(Aging Untold) — People don’t always get to control how life ends, but some get a moment to decide how they’ll say goodbye and who they’ll say goodbye to.
If you are the one saying goodbye, you do not have to stay strong for anyone else, according to the Aging Untold experts.
You are not there to manage anyone else’s emotions
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said a person who knows the end is near is not telling loved ones about it to manage their emotions.
“You need to be getting the support that you need,” Cradduck said.
She said she understands that others are going through the same grief and crisis because they are losing that person.
“But you need the support system,” she said.
If you’re the one hearing the news
Cradduck said people who hear this news from someone can be that support.
“Break down with them and be honest about those emotions, but don’t expect the person that’s dying to be the one that’s holding you up,” Cradduck said.
She said she has seen that happen too many times.
Some people want distance. Others want company.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recalled sitting in church when the minister shared that he had been diagnosed with a terminal illness.
“You could hear a pin drop,” she said.
The minister asked people not to come up and ask him questions or talk to him, O’Rourke said. He said he needed distance and space, but he wanted the congregation to know because they would see physical changes in him.
“I had the utmost respect for that,” she said. “We all have to die on our own terms.”
Others go a different route.
They may say they don’t have much time left and want to spend it together, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said everyone is different.
“You really don’t know how it might hit you either way,” she said.
She listed grief, unfinished business and relationships among the things a person may be dealing with.
Start with what you need, then ask for it
Ambrose suggested a conversation starter: “I wish I had more time, but let’s make the best of the time that’s left.”
Another option, Rogers said, is to say: “This is how I’d like you to celebrate my life.”
O’Rourke said the first step is to think through what you need and then ask for it.
She said some people who are dying don’t want to talk about it. They want to go and experience life, and they don’t want someone looking at them with sympathy.
Living or existing
People have a choice every day to live their lives to the fullest or to exist, Cradduck said. That choice remains after a terminal diagnosis.
“You can live every day until you pass through your final sunset, or you can exist every day,” Cradduck said. “I have seen people do it both ways.”
She said she has seen people who were actively dying who were still doing things they wanted to do and accomplish.
We live in a society that has a problem talking about death and dying, Cradduck said.
“We don’t like to face mortality, and it’s the reason why we don’t plan for it,” she said.
She said she admires anyone who can face it “with the grace and respect for themselves and everyone else around them.”
When you’re invited into the conversation
Ambrose said the conversation can be awkward and people often don’t know how to act. The minister’s request let the congregation off the hook so they didn’t feel they had to address it, she added.
For people who want to talk openly, listeners should engage rather than brush it off by saying, “Oh, Mom, let’s not talk about that,” Ambrose said.
“Give people that peace to be able to speak either way when you’re invited into those conversations,” she said.

title: Letter: Democrats must laser focus on making life better for Americans
Here’s what Joe Biden has to say in his book about Trump’s involvement in Jan. 6 riots
text:
ATLANTA (AP) — Former U.S. President Joe Biden writes in his White House memoir that Donald Trump, at once his predecessor and successor, has deeply damaged the country and world with an administration determined to “tear down institutions and inflame hatreds.”
And the 83-year-old Democrat said the 80-year-old Trump’s years of lies about his 2020 defeat to Biden and the Jan. 6 attacks on the Capitol should “follow him to his grave.”
Biden’s sweeping indictment comes in the first excerpt of “Promise Me, America,” published Monday by The Atlantic. The 46th president’s full memoir is set for a Nov. 17 release. Biden said that while doctors are encouraged by his response to cancer treatment, his activities promoting the book will be limited because of his health.
“Donald Trump led an insurrection,” Biden wrote of the attack by Trump supporters as the U.S. Congress met to certify the 2020 election won by the Democrat. ”His goal was to remain in power after the American people had voted him out of office.
“The rioters weren’t ‘peaceful protesters,” he wrote. “They came armed to stop the official certification of a legitimate election.” He chided Trump for later issuing more than 1,500 pardons to the offenders.
“To this day, Trump and his supporters continue to preen and posture like they’re supporters of law enforcement,” Biden wrote. “Here’s my view: You don’t get to turn a blind eye to cops being punched, speared, sprayed, and brutalized and call yourself a friend of law enforcement. What Trump did on January 6, 2021, should never be forgotten. It should follow him to his grave.”
Biden also laments Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency and his aggressive reversal of many of his policies, especially those intended to address climate change.
“All presidents must confront a feeling that their legacy is vulnerable to the pendulum of politics and the whims of their successors,” Biden wrote. “In my case, that feeling was magnified by the dismissive and destructive nature of Donald Trump, who seemed unable to tolerate the idea that someone else’s accomplishments might be worth building on rather than tearing down.”
Democrats won big, but Biden’s reputation still lags
The memoir’s release comes on the heels of Biden’s fellow Democrats trouncing Republicans in the midterm elections, securing stunningly broad House and Senate majorities and flipping control of several statehouses in a comprehensive rebuke of Trump’s second presidency. But Trump’s return to power two years earlier was itself a rejection of Biden’s one White House term, and many voters still harbor skeptical views of his presidency and his party.
In a lengthy social media post on Sunday, Biden pitched his memoir as the best way he can explain his presidency, “the challenges we faced, the decisions I made and why I made them.”
During his four years in office, Biden confronted the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic fallout, and he worked to restore global alliances that Trump frayed. But he faced widespread concerns about his age, and he abandoned his reelection bid after a disastrous June 2024 debate with Trump. Dogged by lingering inflation and other concerns, Biden’s vice president, Kamala Harris, lost to Trump that November.
Months after leaving office, Biden announced that he’d been diagnosed with prostate cancer. He opened up about his condition in his Sunday social media post, saying he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped” and urging people to let the book speak for him.
Biden said his doctors “continue to be encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment.” But, he acknowledged, “Some days are better than others. It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”
Biden tells of an unusually complimentary Trump
In the excerpt, Biden recounts an unusual Oval Office meeting with Trump days after the 2020 election — well before the Jan. 6 riots.
“‘You know, Joe, if it weren’t for politics, I believe we’d be good friends,’” Trump said, according to Biden.
Trump even commented, “that he’d been relieved he didn’t have to run against me,” Biden added.
Public polling at the time Biden dropped his reelection bid showed him trailing Trump, and Democrats pushed for him to yield out of fear that he could not win.
Biden said he used the meeting to give Trump “a tour of the world,” including the Ukraine-Russia war, NATO alliances, Israel and Gaza and China-U.S. relations. Biden said Trump “focused on the personalities” of world leaders rather than the substance of international relations.
He said that the two-hour meeting left him worried Trump would indeed dismantle much of his presidency. He wrote that Trump’s opening weeks — his Day One executive orders and everything that followed — confirmed his worries about a “crueler government” that “tried to tear down institutions and inflame hatreds” and a president who “took a wrecking ball to our traditions.”
The title echoes Biden’s memoir about his late son
The memoir’s title echoes an earlier Biden book, “Promise Me, Dad,” that he wrote about his son Beau’s cancer and death — a parallel that implicitly acknowledges the former president’s age, condition and the reality that he may not have a long post-presidency to see the direction of the country and the evolution of his legacy.
In that first book, released between Biden’s vice presidency and his 2020 presidential bid, he explained that the title came directly from a father-son conversation around Thanksgiving in 2014.
“Promise me, Dad. Give me your word that no matter what happens, you’re going to be all right,” Biden recalled Beau saying. Beau Biden died six months later.
In his Sunday post, Biden repeated an argument he made often when campaigning and during his presidency, saying the U.S. is unique because it was “built on an idea” that “all of us are created equal.”
“Promise me, America,” he concluded, that, “we’ll never forget it.”

title: Cooper Flagg records 43 points, 10 rebounds as Mavs rally past Pacers
text:

P.J. Washington Jr. could have extended the Dallas lead with four seconds left but missed both free throws, with Indiana’s Obi Toppin grabbing the rebound. The Pacers’ final possession ended with Dallas’ Caleb Martin tipping away a pass by Andrew Nembhard near the sideline.

He hit a season-high seven 3-pointers.

Flagg has four straight double-doubles and five this season.
The Pacers (3-8) were led by Pascal Siakam with 29 points, but only three of those were scored in the second half. Aaron Nesmith scored 18 points with two of his four 3-pointers coming in the final minute.
Siakam hit 8 of 9 from the floor during the first half, including 5 of 6 behind the arc, plus 5 of 6 from the line for 26 points. He was the lone Pacer in double figures in building a 13-point lead that was 66-56 at halftime.

NTSB completes investigation of areas outside Florida Learjet crash excavation site, finds plane parts
The National Transportation and Safety Board said Sunday it has completed its investigation of areas outside the excavation site where the Learjet 60 crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida, and has recovered and identified portions of the aircraft.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: NTSB finds portion of one engine in Learjet crash site as more debris discovered on roofs of homes and buildings
Debris recovered, identified
An NTSB spokesperson told sister station WPBF that investigators have recovered and identified portions of the aircraft, including components from both wings, both engines, the flight deck, vertical stabilizer, horizontal stabilizer, left elevator, aileron sections and multiple flap track assemblies.
Some of the recovered parts have been sent to the NTSB laboratories in Washington, D.C. for closer inspection.
"If you have found or collected any debris from the crash site, please do not keep it or attempt to move, alter or dispose of it," the spokesperson said. "We ask that you contact the NTSB at witness@ntsb.gov to arrange its recovery. Please include a photo of the debris, if possible, in your email. Recovering all available wreckage is critical to the investigation and helping to determine the cause of the crash.
A twisted piece of metal believed to be from Sunday's deadly Learjet crash slammed into a woman's roof less than a mile from the crash site, leaving a hole and causing part of her kitchen ceiling to collapse.
WPBF 25 News Investigates' Terri Parker obtained exclusive photographs of the suspected aircraft wreckage and damage to Ana Escobar's home roof less than a mile from the crash site, leaving a hole and causing part of her kitchen ceiling to collapse
On Tuesday, investigators said they recovered most of the Learjet's left elevator in three pieces, found between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the crash site. The elevator is a control surface on the tail that helps control the aircraft's up-and-down movement.
NTSB board member Tom Chapman said the distance of the debris from the impact crater establishes that the pieces separated before the plane hit the ground.
"What that means exactly in terms of what caused the aircraft to lose control, or whether the loss of this piece was a result of the forces on the aircraft, we don't know yet," Chapman said.
Another witness, Peter DiMaira, discovered what appeared to be pieces of the aircraft's tail at his workplace nearly four miles from the crash site.
NTSB completes its investigation of areas outside the excavation site
 The areas where the NTSB investigation has been completed include Cresthaven mobile home park, some businesses and John I. Leonard High School, though the campus reopened Wednesday. Evacuated residents have not been able to return to the site. The entrance is on Military Trail where the plane crashed, killing all nine aboard.
County spokesman John Jamason told sister station WPBF several things need to be done before the 800 residents can return, including restoring power and water. Sixty-eight residents remain at the Greenacres Community Center, he said.
Palm Beach County spokesman Teri Barbera said deputies are still patrolling the area. The portion of Military Trail remains inaccessible because of the crater.
911 calls released
The crash happened just before 1 p.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1. On Friday, PBSO released 911 calls that reveal the confusion and fear in the moments after a Learjet crashed.
"We need, I think, police because I think a bomb just landed," one caller said.
Another caller described the sound as "like a bomb explosion."
A third caller told 911, "I think an airplane fell or something. There was an explosion."
The 911 operators were working to make sense of the chaotic reports.

title: Mills joins New England governors in seeking $3 billion more for home heating aid
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - Gov. Janet Mills is joining the other New England governors in calling on Congress to increase federal funding for home heating assistance.
Request for LIHEAP funding
The governors are asking for an additional $3 billion for the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, also known as LIHEAP.
“No one should be cold in their homes because Trump decided to wage an unnecessary, unwanted war with Iran,” Mills said.
Heating oil costs in Maine
About half of Maine homes rely on heating oil, which reached a record average of $6.04 a gallon last month.
The governors said families need help as winter approaches.
“For families already living on tight budgets, higher energy bills add to an increasingly difficult financial burden. Seniors on fixed incomes, families with young children, and people with disabilities are especially vulnerable, often facing the difficult choice between maintaining safe temperatures in their homes and meeting other basic needs,” the governors said in the letter.
Federal reserve release
The federal government has also authorized the release of heating oil from a Northeast reserve to help address rising costs.
The full letter:
Dear Chairman Cole, Ranking Member DeLauro, Chair Collins, and Vice Chair Murray:
As winter approaches, we write to thank Congress for its longstanding bipartisan support of the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) and to urge you to provide an additional $3 billion in funding, bringing total program funding to $7 billion, to help vulnerable households manage sharply rising energy costs.
Whether through an increase in the annual appropriation or a one-time emergency supplemental funding, these additional resources are urgently needed.
Across the country, low-income households are struggling with the cumulative impact of rising costs for groceries, housing, insurance, transportation, and other necessities. For families already living on tight budgets, higher energy bills add to an increasingly difficult financial burden. Seniors on fixed incomes, families with young children, and people with disabilities are especially vulnerable, often facing the difficult choice between maintaining safe temperatures in their homes and meeting other basic needs.
LIHEAP provides essential assistance to these households in every region of the country, helping families manage both winter heating and summer cooling costs. While energy needs vary by geography and season, the challenge is the same: ensuring that vulnerable Americans can afford the energy necessary to remain safe in their homes.
These pressures are particularly acute in New England, where cold winters, older housing, and a heavy reliance on delivered heating fuel leave families especially exposed to the dramatic price increases America is currently experiencing. According to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), heating oil prices are projected to increase by approximately 50 percent this winter. NEADA estimates that low-income households across the Northeast could face nearly $1.1 billion in additional heating oil costs alone.
At current funding levels, rising energy prices will erode the purchasing power of LIHEAP assistance, forcing states to reduce benefits or serve fewer eligible households when the need is greatest. While our states are working to mitigate the immediate impact of rising energy costs on vulnerable households and continue to invest heavily in energy efficiency, weatherization, and other long-term solutions, these efforts cannot fully offset the immediate financial pressures facing families this winter.
We recognize the difficult budget decisions confronting Congress and deeply appreciate its longstanding bipartisan commitment to LIHEAP. Given the extraordinary pressures facing America’s poorest households, we urge Congress to provide an additional $3 billion as soon as possible, through increased annual funding or an emergency supplemental appropriation. Timely action will help states sustain assistance and protect vulnerable households from the consequences of unaffordable home energy costs that are far beyond their control. Thank you for your consideration and continued commitment to helping American families meet their essential energy needs.

Cruise ship staffer reportedly treads water in the ocean for nine hours before being rescued
text:
Cruise ship staffer reportedly treads water in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours before being rescued by fishermen
Two fishermen have rescued a man thought to have been treading water off the coast of California for nine hours after falling from a cruise ship.
Grant Garrett and Sean Norton told CNN affiliate KCBS/KCAL that they were around 20 miles from shore when they came across the man in the water on Friday morning.
"I'm like, 'Yeah, it's a human being. Stop the boat; let's get all of our lines in,'" Garrett said.
Norton added that the episode was "surreal."
"Grant and I each got an arm and lifted him up," Norton said. "He was in total shock."
"The only thing he said to me was, 'Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'" Norton said.
He later told them he was a pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise ship named "Ovation of the Seas," and Newport County officials believe the man went overboard about nine hours before he was found, KCBS/KCAL reported.
The man is expected to survive, but Norton said he believes he might not have done so without the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is associated with higher water temperatures in the Pacific Ocean.
"You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees," Norton said. "A different year, no way he makes it."
A spokesperson for Royal Caribbean told CNN: "We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share."
CNN has contacted the U.S. Coast Guard and Newport County lifeguards for comment.

title: These 7 Maine college field hockey and soccer teams earned DIII tournament berths
text:
A disappointing end last season fueled the University of Southern Maine field hockey team in 2026.
The Huskies lost to Keene State in a shootout in last year’s Little East Conference semifinals. They avenged that loss Saturday, beating the Owls 1-0 to win the conference title and earn an automatic berth in the NCAA Division III tournament.
“We set this goal early on,” said USM coach Bonny Brown-Denico, who is in her 28th year leading the program. “Our seniors and captains have been outstanding, helping drive us to this ultimate goal.”
The Huskies were one of the seven Maine programs to earn a spot in NCAA DIII tournaments, whose fields were announced Sunday and Monday. The St. Joseph’s College and Thomas College men’s soccer teams and Husson University women’s soccer teams also earned automatic bids, while the Bowdoin field hockey, Bowdoin men’s soccer and Colby women’s soccer teams earned at-large bids.
Southern Maine (15-7) travels to Clinton, New York, to play Hamilton (11-5) on Wednesday. Hamilton earned an at-large bid.
“I told (the team), ‘If we get to the NCAAs, don’t be grateful just for getting there,'” Brown-Denico said. “‘Believe in yourselves and realize that on any given day, anyone can beat anyone.'”
The Huskies relied on senior leadership and a strong sophomore class this season. Lawrence High graduate Maddie Niles leads the team with nine goals and six assists. Senior forward Bri Townsend, a Nokomis graduate, has eight goals and four assists.
“They’ve taken on the responsibility of really getting better every single day,” Brown-Denico said. “They’ve been so easy with taking feedback and making corrections and instantly changing things when they need. My assistant coach always says, ‘You tell them one thing, they do it immediately.’ They’re the best students.”
The Bowdoin field hockey team earned an at-large bid after going 13-4 and losing to Middlebury 2-0 in the NESCAC semifinals. The Polar Bears have a bye into the first round and, at 11 a.m. Saturday in Brunswick, will host the winner of a game between Amherst and Endicott.
Senior Emily Ferguson has 10 goals and Hanna Balmelli has nine for Bowdoin this season.
The Thomas College men’s soccer team is 12-3-1 and beat Husson in a shootout on Saturday to win the North Atlantic Conference title and an automatic bid. The Terriers fell just short of the NCAA DIII tournament last season, losing to SUNY-Delhi in the conference title game.
“Last year was one of the best teams I’ve had, arguably, but not doing the small things well kind of cost us in the end,” said fifth-year Thomas coach Kyle Fletcher. “Something that we talked about at the beginning of the season was focusing on small details. I think it was a huge step in the learning process, as a coaching staff but as a program as well.”
David Ivarsson has 19 goals and nine assists, while Cody Robinson has nine goals for Thomas this season.
Thomas won’t have to travel far but got a tough draw. The Terriers will face Bowdoin (8-3-5) in the first round at 11 a.m. Saturday in Brunswick. The Polar Bears are ranked 25th in the United Soccer Coaches DIII poll and have three players with 10 points (Jack Banks two goals and six assists; Patrick Brady has four goals and two assists; and Adam Prince has five goals).
“Obviously, Bowdoin’s going to be a real tough test,” Fletcher said.
“The biggest (key),” Fletcher added, “is we can’t give them chances. They’re one of the best teams in the country. We’ve got our hands full. From the opening kick to the final whistle, we have to be at our best.”
The St. Joseph’s men’s soccer team is 9-2-8 and earned an automatic berth by beating Norwich University in the Great Northeast Athletic Conference championship game Saturday. The Monks, led by Windham graduate Nick Marion (10 goals, 8 assists) face Middlebury (10-2-3) at 11 a.m. Saturday in Vermont.
The Colby women’s soccer team (9-4-3) earned an at-large bid for its third trip to the NCAA Division III tournament. The Mules, led by Abigail Jarvi (8 goals), face the University of Mary Washington (12-2-4) on Saturday in Ewing, New Jersey.
Husson (10-5-2), which beat Lesley University 2-0 in the NAC final, will travel to Poughkeepsie, New York, on Saturday to play Tufts.

title: Maine's November Night Sky Is Putting on One Heck of a Show
text:
I've always been fascinated by space. Seriously, I LOVE this stuff. I'm also a huge fan of planetariums, especially the incredible one at Boston's Museum of Science. There's just something about staring up at the stars and realizing how unbelievably massive our universe is that blows my mind.
And this November, Maine's night sky is giving us plenty of reasons to look up!
First, the Northern Taurids meteor shower peaks overnight November 11th into the 12th. WGME says You might only catch a handful of shooting stars per hour, but this shower is known for producing some pretty spectacular fireballs!
Then, November 17th and 18th bring the Leonid meteor shower, where you could spot up to 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions. Fun fact: Those shooting stars are actually tiny pieces of debris left behind by a comet.
And there's more!
On November 15th and 16th, Mars and Jupiter will appear close together in the early morning sky. They're actually millions of miles apart, but from Earth, they'll look like neighbors.
Then comes November's Beaver Moon on November 24th, which is also a supermoon this year. That means it'll appear slightly bigger and brighter than your average full moon.
According to NASA, Mercury will also be easier to spot before sunrise around November 20th, and Uranus reaches opposition on the 25th, making it a great time to break out the telescope.
One of my favorite things about living in Maine is that you don't have to travel far to find some incredible dark skies.
So grab a warm jacket, get away from the city lights, and look up!
Just cross your fingers that the Maine clouds cooperate.
Because sometimes the best show around doesn't require a ticket. Just a clear night and a little curiosity.

title: Ring camera video shows women making racist gestures outside Ole Miss student’s apartment
text:
OXFORD, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - A disturbing video circulating on social media is drawing attention across the Ole Miss campus after women were caught on a Ring doorbell camera making racist gestures outside an apartment where three Black students live.
The video belongs to the daughter of Tasha Bolton, who contacted WMC about the clip.
Bolton’s daughter is an African-American freshman at the University of Mississippi. She shares the off-campus apartment with two other Black roommates.
What the video shows
In the video, three white women can be seen walking past the apartment’s front door. As they pass, two of the women appear to make monkey noises.
The video went viral Saturday after being shared on social media, prompting reactions from students and visitors in Oxford.
Reaction from students and visitors
Sophomore Olivia Landgreve, who does not live at the apartment, said she was upset by what she saw.
“I like to think that people don’t see me like that. I’m just a person like everybody else is. Very upsetting to think that maybe people are thinking other things while they’re looking at me while I walk on campus,” Landgreve said.
Landgreve said she had never experienced anything like this before and was shocked by the video.
Jamie Purcell, who was visiting Oxford from California, had not seen the video until WMC showed it to her.
“It’s disgusting and they’re just not smart, and they’re acting incorrectly to something people should know differently about,” Purcell said.
University statement
On Sunday, the University of Mississippi released a statement condemning the behavior.
“The university is aware of a video depicting offensive, hurtful, and unacceptable behaviors that conflict with our university values and we condemn them. The university has reached out to those targeted by the actions to share information, resources, and support.
“The incident is actively being investigated by the appropriate university offices and processes. It’s important to note that student conduct cases, records, and any potential disciplinary action are protected by the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA).
“We are committed to maintaining a safe and welcoming environment for all of our students, faculty, staff, and visitors and will follow our processes to ensure the well-being and safety of our community.”
Landgreve said seeing the incident was especially upsetting because of the progress she believes the university has made.
“It just kind of upset me a little bit because I feel like the campus has grown so much progress and just seeing things set us back like that is very upsetting,” Landgreve said.
Bolton, who shared the video, does not want to speak with WMC until she has had an opportunity to speak with the university.

title: Judge dismisses case from Dolly Parton’s manager alleging her nephew threatened her estate
text:
(AP) - A Tennessee judge on Monday dismissed a case brought by Dolly Parton ’s longtime manager who was seeking an injunction against her nephew and head of security, alleging he had threatened her estate and its employees.
The manager, Danny Nozell, asked for the dismissal on Thursday after the two sides came to an agreement. The order from Chancellor I’Ashea L. Myles finalizes that request without prejudice, meaning it can be filed again.
Nozell, who runs She’s Alive, an entity founded to manage and protect Parton’s estate, had secured a temporary restraining order against Bryan Seaver and his security company, Squadron Augmented Protection Services, in September.
The complaint seeking the temporary restraining order said Seaver had threatened violence and the destruction of Parton’s legacy and business empire. Nozell wanted to turn the order into a permanent injunction against Seaver. The two sides were to have publicly argued the claims on Tuesday.
Seaver’s lawyers said in a statement Monday that he “cares deeply about his Aunt Dolly, her music, her family, and the legacy she left behind.”
“He has made a career out of protecting his aunt while she was alive and remains committed to Dolly and his family” the statement said. “Mr. Seaver is grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the entire family can continue to grieve peacefully and ensure that the bright light of Dolly’s legacy remains completely untouched.”
The dismissal brings a sudden and quiet end to a serious rift in the beloved country superstar’s inner circle that began while she was sick with cancer and spilled into public view in the weeks after her Aug. 25 death.
Neither side nor court documents have revealed anything about why the complaint was withdrawn, though one court filing said the sides had reached an agreement.
Emails requesting details and comment were sent to lawyers for Nozell and She’s Alive.
Seaver, who Parton had handpicked to announce her death, said in court filings that he considered Nozell a close friend and ally before the restraining order, and said the text messages Nozell cited as evidence of his threats were a “private conversation between two friends who were both frustrated, grieving and discussing strategy.”
Parton was a widely adored singer, songwriter, philanthropist and country music icon who rose from a log cabin in the Tennessee mountains to a stardom that spanned generations with songs including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5” and “I Will Always Love You.” She also left behind a business empire, much of it based in her hometown, that employed many of her close friends and family.

title: Maine deserves greater accountability on hospital commitments
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Denise McDonough is president of Anthem Blue Cross and Blue Shield in Maine,
and Patrick Woodcock is president and CEO of the Maine State Chamber of Commerce.
When it comes to healthcare, Maine is at a critical point.
Across our state, families are struggling with rising costs. Hospitals and other providers face significant financial and workforce pressures. Rural communities are working to preserve access to essential services. Employers and policymakers alike are asking how we can make healthcare more affordable while ensuring Mainers can get the care they need, when and where they need it.
At a moment like this, everyone in Maine’s healthcare ecosystem has a responsibility to put patients and communities first. That includes health plans like ours. It includes providers, policymakers and employers. And it includes Prime Healthcare Foundation.
When California-based Prime Healthcare Foundation sought approval to acquire Central Maine Healthcare, the case presented to Maine was clear: Central Maine was in financial distress and needed a partner with the resources and expertise to help secure its future.
Prime made significant commitments as part of that case. It pledged to invest $150 million in Central Maine’s facilities, employees and technology. It committed to maintaining access to care. And importantly, it assured Maine that local leadership and governance would continue to have a meaningful role in decisions affecting Maine patients, employees and communities.
Those commitments mattered. They mattered to state officials charged with evaluating the transaction. They mattered to community leaders. And they mattered to us. Like many others, we believed that if Prime followed through on its promises, the acquisition could provide needed stability while preserving a strong healthcare institution headquartered in Maine.
Today, there are reasons to be concerned that reality is not matching those commitments. We are seeing indications that consequential decisions affecting Maine healthcare are increasingly being made from afar. Questions remain about the existence and meaningful influence of the local governance that Mainers were told would remain in place. Patients have experienced disruption, and we are witnessing employee dissatisfaction at a time when retaining talented healthcare professionals is already one of Maine’s greatest challenges.
Healthcare is fundamentally local, and accountability to the communities we serve is important. Mainers benefit when decisions about access, affordability, and workforce stability reflect the needs of their communities and are informed by those who understand the challenges they face. Maintaining that local perspective and accountability is essential to ensuring Maine families have access to the care they need.
Maine cannot afford instability in its healthcare system. Our population is among the oldest in the country, many communities face shortages of healthcare professionals, and too many families already struggle with the cost of care. Every organization operating in this environment should be asking the same question: How do we preserve and expand access to high-quality, affordable healthcare for the people of Maine?
Prime has an important role in answering that question.
The path forward should begin with transparency and fulfillment of the commitments that helped make this acquisition possible. Mainers deserve a clear accounting of the promised $150 million investment: what has been invested, where it has been invested and what remains to be done. They deserve meaningful local governance with a genuine voice in decisions affecting Central Maine’s patients, employees and communities. And they deserve confidence that decisions about services will protect access to care rather than create additional disruption.
As healthcare and business leaders, we recognize the extraordinary pressures facing hospitals today. There are no easy answers, and responsible organizations sometimes must make difficult decisions. However, difficult circumstances make accountability and transparency more important, not less. Ultimately, we all benefit when there is stability, and it is essential that the community and the state have clarity on the challenges being faced and the steps being taken to address them. We remain committed to collaboration and welcome new opportunities to work together to address these challenges and strengthen Maine’s healthcare system.
This should not be about California versus Maine, or one healthcare organization versus another. It should be about keeping promises to the people who ultimately matter most: the patients, families, employees and communities who depend on Central Maine Healthcare.
Maine needs a strong and sustainable healthcare system. We need organizations willing to invest here, employ people here and become genuine partners in our communities. And when those organizations make commitments to Maine, we should expect them to keep them.
Prime came to Maine asking for the opportunity to help stabilize Central Maine Healthcare and secure its future. Maine gave it that opportunity. Now Prime must deliver.

title: Burnham woman awaits transfer to Montana on animal cruelty charges
text:
BELFAST, Maine (WABI) - A Burnham woman with multiple animal cruelty convictions in Maine will remain in jail while she awaits transfer to Montana to face similar charges.
Alexis Ingraham appeared by Zoom in a Waldo County courtroom Monday and asked a judge to release her so she could report to Montana on her own.
The judge denied the request for now but appointed an attorney who can ask the court to change her bail conditions.
Montana charges
Ingraham faces four misdemeanor animal cruelty charges in Montana involving four horses. She waived extradition last month.
The state asked for another court date later this month if Montana has not picked her up by then.
Maine sentence on appeal
Ingraham’s two-year jail sentence in the latest Maine case is on hold while she appeals.

title: Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 1/2 years in a British prison for rape and sexual assault
text:
LONDON (AP) — Russell Brand was sentenced Monday to 10½ years in prison for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others during a time when his bawdy behavior was indulged and celebrated during his rise to stardom.
Judge Joel Bennathan denounced Brand’s “casual and arrogant disregard” for any woman who said no to him, and castigated him for the series of lies he told in testimony denying assaults that dated to 2004.
“About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous,” Bennathan said. “You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator.”
Brand showed little emotion during the stinging rebuke. He turned to mouth the words “we’ll be OK” to his wife after he stood up and was led away by court officers after the hearing.
The 51-year-old actor-comedian, known for outrageous stand-up routines and provocative behavior on television and radio broadcasts, as well as battles with drugs and alcohol, had maintained his innocence and testified that all his encounters were consensual.
But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Prosecutor: Brand used fame to carry out crimes
The convictions — years after the #MeToo movement turned a spotlight on sexual abuse by the powerful and famous — raised questions about how Brand’s behavior was tolerated by TV and radio stations he worked for, including the BBC, and those around him.
“Mr. Brand abused the influence and power that came with his fame,” prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said. “He used it to facilitate access to women without which the offending could not have taken place. It also fed his own view that he could commit such offenses with impunity.”
Brand was supported by his wife, father and fans outside court
Brand wore a gray suit and an open collar shirt with a loose white tie. His long, graying hair was pulled back and knotted in a man bun atop his head. He clenched a crucifix in his right hand.
Defense lawyer Ian Winter urged the judge to consider Brand’s good character, saying his only previous conviction was for marijuana possession in 1995 and that he had performed charitable work and helped others overcome drug and alcohol abuse. He also asked the judge to consider the impact of the sentence on Brand’s family, particularly his three young children.
Brand was supported in Southwark Crown Court by his wife, Laura, and his father, Ron Brand. Laura entered the courthouse without Brand, who had been in since custody Thursday’s verdict.
A couple of Brand’s supporters, reflecting his recent conversion to Christianity, held a banner bearing crosses with the words: “Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth.”
Victims tell court it was difficult to see Brand celebrated in public
The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accounts from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand.
One of the women he was convicted of abusing spoke in court about the trauma the crime caused. The others provided statements read by the prosecutor.
A woman whom Brand groped during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004 said that the assault left her in shock and turmoil and made her feel like “damaged goods.”
“It was impossible to escape seeing him all over the media, being celebrated for his disgusting behavior against women like it was all a joke,” she said.
Brand stared straight ahead as she spoke from behind a curtain that shielded her from public view to preserve her identity.
Bennathan said Brand’s entourage may have written off the sexual assault as “laddish,” the boorish and obnoxious behavior for which Brand was known and with which he thought he could get away.
“It was outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal sexual offense, and as it turns out you haven’t got away with it,” the judge said.
Rape victim felt ‘powerless’
A former fan he was convicted of anally raping at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009 said that she was left feeling anxious and humiliated and had difficulty eating and sleeping, and went through periods of heavy drinking.
She said she spent months fearing that she might have contracted HIV and that it took years for her to speak up. She only came forward after police opened an investigation following the documentary.
“I felt that if I reported him, I would not be believed,” she said in the statement read by Karmy-Jones. “His fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance which made me feel powerless.”
Winter, the defense lawyer, argued that Brand should be “regarded as a man who went too far and overrode consent that had been given” following consensual sex.
The judge noted how disrespectfully Brand had treated the woman, including putting her in his phone contacts under “T” for “tart.”
A woman he was convicted of kissing and groping at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 said it had a lasting impact on her life.
“Since the sexual assault ... Russell Brand has managed to move on and even forget,” she said. “Over the years, hearing his voice on television, on social media or seeing his image made me jump.”
A woman says she was silenced by ‘culture at the time’
The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a woman who said the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.
“Immediately after the incident I spoke up, and sadly it was brushed under the carpet by senior management,” she said. “There was a culture at the time which meant I felt I had to just carry on and not talk about it anymore, which meant I did not give myself time to lament on it, boxed it up and pushed it aside.”
Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men’s bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.
Brand, who was known for edgy stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, rose to prominence in the early 2000s hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

title: New England governors call on Congress to tack on $3 billion in heating aid
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Gov. Janet Mills and five other New England governors are calling on members of Congress to provide an additional $3 billion in funding to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program ahead of this winter.
In a letter sent Monday to appropriations leaders in the U.S. House and Senate — including Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins, who chairs the Senate’s committee — Mills and the leaders of Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Connecticut expressed that time is of the essence.
“Whether through an increase in the annual appropriation or a one-time emergency supplemental funding, these additional resources are urgently needed,” the governors wrote.
The $3 billion increase the governors requested would bring the program’s funding to roughly $7 billion.
“At current funding levels, rising energy prices will erode the purchasing power of LIHEAP assistance, forcing states to reduce benefits or serve fewer eligible households when the need is greatest,” the letter says. “While our states are working to mitigate the immediate impact of rising energy costs on vulnerable households and continue to invest heavily in energy efficiency, weatherization, and other long-term solutions, these efforts cannot fully offset the immediate financial pressures facing families this winter.”
In a news release, Mills’ office noted Maine is the most heating-oil-dependent state in the nation, and that roughly 50% of Maine homes rely on oil as their primary heating source.
The price of heating oil in Maine has continued to set records this fall and now rests above $6 per gallon on average. Since the war with Iran began in late February, Maine heating oil prices have spiked roughly 57%.
“No one should be cold in their homes because (President Donald) Trump decided to wage an unnecessary, unwanted war with Iran,” Mills said in a written statement. “That’s why I’m joining my fellow New England governors to call on Congress to release billions in federal funding for LIHEAP to provide immediate relief for vulnerable families as winter approaches.”

title: How to talk about the end of life without feeling pressure to be strong
text:
(Aging Untold) — People don’t always get to control how life ends, but some get a moment to decide how they’ll say goodbye and who they’ll say goodbye to.
If you are the one saying goodbye, you do not have to stay strong for anyone else, according to the Aging Untold experts.
You are not there to manage anyone else’s emotions
“Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said a person who knows the end is near is not telling loved ones about it to manage their emotions.
“You need to be getting the support that you need,” Cradduck said.
She said she understands that others are going through the same grief and crisis because they are losing that person.
“But you need the support system,” she said.
If you’re the one hearing the news
Cradduck said people who hear this news from someone can be that support.
“Break down with them and be honest about those emotions, but don’t expect the person that’s dying to be the one that’s holding you up,” Cradduck said.
She said she has seen that happen too many times.
Some people want distance. Others want company.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke recalled sitting in church when the minister shared that he had been diagnosed with a terminal illness.
“You could hear a pin drop,” she said.
The minister asked people not to come up and ask him questions or talk to him, O’Rourke said. He said he needed distance and space, but he wanted the congregation to know because they would see physical changes in him.
“I had the utmost respect for that,” she said. “We all have to die on our own terms.”
Others go a different route.
They may say they don’t have much time left and want to spend it together, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said everyone is different.
“You really don’t know how it might hit you either way,” she said.
She listed grief, unfinished business and relationships among the things a person may be dealing with.
Start with what you need, then ask for it
Ambrose suggested a conversation starter: “I wish I had more time, but let’s make the best of the time that’s left.”
Another option, Rogers said, is to say: “This is how I’d like you to celebrate my life.”
O’Rourke said the first step is to think through what you need and then ask for it.
She said some people who are dying don’t want to talk about it. They want to go and experience life, and they don’t want someone looking at them with sympathy.
Living or existing
People have a choice every day to live their lives to the fullest or to exist, Cradduck said. That choice remains after a terminal diagnosis.
“You can live every day until you pass through your final sunset, or you can exist every day,” Cradduck said. “I have seen people do it both ways.”
She said she has seen people who were actively dying who were still doing things they wanted to do and accomplish.
We live in a society that has a problem talking about death and dying, Cradduck said.
“We don’t like to face mortality, and it’s the reason why we don’t plan for it,” she said.
She said she admires anyone who can face it “with the grace and respect for themselves and everyone else around them.”
When you’re invited into the conversation
Ambrose said the conversation can be awkward and people often don’t know how to act. The minister’s request let the congregation off the hook so they didn’t feel they had to address it, she added.
For people who want to talk openly, listeners should engage rather than brush it off by saying, “Oh, Mom, let’s not talk about that,” Ambrose said.
“Give people that peace to be able to speak either way when you’re invited into those conversations,” she said.
