title: FDA adds rare vision-loss warning to popular GLP-1 drugs
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Popular weight loss drugs including Ozempic and Wegovy will carry a new warning about a possible rare side effect that can sometimes lead to permanent vision loss, U.S. health regulators announced Monday.
The Food and Drug Administration said the risk will be added to the labeling of all GLP-1 drugs, the blockbuster medications used to treat obesity, diabetes and several other medical conditions. The class includes a dozen injectable or pill-based drugs, including widely used brands like Zepbound and Mounjaro.
The eye condition, known as non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, can cause significant vision loss. The problem, which has been reported with all GLP-1 drugs, is caused by decreased blood flow to the optic nerve, although the underlying cause isn’t understood, the FDA said.
FDA scientists began looking into the problem after the publication of a 2024 medical paper tying the condition to certain patients taking semaglutide, the active drug in Eli Lilly’s Ozempic.
An FDA analysis of more than 125 clinical trials found that the problem occurred in roughly 6 of every 100,000 patients who took a GLP-1 for at least one year. The comparable rate for people taking a placebo or other types of glucose-lowering medications was less than 4 per 100,000, the FDA said.
The agency also found reports of the problem in its electronic reporting system for drug injuries and side effects.
Symptoms of the problem include blurred vision, blind spots, distorted colors and other visual disturbances, according to the FDA. Patients experiencing such problems should contact a health care professional immediately, the agency said.

title: Couple finds at least 25 snakes in newly purchased home
text:
SALVISA, Ky. (WKYT/Gray News) - Jessica and Johnathan Perry bought their first house in August, but their dream home in Kentucky came with an unwelcome surprise.
Three weeks after the purchase, the couple found their first snake.
“I was actually taking out the trash. My son and I were home alone and I walked out the door, and there was a snake on the porch. I immediately called my husband and then my dad to try to get somebody to come out here to get it,” Jessica Perry said. “Then, a few days later, we found another, and a few days later, another. Then one night, about a week after finding the first one, Johnathan and his friend came down in the basement and found two adults and several juveniles in the basement.”
An infestation
The Perrys said they have found at least 25 snakes inside the home.
“At this point, in just a few months, that’s an infestation,” Jessica Perry said.
Multiple home inspections before closing did not reveal a snake den beneath the front porch.
“We hired a contractor to come out and actually dig out the concrete. When they busted through the middle, there were dozens and dozens of snake eggs, new and what looked like several years old,” Jessica Perry said.
‘The Snake House’
Neighbors told the couple the home had a reputation.
“One neighbor had said that, ‘I’m surprised that the previous owners didn’t tell you all that the snakes were free with purchase,’” Jessica Perry said.
Jessica Perry also contacted a previous owner, who told her it was nicknamed the “snake house” when he was a child.
“Now that we have found out that it’s a decades-old problem, what worries us now is that there are multiple dens within the foundation of the home, and in order to eradicate and mitigate that, you essentially have to bust down the entire home, but that’s our worst fear,” Jessica Perry said.
The snakes are not venomous, but the Perrys are worried about their 5-year-old son.
“Not necessarily that we’d be scared that they’d bite him. Snakes like warmth. So, if they were to get in the upper level and get in the bed or whatever, they could curl up around his neck, per se,” Johnathan Perry said.
Searching the basement for snakes has become a daily routine. The family has gotten more cats and cleared brush near a creek, with more work planned for the spring.
“We just bought the home in August and we’re already financially out thousands and thousands of dollars trying to fix an unanticipated problem that we didn’t have, or we didn’t anticipate having when we purchased it,” Jessica Perry said.
“It’s sad to say on a new home we just bought that it’s become a chore, I guess, that every evening we get home, we ask each other, ‘Have you gone to the basement yet to check for snakes?’” Johnathan Perry added.
The work includes removing the back porch to check for another den and addressing potential foundation problems. The process is expected to take months and cost thousands of dollars.
A friend of the family has set up a GoFundMe to help pay for the additional work.
What to do if a snake is found indoors
Kat Dale, lead keeper at the Kentucky Reptile Zoo, said a person who is sure a snake is nonvenomous can carefully remove it.
“If the snake is scared, it might do a couple things, like it might try to bite because it doesn’t understand. It might also musk, which will release a very smelly odor to protect itself, or shake its tail. So, if you understand their behavior and are OK with their reactions when they’re frightened, you could handle it and get them out by hand,” Dale said.
Dale said another option is to guide the snake into a large container or lift it with the end of a broom or a similar object. She emphasized that extermination is not the answer: Snakes benefit nature and help control pests.
If a snake cannot be confidently identified, do not handle it; contact a qualified wildlife professional for help.

title: The system worked in Democrats’ favor. Now what?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Michael Conathan is a former U.S. Senate staffer, a climate and ocean policy expert and served as lead consultant for Maine’s Blue Economy Task Force. He lives in South Portland.
Last Tuesday, years of declining faith in the foundations of American government came to a head. In the face of real fear about the rise of fascism and the death of democracy, the country demonstrated the strength of our founders’ vision.
The blue wave that so many Democrats rode to victories in the midterm elections reminded us that votes still matter. That the collective is more powerful than the billions of dollars spent to drown us out. And that the overwhelming majority of our fellow citizens have had it with the bloviation and excess of the MAGA movement.
Democrats across Maine and around the country earned this historic victory. We built our case, each in our own way, to reach our own audience. The resulting win is not for the punditry or the donor class or the party machine. It’s for everyone who felt forsaken or duped. Everyone who repudiated the political sleight of hand that told us transgender kids in sports is a bigger problem than tax breaks for billionaires. Everyone who despaired as our neighbors were kidnapped and killed by government-sanctioned goon squads in the streets of Minnesota, Maine and Texas.
As the election’s euphoria and afterglow fades to examination and action, Democrats must consider what to prioritize. A wave of this magnitude constitutes a mandate. But a mandate for what?
On Donald Trump’s watch, Republicans made the mistake of taking their newfound voters for granted, assuming those who seized on his pledges of “Make Eggs Cheap Again” and “No New Wars” would join the GOP camp forever. They redrew districts that backfired spectacularly after discarding those promises. Ultimately, their red hubris led them into the path of an overwhelming blue tide.
Democrats should learn from Republican mistakes. As much as this election constituted an endorsement of progressive policies, it was first and foremost a course correction. The mad captain steering our country’s ship seized the wheel and spun us wildly off the chart. Voters have now given us a chance to straighten out and avoid the rocky shoals ahead.
As Democrats now take the controls in Washington and with an even greater majority in Augusta, we should remember that when at the helm of a ship it’s easy to oversteer. To get back on course, you at first turn sharply, then must anticipate the swing of the bow and straighten out before the wind, currents and tide push you too far in the other direction.
This election has brought us from one extreme back to the middle, not to its polar opposite. Republican strongholds in the South and Midwest have not suddenly become bastions of socialism, and they will not tolerate what they perceive to be the imposition of extreme progressive values. The same goes for many Maine districts that flipped blue last week.
An opportunity now exists to translate these wins into lasting, progressive policy change. But doing so will require compromise. Coalition building. Really listening to what voters want, what they fear and how they want to live.
Democrats will leverage their majority to pursue a bold agenda including national priorities such as universal health and childcare, equitable tax reform, climate action, civil rights and rational immigration policy, empathetic foreign policy and diplomacy.
Here in Maine, they will back Governor-elect Hannah Pingree’s stated priorities of housing, healthcare and strong communities. The first order of business is outlining specific actions to achieve those goals.
Then we must take time with independents and Republicans who voted blue. Welcome them the way we aspire to welcome immigrant neighbors. Don’t force them to assimilate immediately. Build bridges. Share meals. Listen. Hear their rationale. And, where we can find alignment, make changes and concessions that reflect their concerns.
We won’t all agree, and they won’t all stay. But this is the way to create a coalition with the staying power capable of creating lasting impact. This is critical, because accomplishing these goals will take time.
Politics is loud and flashy and pointed. But at its core, it exists to do the business of governing by making policy. Creating thoughtful, durable policy is quiet and slow and methodical. And, yes, boring. Which is exactly how the system was designed.
Winning is euphoric, and the victors should celebrate. Policymaking is tedious, and we have to do it anyway. Last week, the system functioned as designed. The guardrails held. The people have spoken.
Now the real work begins.

title: Judge’s ruling could clear way for Lindsay Clancy to be tried again in deaths of her 3 kids
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A judge on Monday denied a motion to dismiss the murder case against Lindsay Clancy, potentially clearing the way for her to be retried next year in the deaths of her three young children.
Clancy’s defense team had asked the court to end the case based on an unusual argument that the judge shouldn’t have declared a mistrial in September when jurors were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. They argued that the judge should have removed the one juror who favored conviction, then allowed jury deliberations to continue.
But Judge William Sullivan disagreed, saying he saw no other option than to declare a mistrial.
“Because the court concludes that there was manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy,” Sullivan wrote.
A spokesperson for Plymouth County District Attorney Timothy Cruz declined to comment.
Clancy has never denied that she killed her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued that Clancy had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior.
Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy had mental health problems, but they said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy, but they haven’t settled on whether they will pursue the same charges or opt for a reduced charge that might be more palatable for the jury.
The next hearing is Nov. 16.
In the motion to dismiss, one of Clancy’s lawyers, Martin Weinberg, argued that the judge should have thoroughly interrogated jurors after the foreperson sent two notes saying the one juror who favored conviction wasn’t following the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt.
Sullivan said that type of questioning is barred by law.
“Because the secrecy of jury deliberations is a bedrock of our judicial system, any inquiry into the jury’s deliberative process would improperly intrude into the jury’s function,” Sullivan wrote.
The judge also said he didn’t believe the jury foreperson’s claim that the holdout juror — identified in court papers by the pseudonym Juror Doe — wasn’t following the law.
“In context, the notes appear to express the foreperson’s belief that Juror Doe must be refusing to follow the law because Juror Doe would not agree with the majority’s view of the case,” Sullivan wrote. “Given that the jury unquestionably had reached an impasse, the Court did not and does not view the foreperson’s notes as reliable evidence of Juror Doe’s inability or refusal to deliberate or follow the law.”
On Monday, Sullivan also denied prosecutors’ request for a gag order while the case remains pending, to avoid influencing a future jury. Clancy’s attorney Kevin Reddington gave interviews during the trial, while prosecutors generally didn’t speak to reporters. Clancy’s lawyers argued that it would amount to an unconstitutional restraint on speech.
Sullivan also denied a defense motion to preserve certain records related to the first trial that potentially could have been used to further investigate the conduct of the juror who wanted to convict Clancy.
“In the Court’s view, Clancy is not entitled to any of the materials sought in this motion,” Sullivan wrote.

title: Trump says he was just kidding about making UFC’s Dana White his press secretary
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump said Sunday he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary after announcing on social media he had offered his close friend the job.
After his party’s deep losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump shook up his administration on Friday by replacing his chief of staff and followed up on Saturday with a post that said he had offered the press secretary job to White. On Sunday, Trump said it was “just a little fun.”
“I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump said, speaking to reporters in Florida before departing for the White House. White is set to visit him at the White House on Monday.
The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump on Friday named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller is the architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies. Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia, who faltered behind the lectern and in interviews, and left the post after five days.

title: Sophomore standouts, and other takeaways from field hockey finals
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
Cheverus remained on top, Nokomis returned after more than a decade away, and Foxcroft Academy put its dominance on display at the field hockey state championships Saturday.
Here are a few takeaways from a raw and rainy afternoon and evening at Edward Little High School:
STELLAR SOPHOMORES
Looking to form a Miss Maine Field Hockey watch list for 2028? You may want to start with players who were on the turf Saturday.
All three champions had second-year players playing central roles in their victories and showing an impressive array of talents.
In the Class A game, Brooke Brunelle — whose sister Sydney is a senior and Miss Maine finalist — was tenacious defending in the midfield and was one of the Stags’ fastest players getting the ball up the field.
She didn’t find the net, but she had an assist on freshman Avery Tinker’s goal, took the ball down the left side for a chance early in the fourth quarter and was a primary ball handler on corners.
In the B game, Maeve Rush of Nokomis dazzled with the ball on her stick. She was the Warriors’ most dangerous player in the open field, showed elimination skills to get around defenders, and had the vision and passing ability to find teammates on the attack.
“The biggest thing I’ve always noticed is the way that she can distribute the ball and her vision,” Nokomis coach Lauren Neal said. “That’s something that not everybody can get to, and having that automatically brings you to that next level.”
In Foxcroft’s 2-0 win in Class C, Addie Rayfield showed why she’s the Penobscot Valley Conference Player of the Year while potting a pair of goals, burying the second on a perfectly placed reverse that beat the goalie inside the right post while she was moving to her left.
“She’s an amazing player,” said senior Jenna Hartford, who assisted on both goals.
GAMER GOALIES
There were no blowouts Saturday, with each game decided by two or fewer goals. The goalies were a big reason why.
In the Class A game, Cheverus turned its pressure into 16 corners but only scored on one of them. Mt. Ararat goalie Jaymie Bergman was excellent (the Eagles’ book credited her for 18 saves). She used the space well in front of the cage to cut off angles, read the ball well through traffic, and got back to prevent Stags forwards from knocking in shots by the posts.
In the Class C nightcap, Foxcroft kept the play almost exclusively in the Winthrop/Maranacook end of the field, forcing netminder Cyara Harriman to keep the Ramblers in the game. She was up for the challenge, making eight saves while frequently batting and kicking balls away to steer traffic from the goal.
As a result, Winthrop kept the game scoreless for over 42 minutes, and kept alive its hopes of an eighth state title against the second-highest scoring team in state history.
DOESN’T HAVE TO BE PRETTY
Cheverus throughout the season showed a knack for the gritty goal, putting a long, bouncing shot toward the net and looking for a stick to deflect it in, or taking a shot on goal and crashing on the rebound to be the first ones to knock it home.
With players like Tinker (20 goals this season), Mary McCartney (16) and Jaylee Radford (13) up front, Cheverus often cashed in that way this fall, and became lethal on corners.
“You don’t get any points for style,” Cheverus coach Andrea Musante said.
Cheverus didn’t need the style points to take a 1-0 lead. Brooke Brunelle took a shot on a corner, with Tinker standing by Bergman awaiting a deflection. Bergman made the initial stop but lost her footing, and Tinker scrambled to the rebound and got the shot off before Bergman could get into position and scored off her pad.
THEY’LL BE BACK?
So what could the matchups next year look like? Well, with none of the teams that played Saturday being gutted by graduation, maybe pretty similar to this year’s.
In Class A, both Cheverus and Mt. Ararat are built well for next fall. The Stags, who have already proven their staying power with four straight undefeated seasons, graduate Sydney Brunelle, center midfielder Ava Martin and McCartney from their starting lineup, but bring back their backfield as well as three of their top five scorers.
Mt. Ararat loses Krystah Coen (the Eagles’ lone scorer Saturday) and Sarah Middleton in the backfield, and Maddy Sweet and Addison Chubbuck up top, but seven starters return and freshman Leah Lafrance is poised to become a top goal scorer in the state. Midfielder Kam Chase and center back Emma Graffam return as the Eagles’ backbone.
In Class B, Freeport was supposed to be rebuilding this year, and instead came within a goal of the state championship. Seven starters will be back, including top threats Dalila McCarthy and Ava Emmons, as well as goalie Lydia Costa.
Nokomis will say goodbye to midfielder MaKenzie Watson, perhaps its top all-around player Saturday, but seven starters, including Rush, impressive freshmen Ava Roundy and defensive standout Ella Toulouse ,are returning.
In Class C, Winthrop will see five starters leave, including two defenders and Harriman, but the Ramblers have shown their ability to contend year-in and year-out. And Foxcroft brings back seven starters, including Rayfield and freshmen Kaydiense Nelson and Lilah French, both of whom thrived on the championship stage. Nobody’s beaten the Ponies in two years, and it’s not going to get much easier.

title: Looking Back week of Nov. 12
text:
Clearwater, Fla.
Some athletes like to run. Others prefer bicycling. And still others swim. David Painter of Bar Harbor, who competed in the Ironman 70.3 challenge here last Saturday, excels at all three. Ironman 70.3 is shorthand for events in which the distances are half those of the original Ironman contests. On Saturday, competitors tested themselves in a 1.2-mile swim, a 56-mile bike race and a 13.1-mile run. For Dr. Painter, who has competed in full Ironman triathlons, Saturday’s event was a chance for him to attain a personal goal — finishing the entire race in less than five hours. He did it with more than five minutes to spare. “It’s a great event. It was unlike anything I’ve done before,” he said on Tuesday. “My goal was to do all three in under five hours and I did that,” he continued. “I’m very happy with that. I had a good race.” With a total time of 4:54:21, Dr. Painter placed in the middle of his age group, coming in 53 out of 112 in his division. Overall there were more than 1,500 entrants. According to Dr. Painter, training on Mount Desert Island got him in good shape for competing on the relatively flat Florida terrain. “Here all we have is hills and mountains.”

title: UMSG approves funding for Alpha Omicron Pi self-defense program
text:
The University of Maine Student Government (UMSG) met on Nov. 3 in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union. During the meeting, UMSG granted final recognition to Students for the Exploration and Development of Space and approved funding for Alpha Omicron Pi’s self-defense program.
Club Business
Shane Barker, president of Students for the Exploration and Development of Space, stood before UMSG to request final recognition. Barker explained how the organization differed from the American Institute of Aeronautics Club and clarified that it will consist of two teams.
The balloon development team will meet Fridays at 1 p.m. and the rocketry development team will meet Thursdays at 5 p.m., both in Room 202 of Barrows Hall. Students for the Exploration and Development of Space will request funding from UMSG for general hardware for the club. The Senate granted final recognition.
Funding Requests
A representative from Alpha Omicron Pi stood before UMSG to request $1,694 in funding for a self-defense program. The program was scheduled for Nov. 8 from 1 to 5 p.m. and would feature two 90-minute sessions. The representative explained that the Office of Fraternity and Sorority Life and a panel would contribute $250 each to cover the remaining costs of hosting the program.
All Maine Women and It’s On Us would co-host the program, which would include a craft room for those who felt overwhelmed by the self-defense activities. The representative stated that $94 of the requested amount would go toward supplies for the craft room. The Senate approved the request.
Upcoming Events
Alpha Omicron Pi was scheduled to host a self-defense event on Nov. 8 in the Bangor Room of the Memorial Union, with sessions from 1 to 2:30 p.m. and 3 to 4:30 p.m.
Veterans Day is Nov. 11, and there will be no classes.
Buffalo Wild Wings will host wing night on Nov. 11 at 6 p.m. in Wells Commons, where 23 different types of sauces will be available. Karaoke will also be held.
A Battle of the Bands event will be held Nov. 13 at 6 p.m. at the Collins Center for the Arts.
The Student Heritage Alliance will host a friends and family fest Nov. 19 from 5 to 7 p.m. in the north pod of the Memorial Union.
With no further matters to discuss, the meeting adjourned.

title: Greene man arrested by Maine State Police and charged with aggravated drug trafficking
text:

title: Maine drought conditions persist despite rainy weekend
Maine Lobstermen's Association hopeful that right whale data is enough to prevent regulations
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Lobstermen's Association hopeful that right whale data is enough to prevent regulations
Following the release of research conducted by the National Marine Fisheries Service, the Maine Lobstermen's Association hopes it is enough to prevent currently paused regulations they say could decimate the industry.
The NMFS has managed the Maine Lobster Fishery since the late 1990s but, following an increase in deaths of the endangered right whale, they began to take action.
In 2023, an appeals court that sided with Maine's lobstermen ordered a pause for certain regulations, which included the expansion of areas that couldn't be fished, a decrease in the number of traps people could use, an increase in the weakness of rope and more. According to the MLA, it was a call for a 90% reduction of risk.
"I really feel genuinely the Maine lobster fishery had a target on its back," stated the executive director of the MLA, Patrice McCarron.
According to the NMFS, which have not provided a comment, 24 right whale calves were identified since the last birthing season. It's the highest since 2009 and the fourth-highest since recording began. That brings the total to 380, including 70 reproductively active females.
"It looks like the risk posed by the fishery is much lower than previously anticipated," said McCarron.
McCarron claimed that data that had originally sparked interest in the regulations on lobstermen were taken from 'worst-case scenarios.'
"The Maine Lobstermen Association never would have sued the federal government," added McCarron. "We never would have had the data we needed, had every lobsterman not consistently said, 'It is not my gear, it is not our gear. We don't see right whales here. We don't see our gear on the whales.'"
The Maine Department of Marine Resources also released a statement on the data, stating that it's positive for Maine's fixed gear fisheries.
It says a meeting scheduled for December will be postponed so the data can be analyzed.
A final ruling on the regulations is expected by the end of 2028, if not sooner.

title: UMaine Culturefest celebrates food and traditions from around the world
text:
Every year, the Office of International Programs (OIP) hosts Culturefest at the New Balance Student Recreation Center, with this year’s event held Saturday, Nov. 7. The floors of the basketball and hockey courts were filled with tables, banners, food and guests milling about. Other than career-related outreach programs, Culturefest seems to be the most heavily attended event of the year, and certainly an anticipated one.
“Everyone likes food,” said Riley St. Pierre, a fourth-year civil engineering student and the president of the Franco-American Resource Opportunity Group (FAROG). St. Pierre was tabling for the group and flipping crepes when I walked over. “It’s such a great event because you get to try food from every culture. Lots that you would never get to try otherwise.”
St. Pierre talked about how food is not only the center of many world cultures, but it manifests in the everyday lives and routines of regular people.
“You know, we’re not from across the world, we’re from right here. But it can be equally as important. We’ve had a lot of people come by and say things like, ‘Oh my god — I’m from Northern Maine’ or ‘I’m from wherever and I used to eat this growing up.’ Sometimes it’s trying new things and sometimes it’s reconnecting with part of your culture that you haven’t seen represented,” said St. Pierre.
Other groups like Diaspora Pa’lante Collective hoped to turn the heads of University of Maine students towards issues they would not naturally encounter.
“My name is Black Wolf; black like the color, wolf like the animal,” said one of the two members behind the booth introducing themselves. “We are an organization that struggles for the independence of Puerto Rico. The majority of information we have here is about the history of that struggle.”
Wolf explained that the group had been invited to Culturefest for the first time this year and that they were excited to table somewhere that young adults could hear their message.
“I don’t think that I’ve had any negative interactions regarding our booth and what we’re trying to represent here. I think our booth has been very educational for people and a lot of people are opening their eyes to the struggle for independence [in Puerto Rico],” said Wolf.
One of the pamphlets on the group’s table drew connections between the experiences of people in Maine, Puerto Rico and Gaza. It highlighted how something that might be an inconvenience to some, such as a power outage, can have life-or-death consequences for others. And if Culturefest is about anything, it is about remembering the diversity of experiences around the world.
A few tables away, the Bangor Chinese School tabled with one of their students excitedly at the front.
“I am Brianna Walton. My Chinese name is Wan Yana, and I’ve been a student since I was in first grade. I am now in seventh grade,” said Walton.
Walton began at the school because of her interest in learning a new language, and her appreciation for the culture grew from there.
“I can tell stories in Chinese, I can play Chinese instruments — I went to China a couple of years ago with my sister and my mother,” Walton said. Because she has no Chinese heritage, Walton’s exploration of Chinese culture has been less based on a set tradition and more related to following her own individual interests.
These three moments of conversation at Culturefest give a disappointingly small glimpse of the real experience. Even in my short time there, much more ground was covered than I could hope to explain to anyone. The scent of food, the many children playing, the looks of excitement on the faces of those behind tables sharing something they care deeply about — it is a very multifaceted event that anyone would benefit greatly from attending.

title: Judge denies key motions in Lindsay Clancy case, clearing path for retrial decision
text:
Judge denies three key motions in Lindsay Clancy case, clearing path for decision about second trial
Three significant motions filed in connection with the case against Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, were denied on Monday by a superior court judge.
Judge William Sullivan, of the Plymouth Superior Court, heard arguments on all three of the motions last week. WMTW sister station WCVB reports that Sullivan issued the following rulings on Monday:
- Sullivan denied without prejudice the prosecution's motion for a gag order, which would have blocked attorneys from speaking to the press about the case. He allowed the prosecution to renew the request "if circumstances change and it can demonstrate that a prior restraint is necessary."
- Sullivan denied a defense motion to dismiss the case on the grounds that retrying Clancy would constitute double jeopardy. He rejected the defense's argument that the lone holdout on the jury should have been replaced before a mistrial was declared.
- Sullivan also denied the defense request for an inquiry into the holdout juror, including allegations of lying on his questionnaire and using a cellphone while in the jury room. "Because Clancy has failed to demonstrate that the requested evidence is relevant and material to her defense at any retrial of the murder indictment, the Court declines to exercise its discretion to order production," Sullivan wrote. "Nor can the Court perceive any valid justification for examining Juror Doe under oath at this point in the proceedings."
Clancy, 36, was on trial over the summer for the deaths of 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan at their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. Her defense argued she was not criminally responsible for murder because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings.
The jury was ultimately deadlocked, with a reported 11-1 split in favor of acquittal after seven days of deliberations. A mistrial was declared.
Last week, when Sullivan asked the prosecutors whether they were planning to pursue another trial, Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague replied, "We're not at that point yet."
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington, however, was more direct.
"I want a trial, and I want it with you, and I want it this spring," he told the judge.
Clancy's case is scheduled to return to court on Nov. 16, and District Attorney Tim Cruz said he would "be talking more" about the path forward after that hearing.

title: US offers $20 million reward for info on Iran’s nuclear program
text:
(CNN) - The United States government is offering a $20 million reward for information on Iran’s nuclear program.
The State Department announced the reward Friday on social media.
The department hopes to get recent information on Iran’s nuclear facilities, equipment and personnel. The department also said the opportunity to relocate may be offered to some informants.
Last year, officials said the International Atomic Energy Agency reported that Iran was able to enrich uranium to 60% purity.
That is a step away from the 90% purity required for nuclear weapons.

title: Probation Violation Keeps Rumford Stabbing Suspect Jailed Without Bail
text:
A man from Oxford County, who was recently placed on probation following a felony drug conviction from 2025, was back behind bars this weekend after police say he allegedly tried to stab someone in the face.
Read More: Maine Gold Scam, Man Sentenced To Nine Years In Prison
According to the Rumford Police Department, 38-year-old Paul Moor of Mexico, Maine, was a suspect in a stabbing incident outside 323 Waldo Street in Rumford on Sunday.
Authorities say they were called to the address just after 4 PM on November 8th for a report of a stabbing. Rumford PD, along with the Oxford County Sheriff's Office, arrived at the scene and determined that two men had been arguing outside the residence. Things started as a shouting match, then took a violent turn when a knife was introduced to the mix and was used to slash one of the men in the face.
"The victim, a 38-year-old Rumford resident, sustained a non-life-threatening facial laceration. He was evaluated at the scene by MedCare Ambulance personnel but declined transportation to the hospital for further treatment...The suspect was identified by the victim and witnesses."
Authorities initially believed, based on preliminary information, that the suspect, Paul Moore, was hiding nearby, so they set up a perimeter and searched for him.
Read More: Maine Drug Busts Net the Seizure of Fentanyl, Cocaine And Illegal Guns
Officers searched the immediate area for several hours and into the next day, but did not find Moore until Monday morning at about 10:15 AM.
They arrested him, and he was taken to the Oxford County Jail and charged with Aggravated Assault. The charges were heightened to a class B Felony because he had allegedly used a dangerous weapon to cause bodily harm to someone.
He would have been allowed out on $1000 cash bail, but since he violated the conditions of his original probation from his original conviction last year, he is being held without bail until he appears in court.

title: BH planning board reviews BRES renovation
text:
Things are moving ahead for Boothbay Region Elementary School's renovations. Sept. 10, the Boothbay Harbor planning board heard from BRES project representative Kendra Marass during its site plan application completeness review.
The project will include two building additions, including a formal entrance with vestibule, administrative offices, new middle school classrooms and student common area, as well as internal renovations throughout, Marass explained. For site improvements, the plan proposes a formal bus and parent drop-off area,additional parking closer to the entrance and pedestrianareas with enhanced Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) accessibility.
The southern parking lot will be restriped to accommodate bus parking, the playground will be moved and a subsurface sand filter will be used for stormwater treatment. For utilities, there will be an electric extension of three-phase from Townsend Avenue to the school. Existingsewer and water will be extended to the additions.
The board unanimously deemed the site plan application complete on the condition that the applicant provide the required fee, indicate the 75-foot wetland setback on the plan maps, provide proof of a Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) Site Location of Development application, and intention to receive a safety fire inspection.
The next step is a public hearing scheduled for Oct. 14 at 6 p.m.
In other business, Mark and Kathie Eldridge proposed landscaping and aesthetic improvements to 19 By-Way, where Romar Bowling Lanes was. According to a project statement from Carson Douglas Landscape Architecture, invasive weed species will be removed from the ledge area in favor of native plantings, the concrete jersey barriers and security fencing will be replaced with a wooden and cable rail fence to match the footbridge, and a wooden viewing deck will be constructed. The current parking lot and Carefree Boat Club building and usage will remain unchanged.
The board praised the idea but said the project's appearance before them was premature. It was recommendedthe Eldridges return to the code enforcement officer to flesh out their application.
Caroline Ivens and Emily Hall presented a change of use for the Christian Science building at 25 Oak St. to become a Pilates studio.This ran into a technical issue since the pair didn'town the building anddidn'tprovide evidence that they had authority to speak on the owner's behalf.
However, Ivens and Hall explained thatpurchasing the building is reliant on planning board approval for the change of use. Chair Merritt Blakeslee recommendedacquiring a letter from the church authorizing them to apply for the property, despite not yet being owners.
The continued public hearing for Boothbay Harbor Waterfront Preservation was rescheduled for Sept. 28.

title: Tigers Kevin McGonigle beats out Red Sox pitcher Payton Tolle for AL Rookie of the Year
text:
Detroit Tigers infielder Kevin McGonigle won the American League Rookie of the Year award Monday night after a stellar all-around season that sets him up to be a franchise cornerstone for the next decade.
Red Sox left-handed pitcher Payton Tolle finished third in the voting, behind Cleveland pitcher Parker Messick.
McGonigle — who played most of the season at just 21 years old — had a .278 batting average and .806 OPS with 18 homers, 72 RBI, 28 doubles and 12 stolen bases while splitting time between third base and shortstop. He’s the first Tigers player to win the award since pitcher Michael Fulmer in 2016 and the first Tigers infielder since Lou Whitaker in 1978.
The Tigers thought enough of McGonigle’s potential that they signed him to a $150 million, eight-year deal in April, just a few weeks into his rookie season. He backed up that confidence by making the All-Star team and helping the Tigers remain in the playoff race for much of the summer.
McGonigle received 28 of 30 first-place votes. The balloting was conducted before the postseason.
Messick had a 12-9 record with a 2.56 ERA and 193 strikeouts while Tolle was 9-6 with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts.
The National League winner will be announced later Monday night.
Red Sox manager Chad Tracy, who took over in April after Alex Cora was fired, and led Boston tot he playoffs, is a finalist for AL Manger of the Year along with Kevin Cash of the AL champion Rays and Will Venable of the White Sox. The winner will be announced on Tuesday.

title: Manhattan rallies past UMaine men’s basketball
Monday Five and Five: From Championship Saturday to Winter Sports
text:
Monday Five and Five: A Gold Ball Comes Home and Winter Begins
That’s a wrap on the fall sports season.
And what a way to finish it.
Five Aroostook County soccer teams played for state championships Saturday, Wisdom brought home its first girls soccer Gold Ball, and four other County teams finished their seasons as state runners-up.
Normally, this is where the calendar would finally slow down.
Not this year.
Some basketball teams are already practicing, girls hockey is underway, postseason soccer honors are coming and the rest of the winter sports calendar isn’t far behind.
So for one final time this fall, here are my five from last week and five things I’m watching this week.
Five From Last Week
5. Madawaska Brings Home the Class D North Championship
Madawaska’s boys had one more big win left in them before heading to the state championship.
The Owls beat Fort Fairfield 2-0 in the Class D North final, with Aiden Gagnon and Josh Querze scoring first-half goals and Aleck Gendreau recording the shutout.
It was the third straight season Madawaska and Fort Fairfield met for the regional championship, and this time the Owls earned the trip south.
Madawaska’s season ended Saturday against Monmouth in the state final, but a Northern Maine championship and a state runner-up finish is still one heck of a season.
4. Fort Kent Girls Make It Four Straight
At this point, reaching the Class C North championship has become familiar territory for Fort Kent.
Winning it has too.
The Lady Warriors shut out Orono 3-0 to capture their fourth straight regional championship.
Reece Doucette scored twice, Hayden Plourde added another and Fort Kent’s defense kept Orono off the board.
That sent Fort Kent to its fourth consecutive state championship game before the Warriors finished as state runners-up against Maranacook.
3. Fort Kent Boys Win It in Overtime
The Fort Kent boys earned their trip to states in about as dramatic a way as possible.
Orono scored first, but Dominic Cyr answered for the Warriors before eventually getting another opportunity almost immediately after overtime began.
Cyr converted the penalty kick just 36 seconds into overtime, giving Fort Kent a 2-1 victory and the Class C North championship.
The Warriors then battled Hall-Dale in Saturday’s state championship before coming up just short, 1-0.
Regional champion. State runner-up. And one unforgettable overtime finish along the way.
2. Wisdom Boys Win a Wild Northern Maine Championship
If you were looking for one of the craziest games of championship week, Wisdom and Piscataquis delivered it.
The Pioneers won 5-4, with Cayden Hargrove scoring four times in the second half.
And somehow that still wasn’t the game-winner.
With just 13 seconds remaining, Zeke Cyr found the back of the net and sent Wisdom to the Eight-Player state championship.
The Pioneers eventually finished as state runners-up to Telstar, but that regional championship game is going to be remembered for a long time.
Four second-half goals from one player and a championship winner with 13 seconds left.
That’s tournament soccer.
1. Wisdom Girls Make History
There really wasn’t another choice for No. 1.
Wisdom’s girls are state champions for the first time in program history.
And they had to come from behind to do it.
Bangor Christian led 1-0 before Emma Soucy tied the game in the second half.
Then Ellie Cyr took over.
Cyr scored twice late, including the goal that put Wisdom ahead for good, as the Lady Pioneers rallied for a 3-1 victory right here in Presque Isle.
Mikayl Michaud made eight saves in goal.
It was also redemption in every sense of the word. Bangor Christian had beaten Wisdom twice during the regular season and defeated the Pioneers 3-0 in last year’s state championship.
This time, Wisdom got the final word.
A first Gold Ball for the program and one heck of a way to close the fall season.
Five to Watch This Week
5. The Rest of Winter Sports Are Almost Here
Enjoy the short break while it lasts.
Next Monday, November 16, practice begins for several more winter sports, including Classes A through D basketball, wrestling, indoor track, boys hockey and winter cheering. Wrestling, boys hockey, indoor track and cheering all list November 16 as their first practice date.
Skiing gets going a week later on November 23.
In other words, the quiet part of November isn’t going to last very long.
4. Girls Hockey Is Already Back
While most winter sports are still waiting, girls hockey has already started.
Practices opened November 2, with the first countable games beginning November 19.
That means hockey is already getting a head start while the rest of the winter calendar begins filling in around it.
3. Soccer Season Is Over, but the Honors Aren’t
The final whistles have blown, but we’re not quite finished talking about soccer.
The postseason honor season is next.
That means All-Aroostook selections will eventually enter the conversation, and I’ll also be working on something new of my own with The Rock to recognize some of the top boys and girls soccer players I watched and covered throughout the fall.
There were too many great performances this season to just close the book after Saturday.
2. It’s Time to Find Our Athletes of the Fall
Athlete of the Week is finished for the fall, but there’s still one more decision to make.
Who were the best boys and girls athletes of the entire season?
Soccer, cross country and golf gave us plenty of candidates, from state champions and regional champions to huge individual seasons and postseason performances.
This week we’ll start putting together the field for Athlete of the Fall, with separate boys and girls honors.
This one should be fun.
1. Basketball Starts Today
Yes, already.
Class S basketball teams are allowed to begin practice Monday, November 9, nearly a full week before Classes A through D get started.
That means several County programs are officially turning the page from fall to basketball today. On the girls side, the North-S division includes Ashland, Easton, Katahdin, Van Buren, Washburn and Wisdom.
Think about that for a second.
Wisdom won a state soccer championship Saturday.
By Monday, basketball season can begin.
That might be the best example possible of how quickly high school sports move around here.
And before long, gym lights, basketball sneakers and winter tournament talk will replace soccer fields and cold October sidelines.
From One Season to the Next
I’m not quite ready to completely close the book on this fall.
There were too many great games, great performances and stories worth recognizing before we move on.
But winter is coming quickly.
Basketball practices are starting, hockey is underway, more winter sports begin next week and we still have Athlete of the Fall and postseason soccer honors to work through.
The fall gave us plenty to remember.
Now we get ready to do it all over again.

title: Judge sets summer 2028 trial for the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk
text:
PROVO, Utah (AP) — The man accused of assassinating conservative activist Charlie Kirk will stand trial in the summer of 2028, a Utah judge ruled Monday.
Attorneys for defendant Tyler Robinson, 23, proposed a trial starting in 2029. But District Judge Tony Graf faced pressure from Kirk’s family and supporters, including President Donald Trump, to speed up court proceedings that already have lasted more than a year.
Robinson has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in the killing of Kirk, 31, as the activist spoke to several thousand people at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025. Robinson could be eligible for the death penalty if convicted.
Graf allocated 105 days for the trial, beginning with jury selection on June 21, 2028. He said the dates balance Robinson’s right to prepare his defense with the rights of Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk, to a speedy resolution.
Erika Kirk’s attorney disagreed with the schedule but said there is no choice but to accept it.
“A trial in the summer of 2028, three years after Charlie’s assassination, does not feel very speedy to the Kirk family,” attorney Jeffrey Neiman told the judge. He had argued the trial should start next October.
In a statement after Monday’s hearing, the Kirk family characterized Graf’s decision as a “delay” and said, “every additional day without justice prolongs our family’s pain.”
Robinson’s defense team declined to comment after the hearing.
The defendant turned himself in a day after the shooting. His lawyers have not offered alternative theories for Kirk’s death.
Prosecutors had said they could be ready for trial by October 2027. Rather than hold the proceedings during the Thanksgiving and Christmas holidays, they proposed a January 2028 start date.
Kirk helped galvanize young voters around Trump during the 2024 election. Trump weighed in on the trial in a social media post last month, saying Robinson should be tried “within a month.” The Republican president criticized Graf, a former prosecutor appointed judge last year, for “taking forever to ask questions that people already know the answer to.”
Utah County prosecutors allege Robinson targeted Kirk for his political beliefs. They say a bullet found in the rifle used to kill Kirk was engraved with the words “Hey Facist! CATCH!” and that Robinson wrote in a text message about Kirk: “I had enough of his hatred. Some hate can’t be negotiated out.”
Robinson’s attorneys said in court documents that they must sift through tens of thousands of files turned over by prosecutors. They plan to conduct extensive investigations into Robinson’s life in search of mitigating factors that could influence his sentence if convicted, and to devote “substantial time” to issues such as jury selection.
___
Associated Press journalist Matthew Brown contributed from Billings, Montana.

title: Batesies Share Halloween Traditions, Past and Present
text:
This Halloween season, Batesies shared what they love about Halloween at Bates and their favorite childhood Halloween.
Reflecting on the “cool experience” of Halloween on campus, Ricky Kamenetz ’28 said, “Being able to dress up and see everybody else dress up…is always a very exciting thing.”
“It’s [Halloween’s] always been one of my favorite holidays. I love the fall. I love candy. I love pumpkins. So I think that it’s wonderful,” Kamenetz said. He added that Bates’ small size makes Halloween an opportunity to build a stronger sense of community.
Salome Gvaramadze ’28 described Halloween as “another reason for students to relax and celebrate…. We have a reason to dress up, go out, and have fun with people,” she said.
Gvaramadze grew up in Georgia and didn’t dress up for Halloween until she was 16. “We didn’t even know what the definition of Halloween was… the general consensus was that it was either the devil’s birthday or something to be feared and avoided,” she said.
Born in New Jersey and raised in Mumbai, Vathsaal Madhusudan ’29 said, “[I] always enjoyed Halloween.” This is despite what he described as a lack of Halloween culture in Mumbai.
Kamenetz reflected that his experience with Bates Halloween reminds him of his childhood memories, “I would just meet up with friends, and obviously we had the trick or treat, that was always superb, because then I’d eat all the candy.”

title: Kraken Black Spiced Rum Just Got a Marvel Makeover, and It's Glitching Out
text:
Kraken Black Spiced Rum’s New Marvel Bottle Looks Like It’s Been Hacked
Marvel fans have another collectible to add to their shelves, and this one comes with a little Caribbean rum history.
Kraken Black Spiced Rum has teamed up with Marvel Television's VisionQuest for a special-edition bottle inspired by the Disney+ series. The collaboration gives the familiar 750ml bottle a digital-age makeover, with a label that looks like it's been pulled straight out of a computer glitch.
The partnership also includes a cocktail kit inspired by the show, blending Kraken Coconut Vanilla with cold brew for a drink called the Glitch Mode Cocktail.
What Does the Kraken 'VisionQuest' Bottle Look Like?
The special-edition bottle features a computer-glitch design covered in digital coding, tying its appearance to the world of VisionQuest.
READ MORE: Who Is the Client on ‘VisionQuest’?
The collectible design is the main attraction for Marvel fans, connecting the series' technology-driven story to the brand's signature sea-monster imagery.
What's Included in the Kraken 'VisionQuest' Cocktail Kit?
The collaboration also includes a kit with the special-edition bottle and ingredients to make the Glitch Mode Cocktail: Kraken Coconut Vanilla Cold Brew.
The drink brings together the rum's coconut-vanilla flavor with cold brew, giving the collaboration a coffee-inspired twist. It's a themed cocktail that nods to the series without requiring fans to decode a computer glitch to figure out what's in the glass.
Why Did Kraken Team Up With 'VisionQuest'?
The partnership brings together two brands with an interest in larger-than-life storytelling. Kraken takes its name and imagery from the legendary sea creature, while VisionQuest continues Marvel Television's story of a complicated character navigating an equally complicated world.
It's also part of a wider trend of spirits brands connecting with entertainment franchises through limited-edition packaging and pop culture collaborations.
READ MORE: Marvel Announces ‘Zodiac’ TV Series for Disney+
In this case, the result is a bottle that puts a recognizable Marvel-inspired spin on Kraken's familiar design.
The special-edition bottle and cocktail kit are available through KrakenRum.com and CocktailCourier.com, as well as in select U.S. states.

title: Maine women’s soccer keeps championship hopes alive with quarterfinal victory
text:
ORONO, Maine — The University of Maine women’s soccer team kept its championship hopes alive on Thursday, Nov. 5, defeating the University at Albany 2-0 in an America East quarterfinal matchup to advance to the conference semifinals against Bryant University. The Black Bears are now two wins away from capturing their fourth consecutive America East championship.
Maine entered the contest fresh off a 2-1 road win against the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, carrying an overall record of 7-5-4. The Black Bears finished third in the conference standings with 14 points and ranked 160th in the RPI, making them the highest-ranked America East team.
On the other side, the UAlbany Great Danes had just drawn 1-1 with the University of New Hampshire on the road, bringing their record to 5-7-3. They finished sixth in the conference standings with 11 points and ranked 207th in the RPI. The result also secured UAlbany’s first America East tournament berth since 2022.
Maine entered the postseason with plenty of experience, having won the previous three America East championships. Fourth-year midfielder Victoria Dungey reflected on the team’s development and excitement about another postseason opportunity.
“We’ve come a long way in terms of who we are as a team, so we’re excited to get to go again now that we’re in a different spot,” Dungey said.
Dungey also discussed the familiarity of competing for an America East championship, describing the postseason routine as something the program has grown accustomed to during her time in Orono.
“Since I’ve been here, we’ve done this, so it’s kind of just routine now,” Dungey said. “All the same thing, and take it day by day and game by game.”
Head coach Scott Atherley acknowledged UAlbany’s recent improvement and emphasized the importance of respecting the opponent while maintaining confidence in Maine’s own abilities.
“They’re probably playing their best stuff right now,” Atherley said. “We have a lot of respect for them.” However, Atherley stressed that the Black Bears needed to focus on their own execution rather than becoming overly concerned with their opponent.
“For us, it’s not so much about the other team and our opponent. It’s about us,” Atherley said.
Maine made an early statement as third-year forward Isabella Meadows scored her eighth goal of the season in the eighth minute to give the Black Bears the lead. The goal moved Meadows into second place in the conference in scoring, one behind third-year Binghamton forward Jahkaya Davis.
UAlbany gradually found its footing, creating several opportunities but failing to convert. The Great Danes continued to apply pressure in the second half, but Maine’s defense held firm. As the visitors pushed forward in search of an equalizer, the Black Bears found space to counterattack.
Second-year forward Sandrine Brault capitalized, blasting a shot past the goalkeeper after UAlbany failed to clear a cross, doubling Maine’s lead. Second-year goalkeeper Elena Barenberg and the Black Bears’ defense then preserved the shutout to secure the 2-0 victory.
Maine finished with a 7-5 advantage in shots on goal despite being outshot 15-9 overall. UAlbany also led in corner kicks, 6-3, including five in the second half, but could not capitalize on its set-piece opportunities.
With the victory, Maine advanced to the America East semifinals, and traveled to face second-seeded Bryant on Sunday, Nov. 8 at 4:30 p.m. The Bulldogs ranked 187th in the RPI and finished 6-6-4, earning the second seed following a strong late-season run in conference play.
Although Maine fought until the end, they were unable to find the back of the net and lost 2-0 to the Bulldogs in the semifinal. This loss concluded their season as they look to continue to build in the Spring.

title: New England governors call on Congress to tack on $3 billion in heating aid
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Gov. Janet Mills and five other New England governors are calling on members of Congress to provide an additional $3 billion in funding to the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program ahead of this winter.
In a letter sent Monday to appropriations leaders in the U.S. House and Senate — including Maine’s Sen. Susan Collins, who chairs the Senate’s committee — Mills and the leaders of Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Connecticut expressed that time is of the essence.
“Whether through an increase in the annual appropriation or a one-time emergency supplemental funding, these additional resources are urgently needed,” the governors wrote.
The $3 billion increase the governors requested would bring the program’s funding to roughly $7 billion.
“At current funding levels, rising energy prices will erode the purchasing power of LIHEAP assistance, forcing states to reduce benefits or serve fewer eligible households when the need is greatest,” the letter says. “While our states are working to mitigate the immediate impact of rising energy costs on vulnerable households and continue to invest heavily in energy efficiency, weatherization, and other long-term solutions, these efforts cannot fully offset the immediate financial pressures facing families this winter.”
In a news release, Mills’ office noted Maine is the most heating-oil-dependent state in the nation, and that roughly 50% of Maine homes rely on oil as their primary heating source.
The price of heating oil in Maine has continued to set records this fall and now rests above $6 per gallon on average. Since the war with Iran began in late February, Maine heating oil prices have spiked roughly 57%.
“No one should be cold in their homes because (President Donald) Trump decided to wage an unnecessary, unwanted war with Iran,” Mills said in a written statement. “That’s why I’m joining my fellow New England governors to call on Congress to release billions in federal funding for LIHEAP to provide immediate relief for vulnerable families as winter approaches.”

Caribbean and Latinx Student Alliance organizes ICE vigil
text:
On Monday, Nov. 2, the Caribbean and Latinx Student Alliance (CALSA) met between the Fogler Library and the Memorial Union to hold a vigil honoring lives lost to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). During the offering ceremony, CALSA officers and faculty spoke about the importance of having these events for the Latin community in the face of ICE brutality.
CALSA officer Sofia Carrasquillo opened the series of speeches by thanking everyone for stopping by and emphasizing what the vigil represented. The second speaker was Micaela Cateriano, who expressed her condolences to the families of those who lost loved ones.
The vigil followed with each officer reading off a total of eight names to honor their lives. The officers were handing out ribbons so that people could decorate a tree. Other students also brought their own offerings, or ofrendas, as a way to recognize those lives.
In a conversation with the Maine Campus, CALSA officers Aylin Noble-Ramirez and Valeria Ixchel Juárez Vergara spoke about the cultural significance of having this vigil on Día de los Muertos, or the Day of the Dead.
“It’s very opening to our culture,” said Vergara. “We’re such a small community here. Many people don’t really know about Día de los Muertos and to have a little celebration of our culture is special.”
Vergara explained that she has been planning this event since last semester and has worked to incorporate her Mexican culture into making this vigil possible. She hopes that these events will help alleviate the fear around diversity and allow others outside of the Latinx community to understand the impact that fear has had.
“This is an important day for a lot of Latinos here,” said Noble-Ramirez. “Having this remembrance for victims of ICE is really meaningful, not just to me but to all the people that showed up today.”
Desiree Peña is the advisor for CALSA and is also the program associate for community inclusion and disability. Peña emphasized the emotional distress that ICE brutality has caused for her.
“I hold my breath every time I open an article. The degrees of separation are really narrow,” said Peña.
Peña said that these events are important because they send a message that ICE enforcement actions will not be tolerated. She called for political change to make sure that this does not continue to impact more people. Peña ended her speech by stating how delighted she was to see how many people support the cause and the people that are directly impacted.
The Maine Campus also spoke to Adrián Arias-Palomo, executive director of the Maine Multi-Cultural Center (MMCC), who began by expressing how heartwarming it is to see people at the vigil. Arias-Palomo says he feels privileged to be the executive director of the MMCC and explained that the goal of the organization is to provide the immigrant community with resources, such as finding housing and employment opportunities.
“It is important to make sure they feel supported and that they know we are here for them. It’s the little acts of kindness that make the difference,” said Arias-Palomo.

title: Daniel J. Crowley Jr.
text:
Daniel J. Crowley Jr., 74, affectionately known as “Danny,” unexpectedly passed away on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026 at Northern Light Mercy Hospital in Portland.
Born at Bethesda Naval Hospital in Maryland on Dec. 26, 1951 to Daniel J. Crowley Sr. (USMC) and Kathryn T. (McLoon) Crowley, he grew up as a U.S. Marine Corps dependent.
Danny attended many schools in various states, including Castner School in Damariscotta, where he had the same first grade teacher as his mom, and Lincoln Academy in Newcastle. When he was a sophomore at Lincoln, he worked at Fairfield’s Diner in Damariscotta busing tables and washing dishes, enjoying the paycheck but especially enjoying the best breakfasts as a reward for his work.
Whether attending schools at Camp LeJeune in North Carolina, Romulus in New York, or Maine, Danny was active in and excelled at several sports, including football, baseball, basketball, and soccer. Although small in size with the nickname of “Peanut,” he earned several athletic awards and recognitions. Dan graduated high school in 1971 from Romulus Central School in New York and obtained a degree in drafting/design from State University of New York Morrisville.
After retiring from the Marine Corps, Kathryn and Dan came home to Damariscotta, then settled in Westbrook, and Danny joined them. He thoroughly enjoyed summer vacations out at Pemaquid Lake in Damariscotta with his family and friends. Danny truly looked forward to those times when he would play cards and, more recently, tussle with Teagan the cat over who would get the best chair first at camp.
Danny was employed at Nichols Portland Inc. Technologies in Portland as a mechanical designer for many years before retiring. While there, his colleagues became friends and continued to keep in touch by playing golf, gathering for breakfast, and participating in football pools. Danny’s ability to analyze team stats and his knowledge of sports usually placed him at the top of the winnings. He was a fan of the Boston Red Sox, Boston Bruins, Boston Celtics, and the … Indianapolis Colts – What!!?? He was also a huge history buff, especially of the Civil War, and had researched his great-grandfather’s role in the Union army.
Danny was predeceased by his parents; uncles, James, Charles “Shike” (Irma), Joseph Charles, George (Dana), Joseph Bernard, and Arthur “Doug” McLoon; and aunts, Florence McLoon, Clara Horie (Everett), and Ruth House (Calvin).
He is survived by his uncle and aunt, John and Martha Cannon, of Rochester, N.H.; brother, Timothy W. Crowley, of Westbrook; sister and brother-in-law, Sheila and Michael Clements, of Augusta; their son, Matthew Clements and his children, Julian, Landon, and Taylor; aunt, Mary Jane McLoon; and several much-beloved cousins.
Relatives and friends are invited to join the family on Saturday, Nov. 21 for a time of visitation from 12:30-1 p.m. with a service to follow at 1 p.m. at the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home in Damariscotta.
Should friends and family desire, please consider donating to the Animal Refuge League of Greater Portland, P.O. Box 336, Westbrook, ME 04098 (arlgp.org/memorial); or to the Marine Corps Reserve Toys for Tots (toysfortots.org).
Arrangements are under the direction and care of the Strong-Hancock Funeral Home, 612 Main St., Damariscotta, ME 04543. Condolences and messages for his family may be expressed by visiting stronghancock.com.

title: Trump after meeting with Qatari PM says he believes war with Iran is militarily ‘effectively over’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) - President Donald Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,” suggesting that — at least for now — he’s not prepared to resume the bombardment that has devastated the Islamic Republic and caused reverberations across the global economy.
The president made a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting earlier in the day with Qatar’s prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.
“Iran militarily is effectively over,” Trump said. “We’re just keeping it the status quo.”
He added that Iran has been “decapitated” but said he is still looking to make sure there’s a long-term solution to ensuring that Iran’s nuclear program is defanged.
It was some of Trump’s most definitive comments about moving away from his threat to resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections had passed.
The president’s Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress to Democrats in last week’s elections. The elections were shadowed by dissatisfaction among the American electorate over the 8-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices that’s impacted nearly ever sector of the global economy.
Trump, over the course of the conflict, has repeatedly said he is on the cusp of ordering U.S. forces to escalate attacks if Iran’s leaders don’t quickly agree to U.S. terms to end the war, only to back down. In earlier cycles, he has also edged away with a last-minute declaration, sometimes at the behest of Gulf allies, that he’s going to give diplomacy more time.
In a posting on social media shortly before speaking to reporters, Trump once again asserted that Middle East allies — Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others — “would prefer the status quo.” Minutes later, in his exchange with reporters, he sought to assure war-weary Americans that there was “positive momentum” and that he saw a “good chance” that the war “could get ended.”
“They’re talking to us, and they’re talking very politely, And we’ll see what happens,” Trump said. He added, “The military action doesn’t seem to be a very necessary thing, but we’re locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes.”
Trump, however, gave no hint of a drawdown of the thousands of U.S. troops who have been shifted to the waters off of Iran and maintain a naval blockade to stem the flow of Iranian oil into the global market.
“We’re keeping it going. We have the greatest military blockade ever,” Trump said.
Qatari officials last week presented proposals on Iran’s nuclear program, according to two Middle East government officials familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The White House declined to comment, though Trump last week alluded to ongoing indirect talks with Tehran.
All the while, Tehran continues to insist on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.
Earlier Monday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has come under fire over the conflict, said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including the possibility of telling Iran: “Hey, we’re done, and we’re going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it.”
The defense secretary has been one of the administration’s most prominent defenders of the war. Critics say the administration launched the war without proper authorization, violated the War Powers Resolution and subverted congressional war-declaring powers.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Hegseth, largely over his execution of the war.
Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with the Iranians and they sign a “strong agreement,” it’s “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” to resume strikes.
Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.
The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
—
AP writers Konstantin Toropin, Samy Magdy and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

title: 81-year-old woman trapped under car for hours in pouring rain before husband finds her
text:
HINGHAM, Mass. (WHDH) - Firefighters rescued an 81-year-old Massachusetts woman who spent four hours trapped under her car in the pouring rain.
Norman Wilbur says he knew something was wrong seconds after a cab dropped him off Friday night at his Hingham home. It turned out his wife, 81-year-old Peggy Wilbur, had gotten trapped underneath her car.
“I walked around, and I heard, ‘Help. Help.’ I said… ‘Peggy, is that you?’ And I looked. I couldn’t even see her because the car was up against it," Norman Wilbur said.
He called 911 as soon as he realized what happened, and Hingham Firefighters arrived within minutes. They used airbags and a spreading safety tool to lift the car off Peggy Wilbur.
Firefighters say the car was accidentally left in neutral and rolled toward the victim, pinning her against a rock wall. Her husband says she had been trapped for four hours in the pouring rain before he found her.
“You couldn’t see her because the wall was here and the car was right up to it,” Norman Wilbur said. “If the door hadn’t swung around, that added a buffer zone, enough of her legs between the wheels and the wall. If that didn’t happen, she would be in hot water.”
Norman Wilbur went with his wife to the hospital. She suffered serious injuries to her chest and legs and now faces a long recovery.
“She’ll be 82 this week, so she’s no spring chicken, as they say, but she’s a tough old Irish girl,” he said.
Firefighters say their thoughts are with the victim and her family.
