title: Cozy Maine skating spots for winter fun
text:
This winter, go all in on ice skating.
There are indoor rinks all around southern and central Maine where you can skate now, even before your local ponds and outdoor rinks are frozen over. There are also some covered rinks where the ice is maintained and skaters are protected from rain or snow.
Some of the indoor rinks are publicly owned or are part of a school or college. Some offer public skating sessions once a week, some almost every day. Some offer special events with music and strobe lights, or skating parties. At least one is free.
Here are some of the indoor or covered skating rinks around southern and central Maine, including, hopefully, one near you.
14 Pomerlau St., Biddeford. biddefordarena.com
This arena has hockey and figure skates available for rent for $5 during public skating sessions, though no pucks or sticks are allowed. Because the arena hosts a lot of hockey teams, public skating is limited and the schedule changes, so check the Facebook page for the latest information. The next scheduled public skating sessions are 11:30 a.m.-1 p.m. Nov. 11 and 6:30-7:50 p.m. Nov. 14. Admission is $5.
36 Hancock Drive, Bridgton. facebook.com
This school arena offers public skating as well as “stick and puck” sessions for hockey players. Hockey players must have their own equipment to participate and anyone under 18 must wear a hockey helmet with a cage. The cost for those sessions are $12. Admission for public skating sessions is $6 and skate rentals are $5. There are upcoming public skate sessions from 4-5 p.m. Nov. 15, 22 and 29 and stick and puck sessions from 5:10-6:10 p.m. Nov. 16, 23 and 30. The monthly schedule is posted on the arena’s Facebook page.
630 Pool St., Biddeford. une.edu
The NHL-size hockey arena here has seats for 900, so you can imagine yourself playing or performing for a crowd. There are open skate or stick and puck sessions (for hockey players) just about every day. On Friday at 9:15 p.m. and Saturday at 6:15 p.m., there will be “cosmic” public skating sessions, with neon lighting, music and a party atmosphere. But the schedules change and the university posts two-week schedules in a pdf on its website. The stick and puck is for skaters 18 and older and helmets with at least a half shield are required. Admission is $3 for children under 17 and $5 for adults. A limited number of rental skates are available for $3.
535 West St., Rockport. midcoastrec.org
This rink offers roller skating in the spring and summer and ice skating in the fall and winter. In November there are public skating sessions just about every day, usually in the early afternoon. There are also early morning “coffee club” skates at 8 a.m. on Wednesday and Friday. There are some stick and puck sessions on the monthly schedule, too. Admission is $8 for adults, $6 for people 60-plus and children 6-12, free for kids 5 and under. Rentals are $5.
985 Turner St., Auburn. norwaysavingsbankarena.com
At this arena, public skating sessions for November are scheduled for 3:50-4:50 p.m. on Sundays. Admission is $5 and skate rentals, in both youth and adult sizes, are $5. The public skating calendar is posted monthly on the arena’s website.
90 Acme Road, Brewer. penobscoticearena.com
This arena near Bangor offers a Frozen Friday Laser Light & Sound Skate from 7:30-9:30 p.m. on Fridays. Admission is $15 and skates can be rented for $5. The party-like events are so popular rink management recommends getting there 30 minutes early. There’s also a quieter Sunday afternoon public skate with no lights and soft music, plus other public skate sessions scheduled at various times. Admission for public skating is $10.
203 Whitten Road, Hallowell. maineicevault.com
Public skates sessions here are for people of all ages and abilities looking for a casual skate. Admission is $12 and skate rentals are $6. Weekend events often sell out, so the rink recommends purchasing advance tickets online. Memberships and discounted 10-packs are also available.
207 Thompson’s Point Road, Portland. thompsonspointrink.com
This popular outdoor rink is covered by an antique train shed roof. It’s located where the Thompson’s Point concerts are held in summer, with a view of the Fore River. The rink is slated to open for the season the weekend after Thanksgiving, with up-to-date schedules posted on the @thompsonspointrink Instagram page. There are daily public skating sessions, which are timed and ticketed. There are also skate rentals, training aids and skate sharpening services.
51 Main St., Kennebunk. kennebunkmaine.us
This open-side rink in downtown Kennebunk is free to all, all the time. Well, November through March, weather permitting. The roof comes down pretty low so the exposure to the outdoors is minimal. The rink is 60 feet by 90 feet and is open 8 a.m.-8 p.m. daily. The rink is town-owned and ice skating and other activities are supported by an endowment set up by town resident Geraldine Waterhouse and her granddaughter, Paige Hill.
225 Park Ave., Portland. portlandmaine.gov
Portland’s city-owned rink hosts hockey, events and public skating. There are public skating sessions just about every day in November, including 90-minute lunchtime sessions on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday and sessions from 1:30-3 p.m. Saturday and Sunday. The times vary from week to week so check the schedule on the website. No sticks or pucks allowed. Admission is $6 and skate rentals are $4.

title: Aging Untold: Why your metabolism changes as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, learn how metabolism changes with age and what may help support it.
Then, we share gentle ways to tell loved ones when time may be short, set boundaries and care for yourself.
Plus, a group of mall walkers is turning ’90s nostalgia into a fun way to stay active and build community.
Your metabolism is like the body’s “power plant” and every organ has its own, according to the Aging Untold experts.
“If you deplete that power in an organ that needs a lot, you’re going to start to see symptoms sooner,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. That is why changes in the eyes and ears show up in older people.
As people age, they gain fat and lose muscle. Muscle plays a role in how the body uses glucose, which provides energy, Rogers said.
Some people who are dying get a moment to decide how they’ll say goodbye to the people they love.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck says the person who is saying goodbye does not need to feel pressure to be strong and manage others’ emotions.
“You need to be getting the support that you need,” Cradduck said.
The people receiving the message are grieving because they are losing that person, but they have the opportunity to provide support for the person who is dying.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said everyone is different in how they handle saying goodbye. She listed grief, unfinished business and relationships among the things a person may be dealing with.
Laura Lyster-Mensh is a death doula at Historic Congressional Cemetery.
Her role at the national landmark in the heart of Washington, D.C., is to promote what she calls “death positivity.”
She helps visitors have healthy conversations about mortality.
Every Sunday morning, mall walkers in spandex, neon and scrunchies gather for three and a half miles of power walking.
Krista Catwood started the group, the Food Court 5000, and said they’ve “become sort of B-celebrities” at the Lloyd Center mall in Oregon.
Catwood said she knew the activity had to be silly, social and shared with others.

title: Actor Donnie Dunagan, original voice of Bambi in classic Disney film, dies at 92, reports say
text:
(Gray News) — Donnie Dunagan, who voiced young Bambi for the original 1942 Disney classic, has died. He was 92.
The Hollywood Reporter was the first to report the news.
Dunagan’s agents confirmed to Variety that he died Nov. 4 of lung cancer.
IMDb lists Dunagan as the voice of young Bambi in the film. The Guardian reports he was just 6 years old when he was chosen for the role.
In the film, adolescent Bambi was voiced by Hardie Albright.
Dunagan also appeared in other films including 1939’s “Son of Frankenstein.”
“Bambi” was his last role. He then enlisted in the U.S. Marines and served three tours in Vietnam. He retired as a major in 1977. For his service, he received a Bronze Star and three Purple Hearts.

title: New program will help people in Maine get to school, work, appointments and more
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - The United Way is launching a new pilot project in Maine to help people get to appointments, work, school and more.
The program is called Keep ME Moving and is funded thanks to support from the John T. Gorman Foundation. The program will help people pay for small car repairs, bus passes, and Lyft rides.
The United Way says requests through 211 Maine related to transportation have increased 90% since 2020 and a recent survey conducted by the United Way in Cumberland and York counties found that transportation was a common challenge.
United Way officials say they expect demand will be high for the limited amount of money available for the program each month. You can also donate to Keep ME Moving to help it stay funded.
“We know that nearly four in ten households in Southern Maine are struggling, and the people experiencing those challenges are the experts on what would make a difference in their lives,” said United Way of Southern Maine President and CEO Dan Coyne. “What we heard repeatedly was that a relatively small transportation problem could quickly spiral into a much larger crisis. A missed shift at work, a missed medical appointment, or an unexpected repair can make it harder for a family that’s already stretching every dollar.”
A 2025 John T. Gorman Foundation report on transportation in Maine found that addressing transportation challenges will require both immediate support for families and longer-term policy solutions. Keep ME Moving is designed to help meet the immediate need.
Who is eligible?
Applicants are currently being accepted by referral from United Way non-profit and employer partners. To be eligible, people must live in a county served by the three United Ways in Maine, be within the ALICE (Asset Limited, Income Constrained, Employed) income threshold, and have a transportation need related to one or more of the following areas:
- Medical, dental, or mental health appointments;
- Work or educational opportunity;
- Child care or school;
- Basic needs, such as groceries or pharmacy.
The fund is administered by United Way of Southern Maine in partnership with United Way of Aroostook.

title: Few museums show the North's Civil Rights Movement. A new one in Harlem is ‘just getting started’
Gunman with far-right views who killed 6 people in Polish city square dies in hospital, police say
text:
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) - People gathered in Krakow‘s main square on Monday evening for a silent march to commemorate the victims of Saturday’s mass shooting, in which a 24-year-old Polish gunman killed six people and wounded 15 others.
Shoulder to shoulder, people walked solemnly through the packed square, some clutching flowers. They placed candles where bullet marks were visible. Polish President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, otherwise political rivals, walked side by side.
The melody from Simon and Garfunkel’s “The Sound of Silence” rang from the tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square. The night after the attack, St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody that plays every hour from that tower, was paused for the first time since World War II. A prayer was read out once the song finished.
The attacker, wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into the main square in Krakow’s Old Town on Saturday and opened fire. The square is a major tourist destination in Poland’s second-largest city. Several foreigners were among the dead and wounded.
The gunman, Michał Oksiński, died at 4:30 a.m. on Monday, authorities said. He had been in critical condition since the attack and had undergone several operations.
Authorities also found the bodies of his sister, mother and father at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. Authorities said that they believed Oksiński killed his family, possibly while they slept, before heading to Krakow.
Authorities investigating the motive
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said Saturday that Oksiński held “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views.
“We are first of all investigating if he was inspired by anyone, if someone helped him,” Eryk Stasielak of the Krakow branch of the national prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press.
He said that authorities are still investigating the attacker’s motives and are trying to access his electronic devices for more information.
Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Gałecka said that authorities were examining the meaning of numerous symbols and patches sewn onto Oksiński’s clothing or found at his home.
Prosecutors said that they found a yellow flag bearing a black snake, known as the Gadsden flag, hanging on the wall of the attacker’s room. The flag originated during the American Revolution and was later adopted by the U.S. Tea Party movement.
Authorities recovered 11 weapons from Oksiński, his car or home, including two AR-15 semiautomatic rifles, prosecutors said.
Oksiński and his father held gun permits. He had trained at a local shooting club, which said in a statement that he “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”
World facing threats from lone actors
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The attackers used knives or sharp objects and some were said to be interested in the far right.
Prime Minister Tusk said that the school attacks were fueled by the online “glorification of violence.” He said that the acts could be associated with “nihilistic violence,” a term used by authorities to describe acts of violence driven by a nihilistic worldview and misanthropy rather than specific political goals.
Oksiński’s military-style equipment and weapons were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe and the world, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague, Netherlands.
He said that even without an explicit link between the attacks in Krakow and at the schools, they could be viewed as part of “a series.”
Tomasz Safjański, a security expert, told Rzeczpospolita newspaper that Poland had experienced its first case of an “active shooter” and that the perpetrator was Polish, even as authorities remain focused almost exclusively on external threats such as Russia’s hybrid warfare.
“We are failing to address the radicalization of young people,” he said. “By focusing on an external enemy, the state overlooks the threat that is growing within our schools, our neighborhoods and online.”
Police officers described as heroes
Officers Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański were patrolling the area when they were called to intervene. Police fired the first shot within three minutes of receiving the initial report. The officers chased the attacker and fired at him with their service weapons as he fired a semiautomatic rifle. Kulik continued firing even after he was shot. Both officers were seriously wounded.
Tusk called them the “real heroes” in a post on X. “They most likely saved the lives of many human beings, without regard for the risk of losing their own lives,” he wrote.
Kulik, 24, was in critical condition, prompting officials to issue an urgent appeal for blood donors. A fundraiser for the officers and their families has so far raised more than 6 million zlotys ($1.5 million).
Krakow’s mayor announced that both officers would be named honorary citizens of the city. Two surgeons who happened to be nearby during the attack helped save the officers’ lives.
Talented artists among the victims
Izabela Woźna, a 53-year-old painter and mother of four, was killed in the attack. She had opened an exhibition of her work in Krakow on Friday evening.
Krakow Academy of Fine Arts confirmed that Magdalena Oksińska — the suspect’s sister — had been one of its third-year students. It said an employee’s sister had also been shot twice.
“Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy said in a statement Sunday.
“Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a social media post accompanied by images of her colorful paintings.
“Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”
Among those killed in the square were citizens from Poland, the U.K. and Austria. The wounded included people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

title: Olivia Raymond Carter
text:
Olivia Raymond Carter, born Jan. 10, 1989, passed away on Oct. 9, 2026 at Maine General Hospital.
Olivia grew up in Waldoboro with her family and went to school there.
She was a hard worker, picking shrimp and shucking clams. She enjoyed going clamming with her uncle Daniel Carter and her father Norman Carter.
Olivia also went lobstering with her dad and enjoyed going on family picnics on the beaches, where she would look for treasures. She also loved going mackerel fishing on the boat.
She lived in Deer Isle for awhile, then moved back home to spend time with her family. Olivia enjoyed going to Seven Tree Pond this summer with her sister Leanne and family. She even went in her wheelchair in the pond; she enjoyed it so much.
Olivia was predeceased by her father, Norman Carter; her partner, Kenneth Judkins; and son, Keegan.
She is survived by her mother, Ramona Carter; sisters, Colleen and husband, Brandon Bissey, Leanne and husband, Joshua Harvey, and Norma Carter; and brother, Jacob Carter.
She is also survived by her nieces and nephews, Lauren, Shelby, Quinntin, Bryent, Owen, Elisabeth, Andrew, Abel, Lukas, Hayden, and Jackson; she loved them all so much.
A celebration of life will be held on Sunday, Nov. 15 at 1 p.m. at West Waldoboro Community Church. Burial will follow at the Hillside Cemetery on Route 32 in Bremen.
A gathering of family and friends will follow at the Bremen Union Church, at 523 Waldoboro Road in Bremen.

title: Democrats flip Georgia state House, giving them new control of at least 12 legislative chambers
13-year-olds charged after intentionally making fair ride swing out of control, deputies say
text:
GROVETOWN, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT/Gray News) — Two 13-year-olds have been charged after deputies said the teens intentionally caused a swing ride at a county fair to go out of control.
A Columbia County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson said the teens had been warned not to grab each other while the ride was in motion.
Video shows the swing ride appearing to become unstable as it slowed.
The video, captured by Kristen Murphy, a mother whose children were on the ride, shows two riders in separate swings appearing to hold on to each other.
A woman was injured when several swings collided, and she left the fairgrounds in an ambulance. Two children were treated for minor injuries.
Murphy said she wanted to get to her children as the ride was in motion.
“This ride has to stop,” Murphy said. “My kids are on it. Something’s happening. I need to get to them.”
Murphy said other parents rushed to the control panel to help her husband slow the ride. She said she noticed injuries after the ride stopped and she reached her children.
The 13-year-olds received paperwork describing their charges and were allowed to leave with their parents, according to the sheriff’s office.

title: Russell Brand faces significant prison term for rape and sexual assaults
text:
Russell Brand faces significant prison term for rape and sexual assaults
Russell Brand faces a reckoning Monday for sexual abuse that occurred just offstage from a public life built around boasts of his erotic exploits.
Brand, 51, could receive a significant prison term after being convicted of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.
The British actor-comedian known for outrageous stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol asserted that he was innocent and all his encounters were consensual.
But a jury of eight men and four women found him guilty of attacking four of six accusers on allegations dating back to 2004. He was cleared of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Brand arrived at Southwark Crown Court in a prison van shortly after his wife, Laura, entered the courthouse without him. Brand had been free during the trial but was jailed following the verdict and did not go home Thursday with his wife.
A couple of Brand's supporters who reflected his recent conversion to Christianity held a banner with crosses that said: “Russell Brand we stand with you. Christ was crucified for telling the truth. Russell is the truth.”
Brand was partly damned at trial by his own words about his obsession with sex and his well-documented life of promiscuity.
Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones called Brand a ruthless, calculating, manipulative “sexual predator” who treated women as a “disposable commodity.”
She quoted from his 2007 memoir “My Booky Wook” to illustrate how his insatiable sex drive led him to cross the line.
“If I want something — whether it’s a job or a woman — I will determinedly, resolutely, remove anything that’s in the way, until I possess the object of my desire,” he wrote.
The accusers came forward following a 2023 investigation by The Times and Channel 4 that aired accusations from women who said they had been sexually abused and degraded by Brand.
Brand was convicted of sexually assaulting a woman during a birthday party at a London bar in 2004, but cleared of orally raping her in a restroom.
He was also found guilty of kissing and groping another woman at a London radio station in 2004 or 2005 and of anally raping a fan at his home after meeting her backstage at one of his comedy shows in 2009.
The final conviction was for sexually assaulting a different woman who says the comedian demanded a massage and pressed his face into her groin during the recording of an advertisement in 2009.
Brand was acquitted of raping another woman in a hotel room during the Labour Party’s annual conference in the seaside town of Bournemouth in 1999, and of attempting to indecently assault a woman by dragging her into the men’s bathroom at the London office of music channel MTV.
The Associated Press doesn’t name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.
Brand, who was known for edgy stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, rose to prominence in the early 2000s hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including “Forgetting Sarah Marshall” and “Get Him to the Greek” and was briefly married to pop star Katy Perry.
In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.

title: No new leads on missing teenager from Turner, nearly a week after she was last seen
text:
No new leads on missing teenager from Turner, Maine, nearly a week after she was last seen
It has been nearly a week since 14-year-old Skylar Rowe was last seen at her grandmother's home on County Road in Turner. She was seen at about 1 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 3, and her grandmother, Valerie Rowe, told Maine's Total Coverage she thinks Skylar may have snuck out of the house while she was babysitting other children in the family.
Skylar lives with her aunt, Tiffani Rowe, who said she has legal guardianship of her niece.
On Monday, the Androscoggin County Sheriff's Office told Maine's Total Coverage there were no updates to the search for Skylar. Police reinforced that they believe Skylar is with her biological mother, Kasey Rowe, and her mother's boyfriend, Michael Rias. Police said Skylar and her mother are no longer in Maine and are possibly headed to Tennessee. Police previously said they could be headed to Memphis.
Police said on Monday that the detective assigned to the case was still looking to contact Skylar and her mother to ensure she is safe.
"Skylar reached out on a private number to her father, William Rowe, and said, 'I'm safe,' and hung up the phone," Tiffani Rowe told Maine's Total Coverage on Friday.
Tiffani Rowe said that phone call was made on Wednesday.
The Androscoggin County Sheriff's Office previously said that, due to Skylar's age and the circumstances surrounding her disappearance, there are serious concerns for her safety and well-being.
Police told Maine's Total Coverage on Monday that their investigation does not involve any other children.
Authorities are asking anyone who has any information regarding Skylar's whereabouts to immediately call 911 or the Androscoggin County Sheriff's Office at 207-753-2599.

title: Paul LePage heads to DC for new member orientation
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (WMTW) - Former Governor Paul LePage says he is headed to Washington, D.C., for new member orientation in the U.S. Congress.
“In the coming weeks and months, I will be laser focused on policies that lower your cost-of-living, bring prosperity back to rural Maine, and crack down on welfare fraud and corruption,” LePage said in a Facebook post Sunday morning.
This comes after Lepage declared victory Wednesday afternoon, and his opponent, Democrat Matt Dunlap, conceded on Thursday.
The Secretary of State’s Office says ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled to start at 10 a.m. Monday, Nov. 9.
In ranked-choice voting races, a candidate must receive more than 50% of first-choice votes as counted on Election Day in order to win the race outright. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the Secretary of State’s Office makes the determination to proceed with a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
The Secretary of State’s Office telling Maine’s Total Coverage that even though Dunlap has conceded, the ranked-choice tabulation is required under state law.
More info about CD2
Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.

title: YWCA MDI to host Children’s Bazaar Dec. 12
text:
BAR HARBOR — For more than four decades, the YWCA MDI Children’s Bazaar has been one of the season’s most beloved traditions, and generations of Mount Desert Island neighbors look forward to it each year. This year’s bazaar will take place Saturday, Dec. 12, 9 a.m. to noon at the YWCA MDI office, 36 Mount Desert St.
The bazaar offers a morning of holiday magic where kids do their own shopping and pick out special gifts for the people they love. Items are priced at just 25 cents or $1, and the entry fee is $1 per child (exact change is recommended). Gifts are new and gently used items donated by local businesses and community members. title: President Trump says he was 'just kidding' about making UFC CEO Dana White his press secretary
text:
Trump says he was 'kidding' about making UFC boss Dana White his White House press secretary
President Donald Trump said Sunday he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary after announcing on social media he had offered his close friend the job.
Related previous coverage in the video player above: UFC CEO Dana White to visit White House after President offers him Press Secretary job
After his party’s deep losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump shook up his administration on Friday by replacing his chief of staff and followed up on Saturday with a post that said he had offered the press secretary job to White. On Sunday, Trump said it was “just a little fun.”
“I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump said, speaking to reporters in Florida before departing for the White House. White is set to visit him at the White House on Monday.
Related video below: UFC CEO Dana White to visit White House after President offers him Press Secretary job
The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump on Friday named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller is the architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies. Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia, who faltered behind the lectern and in interviews, and left the post after five days.

title: Unlikely allies: Why both parties want action on license plate cameras
text:
WASHINGTON (InvestigateTV) — Automated license plate readers have garnered something rare in modern politics: strong bipartisan agreement.
“You have outrage from the far left, and you have outrage from the far right, because you’re verging in this 1984 totalitarian-type environment where there’s nowhere you can go and not be surveilled,” said Rep. Greg Steube.
The Florida Republican sits on the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, and said the scope of the technology’s use by law enforcement — particularly Flock Safety’s nationwide data-sharing network — and concerns about oversight of that use have brought together unlikely allies.
“[It’s] probably one of the very few things that Bernie Sanders and I agree upon,” Steube said.
Senators and House members from both parties told InvestigateTV that action from Congress, not a patchwork of local rules, is needed, and at least nine proposals are now pending or expected on Capitol Hill that would ban or limit mass surveillance technologies like Flock’s.
The push follows InvestigateTV’s year-long investigation into Flock and the growing controversy over license plate cameras as well as a September Senate hearing at which two of InvestigateTV’s interview subjects testified.
‘This needs to be reined in’
Flock Safety, which is by far the largest provider of license plate reader technology to law enforcement, says it has more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states, with more than 6,000 agencies plugged into its data-sharing network.
This means even a small department with a handful of cameras can search the data captured by tens of thousands of Flock devices used by jurisdictions both near and far — and that its camera data is often reciprocally queried by thousands of other departments across the country.
Flock and its proponents assert that this connectivity has led to an increase in crimes solved, but Steube said he sees it as a double-edged sword.
“If it’s a true crime that is being committed, you obviously want law enforcement to have the ability to do that. But if that has that much of a scope and that much power, it obviously in the wrong hands or in abusive hands can be abused.”
Abuse of the system via personal or retaliatory searches is one of the primary criticisms of Flock, and though the company has emphasized the tools it has made available to audit use and flag misuse, the list of officers and law enforcement employees fired or arrested over such abuse has continued to grow.
While some states have passed legislation looking to increase oversight of automated license plate readers, no national rules govern the technology.
“There is no nationwide regulatory framework that says, ‘This is what you can do and not do as it relates to this,’” Steube said. “Even in my district, every law enforcement agency has different rules and policies as to how you can use it and who can use it.”
That patchwork emerged largely because Flock’s nationwide network was pieced together over time via contracts with individual jurisdictions. InvestigateTV found that in some cases those deals were made with minimal public discourse or without a vote by even local officials.
Asked whether Congress needs to vote now to rein things in at the national level, Steube did not hesitate.
“I definitely 1,000% think we need to do that,” he said.
Right after the interview, Steube filed his proposed solution.
He said he thinks the outrage on both ends of the political spectrum is what gives the effort a chance.
“These days, the only thing that definitely passes Congress is something that’s overwhelmingly bipartisan,” he said. “And you’re seeing people on both sides of the aisle talk about how this needs to be reined in.”
The proposals
So far, there have been nine legislative efforts introduced or promised by lawmakers that would seek to put limits on the use of automated license plate readers, with the details varying from warrant requirements to outright bans.
Among the bills that congressional records show have been formally filed:
- H.R. 9800, the Protection Against Mass Surveillance Act, introduced July 21 by Rep. Tim Burchett, R-Tennessee. It would bar federal agencies from buying, deploying or operating automated surveillance systems. Its text names “an automated license plate recognition system, including a Flock Safety camera.” It would also bar state, local and tribal governments from using federal funds for those systems.
- H.R. 10221, the Flock-Off Act, introduced Sept. 2 by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky. It would cut off federal funds for license plate reader and biometric camera systems, including related contracts, subscriptions and data-sharing arrangements, with some exceptions.
- H.R. 10606, the FLAFO Act, introduced Sept. 24 by Rep. Steube. It would generally bar federal agencies from buying, operating or accessing networked license plate reader systems, with access allowed only through a warrant. Exceptions include certain defense and security agencies, emergencies such as terrorism, and missing-person cases. It would tie Justice Department funding for state and local agencies to similar rules.
- H.R. 10691, the Ban Flock Act, introduced Oct. 1 by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York. It would prohibit federal agencies from using license plate readers or their data unless Congress passes a specific authorization law. It would require any authorizing law to limit retention of authorized data at 48 hours.
- H.R. 10822, the ALPR Accountability Act of 2026, introduced Oct. 15 by Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-North Carolina. It includes a warrant requirement for queries, deletion of records within one day, and a ban on indexing “expressive attributes” such as bumper stickers.
Senator Josh Hawley, R-Missouri, has promised legislation that would require similar guardrails, including mandatory audits and limits on data retention, as well as a prohibition on incorporating facial recognition technology.
Other bills address government surveillance more broadly, including license plate readers, such as H.R. 9716 by Rep. Keith Self, R-Texas, and H.R. 8470 by Massie, both of which would require warrants.
InvestigateTV asked Flock about the proposals aimed at the company’s technology.
A spokesperson said:
“Flock’s technology is an important public safety tool for law enforcement agencies across America, helping officers solve serious crimes and find missing people. We support thoughtful, bipartisan legislation that puts strong privacy, transparency, and accountability guardrails in place while preserving law enforcement’s ability to use technology responsibly to keep people safe.”
‘The more questions we asked, the more we felt it was crucial to get to the bottom of it’
Senator Ron Wyden, D-Oregon, made a similar case.
Wyden sent a letter to Flock more than a year ago demanding answers about the balance between privacy and security.
“We decided early on that this was all about warrantless mass surveillance,” Wyden said. “They stonewalled, and the more questions we asked, the more we felt it was crucial to get to the bottom of it.”
Wyden also noted how this concern has bridged across party lines.
“This issue transcends philosophy,” he said. “All over Oregon, all over the country, people are tired of having their privacy rights stomped on. And that’s what’s driving this.”
Whether it’s protecting constitutionally-afforded rights or preventing bad actors from using the technology to stalk and harass, Flock’s position has been that it is ultimately not the company’s job to police the police — that boundaries and accountability are in the hands of local elected officials.
And where some of his colleagues are pushing for federal action, Wyden said he is urging communities to take the decision into their own hands.
“I fall on the proposition that at the local level, people ought to look very carefully,” Wyden said. “And I’m recommending that people close up those cameras. Make it a local choice. People feel very strongly. I mean, my community is 3,000 miles from Washington, D.C. They want to call the shots. They don’t want these cameras.”
But still, Wyden said the company cannot hand off all responsibility.
“Of course, the vendor has a responsibility,” Wyden said. “And particularly, law enforcement is who you look to, to try and strike that balance.”
Constitutional concerns
Steube, the Florida Republican, said in his opinion Congress should write the rules because the network is interconnected nationwide — and at its core is an issue of constitutional significance.
“We should be able to fight child trafficking, kidnapping, armed robbery, all of these things that these cameras help with,” he said. “But we need to make sure that it’s within the United States constitutional framework when we do it.”
Questions on whether the use of technology like Flock’s violates protections against unreasonable search and seizure provided by the Fourth Amendment have been another top flash point.
The company has been adamant that its placement of cameras in public places and safeguards such as its revised default retention period of seven days “protect civil liberties while helping communities prevent, deter, and resolve crime.”
However, in October a federal judge called the technology “a large-scale, dragnet-type surveillance system” and ruled that an Oklahoma officer’s use of it — which was done without a warrant and, the court found, lacked probable cause — was a violation of the Fourth Amendment.
“It becomes constitutionally problematic when law enforcement can indiscriminately and passively catalog your whereabouts over an extended period of time and then use that information for any purpose whenever convenient,” the judge wrote in the ruling.
Wyden said he does not see liberty and security as opposing choices.
“We always wanted liberty. And we always wanted security,” he said. “And I continue to believe that in a country as strong and rich and good as ours, we can have both with smart policies.”
‘An old-fashioned citizens’ issue’
Lawmakers may disagree on the details of how to do it, but the concern about Flock and similar technology and the desire for something to be done have bridged an otherwise ever-deepening political divide on both Capitol Hill and Main Street America.
“Not being stalked and not being harassed is clearly a bipartisan issue. Nobody wants that,” said Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia — where Flock Safety is headquartered.
“Safe from crime, safe from harassment and over-surveillance and stalking. You shouldn’t have to choose one or the other,” he said.
In a press conference following the September subcommittee hearing he hosted on the issue, Hawley, the Missouri Republican, had similar thoughts.
“I think that this is a nonpartisan issue,” he told InvestigateTV. “This is just an old-fashioned citizens’ issue.”
At the hearing, both Hawley and Sen. Cory Booker, D-New Jersey, emphasized the stakes by pulling from issues that normally signal the diametrical opposition of their respective parties: Hawley warned cameras could be placed outside gun shows, gun stores or shooting ranges, while Booker warned a state could use the technology to track and prosecute women who travel for reproductive care.
According to the published calendars, the 119th Congress has just over 20 working days left, and with the unofficial results of the midterm elections pointing to a shift to Democratic control of both chambers, committee assignments and leadership are expected to change once the 120th is convened.
But Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Connecticut, expressed optimism following the September hearing that the relatively unprecedented agreement could indicate action on the near horizon.
“I think there are some clear potential solutions that would have bipartisan support,” he said. “I think there may be an opportunity in the lame duck, if there’s enough consensus.”

title: Crossroads Youth Center crowns Miss Aroostook, Miss Northern Maine titleholders
text:
CARIBOU, Maine (WAGM) - Crossroads Youth Center held its annual regional fundraiser pageants, Miss Aroostook and Miss Northern Maine, on Nov. 1 at the Best Western Caribou Inn in Caribou. The event had 35 contestants. Girls and young women who were crowned will advance to the Maine Academic Scholarship Pageant next fall.
Fundraiser for Maine Snack Food Program
The pageant system places high importance on community service activities. Contestants raised over $4,188 for the Maine Snack Food Program, now in its fifth year.
The program is organized by 2027 USA Ambassador Miss Maine Madelyn Sylvia. The funds are used annually to purchase snack foods for teachers in classrooms throughout Maine.
Donations to the continuing drive can be made through GoFundMe.

title: Aging Untold: Why your metabolism changes as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, learn how metabolism changes with age and what may help support it.
Then, we share gentle ways to tell loved ones when time may be short, set boundaries and care for yourself.
Plus, a group of mall walkers is turning ’90s nostalgia into a fun way to stay active and build community.
Your metabolism is like the body’s “power plant” and every organ has its own, according to the Aging Untold experts.
“If you deplete that power in an organ that needs a lot, you’re going to start to see symptoms sooner,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said. That is why changes in the eyes and ears show up in older people.
As people age, they gain fat and lose muscle. Muscle plays a role in how the body uses glucose, which provides energy, Rogers said.
Some people who are dying get a moment to decide how they’ll say goodbye to the people they love.
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck says the person who is saying goodbye does not need to feel pressure to be strong and manage others’ emotions.
“You need to be getting the support that you need,” Cradduck said.
The people receiving the message are grieving because they are losing that person, but they have the opportunity to provide support for the person who is dying.
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said everyone is different in how they handle saying goodbye. She listed grief, unfinished business and relationships among the things a person may be dealing with.
Laura Lyster-Mensh is a death doula at Historic Congressional Cemetery.
Her role at the national landmark in the heart of Washington, D.C., is to promote what she calls “death positivity.”
She helps visitors have healthy conversations about mortality.
Every Sunday morning, mall walkers in spandex, neon and scrunchies gather for three and a half miles of power walking.
Krista Catwood started the group, the Food Court 5000, and said they’ve “become sort of B-celebrities” at the Lloyd Center mall in Oregon.
Catwood said she knew the activity had to be silly, social and shared with others.

title: Know when to hunt deer, but if you can, spend more time in the wood
text:
Most deer hunters know the best time to be in the woods. However, deer don’t wear watches. They’re in the woods 24 hours a day, and every one of those daylight hours offers the potential for an interaction.
Behaviorally, deer are considered to be crepuscular, which is a fancy way of saying they’re most active around twilight. They may be actively feeding, or finishing their meal before heading off to bed. Either way, the first hour is typically the best hour of the morning for deer hunters.
Deer spend most of their day in bed (what a life). However, that first morning repose is sometimes more of a nap than a full commitment to leisure. Deer are also ruminants. They’ll feed fervently, then lie down and, like a cow, regurgitate and chew on a cud of food. This aids in the digestion of a diet that consists largely of coarse, woody browse in the fall and winter.
Once that task is complete, they may have a little extra space in their complex, four-chambered stomach to fill. An hour or so after the daylight flurry of activity has subsided, there might be a little more movement, as the deer “top off the tank” before seeking their daytime beds. This gives hunters a little more incentive to stay seated for at least the first two or three hours of daylight.
Around hour three, many hunters begin to grow cold, restless, hungry or all of the above. Some will head out of the woods and home to a second breakfast or off to work. Others opt for still-hunting or walking. Either way, the hunter’s movement often creates more deer movement as they inadvertently push deer from their beds. A second, similar increase in activity occurs as more hunters leave the woods for lunch.
In between those waves is another special period that occurs only during the rut. Does have bedded down, but the bucks are still on the prowl and must travel farther and wider to find what they seek. Ask any whitetail guide around the country, and they’ll tell you the best time to shoot a buck during the rut is between 10 a.m. and noon.
If there are doldrums in the deer hunter’s day, they occur over the next 2-3 hours. Natural deer movement is at a minimum. However, there’s still the chance of unnatural deer movement, and the odds increase as you move closer to the time hunters are returning for their afternoon hunt.
Moving from mid-to-late afternoon, daytime deer activity gradually increases as deer stir from their slumber and seek food to fill their now empty stomachs. Odds of intercepting a deer increase with each passing hour until you reach another peak that typically occurs just as the last light is fading.
If your time is limited, the best tactic is to pick peak periods like dawn and dusk. If you have more leeway in how you spend your day, don’t ignore the off hours. As a friend of mine once said, “The best time to be in the woods is when the season is open.”
Bob Humphrey is a freelance writer and Registered Maine Guide who lives in Pownal. He can be reached at: [email protected]

title: A Few Rain & Snow Showers Possible Today & Tuesday As Disturbances Move Through
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The storm system that brought us the soggy weekend will continue to move up into Eastern Canada today. On the backside... an upper-level disturbance will cross the state today giving us a chance for a few isolated rain and/or snow showers throughout the day with a better chance for showers falling across northern parts of Aroostook County. Otherwise expect drier conditions overall today under mostly cloudy skies. There will be a chance to see some breaks of sunshine here and there... but overall clouds are expected to prevail. Temperatures will top off in the 40s to low 50s this afternoon. Skies will be partly cloudy tonight with nighttime temperatures dropping to the upper 20s to mid-30s.
Another disturbance is forecast to move through later in the day Tuesday into Tuesday night. The bulk of the daylight hours will be dry under partly to mostly cloudy skies. Scattered rain and/or snow showers will be possible towards late afternoon and evening and continue into the first half of the night. Temperatures on Tuesday will be similar to today with highs in the 40s to near 50°. Veterans Day on Wednesday looks good with a mix of sun and clouds and high temperatures in the 40s to near 50°. High pressure will nose in for Thursday giving us partly to mostly sunny skies and highs in the 40s.
We’re watching a potential storm for Friday into the weekend. Model data is all over the place with the track of the system. An inland track would mean mainly rain with some snow in the mountains. A track just offshore would lead to minimal or no impacts across the northern parts of the state with a better chance for rain and snow closer to Bangor and to the coast while a track further to our south would keep the storm out to sea and miss us altogether. So at this point... it is too difficult to decide what’s going to play out but certainly looks like a chance for some rain and possibly some snow to impact our forecast late in the week into the weekend. Stay tuned for updates as we get closer.
Rest of Today: More clouds than sunshine. Isolated showers possible. Highs in the mid-40s to low 50s. West wind 5-10 MPH.
Tonight: Partly cloudy. Lows in the upper 20s to mid-30s. West wind 5-10 MPH.
Tuesday: Partly to mostly cloudy. Scattered rain and snow showers possible during the late afternoon and evening. Highs in the 40s to around 50°. West wind 5-10 MPH.
Wednesday: Mix of sun and clouds. Highs in the 40s to around 50°.
Thursday: Partly to mostly sunny. Highs in the 40s.
Friday: Partly to mostly cloudy. Afternoon rain possible... especially closer to the coast. Highs in the upper 30s to mid-40s.

title: This artist uses sunlight to burn designs into wood
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (InvestigateTV) - Billy Keith is a solar artist. He uses sunlight as his tool to create artwork burned directly into wood.
“You learn a lot by standing in the sun all day,” Keith said.
Keith said he introduces himself as “the sun man,” and his goal is to make more art in public.
His work starts with something he cannot hold in his hand: sunlight.
Keith uses a large magnifying lens — a Fresnel lens — to concentrate the sun into a tiny point of light, hot enough to burn designs into wood. Keith works without stencils, printers or shortcuts, creating each piece freehand line by line.
“It’s taken me 16 years to get to where I can do this so fast and smooth over and over again,” he said.
Keith said part of the process is keeping the concentrated point of light moving. When he makes an error, he keeps going.
“No mistakes. I just Bob Ross that. Just keep on going. Happy accident,” he said.
Keith said he got into the art after what he described as a near-death experience.
“Near-death experience after a night out of drinking Easter weekend,” he said.
Keith said he heard what he described as a whisper telling him, “You’re done drinking. Make art with the sun.”
“I did not die… this is what I was saved to do, and I better be doing it,” Keith said.
Keith said each piece has a story. He’s made many trees, landscapes, animals, and plants just to name a few.
“This is the day I saved the cat from a tree,” he said.
Keith sells his work online and travels for events and festivals around the region. He said he likes creating art publicly so he can talk with people about it.
Keith said he can also make solar art in winter as long as the sun is out. He also uses bingo dabbers to paint his work, a method he said he discovered after finding a bingo dabber on the street.

title: Race participants, first responders help save man's life after cardiac arrest in Kennebunk

Race participants, first responders help save man's life after cardiac arrest in Kennebunk
An elderly man who went into cardiac arrest while walking his dog in Kennebunk Sunday morning is alive thanks to bystanders and first responders who quickly stepped in to help.

An elderly man who went into cardiac arrest while walking his dog in Kennebunk Sunday morning is alive thanks to bystanders and first responders who quickly stepped in to help.
An elderly man who went into cardiac arrest while walking his dog in Kennebunk Sunday morning is alive thanks to bystanders and first responders who quickly stepped in to help, according to officials with Kennebunk Fire & Rescue. 
Kennebunk police and fire crews were out providing traffic and safety coverage for the "Cancer Can Suck A Cactus" 5K and 10K race when the medical emergency happened nearby.
In a Facebook post detailing the emergency, Kennebunk fire officials wrote that runners and other bystanders saw the man suddenly collapse and recognized that he was suffering a cardiac arrest. They immediately began CPR and called for a nearby ambulance that was already assigned to the race.
While bystanders continued CPR, the man's implanted defibrillator delivered a shock in an effort to restore his heart rhythm. Once emergency crews reached the man, he was still in cardiac arrest. Personnel from Kennebunk Fire & Rescue continued CPR and began advanced life support measures.
The man later regained his pulse and circulation. He was taken to a hospital in Biddeford and was awake and talking when he arrived, according to officials. 
Fire officials credited the bystanders who recognized the emergency and began CPR, as well as the coordinated response from Kennebunk police and fire personnel.
"You do not have to be a first responder to save a life," wrote Kennebunk Fire and Rescue. "Learn CPR. Be willing to act. You never know when someone will need you."
The department said the incident highlights the importance of the "chain of survival" in cardiac emergencies, including quickly recognizing cardiac arrest, starting CPR and providing rapid emergency medical response.

title: ‘A Christmas miracle’: Stolen nativity scene found miles away
text:
PALMER, Alaska (KTUU/Gray News) - Community tips led to the recovery of a valuable nativity scene that apparently was stolen earlier this week, miles from where it was last seen.
The nativity scene, which sits inside a handcrafted wooden crèche cabin valued at tens of thousands of dollars, went missing from the parking lot at St. Michael’s Parish in Palmer sometime on Tuesday or Wednesday while sitting on a flatbed trailer, according to Father Michael Shields with the church.
Shields said community tips on Facebook led to a reported sighting along the Glenn Highway near Chickaloon.
“So one o’clock [Thursday] night, I got in my car to find it,” Shields said. “So I drove up to Chickaloon to see if I could find it.”
The pastor said he made the late-night drive down the highway but didn’t see it.
Palmer police, however, did. Officers contacted Shields as he was looking for the scene and confirmed they had found it, still in good condition.
Shields said it’s still not known who stole it, but he believes whoever took it abandoned it after the trailer’s tires went flat. He said it was found partly hidden among trees.
“It’s a Christmas miracle because honestly, I didn’t think we were going to get it back, to be honest,” he said.
The pastor said the nativity scene was created over seven years, built and paid for by the parishioners of his church. The figures were molded after the Italian image of Jesus, he said, adding that the figurines are valued at around $25,000 to $30,000.
Shields said the scene will be placed near the Palmer train depot near the center of town.
Shields was heartened by the community response as news of the theft spread quickly on social media.
“It went all through the Valley, Glennallen to Valdez,” he said. “And so everybody showed such beautiful concern and hope.”

title: Why people paid $22 to shop at a vintage market in Portland
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — If buying my first pair of readers last month didn’t make me feel old enough, the most recent Lost & Found Market at Thompson’s Point sealed the deal — and not only because I saw a “vintage” green-and-purple rugby shirt for $75 that brought me right back to picture day.
My reaction to the requirements to attend the event, held in Portland over Halloween weekend, confirmed that I’ve entered a new stage in life: You pay for a ticket and then pay to park to shop for used stuff that costs more than when it was new?
The concept is not for any faint-of-heart fogies, but recognizing that people were indeed choosing to do this — thousands of people, in fact — I left my Walgreens glasses at home and set out to understand why.
My initial interest in attending the event (featuring over 100 vendors, along with food and drinks) was to bear witness to the traffic and parking problems that I heard had plagued it in the past, backing cars up all the way to the interstate.
That didn’t appear to be an issue this time — a result of the ticketing system, according to market founder and organizer Logan Hanson.
Talking to Hanson, I came to understand the need for the tickets, both as a method of crowd control and a way to cover the expenses of the event, including the venue, parking management, insurance and security.
Hanson, who also holds the pop-up market in Bangor and Union where entry is free, said she would prefer not to charge admission in Portland either, but it’s just not feasible.
Plus, you didn’t have to pay for a ticket. Entry to the second day of the market, on Sunday, after it was somewhat picked over, was free. For the same reason, the three timed entry slots on Saturday got progressively cheaper, with tickets starting at $12 and going down to $8 for the last three hours.
The only tickets that sold out were the most expensive ones, for that first time slot, which is also when traffic backed up most, with people waiting in line to park for as long as 11 minutes, said Hanson. At previous markets, the worst traffic delay was up to 45 minutes, she said.
There were also ways to get around paying for parking — a flat rate of $10 for the day, charged by Thompson’s Point. The beautiful fall weekend made walking more plausible for many, whether from home or nearby unattended lots and side streets, if you know a little something about the area (which is all I’ll say to avoid drawing the ire of Libbytown).
Hanson estimated that about 6,000 people came through the doors between the two days, with 850 paying the highest price.
Asked why she thinks so many people are willing to pay to shop, she talked about the treasure-hunt aspect of the market, the nostalgia carried by the items for sale, the sustainability appeal and the opportunity to own something unique.
“I think people are kind of tired of all the soulless junk we’re being peddled,” she said.
As to people who complain about the items themselves being overpriced, she thinks they don’t understand all the time, energy and costs expended by the vendors to curate, purchase, clean, mend and store their wares, not to mention the travel, setup and fee for a spot at the market.
Hanson said some have mischaracterized the event as a thrift market, but it’s not comparable to going to Goodwill.
The vendors are doing that part for you, so you can stroll with a bloody Mary in hand, browsing items that someone with a trained eye has already determined is cool again; so you can leave with a faded T-shirt from a concert that someone else went to, a cookbook from someone else’s church, a mug with someone else’s name on it, a postcard from someone else’s trip.
If you put value on the life an object has lived, paying more to find it first is might be worth it to you, too.

title: Another shake-up at DC Studios: Gunn and Safran out as Skydance appoints Marvel vet Latchman
text:
Another shake-up at DC Studios: Gunn and Safran out as Skydance appoints Marvel vet Latchman
Superman, Batman and the rest of the DC heroes are getting a new boss, yet again.
Skydance Motion Picture Group announced Monday that James Gunn and Peter Safran are stepping down as co-chief executives after four years leading DC Studios. Although their first film leading the superhero factory, “Superman,” reached theaters only last year, their DC run has come to an abrupt end.
Gunn and Safran initially survived Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The studio's merger with Paramount Pictures was finalized just as DC's “Clayface” was released.
However, it turns out Gunn and Safran aren't surviving the merger. Instead, Skydance chairman and chief executive David Ellison is turning to Jeremy Latchman, a veteran of Marvel Studios, to steer DC.
“James and Peter launched a new era for DC Studios and led it through a period of real transformation, resetting the foundation and building a slate we’re incredibly proud of,” Ellison said in a statement. “We’re grateful for their passion, contributions and commitment to this legendary brand.”
Latchman was a leading executive for Marvel, including during the first wave of the Marvel Cinematic Universe with “Iron Man” and “The Avengers.” He also worked with Gunn and Safran on their “Guardians of the Galaxy.”
The changeover will take effect Dec. 1. But a long pipeline of projects already in production ensures that Gunn and Safran's fingerprints will be on DC Studios for a while to come. Gunn is currently in postproduction on the “Superman” follow-up, “Man of Tomorrow.” Other upcoming releases include the series “The People v. Gorilla Grodd” and “The Batman: Part II.”
But the decade's worth of planning that Gunn and Safran instituted will no longer come to fruition. Their reign has been characterized by more idiosyncratic comic book adaptations and genre gambles, like “Clayface,” which fused superhero with horror. (It's grossed $109 million so far.) Earlier this year, “Supergirl” flopped, a major setback in just their second release.
Latchman takes on the roles of president and chief creative officer of DC Studios. He will report to Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, co-chairs of Skydance Motion Picture Group.
“Jeremy brings a deep reverence for DC and its passionate fanbase, recognizing that they are the very foundation of this storied, multigenerational brand,” Goldberg and Greenstein said.
Gunn's biggest success leading DC was “Superman,” which struck a decidedly different and more comedic tone than the previous treatments of the iconic hero in Zack Snyder's “Man of Steel.” But it also didn't reach the box-office heights of the biggest superhero hits, grossing $618.7 million worldwide.
From the start, Gunn, a prodigious filmmaker, was an unusual choice for such a prominent corporate leadership role. In exiting DC, he seemed eager to concentrate again on writing and directing.
“We’re excited to return to what drew us to this job in the first place, which is telling the stories we love, including the next chapter of Clark and Lex’s journey in ‘Man of Tomorrow,'” Gunn and Safran said in a statement.
Latchman had been out of the superhero business. In 2017, he departed Marvel to set up Latchman Pictures, producing films including “Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves” and “Bad Times at the El Royale.”
“I’ve had the privilege to help bring some of the most celebrated superhero stories to life on the big screen, and I’m excited and honored for the opportunity to now lead DC Studios into its next era,” Latchman said.

title: Hallowell police chief reverses recommendation on Quarry Tap Room liquor license
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
HALLOWELL — The Quarry Tap Room’s liquor license was approved for renewal following a packed City Council meeting Monday.
Before the meeting, police Chief Zachary Kindelan wrote an email to council members stating his support for the license renewal, a reversal of a previous letter he wrote with hesitations regarding the license, following a productive meeting with bar and restaurant staff.
Dozens of residents gathered at City Hall for a public hearing, causing the council chambers to reach capacity almost immediately. The meeting was promptly relocated to the upstairs auditorium.
When Mayor George Lapointe asked the crowd to raise their hands if they supported renewing the Quarry Tap Room’s liquor license, nearly every hand in the room went up.
Kindelan and Steve LaChance, one of the owners of the Quarry Tap Room, summarized the results of their recent meeting in which they discussed both of their concerns regarding frequent police calls to the establishment. LaChance emphasized that fewer Saturday late-night music events in November have been scheduled, and their security camera system is in working order.
Several Quarry Tap Room employees and local residents spoke in favor of renewing the license during the public hearing, citing the importance of the establishment to the community.
Brooke Brann, a manager at the Quarry Tap Room specifically for the late-night events, said her fellow staff were scared they were going to lose their jobs and not be able to provide for their families or pay for heating oil if the establishment lost its license.
Brann noted all staff members are continually trained to handle a variety of scenarios.
“In this business, our staff are required and regularly forced to make judgment calls,” Brann said. “Do we get it right 100% of the time? Absolutely not. No one is getting it right 100% of the time.”
Heidi Mills, a server at the Quarry Tap Room for over 10 years, said it is clear how important the Quarry Tap Room is to the local community, noting how much she’s enjoyed seeing families and residents gather there over the years.
“Unfortunately, when you bring people and alcohol together, there will occasionally be individuals who make poor choices. That’s not unique to the Quarry, though,” Mills said. “We have to recognize that difference between the actions of individuals and the intentions and responsibilities of the people that are really in business.”
She also noted how social media has played a role in amplifying negativity around the Quarry Tap Room.
Kindelan had originally written a letter to the licensing board last week stating he would not support the renewal of the liquor license for the tap room, which has been at the center of numerous controversies over the past year, until significant improvements and policies were iumplemented about safety at the establishment.
During the public hearing, Kindelan emphasized he originally wanted to meet with Quarry Tap Room staff before submitting an opinion on the renewal, which was difficult to accomplish in one week. Lapointe and Kindelan both agreed to work on improving communication among city officials to prevent a similar time constraint from occurring in the future.
He also noted in an email to councilors that the public interpretation to his original letter was an “unfortunate circumstance.” He said it was not his intention to prohibit the license from being renewed, but to provide context to his recommendation that the bar make improvements before renewing the license.
The Quarry Tap Room has been at the center of numerous controversies over the past year.
In August, a video of a physical altercation between a bar security staff member and a patron went viral on social media, in which the staffer held a female patron in a headlock.
The patron later posted photos documenting several deep scrapes and bruises on her neck. She also claimed to have suffered a concussion during the altercation.
Kindelan said the matter is currently being reviewed by the Kennebec County District Attorney’s Office, which will decide whether to bring charges in the matter.
On Monday, Maeghan Maloney, Kennebec County district attorney, said the case was reviewed by Aroostook County District Attorney Todd Collins.
Maloney serves on a local nonprofit board with one of the owners of the Quarry Tap Room. While she said she did not have a conflict, out of an abundance of caution she asked Collins to review the case and make a decision on charges.
“I am not able to release (Collins’) decision,” Maloney said.
Collins could not immediately be reached Monday.
Matthew Clancy, the former chief of Maine Capitol Police, stepped down from his position after he was arrested for assaulting a Hallowell police officer in August 2025.
In his original letter to the licensing board, Kindelan, who was sworn in as chief in July, wrote that in his short tenure on the job, his department had been called out to the Quarry Tap Room 15 times, resulting in 11 arrests or summonses. Many of those instances were for people accused of drunken driving after leaving the bar.
City councilors voted unanimously to approve the renewal of the liquor license for the Quarry Tap Room — with the exception of Councilor Walter McKee who recused himself from the vote as he previously represented the Quarry Tap Room in his work as an attorney — a decision which was met with applause from the crowd.

title: Trump says he was just kidding about making UFC’s Dana White his press secretary
text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — President Donald Trump said Sunday he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary after announcing on social media he had offered his close friend the job.
After his party’s deep losses in Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump shook up his administration on Friday by replacing his chief of staff and followed up on Saturday with a post that said he had offered the press secretary job to White. On Sunday, Trump said it was “just a little fun.”
“I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy,” Trump said, speaking to reporters in Florida before departing for the White House. White is set to visit him at the White House on Monday.
The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump on Friday named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller is the architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies. Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia, who faltered behind the lectern and in interviews, and left the post after five days.

title: Patriots’ stars struggle in brutal loss to Packers
text:
FOXBOROUGH, Mass. — Patriots coach Mike Vrabel underlined a universal truth about the NFL following his team’s lethargic 45-27 loss to Green Bay: If your team’s best players don’t perform well, your chances of winning typically evaporate.
New England’s best players — quarterback Drake Maye and cornerback Christian Gonzalez — had performances that rank among the worst of their career.
“We expect a lot more,” Vrabel said.
Maye threw three interceptions for the second time this season, two leading to 14 points for the Packers. He threw just one pick in his previous four games. He’s now tied with the Chargers’ Justin Herbert with an NFL-worst 11 INTs.
Gonzalez had just as bad a night. According to NFL Next Gen Stats, the cornerback gave up seven catches for 105 yards to Matthew Golden and three catches for 82 yards to Christian Watson. It made Gonzalez the only defender since at least 2018 to allow more than 80 yards receiving to two players in the same game.
“Christian had a few plays I’m sure that he’d like to have back,” Vrabel said. “We have high expectations for him, and he certainly does, too. So, I think it’s about answering the challenge this week and then coming back.”
What’s clear is that the team needs both players to course correct quickly as injuries throughout the roster continue to pile and a three-week run of games against Buffalo, Minnesota and Kansas City is less than a month away.
It has put even more emphasis on a matchup with the Detroit Lions on Sunday in Germany, the Patriots’ final game before their bye week. Lose, and they’ll fall to 5-5 and leave little room for error down the stretch.
“We’ve got to bounce back and know that there’s still some games left and we’re battling,” Maye said. “We’ve got to battle. I think that’s it.”
What’s working
Not a lot. But the Patriots did go 2 for 2 in the red zone. Still, this season they’ve converted on just 14 of 24 (58.3%) of their chances inside the 20.
What needs help
The run game. New England’s 94 yards rushing were its second fewest of the season and the second time in three games the Patriots failed to run for at least 100 yards
Stock up
WR DeMario Douglas. The receiver did his part to try to keep the offense moving, catching five passes for a season-high 102 yards.
Stock down
The offensive line. Maye was sacked a season-high four times. While the O-line came in dealing with injuries and had a few more Sunday, it’s something that must be cleaned up if the offense is going to get back on track this week.
Injuries
The biggest concern is running back Rhamondre Stevenson, who was able to jog off the field late in the third quarter, but it was announced later he suffered a knee injury. … Cornerback Carlton Davis III also suffered a knee injury in the second quarter. … In addition, left guard Ben Brown (knee) limped off a few plays after Davis late in the second quarter. … Special teamer Brenden Schooler also aggravated a hamstring injury. … Left tackle Will Campbell walked off with a knee injury in the fourth quarter.
Key number
5 — Number of teams the Patriots will face over their last eight games that currently have winning records.
Next steps
The Patriots head to Munich, Germany, on Wednesday to begin preparations for a matchup with the Lions at FC Bayern Munich Arena, home to the Bundesliga soccer team.

title: Portland Water District secures $8.1M to protect Sebago Lake
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland Water District was awarded an $8.1 million grant to lead a regional watershed protection initiative safeguarding Sebago Lake, a drinking water source for more than 200,000 people.
The money came from the Regional Conservation Partnership Program of the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service. Additional financing comes from $10 million in partner contributions.
The $18 million project will advance stream restoration, forest conservation and forest stewardship across the Sebago Lake watershed from Bethel to Standish.
Maine’s clean water is considered a key ingredient essential to the state’s beverage industry.
Users of Sebago Lake water include Sebago Brewing Co., who owners have credited Portland Water District’s commitment to protecting the lake’s purity. Westbrook-based mainelove sources and packages water from Sebago Lake and packages the consumer product in aluminum cans.
Watershed protection
The latest project builds on an initial $8 million award in 2020 that resulted in the conservation of over 12,000 acres of forest, reconnection of 42 miles of rivers and streams and sustainable management of over 5,000 acres of forest. Watershed conservation and stewardship complement the treatment and monitoring programs by safeguarding water quality before it reaches Sebago Lake.
“Conserving land is essential to protecting Sebago Lake,” said Paul Hunt, the district’s environmental services manager. “This investment strengthens that protection by improving forest health and reconnecting streams.”
Over the next five years, project includes working with interested landowners to purchase conservation easements on high-priority forests to safeguard natural water filtration and prevent development fragmentation. It will provide private landowners with technical assistance and funding for forest management planning, invasive plant and insect control and habitat enhancement. Barriers will be removed and stream crossings improved to promote fish passage, restore natural river flows and build flood resilience.
The measures are expected to improve stream habitat and more than 6,000 acres of forest stewardship.

title: Remains of World War II veteran identified, returned home after 82 years
text:
LYNN, Mass. (CNN) - After more than eight decades, the remains of a World War II veteran are finally home.
Pvt. Joseph Gala was laid to rest in Lynn, Massachusetts, on Thursday.
Gala, who was 21 when he died, entered the military in 1943 and was killed in action the following year in Burma.
His remains were classified as missing in action and remained that way for 82 years. However, DNA advancement helped officials identify his remains.
“And our family, mother, aunt, uncles, grandparents, I know they’re really happy,” Rose DiGregory, Gala’s niece, said.
A ceremony with full military honors was held in the World War II section of Pine Grove Cemetery.
