A New Format for the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall
text:
Athlete of the Fall Is Here With a New Large and Small School Format
Nine weeks of Athlete of the Week are complete, but there is still one major piece of the fall sports season left.
Now it is time to look at the entire body of work.
Nominations are officially open for the 2026 Aroostook County Athletes of the Fall, and this year the awards will have a new format designed to better reflect the different sizes of athletic programs across the area.
Instead of crowning one boys winner and one girls winner, there will be four Athlete of the Fall awards:
Large School Boys Athlete of the Fall
Large School Girls Athlete of the Fall
Small School Boys Athlete of the Fall
Small School Girls Athlete of the Fall
How the School Divisions Will Work
The Athlete of the Fall divisions will not follow individual MPA sport classifications.
Instead, schools are being separated based on the overall size and participation level of their athletic programs.
The Large School Division will include:
Presque Isle
Caribou
Houlton
Fort Kent
All other Aroostook County schools covered during the fall season will compete in the Small School Division.
The goal is to create more balanced comparisons while still recognizing the very best seasons from across the County.
Nominations Will Be Organized by School, Not by Sport
Athlete of the Fall is an overall fall sports award, so athletes from soccer, cross country, golf and other eligible fall sports will all be considered together within their division.
Nominations will be organized by school, making it easier to see the top candidates from across the area.
There is also no one-athlete-per-school limit.
If a school has multiple athletes who put together exceptional seasons, they can all be nominated and considered for the final ballot.
A standout soccer player and a championship-level cross country runner from the same school should both have an opportunity to be recognized.
This Award Is About the Entire Season
Athlete of the Fall is different from Athlete of the Week.
A single huge game can make someone a strong weekly candidate. For this award, we are looking at everything an athlete accomplished from the beginning of the fall through the postseason.
That includes:
Season-long production and consistency, postseason performances, championships and major meet results, individual milestones, importance to the team, leadership, sportsmanship and overall impact.
An athlete does not need to have won Athlete of the Week to be nominated or selected as an Athlete of the Fall finalist.
Likewise, an Athlete of the Week victory does not automatically guarantee a spot on the final ballot.
This is a fresh evaluation of the complete fall season.
What to Include With Your Nomination
Coaches, athletic directors, parents, teammates, fans and community members are encouraged to submit nominations.
Please include:
The athlete's name
School
Sport
Season statistics or accomplishments
Postseason or championship performances
Awards, milestones or other notable achievements
Why you believe they deserve Athlete of the Fall consideration
The more information provided, the stronger the nomination can be when the final ballots are built.
Nominations Close Thursday at 5 P.M.
Athlete of the Fall nominations will remain open through Thursday, November 12 at 5 p.m.
Once nominations close, the top candidates will be selected for each of the four divisions and voting will begin shortly afterward.
That means we will have separate ballots for:
Large School Boys
Large School Girls
Small School Boys
Small School Girls
Nine weeks of weekly voting gave us a chance to recognize incredible individual performances.
Now we get to answer a bigger question.
Who put together the best complete fall seasons in Aroostook County?
Send in your nominations before Thursday at 5 p.m.

title: Characters of the County: John Blodgett Serves His Town and Country
text:
When John Blodgett enlisted in the Marine Corps during his senior year at Medomak Valley High School in 1983, before he was even 18, he did not expect to be in the service for the next 21 years. In fact, up to a few months before he enlisted, Blodgett did not really know what the Marines were, let alone plan to become one.
He was focused on joining a different branch of the military, following in the footsteps of his uncle.
“If you look through my yearbook, it’ll say, ‘Future plans: Join the United States Coast Guard,’” he said.
When it came time to enlist, however, Blodgett learned the Coast Guard had recently experienced major funding cuts and was not taking new recruits. Greater than Blodgett’s desire to join the Coast Guard was his desire to serve in the military, so he started looking at other branches.
Some of his motivation to join up came from his parents. His father, Bill Blodgett, who has served as a Lincoln County commissioner for 30 years, did not seek reelection this year, topping off decades of teaching, serving on various municipal committees, and holding various elected offices. His mother, Carol Blodgett, was similarly involved in leadership positions for many local organizations and civic groups before she passed away in December 2018.
“It was just instilled in me that I’ve got to do something not only for myself but for the community and the United States as a whole,” John Blodgett said.
Additionally, he wanted to take the path less traveled.
“I wanted to do something not everyone did,” Blodgett said.
So he looked into other military branches, and in January 1983, at the age of 17, Blodgett enlisted in the Marine Corps. Blodgett said when he joined, the Marine Corps was a smaller service. According to the Center for Naval Analyses, the Marine Corps consistently had the smallest number of active members by about 200,000 from 1973-2017.
Blodgett graduated from high school that June, and at the end of August, shortly after his 18th birthday, he was on a plane to Parris Island, S.C. for boot camp. Blodgett remembers the exact date: Aug. 23, 1982.
“First time on a plane, first time away from the family for a long extended period of time,” he said.
After boot camp, Blodgett attended transportation school, graduated in 1984, and was assigned to Okinowa, Japan. He was originally assigned to driving trucks on the base, but when he got there, Blodgett found himself working for the U.S. Postal Service.
“I drove the mail all around Okinowa, Japan,” he said.
Blodgett spent two years delivering mail in Japan, returned to America in 1986, and was sent back to Japan in 1987, where he spent another two years. From Japan, he was deployed to Korea three different times, and was able to attend the 1988 Seoul Olympic Games.
“I can say I’ve been to the Olympic Games,” Blodgett said.
He returned to America in 1989, to Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton in California where he was stationed.
In August of 1990, Blodgett was preparing to go to Turkey. Instead, Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait, and Blodgett was sent to Saudi Arabia as part of Operation Desert Shield, the initial phase of the Gulf War.
Blodgett said on the plane to the Middle East, he could tell the situation was serious because everyone was being given handfuls of ammunition.
“Usually you have to sign your life away to get stuff,” Blodgett said. “But they just said, ‘Pack your pockets.’ So we knew that was it … We were flying over to war.”
Blodgett was in the Middle East for Operation Desert Shield and then Operation Desert Storm. Early in 1991, he returned to Camp Pendleton in California.
Throughout his time serving in America and in other countries, there was never any question in Blodgett’s mind about where he would eventually end up: It was always going to be Waldoboro.
“Even in the Marine Corps when I was traveling around, I always knew what was going on in Waldoboro,” he said.
In 1992, Blodgett attended the Marine Corps Recruiting and Retention School in San Diego in order to become a recruiter. He said he hoped this would allow him to be “closer to home,” meaning Waldoboro.
Blodgett remained in recruiting the rest of his military career, until his retirement from the military with the rank of Master Sergeant in 2004.
He married his wife Tanya in 2002, and they still live in Waldoboro. Their daughter, Kelsie Lee, and her husband, Josh Lee, live nearby in Friendship with Blodgett’s four grandchildren: Nathan, Beau, Wayland, and Ella.
Blodgett currently works for Back Meadow Farm Land Development in Boothbay, driving big vehicles like the Peterbilt dump truck he parks by his garage. Tanya Blodgett works at the Waldoboro town office.
In 2023, John Blodgett was elected to the Waldoboro Select Board. In June 2026, he was reelected to the seat.
Blodgett said any leadership skills he may have are the result of his time in the Marine Corps.
“The Marine Corps helped me develop,” he said. “I don’t have a problem talking to people now.”

title: Voices of Honor
text:
Roger Belanger, Auburn
I for sure am no hero.
I did my duty and served my country. Enlistment in the U.S. Navy in 1967 took me to the oceans of Vietnam. I worked in the Operations’ office and was assigned to the ship’s photography section to photograph each launch and recovery of the ship’s air squadrons.
Positioned in the middle of the catapults, I would take movies of each launch as they passed by several feet away and again when they returned. These were needed in the event of a malfunction or a crash. Dangerous, yes, our position put us at great risk but no weapon in my hands. Unlike my two brothers who faced the enemy with their rifles in hand, I only faced possible mishaps.
After my WestPac cruise, I returned to the U.S.A. and was assigned to Combat Camera Group Atlantic Fleet. I never understood how I was chosen for this position, but it allowed me to travel the world and work on various secret missions as a motion picture photographer.
This unit was an elite photography documentary unit. I was trained as a motion picture photographer, but we also had still photographers and we were certified in aerial photography and underwater diving. My specialty was aerial, and it allowed me to work as an aircrewman on many different types of helicopters, prop and jet planes. As a young man, this was the highlight of my enlistment.
I am proud of my service and I later served in the U.S. Coast Guard Reserve. Duty to the country is important to me. I have traveled to many places and witnessed luxury and poverty. We have a great nation, and with that we have a responsibility to serve and protect our heritage and our future. Freedom is not free. As in Vietnam, the World Wars, and the latest fight over global terrorism, thousands have sacrificed their time and, most importantly, their lives. Most believed that our nation needs to be cherished, held to high esteem and protected. We live in a time of great danger to our society. We need to instill in our youth that Freedom is not Free. It is a privilege to live in the U.S.A. and serving our nation is an honor.
Robert Dorr, Waldoboro
June 1954
I joined the Air Force at age 17, went to Sampson AFB for basic training, then to Amarillo, Texas, for training as a jet aircraft mechanic.
In February 1955, I was stationed in Misawa, Japan, for two years. I was crew chief on three T-33 jet fighter trainers. I accumulated many hours of flight time in the back seat of my planes, on operational checks and fun rides. The off-time life was good in Misawa, and the friendships were strong. I enjoyed life in Japan. I traveled on deployment to the Philippines, Okinawa, and Korea, along with many bases in Japan. It was a time of growth, learning responsibility for the planes and pilots who flew them.
I returned to the States and Dover AFB in 1957. I was discharged in early 1958. The military set the tone for my life. You don’t have to thank me for my service, because my military experiences gave me education, a lifetime community, responsibility and affirmation. After the service, I completed my high school education at Greely High School in Cumberland, received a BA in psychology from the University of Southern Maine, and a master’s degree in divinity and pastoral counseling and psychology from Boston University.
Thank you, America, for your service to me and the life I have.
Tony Scarpelli, Portland
The day the world nearly ended.
I’ve been reading in the paper about the Cuban missile crisis; I was involved.
In October 1962, I was at the East Coast Relay Station in Frederick, Maryland, 50 miles from Washington, D.C. This was the country’s long-range communications site. The world’s radio communications came through us to and from Washington, DC. There were large transmitter antenna farms all over the world that would blast radio waves off the ionosphere to receiver farms all over the world beyond the curve of the Earth. I was in the Army and was a facilities controller. I fixed long-range communications problems.
One day in 1962, a U-2 spy plane took pictures of a bunch of Russian atomic missiles in Cuba. President Kennedy didn’t like that very much and told Cuba to get them out, or else. He decided to send in the military. That day, I was given the task of setting up communications with the Navy carriers in the sea near Cuba and Washington, D.C. The only way we had, at that time, to communicate with the ships was UHF radio. So some sailors on the ships and I got our old radios (we hardly used UHF anymore) connected together.
Cuba decided to have the Russians take back their atomic missiles. Kennedy’s guts saved the day, and us. It was quite exciting for me as a 19-year-old.
In Honor and Loving Memory of George Hamel
Airman 2nd Class – Petty Officer, U.S.S. Gilbert Island
Thank you for serving our country and helping to keep us free and for teaching us the value of service, honor, duty and love.
You will always be our HERO.
We Love and Miss You Every Day,
Your Family
In Honor of Ervin H. Tyler
US Army, P.F.C. INF.
June 17, 1921 – Nov. 17, 2020
The courage and bravery you showed continues to serve as an inspiration to us as we face life challenges.
Love, Your Family
Jeff von Freymann, MBA, DBA, Kennebunk
From an 84-year-old veteran’s Air Force military service and a lasting memory.
(Four years of active-duty Air Force service; Cold War noncombat service; 15-month remote foreign assignment).
At the end of my 15 months of overseas duty in Turkey, I was ordered to report to Fort Meade in Maryland to finish my active-duty service. I left with a smile, having spent some time in class there learning about Turkish history, visiting Istanbul two or three times and its wonderful Topkapi Palace Museum, the ancient Hagia Sophia, the exquisite Blue Mosque and lavish sultans’ palaces, the marketplace, and the bridge connecting Europe to Asia over the Bosporus. I also spent six weeks taking college classes in Germany.
On my return, to my surprise, I was assigned to the NSA and worked in the critical command center as a communications status reporter. Promoted to sergeant before leaving Turkey, I still did not have a handle on how vast and important our work had been there. Once in the NSA command center, working the night shifts to report to the director each morning on world security status, I realized how important each of our contributions really was, where we fitted in, and how we were appreciated for what we did. Also, while on duty, it was heartbreaking to hear President Johnson call each night after 2 a.m. with his request for the body count of our troops killed in Vietnam. I will never forget those calls.
In the words of our gifted New England poet, Robert Frost, and his famous poem, “The Road Not Taken”: “Two roads diverged in a yellow wood … I took the one less traveled by, and that has made all the difference.”
Really? Maybe. But there is no going back. (And no one I met during my four years of service was a sucker or loser.)
In Honor of Sergeant Philip C. Buck
U.S. Army Air Corp – WWII
November 13, 1920 – March 29, 2007
You are in my thoughts and prayers from morning to night and from year to year.
Sadly Missed by Son, Mike
In Honor of Norman B. Buck
January 12, 1924 – August 25, 2013
Always in my heart.
Sadly Missed by Nephew, Mike
Lega Sammut-Medcalf, Bridgton
From Marcel Ernest Sammut’s memoir, (Bridgton resident, now deceased)
While we were at the foot of Mount Etna, I was informed to go on patrol at night with my platoon. The scope of our mission was to climb the mountain by moonlight to find the position of the enemy. We were supposed to remain there for a few days if necessary. We were also warned that we could expect to meet a German patrol. My role was to interrogate military or civilian Italians who could inform us of the enemy position.
We waited for two mules to carry our food, water, and blankets. At last, a man came with a horse and a donkey! What a choice! It is well known that horses and donkeys are bad mountain climbers. However, the man told us that he couldn’t find mules and that we had to accept what he could find. So, we loaded the horse and the donkey and marched toward a bridge. The horse crossed the bridge, but alas, the donkey refused.
We tried all sorts of stratagems to no avail, including the use of a baton. The use of the baton was a mistake because the donkey kicked left and right and disappeared into the darkness, taking away part of our food and water.
We had no time to waste. The mission had to go on. The first phase of our march was not very difficult as we walked on an almost flat path. But the slope increased rapidly, and we encountered many rocks. From time to time, we could hear the clicking of horseshoes as the horse scrambled along the rocks.
It was midnight, and we were exhausted. The leading officer told us to have a rest. I laid down my haversack and rifle and sat on the rocky ground. We found ourselves surrounded by a wall of silence. We were all sleeping or half-asleep; even the horse was sleeping. Suddenly, we heard a rifle sliding over the rocks and then a very loud gunshot. The horse kicked many times, stood up on its front legs and ran down the hill, carrying away our precious food and water. Fortunately, nobody was hurt, but could the enemy have heard the shot, and were we now exposed to crossfire? We felt that we were on the verge of being caught. Fortunately, nothing happened. The surrounding silence remained silent.
Gary Perlmutter, Cumberland
Somewhere at sea.
My Dad, who never talked about his service or awards he received, served in the 783rd Military Police Battalion during WWII and was in France when Paris was liberated. His modesty was evident during his funeral when, unbeknownst to us, he received an Army Honor Guard Salute for his service and awards. When he passed, we found a suitcase of letters he sent to his parents and relatives during his time of service. The letter attached is a poem he sent to his “folks” as well as a photo of him, and I salute all those who served, present and past, as well as what has become known as the “greatest generation ever.”

title: Trump says his deportation policy ‘might have been too tough’ for voters in the election
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.
Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS’s “60 Minutes” in an interview that aired on Sunday: “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”
He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority. “The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it’s something -- I think that’s something that’s actually doable,” he said in the interview.
Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff.
“Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media Sunday after the interview aired. “Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That’s not a course correction. That’s a promotion.”
The president’s immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring. Two U.S. citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations.
Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress.
Trump said he believes that “killers” and “drug dealers” in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay “if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.”
Trump says he may stay on the sidelines for the 2028 race
On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Trump hinted at staying neutral.
Asked whether he’d endorse a potential successor, the president said “probably, not necessarily.”
“We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with,” Trump said in the interview.
Asked about possible candidates other than Vice President JD Vance, Trump only named Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is viewed as a possible 2028 contender.
“I think Marco’s great,” Trump said. “But there are many others and I’d rather not mention their names. There’s some senators that are excellent. I know ’em all, I like ’em a lot.
“So I may or may not get involved. I don’t know. Maybe I’m better off not getting involved,” Trump said.
Trump brushes aside questions about becoming wealthier while in office
During the midterms, Democrats sought to make the president’s personal wealth a campaign issue. About half of voters nationally said government corruption was “crucial” for their vote for Congress, according to the AP Voter Poll.
Asked how his net worth went up by $3 billion since returning to the White House, Trump said he doesn’t pay much attention to it and said his sons look after the family business.
“I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don’t care. I make — I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I’d have. And I guess it’s gone up. I don’t even know,” he said.
Trump was asked whether he thinks people from foreign countries investing in the company he co-owns with his sons are trying to buy influence. “I don’t know. But that’s true — look, every president has a problem,” he said.
Trump, who survived an assassination attempt while campaigning for reelection in 2024 and has lashed out against his political foes, was asked whether he could forgive his enemies. He said it would be easy to say yes.
But he added: “I probably cannot do that, no, because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.”

title: Blood test could offer less invasive way to aid Alzheimer’s diagnosis
text:
(Aging Untold) — A familiar bike ride with her husband became frightening for Kathi Rigby when she suddenly struggled to communicate.
“I couldn’t get words from my brain to my mouth,” she said.
Rigby was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease in 2022. The news, she said, “was like a slap in the face.”
How the blood test works
Brain scans or tests of spinal fluid are often required to diagnose Alzheimer’s disease, but a blood test to detect amyloid plaque in the brain, a key marker of the disease, could offer a less invasive way.
In May 2025, the Food and Drug Administration cleared the Lumipulse, the first blood test cleared by the agency to aid in diagnosing Alzheimer’s disease.
“It’s a game changer. It’s indicated for people who are 55 years of age or greater with symptoms of cognitive decline,” Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician and Aging Untold host, said.
Researchers suggest that if a patient tests positive, there is a greater than 90% chance that they have amyloid plaque in their brain.
The FDA has cleared the blood test for use only in patients 55 and older who are already experiencing memory problems. The agency cautions that this is not intended as a standalone diagnostic tool for Alzheimer’s. Results should be interpreted alongside a patient’s medical history and other assessments, such as cognitive testing.
Why early evaluation matters
Rogers said identifying Alzheimer’s earlier can help people and their families plan and consider care options.
“I think it’s very welcoming because we know that like many diseases, especially Alzheimer’s, the earlier that you catch it, the more you can make an impact on quality of life,” she said.
For Rigby, early detection allowed her to participate in a clinical trial of a drug intended to remove brain plaque.
Her husband, Brent, said, “95% of the plaque was removed.” Rigby’s experience does not indicate how a treatment will work for someone else.
Rigby said the treatment made a difference for her.
“I want to be Grandma, and I want them to know that I love them—and I know them,” she said.

title: This walking club for seniors calls members ‘Golden G.O.A.T.s.’
text:
GEORGETOWN COUNTY, S.C. (Aging Untold) — A walking club for seniors in South Carolina calls itself the “Golden G.O.A.T.s.”
The goal of the club is to stay fit and have fun. Members walk up to three miles three days a week.
Member joined to walk and be around people
“I’ve always enjoyed walking. I wanted to be able to be among people because I like people,” Virginia Holladay, a member of the group, said.
She addressed the unique name for the members.
“You know — you don’t want to be called an old goat. I think it’s a healthy benefit for us,” she said.
Camaraderie along with cardio
Aging Untold host Amy O’Rourke said the “camaraderie” is as important as the cardio.
“Golden G.O.A.T.s walking together hit me on so many levels. It’s the camaraderie of the interaction between all of them. It’s being in nature and feeling the ground and getting that fabulous air, and then all the exercise that they’re getting. They’re moving their body, so on every single level they’re hitting all the points that you want to hit,” O’Rourke said.
‘Iron G.O.A.T.’ title earned at nearly 600 miles
John Kester walked nearly 600 miles with the group and earned the title “Iron G.O.A.T.”
He said he likes the social aspect of the group.
“Talks continuously while we’re walking. We’ve gotten to learn about each other — so it’s a good social get-together,” Kester said.
O’Rourke also spoke about goals.
“When I think about having a goal and having that purpose, I think of how excited I would be, and I think others would be, having that goal and then accomplishing it, and then setting up the next one and having an inner purpose is so meaningful,” O’Rourke said.

title: Windham state representative requests recount
text:
Rep. Barbara Bagshaw, R-Windham, has requested a recount one week after losing her seat by a margin of 139 votes. Bagshaw received 2,498 votes, while challenger Bradley Youngs totaled 2,637.
Bagshaw, who has represented Windham in the Maine State House since 2022, previously drew scrutiny for her attendance at the “Stop the Steal” Rally in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 6, 2021.
During a Nov. 6 appearance on the “Voice of Maine” radio show, Bagshaw claimed that the lines for same-day voter registration in Windham were filled with people she described as “foreign looking,” who arrived en masse late in the day. In the same interview, Bagshaw said she had reached out to the Department of Homeland Security, asking them to run everyone who voted that day through the department’s SAVE database, which is intended to screen for noncitizen voters, and has been criticized for falsely flagging U.S. citizens.
Windham Town Clerk Anthony Blasi said the town didn’t see an unusual volume of voter registrations for a statewide election, and that it was not uncommon for there to be an uptick in voters during the final hours of election day.
Jana Spaulding, deputy secretary of state for communications, said the department will not release a schedule for recounts until all requests are in by the Nov. 10 deadline. Recounts, she said, typically take about a day.
A candidate is required to pay a deposit to a municipal clerk when requesting a recount, according to state statute. The fee may be waived if the margin is below 1.5%-2.5%, depending on the amount of votes cast in total. The margin in Windham race, 50.5% to 47.8%, or 2.7 percentage points, with a total vote count of 5,224, is above the maximum number for a fee waiver.

title: Underwater hockey is growing one player at a time
text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (InvestigateTV) — Inside Green Bay’s Kroc Center, athletes from small towns around the region are joining together to play a sport you probably haven’t heard of: underwater hockey.
Peter Covach is president of the Green Bay Underwater Hockey Club.
Molly Banks has been around the sport her entire life.
“My parents actually met playing the sport probably 30 years ago,” Banks said. “Our whole family’s just been kind of hockey nuts since then.”
The 24-year-old will represent the U.S. later this year in Turkey as a member of the elite U.S. women’s team and is trying to help grow the sport one player at a time.
“Every time it comes up it’s always kind of a lecture, like, ‘Oh yeah, people don’t know about it,’” Banks said. “Because it’s such a small sport, getting people into it young is really important to help the sport grow, so as much as we can get the youth interested, it’s awesome for the sport and it’s awesome for the kids.”
Adalind Meyer is an up-and-coming player with the Green Bay club.
“Underwater hockey’s pretty fun and also I get to go underwater and hold my breath for a long time,” Meyer said, explaining what she likes about the sport. “Being on a team, yeah and going underwater and flicking the puck very far.”
The group is hopeful others will join for some underwater excitement.
“Being able to keep an open mind with it, because once you break through and get comfortable, it really is so much fun,” Banks said.
Covach said team spirit is important in the sport.
“It’s probably the worst spectator sport in the world, you need to have goggles on, be in the water looking at the play as it’s happening,” Covach said. “All you need to do is have a swimsuit and be able to swim from back and forth from the end of the pool to the other side. We have the gear, we have the coaching — people can come into any practice, and we’ll show them the basics and hopefully they’ll continue to play with us.”
While the season typically runs during the winter months, Covach says people are always able to get more information by visiting the team’s Facebook page.

title: Another ALDI in Maine? Windham planning board takes up proposal

text:
Another ALDI in Maine? Windham planning board taking up proposal
Maine's first ALDI opened in Portland earlier this year. Now, it appears the discount grocer is looking to open a second location.
On Monday evening, the Windham Planning Board is scheduled to discuss a site plan submitted by ALDI to build a new store on Route 302, in front of Walmart and next to McDonald's.
Video in the media player above is from the store in Portland.
The proposal calls for a 19,720-square-foot store with a canopy and covered walkway, 98 parking spaces, a truck delivery drive from Roosevelt Trail, and a reconfigured entrance at the existing McDonald’s driveway on Roosevelt Trail.
The bank building that currently sits between McDonald's and M&T Bank would be torn down.
The sketch plan application was submitted on Sept. 22. There are still several steps the proposal must clear before construction could begin.
ALDI touts itself as having the lowest prices of any national grocery store brand.
ALDI is headquartered in Germany and has more than 12,500 stores around the world, including more than 2,400 locations in the United States.
ALDI initially planned to open its first store in Maine in the former Big Lots on Brighton Avenue before the end of 2025, but that was pushed back. In October 2025, a spokesperson said they hoped to open in the first part of 2026. The company then told Maine's Total Coverage that it expected to open the Portland location in March before finalizing an opening date of March 26.

title: Moose calling is an art and an exercise in patience
text:
Of all my assorted big game hunts, the celebrated Maine moose hunt gets top billing for just plain fun, challenges and, at times, downright frustration. Over the years I have either hunted with a permit or have been part of a moose hunting party. Most of my hunts have been cow hunts, except for two bull hunts. My last hunt, this fall, was a bull hunt, and my chainsaw power winch and I were invited along as guests.
Moose sign was as plentiful as I have ever seen, but sightings were scarce. At the least three times we had bulls answering our cow-in-heat calls only to “hang up” just out of range or in thick cover. Frustrating! Common sense said that our calling strategy or techniques were just not up to snuff. What were we doing wrong?

title: Trump after meeting with Qatari PM says he believes war with Iran is militarily 'effectively over'
text:
Trump after meeting with Qatari PM says he believes war with Iran is militarily 'effectively over'
President Donald Trump on Monday told reporters he believes the war in Iran "militarily is effectively over," suggesting that — at least for now — he's not prepared to resume the bombardment that has devastated the Islamic Republic and caused reverberations across the global economy.
The president made a surprise visit to the White House briefing room after meeting earlier in the day with Qatar's prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.
"Iran militarily is effectively over," Trump said. "We're just keeping it the status quo."
He added that Iran has been "decapitated" but said he is still looking to make sure there's a long-term solution to ensuring that Iran's nuclear program is defanged.
It was some of Trump's most definitive comments about moving away from his threat to resume strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections had passed.
The president's Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress to Democrats in last week's elections. The elections were shadowed by dissatisfaction among the American electorate over the 8-month-old war, which has led to a surge in fuel prices that's impacted nearly ever sector of the global economy.
Trump, over the course of the conflict, has repeatedly said he is on the cusp of ordering U.S. forces to escalate attacks if Iran's leaders don't quickly agree to U.S. terms to end the war, only to back down. In earlier cycles, he has also edged away with a last-minute declaration, sometimes at the behest of Gulf allies, that he's going to give diplomacy more time.
In a posting on social media shortly before speaking to reporters, Trump once again asserted that Middle East allies — Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait and others — "would prefer the status quo." Minutes later, in his exchange with reporters, he sought to assure war-weary Americans that there was "positive momentum" and that he saw a "good chance" that the war "could get ended."
"They're talking to us, and they're talking very politely, And we'll see what happens," Trump said. He added, "The military action doesn't seem to be a very necessary thing, but we're locked and loaded, ready to go for any reason that changes."
Trump, however, gave no hint of a drawdown of the thousands of U.S. troops who have been shifted to the waters off of Iran and maintain a naval blockade to stem the flow of Iranian oil into the global market.
"We're keeping it going. We have the greatest military blockade ever," Trump said.
Qatari officials last week presented proposals on Iran's nuclear program, according to two Middle East government officials familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The White House declined to comment, though Trump last week alluded to ongoing indirect talks with Tehran.
All the while, Tehran continues to insist on several concessions from the U.S., which Trump has declined in the past. Among the core demands Iran says must be met before engaging in nuclear talks: ending the U.S. blockade on Iran's ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.
Earlier Monday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who has come under fire over the conflict, said the next steps on the war are up to Trump, including the possibility of telling Iran: "Hey, we're done, and we're going to watch your nuclear material. You better not move it."
The defense secretary has been one of the administration's most prominent defenders of the war. Critics say the administration launched the war without proper authorization, violated the War Powers Resolution and subverted congressional war-declaring powers.
Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky moved Monday to force a vote to impeach Hegseth, largely over his execution of the war.
Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with the Iranians and they sign a "strong agreement," it's "highly unlikely it's going to be necessary" to resume strikes.
Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.
The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.
—
AP writers Konstantin Toropin, Samy Magdy and Seung Min Kim contributed reporting.

title: Studio Art Theses: A Preview
text:
The senior thesis. Dread it, run from it, it arrives all the same. Thesis can take many different forms, depending on your major. Some majors have their thesis planned out before the semester even starts. Studio art majors, however, have the complete opposite.
When asked about the studio art thesis process, studio art majors Carly Buck ’27 and Penelope Ratz ’27 shared that both their advisors told them the same thing, that they should have no idea what they want to do until the second semester. The first semester is simply a period to create as many pieces as possible with their chosen medium.
Ratz chose painting, taking inspiration from Impressionist painters like Fairfield Porter and Louis Dodd for her thesis. Ratz said, “I farmed a bunch of credits in art 101 classes.” She spoke on how her biggest challenge when making art was in thinking contemporarily.
It wasn’t until Ratz’s semester abroad in Florence, Italy, that she finally got a grasp on what type of paintings she wanted to do. Penelope explained, “I was drawn towards nature.” She added, “I like paintings where you can see the strokes of the paint brush.” She spoke about how seeing the strokes allows you to see the process and decisions made by the painter even years after the piece is finished.
While Ratz is still in the beginning stages of deciding what she wants to do for her thesis, if what I saw in her studio was anything to go by, whatever she’ll end up making will be something that Bates students should be excited to see.
Carly Buck is doing pottery for her thesis and is drawn towards making pieces out of porcelain, instead of the more common earthenware and stoneware. Buck shared her reasoning, “The outcomes of my pots are much more predictable. Porcelain is forgiving, and if you practice using it enough, you can learn to work with it.” This means that even if she were to mess up on the pottery wheel, it is always possible to fix her mistakes with porcelain.
Buck is inspired by traditional Japanese porcelain pieces, like Japanese tea sets or vases, and you can see that in her work. She has a preference towards throwing, making pottery, rather than glazing and painting. She explains, “I feel like I have a lot of control over the form of my bowl. Whereas when you fire something, you’re like surrendering it to the kiln and it kind of does what it wants.”
Like Ratz, she is still unsure about what her final project will look like. Whatever it is, I’m sure it’ll be bound to leave you in awe.
If you want to see the final results of their work, and the work of all the other studio art majors at Bates, keep a look out for the Annual Senior Thesis Exhibition, happening from mid April all the way through May, where all the studio art majors will present their work to the community. If you don’t want to wait, head to the open arts studios in Olin on Nov. 18th to see the works in progress of all studio art majors. I’m sure you won’t be disappointed.

title: UMF student named Peace Corps ambassador, eyes global service
text:
FARMINGTON — University of Maine at Farmington junior Maygin Leighton has never traveled outside New England, but she hopes to take her commitment to community service around the world through the Peace Corps.
Leighton, a Baileyville native majoring in biology with minors in climate change solutions and international and global studies, has been selected by the national Peace Corps program to serve as UMF’s campus ambassador, according to an Oct. 19 university announcement.
The position allows Leighton to introduce fellow students to international service opportunities while preparing for her own future through UMF’s Peace Corps Prep certificate program, the only one offered in Maine.
“Coming from a small town, I’m very community-minded,” Leighton said. “One person can have a huge impact in this world. My high school experiences helped me to be more confident and outspoken, and I have brought those strengths with me to my UMF experience.”
Campus ambassadors promote the Peace Corps’ mission, connect with student organizations and provide information about volunteer opportunities.
Leighton is also enrolled in UMF’s Peace Corps Prep program, which combines academic coursework, practical experience and professional development. Participants complete classes related to international service, gain experience through volunteering or internships and develop intercultural and leadership skills.
Students who complete the requirements receive a Peace Corps certificate recognizing their preparation for international service. The certificate can strengthen an application, although it does not guarantee acceptance.
Leighton hopes to join the Peace Corps after graduating in 2028, with particular interests in environmental conservation, marine biology and wildlife.
“The thought of leaving home for an extended period is exciting … and also a little intimidating,” she said in an Oct. 16 university profile.
Her interest in the Peace Corps developed partly through Linda Beck, a former volunteer who served in Senegal and introduced her to the university’s preparation program.
Leighton initially entered college as an education major because she wanted to help others, but later switched to biology while maintaining her interests in education and the environment.
She also helped establish UMF’s Global Connections Club and serves as its president. The organization encourages students to explore international cultures and perspectives.
“Being aware of what is happening in other countries is important,” Leighton said. “I want to give students as many opportunities as possible to learn about different parts of the world.”
Her other campus activities include Rotaract, JMG and the Johnson Scholars Peer Mentoring program. She also hopes to complete an internship at a national park or wildlife rehabilitation center.
After serving in the Peace Corps, Leighton plans to pursue a master’s degree in biology and is considering a career as a college professor.
Although she has not yet applied to become a Peace Corps volunteer and does not know where she might serve, Leighton hopes the experience will allow her to combine her interests in science, education and community service beyond Maine.

title: Biden says cancer has not stopped him, but it will limit his book promotion

title: Ohio State suspends fraternity while investigating a video showing men engulfed in flames
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A fraternity at Ohio State University has been temporarily suspended while authorities investigate a video that appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames.
A video shared on social media shows a large group of people standing outside, many wearing the school’s red and white colors, laughing and shouting while a man sits on the ground with his sweatpants on fire. He then lunges at a second person and tackles him. The second man’s clothing also catches fire, and they both roll on the ground removing their clothes as several onlookers intervene. One appears to be holding a small fire extinguisher.
University spokesperson Benjamin Johnson said the school has placed Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension while it investigates, and has referred the matter to university and Columbus police. The university did not say how the fraternity is linked to the event, whether the burned men are students or what condition they were in Monday.
“The university is aware of this extremely concerning incident, and the individuals in question are receiving medical care,” Johnson said in a statement. “Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university’s values.”
Columbus Police Sgt. Joe Albert said it appears the matter took place on Saturday. Police did not receive any calls for service at the location, but someone called police Sunday evening reporting that the video was circulating online, he said.
Steve Mitchell, CEO of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, said behavior that violates its high standards has no place in its organization and it will take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable based on the investigation.
“We take this matter seriously and are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident while working closely with university officials and local law enforcement,” he said in a statement.
More than 60,000 students are enrolled at the university.
The episode comes as fraternities are back in the national spotlight in the wake of a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
___
Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

title: South African police arrest 9 foreigners for trying to join Russia-Ukraine war
text:
South African police arrest 9 foreigners for trying to join Russia-Ukraine war
Nine foreign nationals suspected of violating South African mercenary laws by trying to travel from South Africa to Russia to fight in the war between Russia and Ukraine have been arrested, police said Monday.
Police arrested the suspects, aged between 20 and 26, late Sunday night at O.R. Tambo Airport and at a nearby hotel in Johannesburg’s Bruma neighborhood, according to Col. Katlego Mogale.
The suspects were preparing to board flights to Russia when officers intervened after an investigation involving Interpol and local and international law enforcement agencies, police said. They did not identify the suspects’ nationalities nor which side they allegedly planned to join.
Video: Russian missile strikes on former Ukraine school
The nine are expected to appear before the Kempton Park Magistrates’ Court on charges relating to alleged violations of South Africa’s Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act. The law prohibits mercenary activity and regulates military assistance to parties in foreign conflicts, including recruitment and training. Its provisions also apply to foreign nationals acting within South Africa. Police did not give a date for the accused to appear in court.
The arrests come amid growing concern that Africans are being recruited to fight for Russia, sometimes through promises of civilian jobs that lead to the battlefield. An investigation by a nonprofit data journalism and technology organization, Code for Africa, cited by the Institute for Security Studies, identified 289 websites, domains and social media profiles used to lure recruits through false advertising and promises of generous benefits.
South Africa has helped repatriate several citizens it said were lured into the conflict. Police investigated allegations that Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla, a daughter of former South African President Jacob Zuma, helped lure 17 South African men to fight for Russia under promises of security training. She denied wrongdoing and resigned from Parliament in November 2025 following the allegations. Zuma-Sambudla was never formally charged but was highlighted among those who were investigated.
In a separate case, a radio presenter, Nonkululeko Mantula, was charged in late 2025 with allegedly recruiting four South African men to join Russia’s military. The men also faced charges under South Africa’s foreign military assistance law.
In neighboring Zimbabwe, authorities said in March that 15 citizens had been killed in the war in Ukraine and that they were seeking the return of 66 others. Information Minister Zhemu Soda said recruits were promised well-paid jobs but had their travel documents confiscated and were forced into combat.
Kenya’s government said in February that more than 1,000 citizens had been recruited to fight for Russia. Families protested in Nairobi in March, demanding their relatives’ return and the prosecution of those responsible.
Following a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow in October, Ghana and Kenya said they had secured Russian commitments to stop enlisting their citizens. Ghana’s Foreign Ministry said the assurance covered both irregular recruitment and voluntary enlistment.

title: Trump and his Justice Department stand defiant as Democrats ready an investigative blitz
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump and his Department of Justice are taking a combative stance toward Democrats after their election victories in the midterms, signaling intense conflict to come as lawmakers prepare aggressive investigations into the executive branch next year.
Trump set the tone, declaring on social media that investigative requests already made by Democrats are “extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable.” Attorney General Todd Blanche echoed the Republican president and said criminal investigations of Democrats are possible.
“They are not allowed to just go around threatening existing members of the administration, to go around threatening companies, and that’s what President Trump is extremely worried about and he should be,” Blanche said as he and congressional Democrats appeared on the Sunday news shows to discuss the repercussions from last week’s elections.
Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, is preparing investigations into what he calls the “Trump crime family.” He said Democrats are not going to be intimidated.
“The days of us not fighting back are over,” said Garcia, D-Calif.
The early rhetoric sets up a showdown ahead that will likely define Trump’s remaining two years in office and test the power of Congress to put a check on the White House. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
Democrats have made clear that impeachment is an option.
If there are people who have been “shortchanging the American people, screwing over the American people, or stealing from the American people, then they need to be held accountable in a manner consistent with Congress’ role, constitutionally,” said Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
Some Democrats are worried about overreach
But the investigative onslaught is also a source of tension for Democrats, with many warning that delivering on their central promise to voters — actions to lower the cost of living — must take precedence.
Some fear their resounding wins Tuesday that have given them healthy majorities in the House and Senate will prove fleeting if conflict with Trump defines the agenda.
Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat elected to the chamber from Kansas in 94 years, expressed skepticism about impeachment, saying his campaign was about trying to bring people together. He said he does not want the next two years to be spent “dividing our country further.”
“I’m not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails,” Hamilton said. Still, Hamilton said he understands that some investigations are necessary, and Democrats “have to look at what’s happened in Washington.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, said he wants to hold Trump accountable, but warned there was only so much time.
“We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Sanders said. ”We’ve got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”
Jeffries casts doubt on working with Stephen Miller
Jeffries, who is on the cusp of becoming the nation’s first Black House speaker, was asked on election night about the prospects of working with Trump. He said he would be ready to work with the other side of the aisle “whenever and wherever possible to deliver real results.”
Jeffries on Sunday criticized Trump’s choice of longtime adviser Stephen Miller to succeed Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, calling him an “awful choice” and cast doubt on the prospect of working with him.
“There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people,” he said.
Democrats across the ideological spectrum have been critical of the appointment of Miller, an architect of Trump’s mass deportation machine that became an issue in the midterm elections. Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll.
Jeffries also said he supports a pending resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Jeffries said Democrats would be discussing it when they return to the Capitol this week. “Hegseth has got to go,” he said.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said.
Hegseth in a video dismissed the impeachment push as “all about the politics of personal destruction.” He said it “won’t work with me.”
New senators express skepticism about Schumer
At least two new incoming Democratic senators expressed some reservations Sunday about Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who’s expected to be reelected to his post after leading his party back to the majority.
Hamilton said he’s told Schumer, who is currently running unopposed, that he means no disrespect but that the New Yorker is a polarizing figure in Kansas and Hamilton is aiming for someone less divisive.
“What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the center, somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together,” Hamilton said. “It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”
Hamilton said he wants to get to know the other Democratic senators better before he makes any recommendations.
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, whom Schumer did not back in the Democratic primary, said he had been committed to Sen. Chris Van Hollen, but acknowledged that the Maryland Democrat does not appear to be running for the post.
El-Sayed said he and Schumer, who put $67 million into El-Sayed’s general election campaign, “figured out how to work together” after the primary.
“The question to me is, who wants to be the leader who’s going to make sure that we deliver on the mandate that we just got?” El-Sayed said.
Blanche was interviewed on “Fox News Sunday” and CNN’s “State of the Union.” Garcia also was on CNN, Jeffries spoke on ABC’s “This Week,” Hamilton and Sanders were on CNN and NBC, and El-Sayed appeared on ABC.
___
Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Post-election and ‘free at last’
text:
Martin Luther King, Jr. once proclaimed, “Free at last, free at last, thank God Almighty, we are free at last.”
Following the resounding defeat of Republican candidates for various local, county, state and federal offices, in this year’s midterm elections, we are now “free” to heal the severe wounds inflicted upon this country by President Donald Trump and his enablers and, therefore, begin the long and rather difficult process of allowing justice and fair play to again govern America.
The road ahead — to find equitable solutions for wealth inequality, healthcare, housing and ample food supplies, to name a few of the important and vital areas — will be long and cumbersome. However, as a country, America must continue this necessary process until and after the 2028 elections, to ensure a steady movement of progress to be made.
But, now for the present, we are “Free at last …”
John Mishler
Harpswell

title: Trump pushes for permanent daylight saving time: ‘It’s so dark outside, so early’
text:
WASHINGTON D.C. (Gray News/AP) — President Donald Trump renewed his call to end the twice-yearly clock change by making daylight saving time permanent.
“Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act. It’s so dark outside, so early (Sunset was 5:06 P.M., and it was dark by 5:31 P.M. — Isn’t that ridiculous?),” the president said on his social media platform, Truth Social.
Daylight saving time is that period between spring and fall when clocks in most parts of the United States are set one hour ahead of standard time.
On July 14, the House approved a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent. The vote was 308-117. However, the bill did not pass the Senate before Americans switched their clocks on Nov. 1.
Supporters argue that ending the time change would provide more daylight when Americans are most active. But opponents say commuters in some states wouldn’t see the sun until after 9 a.m.
Congress passed a law in 1973 establishing year-round daylight saving time as an experiment, which began in 1974. Lawmakers ended the experiment early as support declined, partly because of concern for children walking to school in the dark.
Trump, with the GOP coming off a shaky midterm election, promised to keep working to get the bill to his desk.
“I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done,” the president said. “The House sent it over to the Senate with great bipartisan support, numerous times (308-117), but the Senate didn’t take it up. We have far bigger priorities, but I will keep fighting for this!”

title: Does Maine count votes for undeclared write-in candidates in state and federal elections?
text:
No.
In state and federal elections, Maine doesn’t count write-in votes for anyone who didn’t file a declaration of candidacy.
Votes for undeclared write-ins are recorded as blanks, but other votes on the ballot remain valid.
Blank votes still count toward the total ballots cast. In Maine’s 2026 2nd Congressional District race, preliminary results showed 123 votes for declared write-ins and 6,017 blanks. Because those votes count toward the total, no candidate reached a majority, requiring a ranked-choice runoff.
Municipal elections have different rules. Towns and cities may require write-in candidates to declare, but even those that do must count undeclared write-ins if no candidate appears on the ballot or a nominee withdraws.
Municipalities without that requirement also must count undeclared write-ins if they outnumber a listed candidate’s votes. Clerks are not required to count votes for fictional or dead people.
This fact brief is responsive to conversations such as this one.

title: Hallowell police chief changes stance on renewal of bar's liquor license
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Hallowell police chief changes stance, now recommends renewal of Quarry Tap Room's liquor license
Just days after informing the Hallowell City Council that he would not recommend renewing the Quarry Tap Room's liquor license, Hallowell Police Chief Zachary Kindelan said he is now comfortable with recommending the license renewal.
The City Council is set to consider a motion about whether to approve the renewal of a liquor license for the bar and grill at 122 Water St. during a meeting that starts at 6 p.m. Monday.
On Thursday, Kindelan sent a letter to the City Council, in which he said that he could not recommend the renewal of the Quarry Tap Room's liquor license. According to Kindelan, there have been at least 15 incidents involving the establishment since he became police chief in July.
In his initial letter, Kindelan went on to say that he had seen no improvement in liquor enforcement after conversations with Quarry Tap Room staff, and that he also had concerns about the fact that some security camera equipment was broken and that the security team had no set policies for how to deal with certain situations.
Quarry Tap Room owner Steve LaChance said that ownership and management met with Kindelan and other officials on Monday, and that the issues in Kindelan's letter have largely been addressed.
"To me, it's just silly that it got to this point," LaChance said. "We've had a lot of employees in the last few days worrying about their jobs. I mean, it was uncalled for, I think. Hopefully, we'll get it situated this evening."
Kindelan then sent another letter to the City Council on Monday following his meeting with LaChance and other members of the Quarry Tap Room team. In the updated letter, Kindelan said he is now comfortable with recommending the renewal of the establishment's liquor license.
"The Quarry Tap Room staff and I had a great discussion and I am happy with the outcome," Kindelan said in the letter he sent to the City Council on Monday. "I appreciated the conversation where we could all address concerns on both sides and work towards better serving the city of Hallowell."
In Monday's letter, Kindelan noted that there was a short amount of time that was available to try and make a recommendation, and characterized the public interpretation of his initial letter as "unfortunate."
"I take my responsibility to this community seriously. With that in mind, my initial recommendation was based only on the information that was available to me at the time," Kindelan said. "My letter to the Council was never an attempt to not have the license renewed, but to provide context to my recommendation. My role is to look at these matters objectively, identify public safety concerns, and make recommendations based on that information. As with most things in law enforcement that evolve rapidly, my new recommendation is based upon the relevant information now available to me following the meeting with staff."
Kindelan said he is happy that all sides were able to sit down, communicate and reach a goal of working together for the betterment of the city.

title: Ranked-choice voting tabulation for Maine's CD2 race gets underway
text:
Ranked-choice voting tabulation for Maine's 2nd Congressional District race continues
Democrat Matt Dunlap has already conceded to Republican Paul LePage, but a tabulation still needs to be conducted
Ranked-choice voting tabulation for Maine's 2nd Congressional District race continues
Democrat Matt Dunlap has already conceded to Republican Paul LePage, but a tabulation still needs to be conducted
The ranked-choice voting tabulation that will determine the official results of the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat in the U.S. House of Representatives is underway.
State Auditor Matt Dunlap, the Democratic candidate, has conceded the race to Republican former Gov. Paul LePage, but Maine Secretary of State Shenna Bellows said that even though Dunlap conceded, the ranked-choice tabulation must still be completed in order to have a certified election under state law.
"Paul is already at work in Washington, D.C., while the perfunctory process plays out back home," LePage campaign strategist Brent Littlefield said in a statement shared Monday. "Just like our opponent who conceded, we are confident in the outcome."
The tabulation, which started Monday morning, is being conducted at the Maine Department of Public Safety Headquarters, which is located at 45 Commerce Drive in Augusta. The process is open to the public and will be livestreamed on the Secretary of State's YouTube page.
Bellows said that while her team made some really good progress between 10 a.m. and 5 p.m. Monday, the most likely outcome is that the tabulation will be finished sometime Friday afternoon.
The tabulation process resumed at 9 a.m. Tuesday. Click here to watch the livestream of Tuesday's work.
In ranked-choice voting races, like the race for CD2, a candidate must receive more than 50% of first-choice votes as counted on Election Day in order to win the race outright. Last week, the Secretary of State's Office announced that there were 341,248 total ballots cast in the race, with 170,263 votes for LePage (49.894%), 164,845 votes for Dunlap (48.307%), 123 votes for declared write-in candidates (0.036%) and 6,107 blank votes (1.763%). The lone declared write-in candidate in this race is Gregory Ward, an independent.
If no candidate receives more than 50% of the total ballots cast, the Secretary of State's Office makes the determination to proceed with a ranked-choice voting tabulation.
Bellows said the first step in the process will be to verify the vote totals from every municipality to ensure accuracy. Then, the votes are tabulated in rounds, with the lowest-ranked candidate eliminated in each round until there are only two candidates remaining. The candidate determined to have received the majority of the votes — more than 50% — in the final round is declared the winner.
More info about CD2
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.

James Gunn on DC Departure: ‘Incredibly Relieved and Excited’
text:
James Gunn Responds to DC Departure: ‘Incredibly Relieved and Excited’
DC fans might have been shocked to learn that James Gunn and Peter Safran are done at DC just four years into their tenure as co-CEOs of DC Studios, and the chief engineers of their new film and TV universe.
Gunn himself? He says he’s “incredibly relieved and excited.”
In a long statement posted to his Instagram account, Gunn said that working as DC co-CEO has been “a dream come true” but he also revealed that his time running the company “has been trying, to say the least.”
“When I was a kid growing up in Manchester, Missouri, I used to write and draw my own comics with a mix of DC Comics characters and my own characters,” Gunn wrote. “Having full access to these characters to do whatever we wanted has been a dream com true. I didn’t know if I wanted this job when it was offered to me, but I just couldn’t pass up the unique opportunity. I’m glad I took the job.”
But, he added, “what only the closest people to me have known over the past four years is my time at DC Studios has been trying, to say the least. I dislike the at-times corporate nature of the job (thanks to Peter for taking the brunt of that). I’m always a very hard worker, but as a filmmaker I would at least get to take short breaks to unwind, and I’ve stolen even that time from both myself and my loved ones over the past four years.”
READ MORE: Every DC Comics Movie Ever, Ranked From Worst to Best
Gunn says he’ll miss his co-workers and the job of watching over the DC library of characters like Superman, Batman, Wonder Woman, and the rest of the Justice League.
“But,” he also said, “I’m also incredibly relieved and excited to get back to pure filmmaking.”
Gunn also revealed that he’s “just been engaged on another DC project which I’m writing.” He didn’t specify what that project is, and given the end result for most of the DC projects that Gunn and Safran announced (i.e. they never came out, and now likely never will) it’s probably not wise to get your hopes up too high for whatever Gunn is writing for DC next.
Gunn’s Man of Tomorrow, on the other hand, is definitely coming out. That’s scheduled to open in theaters on July 9, 2027. His interviews about the film, and his time at DC, should be pretty interesting.

title: This woman helps cemetery visitors talk openly about death
text:
WASHINGTON (Aging Untold) — A historic cemetery in the nation’s capital has hired a death doula to help visitors have healthy conversations about mortality in what might be a first for such institutions.
An end-of-life doula, or death doula, is a person who offers services for end-of-life care, from planning final moments to providing respite for exhausted caregivers.
Promoting “death positivity”
Laura Lyster-Mensh, the death doula at Historic Congressional Cemetery, a national landmark in the heart of Washington, D.C., said her role focuses on promoting what she calls “death positivity.”
“The greatest thing that I can do here at the cemetery is promote death positivity and I walk around with people in the cemetery, and we just talk openly about death — unafraid, curious, sometimes awkward,” Lyster-Mensh said.
She acknowledged the concept might seem insensitive to those who are grieving.
“I think at first, to hear death positivity could seem even disrespectful,” she said. “I actually think that death positivity is about living better. Because what are we afraid of? When we turn that and we look at it as boundaries on our life that make life precious, we can feel better.”
Death cafes and conversation cards
Lyster-Mensh conducts her work through various methods, including regular events, including “death cafes.” She sets out tea, cookies and a deck of cards called “the death deck,” which is designed to start conversations about mortality.
“At first people will say, ‘Death, oh, I don’t want to do that.’ But you pull out one of these cards and you start talking and you learn things about the people that you care about and you start real conversations,” she said.
She said these conversations are often uncomfortable for people to initiate until it’s time or too late.
When asked for advice about living, Lyster-Mensh said people should slow down.
“I think we try to speed through everything. We try to speed through grief. We try to speed through happy moments, we hoard it. But you can’t really be present if you’re hoarding it,” she said.

title: InvestigateTV+: Is tracking ALS possible?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at how better tracking of ALS cases could reveal why more people are getting sick.
Then, scammers can get ahold of your address and register it as a front for fake companies. We uncover the risks for homeowners and why officials say it’s so hard to stop.
Plus, an artist shows us how he “draws with daylight,” creating one-of-a-kind pieces of art.
Tracking ALS cases
A cure for ALS is much more complicated to find than a treatment, in part because no one knows why people get it, how to stop it or what causes it. Among experts, there are suspicions that pollutants in the environment play a role.
Researchers said they could better study that if they knew where ALS patients were located.
Fake business, real problem
Imagine your name and home address are used to start a business, but you have nothing to do with it.
There are reports of this happening in several states of fraudulent companies registering with random addresses. Experts say it can cause trouble for unsuspecting property owners.
Underwater...hockey?
Inside Green Bay’s Kroc Center, athletes from small towns around the region are joining together to play a sport you probably haven’t heard of: underwater hockey.
Peter Covach is president of the Green Bay Underwater Hockey Club.
“You’ve got a weighted puck, sits at the bottom of the pool, and it moves up and down the pool like soccer or hockey,” Covach said.
Using the sun for art
Billy Keith is a solar artist. He uses sunlight as his tool to create artwork burned directly into wood.
“You learn a lot by standing in the sun all day,” Keith said.
Keith said he introduces himself as “the sun man,” and his goal is to make more art in public.

title: New data shows US crime is down across the board
text:
New data shows US crime is down across the board
New data shows US crime is down across the board
Crime rates are dropping in the U.S., according to new preliminary data from the Bureau of Justice Statistics.
Property crime rates fell nearly 20%, and violent crime was down about 10% from 2024 to 2025, per the latest data from the National Crime Victimization Survey.
The NCVS surveys U.S. households to provide a picture of crime beyond what gets reported to police.
"There’s a dark figure of crime," said Thaddeus Johnson, Council on Criminal Justice senior fellow. "We know that all crime is not reported or known to police."
Violent crime rates improve
In total, about 7.5 million people were estimated to be victims of a violent crime in 2025.
Nationally, that means about 25.7 out of every 1,000 people aged 12 or older experienced a violent crime like rape, robbery or assault. Homicides were not included in the NCVS.
According to the survey, about 800,000 people were the victims of rape or sexual assault last year, down about 12% from 2024. Cases of sexual violence tend to be among the most underreported crimes to police.
Simple assaults, which are attacks without weapons that result in non-major injuries, are the most common type of violent crime reported, accounting for about 70% of violent crimes reported through the survey.
Excluding simple assaults, there was a 25% drop in all other types of violent crime.
Property crime is down as well
Nearly 15 million U.S. households were the victims of property crime in 2025, according to the preliminary NCVS data. That’s about 111 out of every 1,000 households.
General theft — the unlawful taking or attempted taking of a person's property or money — was the most common, accounting for more than 75% of property crimes.
Trespassing dropped 34% from 2024 to 2025, and motor vehicle theft dropped 29%.
Why are the rates dropping?
According to experts, there’s no one factor that is causing the across-the-board declines in crime rates.
"Everybody can take credit, and nobody can take credit," Johnson said.
CCJ recently conducted a focus group with leading crime scholars to assess the factors influencing the homicide rate, which has also dropped in recent years.
The scholars found that six factors stood out:
- Community violence intervention programs
- A return to normal after disruptions from the COVID-19 pandemic
- Increased law enforcement deterrence that targets high-risk individuals
- Increased local government capacity and social services
- Increased public safety and support resources
- Increased proactive police enforcement
The White House has pointed to increased immigration enforcement and President Donald Trump's focus on crime — which included deploying the National Guard to several U.S. cities — as reasons for the drop.
But scholars say there isn't strong evidence.
"There is no evidence that the National Guard or immigration enforcement pushed the envelope when it came to reducing crime," Johnson said. 
Crime was already headed down in many cities before Trump shone a spotlight on the issue.
While the DOJ recently changed its methodology for collecting the NCVS — which means we can't compare 2025 data to past years — over the past 30 years, crime rates have been trending downwards across the country.
In 2024, both the old and new survey methods were used which does allow researchers to compare 2024 to 2025 using the new methodology.

title: Maine women’s basketball opens season with dramatic win over Siena
text:
ORONO, Maine — The University of Maine women’s basketball team opened its season this week against Siena University on Thursday, Nov. 5.
The Black Bears ended last season in heartbreak with a loss to the University of Vermont in the conference championship. In the America East preseason poll, Maine was picked to finish fourth in the conference and predicted to miss the NCAA Tournament. One win away from the Big Dance last year, the team enters this season with a chip on its shoulder and a point to prove.
That journey began with a home game to open the season against Siena, a team that had already scored a win against Brown University a week before.
Maine entered this game with a new-look lineup after losing star forward Adrianna Smith to graduation after last season. The updated game plan would revolve around a new leader, fourth-year center Lizzy Gruber.
Gruber started the game with Maine’s first points and officially got the season underway with a successful midrange jump shot.
The first-quarter plan was to establish a strong defense and hold Siena’s offense to a low-scoring period. As the quarter went on, Maine was successful, holding the Saints to only 12 points in the entire first quarter.
Maine entered the second quarter with a seven-point lead and momentum swinging entirely in its direction. Second-year guard Maddie Fitzpatrick drove through the lane for a layup just minutes into the quarter, pushing the Maine lead further and keeping the pressure on Siena.
The half ended with Maine controlling a 30-22 lead, holding Siena to zero baskets throughout the final five minutes of the quarter.
The second half began with more of the same. Maine went on an offensive run and scored 22 points while holding off Siena’s halftime adjustments to maintain the lead. Maine entered the final quarter with a 52-42 lead and full control over the game.
The game began to shift in the fourth quarter. Through just the first five minutes of play, Siena had found a way to come all the way back and shock the Black Bears with a 59-58 lead with just five minutes to play.
Maine punched back with two consecutive 3-pointers from second-year guard Lala Woods and second-year guard Olivia Alvarez. Siena countered with a 3-pointer of its own.
The clock was down to under 30 seconds, and the score was tied at 68.
With just 13 seconds left, Alvarez drove to the basket and hit a game-winning layup over the Siena defense. Maine had won in dramatic fashion and opened its season with a victory.
Gruber led Maine with 18 points, and the Black Bears shot 45% from the field.
Maine will return to the Pit next week to host the University of Oregon on Thursday, Nov. 12, and Red Panda will be performing at halftime.
