title: Who’s going to run Hannah Pingree’s government? We have an early idea.
text:
AUGUSTA — Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree has no time to lose.
With less than 60 days until her inauguration, she’s got to make dozens of hires — decisions that will shape the course of her administration. An array of officials from the Gov. Janet Mills era have already announced over the past few months their plans to step down and let new faces join the Pingree administration.
We already know some of the key figures involved in staffing Pingree’s team. Pingree said she will announce the rest of the transition staff Tuesday morning during a news conference in Augusta.
The staffers we already know about have resumes that include working for both Democratic and Republican officials. They have ties to the Wabanaki Alliance, Planned Parenthood and other groups. They signify both Pingree’s pragmatism and — particularly on the issue of tribal sovereignty — her efforts to pivot away from Mills on certain fronts.
Pingree, 50, said after Tuesday’s election victory that she is now accepting applications on a rolling basis to serve in her administration. She and Mills had lunch Friday at the Blaine House after meeting with reporters in the morning to say how they are working together on the transition.
Without referring to former Gov. Paul LePage by name, Mills said “this is quite different than eight years ago,” alluding to less cooperation when she took over from the Republican.
It is too soon to speculate on who may lead certain departments. Pingree said she has been meeting with current agency heads and will interview or accept resumes for every Cabinet position. Asked about any plans to restructure or create new offices, she said she is open to “better ways to do things” and that she met a few weeks ago with former Gov. Ken Curtis, a Democrat who in 1972 made a major reorganization by consolidating 150 independent agencies into 16 departments.
Pingree is set to be sworn in on Jan. 6. Ahead of the inauguration, here are a few names of transition team and campaign staffers who will play key roles.
LEADING THE TRANSITION
The co-chairs of Pingree’s transition team are two people familiar to those who have closely followed the State House over the years.
Maulian Bryant is a member of the Penobscot Nation and the executive director of the Wabanaki Alliance, which represents the four Native American tribes in Maine and advocates for tribal sovereignty legislation that Mills vetoed in 2023. Although Mills and leaders of the tribes made progress on certain policy changes toward the end of her tenure, Pingree has said she will sign the sweeping proposal within 100 days that Mills blocked to allow the tribes to benefit from federal laws that do not currently apply to them.
Bryant was previously the Penobscot Nation ambassador to the state and remains a member of the tribal council and the Maine Climate Council.
Her transition team co-chair is Roger Katz, a former Augusta mayor who served as a Republican state senator from 2010-18. Katz, a lawyer, chairs the University of Maine System board of trustees. He is a moderate who has criticized his party’s more hardline figures like President Donald Trump and former Gov. Paul LePage.
Katz and Pingree launched a political talk show together in 2014 called “The Maine Event” that aired on public television.
“Roger Katz and Maulian Bryant bring the experience and judgment I want at the table as we build this administration,” Pingree said in a statement. “They will be leading a group of volunteers from across Maine who will help me find leaders who put results first and reflect the best of Maine: integrity, accountability, public service and shared optimism about improving the lives of Maine people.”
MORE FAMILIAR FACES
Scott Ogden and Karen Geraghty will direct Pingree’s professional staff transition, focusing on more of the behind-the-scenes work that goes into getting a new administration up and running.
Ogden previously served as a spokesperson and deputy chief of staff to Mills, as well as an aide to U.S. Sen. Angus King, I-Maine; former U.S. Sen. Olympia Snowe, R-Maine; and to U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, the 1st District Democrat. Ogden will coordinate personnel decisions, “legislative and policy agenda development” and “day-to-day operations,” according to a Pingree news release.
Geraghty previously led philanthropic efforts at Planned Parenthood of Northern New England and served as a Portland mayor and city councilor. She will direct planning of the inauguration.
Pingree’s team has not yet confirmed the location of the Jan. 6 inauguration, as the aging Augusta Civic Center that has hosted past inaugurations will be closed for renovation work.
OTHER PINGREE STAFFERS
It is not unheard of for campaign staffers to move into official roles if a candidate wins office. Pingree’s campaign manager, Jonny Asen, is one name to watch given his extensive resume.
Asen, who works in government relations and political consulting for the law firm Bernstein Shur, worked under former President Barack Obama for five years, rising to the rank of chief of staff for the White House’s legislative affairs director.
Asen also served as senior adviser to former Maine House Speaker Mark Eves, D-North Berwick, who led the state House of Representatives from 2012-16, and as chief of staff to Freeport Democrat Sara Gideon, who led the Maine House from 2016-20. Asen was then senior adviser for the Maine operation of former Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign. Harris won Maine handily while losing the 2nd Congressional District to Trump.
It is unclear how many campaign staff will stay on to work for Pingree’s administration, such as deputy campaign manager Ellie Edgell, who previously worked on campaigns in Michigan for figures such as U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin.
It is also not yet known who will serve as Pingree’s chief spokesperson. Pingree’s campaign spokesperson, Mary-Erin Casale, will serve in the transition role through the inauguration.
Pingree led Mills’ Office of Policy Innovation and the Future from 2019 until launching her gubernatorial campaign last year, so she has plenty of connections in that office who may continue to serve in her gubernatorial administration.
As for Mills, the 78-year-old former attorney general who is in her final weeks in office and who made an unsuccessful bid for the Democratic nomination for the U.S. Senate, she kept it brief Friday when asked what is next for her.
“Well, I have a few irons in the fire,” Mills said, “and I’ll know in January.”

Photo Story: Life, death and birth on Witter Farm
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The students get to work at 6 a.m. and leave at 10:30 p.m. or later. They are there for the birth, life and death of the animals they take care of. These students work on Witter Farm, also called the J. Franklin Witter Teaching & Research Center, located only a five-minute drive from campus.
As part of their classes, animal and veterinary science (AVS) students work on Witter Farm, in Old Town, Maine. Though it is a part of their education, Rose Arsenault, a second year AVS student, describes the farm chores as being “More of an unpaid internship than a class.” Despite this, these students know that the skills they learn here will be essential, as they learn how to take care of the cows and manage their health.
The schedule can be grueling. There are four shifts throughout the day: “AM chores,” which start at 6 a.m.; “Noon Check,” which starts at 11 a.m.; “PM chores,” which start at 4 p.m.; and “Night Check,” which starts at 10 p.m. Students are often awake by 5 a.m. to get ready, and those who work late can be there until 11 p.m. or later. Their schedules are built around their other classes, which can lead to a lot of early morning and late-night shifts. This is the case for Briana Alves, a second-year AVS student who said she works an average of two to three shifts a week, mostly consisting of “AM chores” and “Night Check.”
The job can frequently be taxing, both mentally and physically. Emma Carlsen, a third-year AVS student, said “I really don’t like being here when it’s cold.” The weather on the farm is a common complaint among students, who have to be there in the cold and heat, rain and shine. The students also have to deal with the reality of farm life. Alves stated that one of the hardest things for her was losing Wynonna, a 3-year-old cow, who died following an accident involving another cow.
However, farm work is not all bad. The students become quite attached to the cows, with Alves saying that her favorite part of the job is getting to cuddle the cows, and Carlsen stating that “I just love interacting with the animals; I love learning their little quirks.” Their attachment to the cows can make the work emotionally taxing, particularly as they care for their favorite calves through birth, life and death. But still they persevere. Day and night, rain and shine, in sickness and in health, the students of Witter will be there.

title: Credit counselor says stigma should not keep people from seeking debt help
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — People enrolled in Money Management International’s debt management plans now owe more than $1 billion in credit card and personal loan debt, the most the national nonprofit has seen in 13 years.
More than 60,000 people are enrolled. Many are putting everyday expenses such as groceries, gas and car repairs on credit cards as prices have jumped about 30% since 2019.
Ted Rossman, with Money Management International, said inflation, high interest rates and the rising cost of living are behind the numbers.
“The story behind the story is inflation, high-interest rates, just the rising cost of living that is really straining household budgets,” Rossman said. “And we’re going back to some unpleasant numbers that followed the financial crisis.”
Rossman said some households are clearly showing stress. Even for people who are working and getting raises, pay is often not enough right now to keep up with rising prices for gas, groceries, housing, medical bills and child care.
Rossman said people who are struggling should not wait to ask for help.
“Definitely speak up, ask for help, don’t be ashamed,” Rossman said. “There’s such a stigma around credit card debt, which I think is unfortunate. There’s this feeling that if you have credit card debt you did something irresponsible, right? A big vacation, shopping spree, no… in reality it’s usually practical things, it’s medical bills, it’s car repairs, it’s gas, it’s groceries, so take the shame out of it.”
Rossman said half of credit card holders carry debt from month to month, and the key is working to break the pattern. Options include connecting with a nonprofit credit counselor, taking out a personal loan or trying a zero percent balance transfer card to consolidate and pay down debt.

title: 2026 Portland Press Herald Fall Athlete of the Week: Week 9
How fake businesses can become a real problem for you
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PHOENIX, Az. (InvestigateTV) — Imagine your name and home address are used to start a business, but you have nothing to do with it.
There are reports of this happening in several states of fraudulent companies registering with random addresses. Experts say it can cause trouble for unsuspecting property owners.
Morgan Johnson doesn’t own a furniture store or run a toy wholesaler, but there’s paperwork that sure makes it look like she does. Three times in the past year, someone has created limited liability companies in her name at her address.
Johnson discovered the fraud after receiving mail about pending credit accounts she never opened.
“I freaked out a little bit about it because it felt so intrusive,” she told On Your Side.
Fraudsters create fake LLCs with the goal of cashing in, often passing bad checks or opening a line of credit they’ll never repay.
“The bottom line is it’s not for a good reason,” said Tanya Gibson, the director of the Corporations Division at the Arizona Corporation Commission. “It’s a huge problem.”
According to data from the agency, the Corporations Division received 208 complaints about fake LLCs in September 2025. After a new system launched in early 2026, complaints dipped, but rose again to 180 in May 2026.
Why it’s easy to create a fake LLC
Currently, anyone can create an LLC online using only a name and address. No identification is required.
“We have no way to verify if that person has the ability to use an address,” said Gibson.
Gibson said she wants the law changed to give the division authority to validate information and deny filings if fraud is suspected.
In the meantime, changes are coming to make it tougher to file for fake LLCs. “[By July 1], we’re going to have our online ID verification, which will require a photo ID, front and back, and a selfie,” Gibson explained. “Then the software runs the information against multiple databases. You either come back verified or not. If you come back verified, you get a stamp on your account, and you’re free to file. If you are not verified for whatever reason, you will get a message saying that you need to come into the office to file.”
Gibson acknowledged the state cannot prevent fraud completely.
“We’re trying to throw as many hurdles in place as we can,” she said.
Once the state receives a complaint about a fake LLC, it can take months to get it dissolved. In the meantime, the division marks the status as pending inactive and not in good standing and flags it as undeliverable to alert banks and credit agencies.
Johnson said flagging fake LLCs isn’t enough.
“We need to do a lot more,” she said.
How to check for fraud
Fake LLCs could go unnoticed if victims don’t receive mail about them. Gibson said the agency often sees clusters of addresses, suggesting fraudsters are pulling lists of people and addresses at random.
Residents should check their own address for unauthorized LLCs and file a complaint with your secretary of state’s office.

title: Trump and his Justice Department stand defiant as Democrats ready an investigative blitz
text:
(AP) - President Donald Trump and his Department of Justice are taking a combative stance toward Democrats after their election victories in the midterms, signaling intense conflict to come as lawmakers prepare aggressive investigations into the executive branch next year.
Trump set the tone, declaring on social media that investigative requests already made by Democrats are “extortion at the highest level, and they should be held accountable.” Attorney General Todd Blanche echoed the Republican president and said criminal investigations of Democrats are possible.
“They are not allowed to just go around threatening existing members of the administration, to go around threatening companies, and that’s what President Trump is extremely worried about and he should be,” Blanche said as he and congressional Democrats appeared on the Sunday news shows to discuss the repercussions from last week’s elections.
Rep. Robert Garcia, who is poised to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee in the next Congress, is preparing investigations into what he calls the “Trump crime family.” He said Democrats are not going to be intimidated.
“The days of us not fighting back are over,” said Garcia, D-Calif.
The early rhetoric sets up a showdown ahead that will likely define Trump’s remaining two years in office and test the power of Congress to put a check on the White House. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters.
Democrats have made clear that impeachment is an option.
If there are people who have been “shortchanging the American people, screwing over the American people, or stealing from the American people, then they need to be held accountable in a manner consistent with Congress’ role, constitutionally,” said Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York.
Some Democrats are worried about overreach
But the investigative onslaught is also a source of tension for Democrats, with many warning that delivering on their central promise to voters — actions to lower the cost of living — must take precedence.
Some fear their resounding wins Tuesday that have given them healthy majorities in the House and Senate will prove fleeting if conflict with Trump defines the agenda.
Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, the first Democrat elected to the chamber from Kansas in 94 years, expressed skepticism about impeachment, saying his campaign was about trying to bring people together. He said he does not want the next two years to be spent “dividing our country further.”
“I’m not as interested in impeachment as setting up guardrails,” Hamilton said. Still, Hamilton said he understands that some investigations are necessary, and Democrats “have to look at what’s happened in Washington.”
Sen. Bernie Sanders, a Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats, said he wants to hold Trump accountable, but warned there was only so much time.
“We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump,” Sanders said. ”We’ve got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives.”
Jeffries casts doubt on working with Stephen Miller
Jeffries, who is on the cusp of becoming the nation’s first Black House speaker, was asked on election night about the prospects of working with Trump. He said he would be ready to work with the other side of the aisle “whenever and wherever possible to deliver real results.”
Jeffries on Sunday criticized Trump’s choice of longtime adviser Stephen Miller to succeed Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, calling him an “awful choice” and cast doubt on the prospect of working with him.
“There’s not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we’re committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people,” he said.
Democrats across the ideological spectrum have been critical of the appointment of Miller, an architect of Trump’s mass deportation machine that became an issue in the midterm elections. Nationally, about 6 in 10 voters said the administration’s actions on immigration enforcement had “gone too far,” according to The AP Voter Poll.
Jeffries also said he supports a pending resolution from Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Jeffries said Democrats would be discussing it when they return to the Capitol this week. “Hegseth has got to go,” he said.
“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said.
Hegseth in a video dismissed the impeachment push as “all about the politics of personal destruction.” He said it “won’t work with me.”
New senators express skepticism about Schumer
At least two new incoming Democratic senators expressed some reservations Sunday about Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who’s expected to be reelected to his post after leading his party back to the majority.
Hamilton said he’s told Schumer, who is currently running unopposed, that he means no disrespect but that the New Yorker is a polarizing figure in Kansas and Hamilton is aiming for someone less divisive.
“What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the center, somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together,” Hamilton said. “It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”
Hamilton said he wants to get to know the other Democratic senators better before he makes any recommendations.
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, whom Schumer did not back in the Democratic primary, said he had been committed to Sen. Chris Van Hollen, but acknowledged that the Maryland Democrat does not appear to be running for the post.
El-Sayed said he and Schumer, who put $67 million into El-Sayed’s general election campaign, “figured out how to work together” after the primary.
“The question to me is, who wants to be the leader who’s going to make sure that we deliver on the mandate that we just got?” El-Sayed said.
Blanche was interviewed on “Fox News Sunday” and CNN’s “State of the Union.” Garcia also was on CNN, Jeffries spoke on ABC’s “This Week,” Hamilton and Sanders were on CNN and NBC, and El-Sayed appeared on ABC.
___
Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick and Lisa Mascaro in Washington contributed to this report.

title: ‘He was loved by everyone’: Family mourns pilot killed in crash weeks before daughter’s birth
text:
WAYCROSS, Ga. (WALB/Gray News) — A pilot killed in a small plane crash at the Waycross-Ware County Airport has been identified as a husband and father.
Amanda Scheuing identified the pilot as her husband, Tim Scheuing.
According to the Federal Aviation Administration, a Beechcraft BE35 crashed during takeoff at Waycross-Ware County Airport around 11:15 a.m. Friday, Nov. 6.
Amanda Scheuing remembered her husband as a devoted father, husband and Christian.
“Words are hard to process right now.... He was the absolute best person I have ever known. I couldn’t have asked for a better husband or a better father for our kids,” she said.
She said they met while working together when she was 16 and began dating shortly afterward. The couple celebrated their 20th wedding anniversary this year and have a 16-year-old daughter, with another daughter due in three weeks.
“He was funny, quick-witted, adventurous and a helping hand to anyone,” she said.
Amanda Scheuing said her husband was a pilot, flight instructor and owner of Runway One Nine Aviation. She thanked the community for its outpouring of love.
“He was loved by everyone and touched so many lives,” she said.
She also thanked the emergency crews, first responders and airport staff, as well as the couple’s family, friends and church family.
The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the cause of the crash, with the FAA also investigating.

title: Ohio State suspends fraternity while investigating a video showing men engulfed in flames
text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — A fraternity at Ohio State University has been temporarily suspended while authorities investigate a video that appears to show two panicked men engulfed in flames.
A video shared on social media shows a large group of people standing outside, many wearing the school’s red and white colors, laughing and shouting while a man sits on the ground with his sweatpants on fire. He then lunges at a second person and tackles him. The second man’s clothing also catches fire, and they both roll on the ground removing their clothes as several onlookers intervene. One appears to be holding a small fire extinguisher.
University spokesperson Benjamin Johnson said the school has placed Sigma Alpha Epsilon fraternity on interim suspension while it investigates, and has referred the matter to university and Columbus police. The university did not say how the fraternity is linked to the event, whether the burned men are students or what condition they were in Monday.
“The university is aware of this extremely concerning incident, and the individuals in question are receiving medical care,” Johnson said in a statement. “Ohio State is committed to a safe and healthy environment and expects students and student organizations to uphold that commitment and the university’s values.”
Columbus Police Sgt. Joe Albert said it appears the matter took place on Saturday. Police did not receive any calls for service at the location, but someone called police Sunday evening reporting that the video was circulating online, he said.
Steve Mitchell, CEO of Sigma Alpha Epsilon, said behavior that violates its high standards has no place in its organization and it will take appropriate action to hold those responsible accountable based on the investigation.
“We take this matter seriously and are actively investigating the circumstances surrounding the incident while working closely with university officials and local law enforcement,” he said in a statement.
More than 60,000 students are enrolled at the university.
The episode comes as fraternities are back in the national spotlight in the wake of a former Cornell University student’s lawsuit saying she was gang raped at a fraternity party in 2024.
___
Ramer reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Democrats pick up seats in the state legislature
In the Maine Senate, Democrats now have a "supermajority".
Maine Democrats pick up seats in the state legislature
In the Maine Senate, Democrats now have a "supermajority".
The blue wave we saw across the country last week is also happening in the Maine Legislature. Democrats not only keeping their majority, but flipping close to two dozen seats blue.
"Democrats still need our votes to do anything that requires a two-thirds vote, such as amending the constitution, passing a two year state budget," Rep. Ken Fredette, R-Newport, said.
Fredette is the new House Republican leader and he said he's hopeful Governor-Elect Hannah Pingree works with the Republicans and Democrats on budgets, but also on an issue that will impact many Mainers very soon, heating oil.
"I think we need to really look at how Maine people are going to be affording higher heating costs," he said. "And how is it that we, as the legislature and or the governor might be able to work on something."
According to the Associated Press, the balance of power in the Maine House of Representatives is 86 Democrats, 60 Republicans, 3 unenrolled and 2 races have not yet been called.
In the Senate, 23 Democrats, 11 Republicans and 1 race not called.
Democrats in the Senate now have a "supermajority", meaning they have two-thirds of the members, giving them veto power.
"This was made possible by the folks that we have running for office," Maine Senate President Mattie Daughtry, D-Brunswick, said.
She added that she hopes to work across the aisle with Republicans to pass bipartisan legislation, agreeing with Fredette that the cost of heating oil is something the legislature needs to work on right away.
She's also taking a moment to recognize the historic nature of this incoming state senate.
"We're going to have the largest amount of women serving in the state Senate in Maine's history. That's a big deal. That type of representation matters," she said.
The next legislature will be sworn in on Dec. 2.

title: The race for Maine attorney general is down to a state lawmaker and Yarmouth lawyer
text:
A state senator from Cape Elizabeth and a lawyer from Yarmouth are competing to win enough support from Maine lawmakers to become Maine’s next attorney general.
Sen. Anne Carney, a Democrat who has served in the Senate since 2020, and Tim Shannon, a lawyer who previously served on the Yarmouth Town Council, are hoping to succeed Attorney General Aaron Frey, a Democrat who is termed out this year after first winning the state’s top legal job in 2018.
Carney, 63, has been holding conversations with fellow Democratic lawmakers who grew their majorities in each chamber in last week’s midterm elections. The elections also saw Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree win the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills and keep the Blaine House in Democratic hands.
Carney wrote in a statement she is “talking with legislators one by one and working hard to earn each of their votes.”
“This is a moment when Maine needs an attorney general ready to defend our constitutional rights and our state from day one,” Carney wrote in a Friday email. “Every legislator represents an important part of Maine, and I’m building a coalition that reflects the statewide nature of this job and the urgency we all feel.”
Meanwhile, Shannon, 54, said he would focus on pushing back against Trump if elected.
“The Trump administration is a threat to our country, our state and our democracy, and it’s had a negative effect right here in Maine,” Shannon said in a Monday phone interview, adding he has received “lots of support” from the Democratic lawmakers he has spoken with so far.
He listed consumer protection, “predatory social media companies that employ addictive algorithms” targeting kids and “corporate polluters” as among the things he would tackle as attorney general.
“I found a very receptive audience for all of those points,” Shannon said.
The 186-member Maine Legislature and its new crop of lawmakers will hold a joint session Dec. 2 to vote on selecting constitutional officers. Maine is the only state in the country where legislators, rather than voters or the governor, pick the attorney general, secretary of state, state treasurer and state auditor.
The attorney general is the state’s chief lawyer, representing Maine and its agencies in court. The attorney general’s office prosecutes homicides and other major crimes; works with Maine’s elected district attorneys; and gives legal opinions to the governor, Legislature and state agencies. Frey, a former state representative from Bangor, made $163,716.80 in salary last year, per state records.
Carney, who served one term in the Maine House from 2018-20 before joining the Senate, practiced civil rights, employment and municipal law at Portland-based Norman, Hanson and DeTroy LLC for 17 years before serving for eight years as the in-house volunteer attorney with Pine Tree Legal Assistance.
In that latter role, Carney provided free legal representation to low-income Mainers, women who were sexually assaulted at work, migrant farmworkers and others facing discrimination. She is a University of Maine School of Law graduate.
Her work in the Legislature has included time chairing its Judiciary Committee, which handles an array of legal matters and judicial appointments. Carney has sponsored legislation aimed at tackling Maine’s stubborn public defense challenges, among other issues.
Shannon works in intellectual property litigation for a national law firm. The Harvard Law School graduate served on the Yarmouth Town Council from 2018-24, including a term as chair, and previously worked for Portland firm Verrill Dana. He sought the attorney general position in 2018, when Frey beat out Shannon after Democrats took four ballots to settle the race that started with five contenders.
Mills and Frey, who succeeded Mills as attorney general, have gone up against President Donald Trump’s administration numerous times in recent years and joined multistate lawsuits seeking to block certain Trump actions. The next attorney general can expect more of that, though the president’s party suffered heavy losses in last week’s midterms and will not control Congress for the last two years of his time in the White House.
The new attorney general may also inherit an ongoing investigation into the deadly July shooting in which an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent killed a Colombian man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was living in Biddeford with his wife and young daughter.
State Treasurer Joe Perry and Secretary of State Shenna Bellows have indicated they will seek another term in their roles and are not currently facing challengers, while State Auditor Matt Dunlap’s current term ends in 2029.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Nov. 9 to correct the salary of current Attorney General Aaron Frey.

title: Portland Stage introduces open captions to make theater more accessible
text:
Portland Stage is introducing a new accessibility feature for the second show of its 53rd season.
During performances of “Rooted” on Nov. 11, 14 and 19, the organization will offer open captions, where spoken words, character names and descriptions of contextual sound effects are displayed on a 3-foot-wide screen positioned beside the stage.
The screen is pulled out specifically for open captions performances, and can be folded back against the wall out of view when it’s not being used.
The technology has been used in live opera productions since the 1980s and in theaters since the late ’90s. In Maine, the Ogunquit Playhouse started using open captions in 2023.
“We’re looking at ways which would have the greatest impact for potential audiences, ” said Anita Stewart, Portland Stage’s artistic director.
The technology for open captions has advanced and gotten less expensive, so the timing was right, she said.
Stewart said the captions will be visible from most seats in the theater, and the monitor is designed to not emit a distracting glow.
“The best seating is probably on the side close to it, but because this is a whole pilot project, we’re also testing it out and we’re gonna let people tell us,” she said. Stewart suggested patrons contact the box office when purchasing tickets because staff will be able to suggest ideal seats.
Portland Stage purchased the monitor and a computer to run the open captioning system, which Stewart describes as a slideshow. Staff members and apprentices manually enter the script, and each captioned performance requires a dedicated operator to follow along and advance the slides as the dialogue unfolds.
Bringing open captioning to Portland Stage cost about $20,000. Roughly half went toward equipment and hiring an electrician. The remainder covers ongoing costs, including entering the text and paying a dedicated operator for each captioned performance.
Portland Stage received some of the necessary funds from the Maine Theater Fund grant program, which helped to underwrite the cost of the hardware. “It’s not fully covering the costs, but it’s a huge help,” said Stewart.
Portland Stage has previously offered performances with American Sign Language interpreters, but Stewart said that approach comes with challenges. Interpreters must attend rehearsals to familiarize themselves with a production, requiring a considerable investment of time.
“In our experience, the number of people who are well-versed in American Sign Language is fairly limited,” Stewart said, pointing to both the expense and the shortage of qualified interpreters.
Stewart compared the difficulty of using open captions to an orchestra performance, where the conductor is controlling the tempo of the music and the musicians. During a play, a stage manager directs light and sound cues. The open captions operator wears a headset to listen to the stage manager while closely monitoring the flow of the show from a monitor.
“It’s a live performance, so the tempo of a show will change. It can be up to five minutes faster, depending on if an audience isn’t laughing. Things are very fluid, therefore those lines need to have that fluidity,” said Stewart.
Portland Stage did a test run during a few performances of “Arcadia,” which ran from Sept. 30 to Oct. 25. “It was great, and people really responded,” Stewart said.
Stewart said the quirky “Rooted” will provide another opportunity to see how the system works. “This is an excellent play to do it with,” she said. ” ‘Arcadia’ was hard because it was so text-heavy. This one is a little bit less text so we’re really gonna see how it functions along with the audience.”
To purchase tickets for Portland Stage productions, visit portlandstage.org or call 207-774-0465. The box office at 25A Forest Ave. in Portland is open from noon-5 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday, and two hours before showtime.

title: InvestigateTV+: Is tracking ALS possible?
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at how better tracking of ALS cases could reveal why more people are getting sick.
Then, scammers can get ahold of your address and register it as a front for fake companies. We uncover the risks for homeowners and why officials say it’s so hard to stop.
Plus, an artist shows us how he “draws with daylight,” creating one-of-a-kind pieces of art.
Tracking ALS cases
A cure for ALS is much more complicated to find than a treatment, in part because no one knows why people get it, how to stop it or what causes it. Among experts, there are suspicions that pollutants in the environment play a role.
Researchers said they could better study that if they knew where ALS patients were located.
Fake business, real problem
Imagine your name and home address are used to start a business, but you have nothing to do with it.
There are reports of this happening in several states of fraudulent companies registering with random addresses. Experts say it can cause trouble for unsuspecting property owners.
Underwater...hockey?
Inside Green Bay’s Kroc Center, athletes from small towns around the region are joining together to play a sport you probably haven’t heard of: underwater hockey.
Peter Covach is president of the Green Bay Underwater Hockey Club.
“You’ve got a weighted puck, sits at the bottom of the pool, and it moves up and down the pool like soccer or hockey,” Covach said.
Using the sun for art
Billy Keith is a solar artist. He uses sunlight as his tool to create artwork burned directly into wood.
“You learn a lot by standing in the sun all day,” Keith said.
Keith said he introduces himself as “the sun man,” and his goal is to make more art in public.

title: Why your metabolism changes as you age — and what you can do now
text:
(Aging Untold) — Metabolism is how your body makes and uses energy, burns fuel, keeps up strength and recovers from day to day.
As we get older, that process can change and affect how we feel and how our bodies function.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said metabolism is about much more than the number on the scale.
Metabolism is the body’s ‘power plant’
“Metabolism really is the language of your cells, and your cells operate on energy,” Rogers said. “What’s supplying that energy is these little battery packs called mitochondria.”
Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck compared metabolism to the body’s “power plant.”
Mitochondria are the batteries that power it and every organ has its own power plant, Rogers said.
“The brain requires a lot of power, the heart requires a lot of power,” Rogers said. “If you deplete that power in an organ that needs a lot, you’re going to start to see symptoms sooner.”
That is why changes in the eyes and ears show up in older people, she said.
“They require a lot of power, so that’s why you see the healing start to go and the eyesight start to go quickly,” Rogers said.
When cells can’t produce the energy they need, Rogers said, people can notice changes in how they think and feel.
“When you cannot produce the energy for all your cells that is needed, you’ll experience things like brain fog or fatigue or just simply being out of it,” Rogers said.
She said that energy supports the whole body.
“Your heart has to beat. Your brain has to think. You have to breathe. Your immune cells have to fight infection. Everything depends on having energy,” Rogers said.
Metabolism is more than weight
Cradduck said many people think of metabolism only in terms of weight gain. It also affects how an older person processes medications.
“Think of aging as losing energy,” Rogers said. “It’s the cellular energy that’s progressively being lost as you age. That’s why we start to see the symptoms that we associate with aging.”
Why strength training matters
As people age, they lose muscle and gain fat, a condition called sarcopenia, Rogers said. And many of the hormones people lose with age are tied to maintaining muscle mass.
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke said people often turn to weight loss and overlook strength.
“What I see happen is people will go on a weight loss thing, and they think they need to lose weight, and they forget that they really need the strength,” O’Rourke said. “So it’s a positive thing to gain weight because it could mean that your muscles are getting stronger.”
O’Rourke recommended strength training two to three times a week as people get older.
“To the younger people out there, I’d say start strength training now, so that you don’t have such a cascading effect when you get older,” O’Rourke said.
How muscle connects to glucose
Rogers explained that muscle plays a role in how the body uses glucose. She said glucose provides energy and has to be taken up by muscles to be used for energy.
“Insulin resistance is when your muscles will not take that glucose up, And that’s where prediabetes and all that starts, at the level of the muscle. So the more muscle that you can build, the better you can help that process,” Rogers said.
Type 2 diabetes is showing up earlier, Rogers said, and cited metabolic inflexibility, which she described as the inability to go back and forth between using fat for energy and using carbs for energy. Your cells should be able to go back and forth.
“That makes you very efficient, and we’re losing that efficiency because of things like toxins, inflammation,” Rogers said.
Building health instead of waiting to manage disease
Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said the focus can be on creating health and energy rather than waiting to manage disease.
Rogers listed muscle stimulation, inflammation control, toxin removal, good nutrition and good sleep.
Key takeaways
- Metabolism is about energy, not just weight. Every cell runs on energy, including the heart, brain, lungs and immune cells.
- Muscle is a primary metabolic driver. Losing muscle mass as you age is one thing that can slow metabolism.
- Aging is the slow loss of cellular energy. When mitochondria slow down, your overall vitality drops.
- Life is about function, not weight. A healthy metabolism gives you the physical strength to stay capable.

title: Police Beat: 10/28 to 11/6
text:
10/29:
At 9 a.m., the University of Maine Police Department (UMPD) received an information complaint at DeMeritt Forest. The caller reported a tent in the area, but when officers responded, the area was clear.
At 10 p.m., UMPD received a disorderly complaint at Beta Theta Pi. Officers responded and found an inebriated student rolling around in the leaves and acting erratically. She denied any drug use. The University Volunteer Ambulance Corps (UVAC) was called and the student was transported for medical attention. She was referred to Student Conduct. The complaint was reclassified to an intoxication complaint.
At 11 p.m., UMPD received a disorderly complaint at Beta Theta Pi. The caller reported that two men were fighting. Officers responded and determined that both were drunk and underage. They were referred to Student Conduct.
10/30:
At 12 a.m., an information complaint was filed at Somerset Hall. A resident assistant had seen a bottle of alcohol in a dorm. Officers made contact with the occupants of the dorm and found that both were underage. The alcohol was confiscated and the students were referred to Student Conduct.
At 2 p.m., UMPD received a theft complaint at Fogler Library. The caller reported that a painting was stolen. Officers responded and found that the painting had been picked up by an art restorer who had notified library staff of their plan. The complaint was reclassified to an information complaint and no further action was taken.
At 7 p.m., an information complaint was filed at the University Mall. The caller reported that there was an unauthorized campfire taking place. Officers responded and found that the hosts had taken the proper steps to authorize the campfire, so no further action was taken.
At 7 p.m., UMPD received an erratic vehicle complaint at the Alfond Sports Arena. The caller reported that a vehicle had driven by too fast. Officers were able to obtain the license plate number and contacted the owner of the vehicle. The vehicle owner has not responded yet.
At 11 p.m., UMPD received an information complaint at Phi Eta Kappa. The caller reported that there were minors being served alcohol at a party. Officers performed several drive-by checks and did not find a reason to enter the building. No further action was taken.
At 11 p.m., UMPD received a disorderly complaint at Penobscot Hall. The caller reported that a non-student was refusing to leave the dorm. Officers responded and found the person outside the dorm and unable to get inside. The person refused to identify themself and they were determined to be trespassing.
10/31:
At 12 a.m., a criminal mischief complaint was filed at Somerset Hall. A mirror in one of the first-floor bathrooms had been spray-painted. The mirror was cleaned.
At 12 a.m., an information complaint was filed at the Collins Center for the Arts. A custodian reported that there was supposed to be someone else on shift with them, but they never showed up. Officers made contact with the custodian’s supervisor and found that the other person had quit.
At 1 a.m., UMPD received an assault complaint at Alpha Sigma Phi. The caller reported that he had been punched in the head by an unidentified man. He did not need medical attention.
At 1 a.m., UMPD received a traffic offense complaint on Long Road. Officers responded and found a student drinking and driving. The driver was arrested for operating under the influence.
At 7 a.m., UMPD received a violation of conditions of release complaint at the Memorial Union. A non-student had bail conditions prohibiting them from being on university property. Contact was made with the person and they were arrested.
At 4 p.m., a domestic family fight complaint was filed at Knox Hall. The caller reported that a male and a female had been arguing. Officers responded and the people implicated in the report denied arguing. They were issued a Title IX report and referred to Student Conduct.
At 7 p.m., UMPD received an information complaint at Aroostook Hall. The caller reported that there was someone wearing a mask and dressed in all black who appeared to have a firearm. Officers responded and found that the firearm was fake and part of the person’s Halloween costume. The situation was explained to the individual and they were referred to Student Conduct.
At 11 p.m., UMPD received a disorderly complaint at Delta Tau Delta. Someone had heard a scream. Officers responded and made contact with individuals in the area, but could not determine where the scream came from.
At 11 p.m., an intoxication complaint was filed at Kennebec Hall. There was an inebriated male running around the building. Officers made contact, determined that he was underage and referred him to Student Conduct.
At 11 p.m., a disorderly complaint was filed at Stodder Hall. The caller reported that a former student had entered the hall and was throwing full water bottles at people. Officers responded and found the individual outside and unable to get back in. He was issued a criminal trespass warning and arrested for disorderly conduct.
11/1:
At 2 a.m., UMPD received a criminal mischief complaint at Knox Hall. A window had been broken. There are no other details at this time.
At 10 a.m., UMPD received a report of a theft of a vehicle at the Hilltop Commons parking lot. A student had parked his car there the day before, and received a call from his mother saying that the Auburn Police Department found his car in Auburn. Officers are reviewing surveillance footage from the area.
At 1 p.m., UMPD received another report of a theft of a vehicle at the Hilltop Commons parking lot. A student had left his wallet and keys in his car and someone had moved it to the overnight parking lot. His credit card had also been used. Officers are reviewing surveillance footage from the area.
At 2 p.m., a information complaint was filed at Somerset Hall. A student was receiving text messages from an unknown number. They blocked the number and the messages ceased.
11/2:
At 1 a.m., UMPD received a suspicious complaint at Page Farm. Officers responded and found that a student had fallen asleep in a tree. UMPD said this is not an uncommon occurrence for this particular student. He was advised that if he kept falling asleep in trees, officers would keep coming to wake him up. No further action was taken.
At 1 p.m., a suspicious complaint was filed at the Satellite Lot. A worker had gone hunting and returned with his vehicle covered in blood and dirt. Officers responded and found that the blood came from a deer. The worker was asked to clean his vehicle.
At 7 p.m., a theft complaint was filed at Somerset Hall. The caller reported that their electric scooter had been stolen. There are no cameras on the outside of the building, so no further action was taken.
11/3:
At 3 p.m., UMPD received a theft complaint at the Memorial Union. The caller reported that their skateboard had been stolen. Officers reviewed surveillance footage from the area but found nothing.

title: Maine Shows Its True Colors in Ranking of America's Most Charitable States
text:
Maine Shows Its True Colors in Ranking of America’s Most Charitable States
Congrats, Maine! Way to continue showing our true colors when it matters most. And that’s by being a very charitable state. In fact, one of the most charitable in the entire country.
How Charitable is Maine Compared to Other States?
Maine's overall survey score was a 60.53 out of a possible 100 points. The scoring was based on two major categories: Volunteering & Service and Charitable Giving. The categories were broken down into 17 subcategories to make the study as accurate as possible. You can read more about the methodology here.
Maine ranked below average for charitable giving, coming in at 36st overall. However, the state truly stood out in terms of volunteering and community service, securing an impressive 6th place. This ranking was also the highest of any state in New England, once again proving that Mainers are truly the best.
Having worked at a nonprofit in Maine, I can say these numbers ring true. I witnessed firsthand how incredibly generous Mainers are, always eager to help however they can. And it wasn’t just people directly connected to the organization; I’d see that same spirit from folks with no personal stake at all. This state really is one of a kind. People here just want to take care of each other.
Again, no one should be surprised. This state has one of the largest collective hearts you can find. Maine is one big community, and it really shows.

title: Gunman with far-right views who killed 6 people in Polish city square dies in hospital, police say
text:
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) - People gathered in Krakow‘s main square on Monday evening for a silent march to commemorate the victims of Saturday’s mass shooting, in which a 24-year-old Polish gunman killed six people and wounded 15 others.
Shoulder to shoulder, people walked solemnly through the packed square, some clutching flowers. They placed candles where bullet marks were visible. Polish President Karol Nawrocki and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, otherwise political rivals, walked side by side.
The melody from Simon and Garfunkel’s “The Sound of Silence” rang from the tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square. The night after the attack, St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody that plays every hour from that tower, was paused for the first time since World War II. A prayer was read out once the song finished.
The attacker, wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into the main square in Krakow’s Old Town on Saturday and opened fire. The square is a major tourist destination in Poland’s second-largest city. Several foreigners were among the dead and wounded.
The gunman, Michał Oksiński, died at 4:30 a.m. on Monday, authorities said. He had been in critical condition since the attack and had undergone several operations.
Authorities also found the bodies of his sister, mother and father at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. Authorities said that they believed Oksiński killed his family, possibly while they slept, before heading to Krakow.
Authorities investigating the motive
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said Saturday that Oksiński held “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views.
“We are first of all investigating if he was inspired by anyone, if someone helped him,” Eryk Stasielak of the Krakow branch of the national prosecutor’s office told The Associated Press.
He said that authorities are still investigating the attacker’s motives and are trying to access his electronic devices for more information.
Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Gałecka said that authorities were examining the meaning of numerous symbols and patches sewn onto Oksiński’s clothing or found at his home.
Prosecutors said that they found a yellow flag bearing a black snake, known as the Gadsden flag, hanging on the wall of the attacker’s room. The flag originated during the American Revolution and was later adopted by the U.S. Tea Party movement.
Authorities recovered 11 weapons from Oksiński, his car or home, including two AR-15 semiautomatic rifles, prosecutors said.
Oksiński and his father held gun permits. He had trained at a local shooting club, which said in a statement that he “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”
World facing threats from lone actors
Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The attackers used knives or sharp objects and some were said to be interested in the far right.
Prime Minister Tusk said that the school attacks were fueled by the online “glorification of violence.” He said that the acts could be associated with “nihilistic violence,” a term used by authorities to describe acts of violence driven by a nihilistic worldview and misanthropy rather than specific political goals.
Oksiński’s military-style equipment and weapons were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe and the world, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague, Netherlands.
He said that even without an explicit link between the attacks in Krakow and at the schools, they could be viewed as part of “a series.”
Tomasz Safjański, a security expert, told Rzeczpospolita newspaper that Poland had experienced its first case of an “active shooter” and that the perpetrator was Polish, even as authorities remain focused almost exclusively on external threats such as Russia’s hybrid warfare.
“We are failing to address the radicalization of young people,” he said. “By focusing on an external enemy, the state overlooks the threat that is growing within our schools, our neighborhoods and online.”
Police officers described as heroes
Officers Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański were patrolling the area when they were called to intervene. Police fired the first shot within three minutes of receiving the initial report. The officers chased the attacker and fired at him with their service weapons as he fired a semiautomatic rifle. Kulik continued firing even after he was shot. Both officers were seriously wounded.
Tusk called them the “real heroes” in a post on X. “They most likely saved the lives of many human beings, without regard for the risk of losing their own lives,” he wrote.
Kulik, 24, was in critical condition, prompting officials to issue an urgent appeal for blood donors. A fundraiser for the officers and their families has so far raised more than 6 million zlotys ($1.5 million).
Krakow’s mayor announced that both officers would be named honorary citizens of the city. Two surgeons who happened to be nearby during the attack helped save the officers’ lives.
Talented artists among the victims
Izabela Woźna, a 53-year-old painter and mother of four, was killed in the attack. She had opened an exhibition of her work in Krakow on Friday evening.
Krakow Academy of Fine Arts confirmed that Magdalena Oksińska — the suspect’s sister — had been one of its third-year students. It said an employee’s sister had also been shot twice.
“Nothing will ever be like before. The delicate tissue of our academic community was painfully wounded,” the academy said in a statement Sunday.
“Magdalena Oksińska, 21 years old, a queer person, was an absolutely talented painter, photographer, poet and writer,” architect Pavko Krajka wrote in a social media post accompanied by images of her colorful paintings.
“Her death is a great loss for Krakow, Polish, European and queer culture.”
Among those killed in the square were citizens from Poland, the U.K. and Austria. The wounded included people from Britain, Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

title: The race for Maine attorney general is down to a state lawmaker and Yarmouth lawyer
text:
A state senator from Cape Elizabeth and a lawyer from Yarmouth are competing to win enough support from Maine lawmakers to become Maine’s next attorney general.
Sen. Anne Carney, a Democrat who has served in the Senate since 2020, and Tim Shannon, a lawyer who previously served on the Yarmouth Town Council, are hoping to succeed Attorney General Aaron Frey, a Democrat who is termed out this year after first winning the state’s top legal job in 2018.
Carney, 63, has been holding conversations with fellow Democratic lawmakers who grew their majorities in each chamber in last week’s midterm elections. The elections also saw Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree win the race to succeed Gov. Janet Mills and keep the Blaine House in Democratic hands.
Carney wrote in a statement she is “talking with legislators one by one and working hard to earn each of their votes.”
“This is a moment when Maine needs an attorney general ready to defend our constitutional rights and our state from day one,” Carney wrote in a Friday email. “Every legislator represents an important part of Maine, and I’m building a coalition that reflects the statewide nature of this job and the urgency we all feel.”
Meanwhile, Shannon, 54, said he would focus on pushing back against Trump if elected.
“The Trump administration is a threat to our country, our state and our democracy, and it’s had a negative effect right here in Maine,” Shannon said in a Monday phone interview, adding he has received “lots of support” from the Democratic lawmakers he has spoken with so far.
He listed consumer protection, “predatory social media companies that employ addictive algorithms” targeting kids and “corporate polluters” as among the things he would tackle as attorney general.
“I found a very receptive audience for all of those points,” Shannon said.
The 186-member Maine Legislature and its new crop of lawmakers will hold a joint session Dec. 2 to vote on selecting constitutional officers. Maine is the only state in the country where legislators, rather than voters or the governor, pick the attorney general, secretary of state, state treasurer and state auditor.
The attorney general is the state’s chief lawyer, representing Maine and its agencies in court. The attorney general’s office prosecutes homicides and other major crimes; works with Maine’s elected district attorneys; and gives legal opinions to the governor, Legislature and state agencies. Frey, a former state representative from Bangor, made $163,716.80 in salary last year, per state records.
Carney, who served one term in the Maine House from 2018-20 before joining the Senate, practiced civil rights, employment and municipal law at Portland-based Norman, Hanson and DeTroy LLC for 17 years before serving for eight years as the in-house volunteer attorney with Pine Tree Legal Assistance.
In that latter role, Carney provided free legal representation to low-income Mainers, women who were sexually assaulted at work, migrant farmworkers and others facing discrimination. She is a University of Maine School of Law graduate.
Her work in the Legislature has included time chairing its Judiciary Committee, which handles an array of legal matters and judicial appointments. Carney has sponsored legislation aimed at tackling Maine’s stubborn public defense challenges, among other issues.
Shannon works in intellectual property litigation for a national law firm. The Harvard Law School graduate served on the Yarmouth Town Council from 2018-24, including a term as chair, and previously worked for Portland firm Verrill Dana. He sought the attorney general position in 2018, when Frey beat out Shannon after Democrats took four ballots to settle the race that started with five contenders.
Mills and Frey, who succeeded Mills as attorney general, have gone up against President Donald Trump’s administration numerous times in recent years and joined multistate lawsuits seeking to block certain Trump actions. The next attorney general can expect more of that, though the president’s party suffered heavy losses in last week’s midterms and will not control Congress for the last two years of his time in the White House.
The new attorney general may also inherit an ongoing investigation into the deadly July shooting in which an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent killed a Colombian man, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was living in Biddeford with his wife and young daughter.
State Treasurer Joe Perry and Secretary of State Shenna Bellows have indicated they will seek another term in their roles and are not currently facing challengers, while State Auditor Matt Dunlap’s current term ends in 2029.
Editor’s note: This story was updated on Nov. 9 to correct the salary of current Attorney General Aaron Frey.

title: Enough about Sen. Margaret Chase Smith
text:
In a recent New York Times article, Senator Susan Collins compared herself to former Senator Margaret Chase Smith, saying they had both “taken a lot of tough votes.” And that she (Collins) had “stood up for what I believe in.”
The article ends with a quote from Collins, “I have now had my Margaret Chase Smith moment.”
Wrong. Sen. Margaret Chase Smith is remembered for a brave and principled stand against Joseph McCarthy’s “Red Scare.” Collins will be remembered as a calculating politician who carefully chose her “battles” in order to maintain a false reputation as a moderate in order to remain in power.
Collins had an opportunity, in her final term, to earn a “Margaret Chase Smith moment.” Collins knew what Trump and the MAGA culture he fostered was all about. She knew about the greed and corruption. Trump’s pardoning of the Jan. 6 criminals alone should have made that obvious.
Collins blames voter backlash against Trump for her loss. But it’s her appeasement to Trump that was the cause. If she had truly embraced Sen. Smith’s courage and stood for what was right, she might have won; Maine people admire courage.
John Gold
Saco

Portland officials are still unsure about plans to move Downeaster train station
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Portland city officials are still not convinced the proposal to relocate the Downeaster train station to outer St. John Street is the right path forward.
The Portland City Council members heard from stakeholders and weighed in with their opinions at a workshop on Monday, where they decided they will vote on one of three recommendations at a council meeting in December.
In August, the Northern New England Passenger Rail Authority, which operates the Downeaster, received $48 million in federal funding to relocate the train service’s Portland station to the authority’s preferred spot.
However, city staff and elected officials were caught off guard by that announcement because of a lack of local and regional support for the authority’s preferred location, as well as their own preference for using Union Station Plaza, farther down St. John Street.
Rail authority officials have argued that the move from the Portland Transportation Center to a swath of land between St. John Street and Northern Light Mercy Hospital would reduce travel time by roughly 15 minutes and expand rail service, and that its application for the funding was for that specific location.
The project is estimated to cost roughly $60 million, with a proposed $12 million match in state funding.
The three options the council will consider are to recommend the train station be left where it is; that the city’s preferred site be further explored; or that the rail authority’s preferred site move forward, with stipulations around other enhancements in the area.
Representatives from the rail authority, Greater Portland Council of Governments, and city staff outlined their arguments at — and ahead of — the workshop on Monday.
In a memo issued before the workshop, city staff recommended against proceeding with the train station relocation and suggested that the state prioritize transportation funding for more urgent needs. Staff say the rail authority’s preferred site goes against nearly every zoning and long-term planning document in place, and that its chosen location is heavily weighted toward rail operations.
An analysis from city staff said Union Station Plaza would provide better bicycle and pedestrian access and better public transit connections, noting that it’s closer to Congress Street workplaces, businesses, residential neighborhoods and recreational sites like Hadlock Field.
The rail authority has argued that its chosen site would strengthen pedestrian mobility between two areas of the city — the Fore River Parkway/Libbytown neighborhood and the West End/Western Promenade — that are currently split by the railroad.
At Monday’s workshop, it also cited barriers to the city’s preferred site, including a lack of needed buy-in from the county and MaineHealth to make it work.
A GPCOG memo, written by Executive Director Kristina Egan, argues that moving the station from its current location would weaken the transportation hub at Thompson’s Point by splitting rail from buses.
“Should we spend $60 million in public dollars to move the station away from the
connections we’ve already built?” she said.
According to a memo, the city and GPCOG staff previously outlined concerns with the rail authority’s process and suggested that the advantages of Union Station warranted a more in-depth analysis that compared both St. John Street options to the existing Thompson’s Point location. However, that analysis was never completed, and staff said a subsequent effort to engage a mediator reached “an early impasse.”
City staff and GPCOG also argue that the proposed $12 million in state funds has not yet been committed to the new station, and that if the funding did become available, it should be spent on higher priorities in the region.
Those include a new Metro facility and buses, and needed pedestrian infrastructure along corridors like Forest Avenue, as well as elsewhere in southern Maine, the GPCOG memo states.
“This is a discretionary project, and Portland and the region face substantial state funding limitations related to higher-priority needs … that would benefit more people,” Kevin Kraft, the city’s planning director, said before the meeting.
GPCOG also said using the state funding on the station instead of on Metro infrastructure “widens the equity gap.” The presentation says 86% of bus riders have household incomes of under $50,000 compared to just 5% of train riders.
An estimated $4 million of the $60 million budget would go toward the costs of property acquisition, which the city says would displace several businesses. The staff memo said the location at Union Station, which is owned by MaineHealth, could move forward without displacement.
Mayor Mark Dion has previously said that MaineHealth has not been interested in selling, which complicates the city’s position.
Councilors Wes Pelletier and Regina Phillips were ardent in their opposition to the rail authority’s preferred site and the process to date.
“For us to get strong-armed like this, we are not a partner,” Pelletier said.
Councilor Sarah Michniewicz said she was not certain the 15-minute gain for rail passengers outweighs the drawbacks of the authority’s preferred site.
“I’m not sure that the motivation to relocate the entire station makes sense,” she said.
Councilor Kate Sykes expressed openness to making the authority’s preferred site work, noting that $48 million is a lot of money not to use.
Dion also expressed the need to be open, noting the city doesn’t have “a veto,” and rather can only make a recommendation and hope the rail authority and state comply.
“Unless somebody can tell me that we have the ability to veto … then we should devote our energies to provide what we can do to make (the rail authority’s preferred site) the best possible site,” he said.

title: FBI investigating ‘suspected homicide’ aboard cruise ship out of Texas
text:
HOUSTON (AP) — The FBI is investigating a “suspected homicide” aboard a cruise ship that returned to port after departing from Texas, and a suspect is in custody, the agency said Monday.
The FBI did not say whether any charges had been filed. The name of the suspect was being withheld pending notification of the victim’s family, the agency said on the social platform X.
The MSC Seascape, which took off from Galveston, is a towering white vessel that has 2,270 cabins, more than 1,600 crew and can host nearly 5,900 guests, according to the company’s website.
“On reporting a guest incident aboard our ship, we were instructed by the authorities to return to the Port of Galveston,” MSC Cruises said in a statement. It added that it was cooperating with authorities and providing support to those impacted.
The company said the vessel has resumed its voyage and left Galveston as of Monday afternoon.
MSC Seascape currently runs from Galveston to the Caribbean for five- and seven-night stays, according to the company’s website. The ship switched from Miami to Galveston last November, according to a statement.
Homicide investigations on cruise ships are uncommon. Earlier this year, a teenager was charged with murder and aggravated sexual abuse in the death of his 18-year-old stepsister on a Carnival Cruise ship out of Florida.
